item.title: Five hundred years of furniture timber
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Five hundred years of furniture timber
Percy Macquoid, opening *A History of English Furniture* in 1904, split the fashionable English house into four timber piles: oak to 1660, walnut to 1720, mahogany to 1770, satinwood after that. Walk a country-house corridor and the scheme still works on the hand — blackened joined oak, faded oyster walnut, a red-brown splat, a yellow card table. It fails as soon as you leave that corridor. A Gdansk wainscot in an English chest is a Baltic object. A Philadelphia high chest is mahogany on yellow-poplar. A Thonet café chair is Moravian beech. A Ming yoke-back is huanghuali. Macquoid named a London clock. The trade ran several clocks at once.
![Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/timeline.svg)
*Figure 1. Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.*
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## What a furniture wood is asked to do
A furniture wood is a species a shop will dry, face, joint, and either show or hide. Beech made Thonet’s café empire and also laundry pegs. Yellow-poplar lined Philadelphia drawers and also the cores of cheap veneered suites. The difference is the job, not a moral ranking of trees.
Three behaviors decide whether a wood stays in the rack.
Hardness and density. The USDA Forest Products Laboratory reports side hardness (Janka) and specific gravity at 12 percent moisture in the *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190, 2010, tables 5–3a and following). White oak sits near 1,360 lbf and SG 0.68; black cherry near 950 lbf and 0.50; eastern white pine near 380 lbf and 0.35; Honduran mahogany near 800 lbf and 0.45–0.50 (imported-woods chapter / Kukachka FPL-125). Those numbers explain why a pine tavern table dents under a buckle and a maple counter does not. They do not explain fashion. Fashion is why cherry was a secondary wood in one decade and a show wood in the next.
Movement. Wood shrinks across the grain as it dries, more tangentially than radially (FPL-GTR-190, ch. 4). Quartersawn stock moves less in width. A door flatsawn in 1710 and hung in a heated apartment in 2010 will tell you this without a hygrometer. Frame-and-panel is not a style. It is manners for a wide board. Breadboard ends, floating panels, slotted screws, and later plywood grounds are all answers to the same geometry.
Workability. Interlocked grain (elm, sapele) tears under a plane. Silica (teak) dulls edges. Open pores (oak, ash) drink filler. Fine texture (maple, boxwood, pear) takes a polish that looks like light under glass. Shops chose woods for the tool in hand as much as for the color in the plate book.
## Trade is the hidden style
English oak furniture of 1550 is not simply English oak. Dendrochronology on panels and chests keeps pointing to the south-eastern Baltic — the hinterlands of Gdansk, then Königsberg and Courland — for the slow-grown, radially split boards sold as wainscot (*wagenschot*). Haneca and colleagues (2005) showed how art-historical oak can be provenanced by ring patterns. In 1565, they note, 85 percent of wainscots passing the Danish Sound shipped from Gdansk. London joiners mixed that imported stuff with home oak. A linenfold chest can be a North Sea object even when the carving looks local.
Walnut’s English fashion after 1660 rode Dutch and French taste and a veneer technology that wasted less of a scarce, figured log. American black walnut, *Juglans nigra*, did a different job in the colonies: it was a primary solid wood, wide and available, and it still is in the central hardwood belt.
Mahogany’s English story is a statute. Adam Bowett killed the old connoisseur dates (Macquoid’s 1733, Cescinsky’s 1748) for the duty change. The Naval Stores Act of 1721, in force 1722, took the import duty off British West Indian timber. Jamaica wood that had not been worth the freight became, in the port books, cheap enough to carve in the solid. Thomas Ripley, advising the Admiralty, called mahogany cheaper than deal or wainscot when Navy ships carried it freight-free (*Georgian Group Journal*, 1997). The rococo splat did not invent mahogany. A tax cut and a sugar island did. Logging gangs and enslaved labor sit in those records. A dining table can be beautiful and still be a receipt from an extractive system.
## Joinery follows the fiber
Draw-bored mortise and tenon in riven oak holds because the pin, driven slightly offset, pulls the shoulder tight as the oak moves; Chinnery’s *Oak Furniture* is still the long walk through that joint. A mahogany splat can be thinner than a walnut one because the fiber is long and even enough to take a carved piercing without crumbling — the claim R. W. Symonds made and Bowett complicated. An elm Windsor seat takes four tapered legs because the interlocked grain will not split out to the rim (Evans, *Windsor-Chair Making in America*). Beech takes Thonet’s steam bend; maple takes a turned bead; boxwood takes a stringing line a millimeter wide.
When the fiber changes, the joint changes. Veneer on a deal carcase (walnut age) is a different contract from a joined oak stool. A crotch-mahogany face on yellow-poplar (American Empire) is a different contract from a solid Jamaica dining leaf. Plywood’s cross-band is the industrial version of the floating panel. The glossary and the cut chapters in this series are not technical asides. They are half of period style.
## The other clocks
In the German-speaking lands after the Napoleonic wars, Biedermeier shops made a virtue of pale birch, pear, and cherry. In Denmark a century later, oak and teak and a little rosewood became an export look. In the United States the Shakers kept maple, cherry, and pine while Renaissance Revival factories drowned parlors in black walnut. Gustav Stickley and the English Arts and Crafts men dragged quartersawn oak back into the polite room and fumed it with ammonia so the tannins went brown.
Michael Thonet’s No. 14 chair, 1859, is six pieces of steamed beech (V&A W.31-2011). Alvar Aalto’s Paimio seating is Finnish birch laminate. Charles and Ray Eames’s plywood chairs learned their compound curves on a 1942 wartime splint (V&A plywood history). None of these fit an Age of Mahogany.
## Substitutes and paper
By 1900 Cuban mahogany (*Swietenia mahagoni*) was already a memory in commercial sizes. Honduran *S. macrophylla* took the name, then African *Khaya* and *Entandrophragma*. Brazilian rosewood (*Dalbergia nigra*) went onto CITES Appendix I; the rest of *Dalbergia* followed onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017. Big-leaf mahogany’s neotropical populations entered Appendix II in 2003 (in force 15 November 2003). The U.S. Lacey Act as amended in 2008, and APHIS Phase VII declarations (1 December 2024), make a binomial on an invoice part of the piece.
Particleboard and veneered MDF are furniture woods in the only sense that counts: they are what most people now own. They move less than solid flatsawn oak. They fail in water. They can be named without apology. They cannot be named as walnut.
## How to walk the house
Start with the cut. A linenfold panel that is still flat after four centuries is usually riven or quartered. A two-board mahogany top with matching cathedrals is flatsawn and proud of it. A run of dining-chair legs that do not match is usually a flatsawn run. The glossary that follows is the field kit: three faces from one log, pore classes, and the shop words that name too many trees. Figure 3 lives there.
Then take a wood you already own, or walk Macquoid’s English stairs — oak, walnut, mahogany, satinwood — and keep going into the rooms he barely named: Baltic wainscot, Dutch shipping, navy reserves, American pines, campaign teak, Thonet beech, factory maple, CITES paper. Figure 1 and Figure 4 above are the map and the scatter. The later figures sit where the lane, the cut, or the appendix is the subject.
Open a drawer wherever you are. Secondary wood is the honest half of the piece: yellow-poplar under Philadelphia mahogany, deal under a Dutch *kast*, pine under a painted New England chest. The show face is the fashion. The interior is the mill.
Arkansas sits in this history without a costume. White oak, red oak, cherry, walnut, hickory, ash, and pine are the same genera that filled American shops in 1800. The difference is second-growth rings, kiln schedules, and a legal paper trail. Bradley Brand works those hardwoods. The useful question is still the shop question: what will the board do — swell, dent, darken, take a finish, outlive a fashion — and what joint did someone cut to live with that.
Macquoid gave a staircase. The house has more rooms than he drew.
## Sources
Macquoid, *A History of English Furniture*, 1904–08. Bowett, *The English Mahogany Trade 1700–1793*; “Thomas Ripley and the use of early mahogany,” *Georgian Group Journal* 7 (1997). Haneca et al., *Journal of Archaeological Science* 32 (2005). USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (2010). Chinnery, *Oak Furniture*. Evans, *Windsor-Chair Making in America*. CITES 2003 mahogany release; CoP17 *Dalbergia*. USDA APHIS Lacey Phase VII. V&A plywood history; V&A Thonet W.31-2011.
See: `glossary-grain-and-cut`, `baltic-oak-renaissance`, `mahogany-chippendale`, `conservation-today`.

item.title: Grain, cut, and the words shops actually use
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Grain, cut, and the words shops actually use
A log is a cylinder of tubes. How you slice the cylinder decides the face you stain, the way a table top cups, and whether an oak chair looks like a cathedral or like a rayed stone. Fashion has picked sides for five hundred years. The physics has not changed. This draft is the field kit for every later slug: the three cuts, the pore classes, the words that mean too many trees.
![Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.](../assets/grain-cuts/sawn-orientation.svg)
*Figure 3. Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.*
## Three faces from one tree
Flatsawn (plain-sawn) boards are cut tangent to the rings. On the face you get arches — the cathedrals of oak and ash. The width of the board is mostly tangential grain. Tangential shrinkage is the large number in the *Wood Handbook* tables (FPL-GTR-190, ch. 4). A flatsawn white-oak board will move more in width, and it will cup so the rings try to flatten. That is not a defect. It is geometry.
Quartersawn boards are cut so the rings run nearly perpendicular to the face. The face is radial. In oak, the medullary rays — ribbons of tissue that ran from pith to bark — show as flakes. English joiners and later Arts and Crafts catalogues called the look silver grain or tiger oak. Radial shrinkage is smaller. A quartersawn top still moves, but it stays flatter and wears its width change more evenly.
Riftsawn is the compromise: rings at about 30 to 60 degrees, straight stripe, fewer flakes. Chair shops like it for legs that must match. Yield is worse than flatsawing. A mill that sells “quartered and rift” as a mixed bundle is telling you to specify flake if you want flake.
Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*, is the shop book for this geometry. Figure 3 above is the same argument in one diagram.
## Before the circular saw
Medieval and early modern oak furniture often started as riven stock, not sawn. A wedge follows the rays. The board you get is naturally quartered. That is why a 16th-century linenfold panel can be thin, wide, and stable in a way a cheap 19th-century oak sideboard is not. Baltic wainscot, the *wagenschot* of the Gdansk trade, was typically cleft or sawn to keep the face radial (Haneca et al. 2005; KNOB wainscot literature). Buyers in London and the Low Countries paid for dryness and for that radial cut.
When pitsaws and later water-powered sash mills took over, flatsawing won on yield. You get more wide boards by slabbing the log. Walnut veneer in the late 17th century is a different conversion: the log is too precious to quarter for solidity, so you glue a thin face to a cheaper carcase and let the substrate argue with the weather.
Mahogany in the 18th-century solid — Bowett’s cheap Jamaica wood after 1721 — was often flatsawn because the logs were huge and the shops wanted width for dining tables. A two-board mahogany top with matching cathedrals is a flatsaw trophy. Quartersawn mahogany exists; it is quieter. The ribbon in some *Swietenia* and later in sapele is interlocked grain, not oak-like rays.
## Pores, rings, rays
Hardwoods have vessels. On the end grain they are holes. On the face they are grooves or dashes.
Ring-porous woods (oak, ash, elm, teak, hickory) lay a row of large earlywood pores each year. You can count rings with a thumbnail. The face shows a strong grain that filler and stain love. Diffuse-porous woods (maple, cherry, birch, yellow-poplar, true mahogany in a quieter way) spread smaller pores through the ring. The face can look satiny. Semi-ring-porous woods (walnut) sit between.
Softwoods have no vessels. They have tracheids. Pine shows resin canals and a jump from earlywood to latewood that is loud in southern yellow pine and shy in eastern white pine. If you think you are looking at maple and you see a resin canal, you are not looking at maple.
Rays are the other tell. Oak rays are large enough to be a design element when quartered. Beech and sycamore have crowded rays that speckle a quartered face. European “sycamore” in the furniture trade is *Acer pseudoplatanus*, a maple. American sycamore is *Platanus*. The word is a trap. Boxwood rays are fine; the wood looks almost like a pale meat.
A 10× lens and a cut end grain beat a phone photograph of a finished top.
## Joinery that assumes a cut
Frame-and-panel assumes the panel may shrink. The groove is deep enough that a flatsawn oak panel can lose width and still sit. The stiles and rails are often closer to quartered so the frame stays true next to glass or a door edge.
A breadboard end across a flatsawn top must slot-screw or pin in elongated holes. If the pins are tight, the top splits. If the breadboard is glued across the whole end, the top splits. Eighteenth-century shops knew this. Some nineteenth-century factories forgot.
Draw-boring in oak likes riven or quartered stiles: the pin crushes fibers in a predictable direction. In interlocked elm you do not draw-bore a seat; you drive a tapered leg into a bored hole and wedge it from above.
Veneer assumes a ground. Hide glue on deal or yellow-poplar is the historic sandwich. A plywood ground is the 20th-century sandwich: cross-bands cancel movement. A paper foil on particleboard is a photograph of grain. The edge tells you which contract you bought.
## Names that mean too many trees
Mahogany in a 1760 London bill is likely Jamaican *Swietenia*. In a 1960 American suite it may be *Khaya*, sapele, or a photograph on lauan. Rosewood may be *Dalbergia nigra*, East Indian *D. latifolia*, or a stained substitute. Cedar in a blanket chest is often *Juniperus virginiana*. Cedar in a Spanish colonial chest may be *Cedrela odorata*. Sycamore is a fight between continents. Fruitwood on an eight-foot table is a stain name.
CITES and the Lacey Act do not care about poetry. The later conservation drafts in this series use binomials on purpose.
## How to see it on a piece you did not make
Look at the end grain. Rings running across the thickness, parallel to the face, mean flatsawn. Rings running through the thickness, end-on, mean quartered. If you cannot see the end, look at the face: cathedrals versus straight stripe plus flake (oak) or ribbon (interlocked tropicals).
Look at wear. Chair seats that were flatsawn cup toward the bark side. Tabletops with breadboard ends: if the pins elongated into slots, someone understood tangential movement.
Look at the period. A 1600 joined chest with ray flake is doing its job. A 1905 sideboard with loud flake is announcing a movement. A 1970 oak suite with printed grain on a veneer of unclear species is announcing a factory. Printed grain has no end-grain rings.
## Cost
Quartering wastes the log. That is why Baltic wainscot was dear, why Gillows in Lancaster could pay nearly mahogany prices for Danzig oak in 1740 (Bowett, provincial woods paper), and why a true quartersawn white-oak dining table still costs more per foot than a flatsawn one from the same kiln charge.
Mills now cut quartered and rift as a mixed bundle. Designers who want flake must say flake. Designers who want straight grain for a run of doors should say rift.
A Windsor seat is a cut lesson you can sit on. English shops often used elm because the interlocked grain will not split out to the rim when four tapered legs go in (Evans). American shops used pine and poplar too. The seat is thick and usually flatsawn; it cups. The bow wants a riven or steam-bent stick — ash, oak, hickory, sometimes yew — because a flatsawn oak bow with a cathedral on the face will break toward the bark on a tight radius. The glossary’s three cuts are not museum talk. They are why a chair stays a chair.
Rotary veneer is the other conversion the figure does not draw. A log on a lathe, peeled like a paper towel, gives wide wild cathedrals and a cheap face. Sliced veneer — crown or quarter — is how you get a walnut crotch or an oak flake on a door. The plywood draft takes the sandwich. Here it is enough to say: the cut of the face and the cut of the ground are two decisions. A quartered oak flake on a particleboard core is a photograph of a radial board glued to a fiber that does not have rings.
Moisture content sits under every cut. FPL-GTR-190, chapter 4, is the handbook. Wood shrinks as it dries, more tangentially than radially, for most species about one-and-a-half to two times. A flatsawn panel in a heated apartment is the large number. A quartersawn stile next to glass is the small number. The moisture draft (`moisture-wood-movement`) walks a door through a winter. This page only needs the rule: name the cut before you name the finish.
The later drafts — `quartersawn-arts-crafts`, `flatsawn-panel-figure`, `rift-cut-flooring`, `moisture-wood-movement` — take each cut into a room. This page is the vocabulary. Figure 3 is the picture. Keep both in your head when a catalogue says “solid oak” and the edge is 0.6 mm of something on a fiber core.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190, ch. 4–5. Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*. Haneca et al. 2005. Bowett, “Furniture woods in London and provincial furniture 1700–1800.” Chinnery, *Oak Furniture*.
See: `quartersawn-arts-crafts`, `flatsawn-panel-figure`, `rift-cut-flooring`, `moisture-wood-movement`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Baltic oak and the Renaissance panel
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Baltic oak and the Renaissance panel
A linenfold chest in a London hall can look as local as the parish. Lift a panel and send a slice of the end grain to a dendrochronologist and the rings often refuse England. They match the slow-grown oaks of the south-eastern Baltic — the hinterlands that fed Gdansk, then Königsberg and Courland — the boards the trade called wainscot and the Dutch called *wagenschot*. Haneca and colleagues, writing in the *Journal of Archaeological Science* in 2005, showed how art-historical oak can be provenanced by those ring patterns. In 1565, they note, 85 percent of the wainscots that passed the Danish Sound shipped from Gdansk. The carving may be English. The fiber is a North Sea cargo.
![Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/trade-lanes.svg)
*Figure 2. Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.*
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## The tree the ports sold
European furniture oak is mostly *Quercus robur* (pedunculate) and *Q. petraea* (sessile). Dealers later sold it as Danzig, Riga, Polish, Slavonian, French, or English oak depending on the quay and the century. The USDA *Wood Handbook* does not give a single FPL-equivalent Janka for *Q. robur* `[CITE NEEDED for a bench-copy imported-woods number]`. American white oak, the nearest handbook neighbor, sits near 1,360 lbf and specific gravity 0.68 at 12 percent moisture; northern red oak near 1,290 lbf and 0.63 (FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a). Figure 4 puts those two among the series anchors. Slow-grown Baltic stock is often finer and more even than a wide-ringed second-growth American board. The binomial does not tell you the ring count. The Sound does not either. A splitter in the Vistula hinterland did.
Both European species are ring-porous. Large earlywood vessels open each spring; latewood closes the year. Tyloses plug many heartwood pores in the white-oak group, which is why tight cooperage and ship planking follow the same trees that made panels. Red-group oaks keep the pores open. A Renaissance wainscot is a white-group story: liquid stays out, the board takes a radial face, and the medullary rays — ribbons from pith to bark — show as flake when the cut is true.
The *Wood Handbook* (ch. 4) treats tangential shrinkage as commonly about one and a half to two times radial for many hardwoods. A radially split or quartersawn Baltic board moves less in width than a flatsawn slab from the same log. That is why a thin linenfold panel can stay quiet in a groove for four centuries, and why a cheap 1890 oak sideboard, steam-sawn tangent to the rings, cups toward the bark.
## Gdansk, the Sound, and the driest boards
Wainscot is a cargo word, not a mood. Tomasz Wazny’s work on Gdansk export oak, cited throughout the Haneca paper, is the port-side half of the dendro story. The Danish Sound Toll at Helsingør taxed the boards as they left the Baltic. Western buyers in London, Antwerp, Amsterdam, and the Hanse towns paid for dryness and for a radial face. The KNOB bulletin literature still quotes the period instruction: the driest wainscots you know how to get. That is a specification, not a proverb.
Figure 2 draws the Baltic oak lane beside Atlantic mahogany and Indian Ocean teak. They are parallel supplies, not a relay. In the sixteenth century the oak lane is the one that matters to a joiner. Königsberg and Courland rose as Gdansk’s share fell; Riga’s name stuck to a grade long after the quay mix changed. Home oak built frames, posts, and anything a shop could hide. Imported boards often made the faces — the linenfold, the carved frieze, the panel a guest would touch.
A London joiner in 1550 did not need a botanist. He needed a balk that had already been cleft or sawn to keep the rings on end in the thickness. A wedge follows the rays. The board you get is naturally quartered. Baltic *wagenschot* was typically converted that way (Haneca et al. 2005; the KNOB wainscot essays). Pitsaws could still rotate a balk and take radial cuts. They usually did not unless the buyer paid. Width is money. The radial face was the dear face.
Do not invent a named voyage or a price from a blank register. The Sound Toll books exist; a writer who has not opened a year-page should say so. Later, in 1740, Gillows of Lancaster could still pay nearly mahogany prices for Danzig oak (Bowett, provincial woods paper). That sentence is a late echo of the same grade, not a Renaissance invoice.
## What Renaissance shops asked the board to do
Macquoid’s *Age of Oak* (1500–1660 in *A History of English Furniture*, 1904–08) is a London clock. The Baltic trade is older than his first date and wider than England. Netherlandish and French joiners used the same cargo. A Flemish linenfold and an English one share a fiber before they share a carver. The Renaissance in this draft is the hour when radially split oak, imported in quantity, met a fashion for framed panels, carved folds, and joined chests that replaced the boarded box in polite rooms.
Oak planes if the grain is straight and the irons are sharp. Quartersawn stock picks up at the rays. Interlocked or wavy boards tear. Tannin is the daily chemistry: iron and damp oak write a black stain — the old ink, the ruined clamp mark. Water-based finishes raise the grain into needles. Oil and wax leave the pores open and the flake bright. A shop that wants the sixteenth century back skips the Victorian filler that hid the structure on purpose.
The wood is hard enough to take a draw-bored pin and still be carved. It is not the carvable evenness of later mahogany. A linenfold is a gouge-and-veiner job on a radial face; the fold reads because the ray flake catches light differently from the ground. That is anatomy doing the work of ornament.
## Joinery
The joint that holds this hour together is the draw-bored mortise and tenon. The pin is driven through a hole in the tenon that is offset a hair toward the shoulder. As the pin goes home it pulls the shoulder tight. Oak crushes in a predictable direction if the stile is riven or quartered. Years on, the pin lozenges in the hole as the wood dries. Victor Chinnery’s *Oak Furniture: The British Tradition* is still the long walk through that joint and the forms that use it: the joined stool, the press, the court cupboard, the chest with stiles and rails around a floating panel.
Frame-and-panel is not a style. It is manners for a wide board. The groove is deep enough that a panel can lose width and still sit. The stiles and rails stay closer to quartered so the frame remains true. A boarded six-board chest — nailed or pegged, no frame — is the older, cheaper cousin. Both exist in the same decades. The joined chest is the one that wants Baltic faces.
Linenfold sits on that panel. The carver works the radial face; the back can be riven-rough. Dowelled or grooved into the rails, the panel must float. Glue it tight and the next dry winter splits the fold down a vessel line.
Haunched tenons at the corners of a frame keep the mortise away from the end grain of a stile. A muntin between two panels is a third stile with two grooves. Pins are oak, sometimes a slightly darker piece so they read. Iron nails appear in boarded work and in later repairs; they stain.
A chest lid that later becomes a table top is a common afterlife. Look at hinge scars and a leftover till. The Baltic panel does not care what century reused it. The ring pattern still points east.
## Conservation
Oak in the American and European mains is not a CITES appendix story. It is a forestry story: high-grading of slow-grown clears, oak wilt and sudden oak death in some regions `[CITE NEEDED for a current range map if counties are named]`, and a market that still asks second growth to behave like 1565 wainscot. Plantation oak exists. It is not Gdansk hinterland oak. Tight rings must be written on the purchase order, or the buyer pays for antique stock and accepts iron stains and sapwood worm.
A Renaissance panel in a museum is a documented object. A “linenfold chest” from an unnamed warehouse may be a Victorian Gothic revival with steam-sawn oak and a stain. End grain tells: rings through the thickness and a fine ring count support the Baltic claim; wide rings and a cathedral face do not. Dendrochronology is the only honest provenance for “Baltic.” A dealer’s country of origin on a tag is not.
Repair a split panel with a spline or a butterflied patch in oak of similar ring and cut. Do not flood the face with a film finish that fills the pores the first shop left open. Iron stains at old hinges are history; bleaching them for a kitchen island is a different object.
Arkansas white oak still quarters, and the flake is the same anatomy a Gdansk splitter sold. The rings are wider. The kiln ticket is new. That is the whole local sentence.
## What to look for
On an old piece: ray flake on a thin panel, a draw-bored pin that has lozenged, sapwood worm, a black line where a clamp or a nail met tannin. On a new “Renaissance oak” suite: printed grain with no end-grain rings, or a 0.6 mm oak face on a fiber core. On a claim of Baltic: ask for a ring study or be quiet. Haneca’s method is available. A port name on a hang-tag is not a Sound Toll page.
Macquoid named an English age. The panel in the chest may have paid a Danish clerk on the way.
## Sources
Haneca, Kristof, et al. “Provenancing Baltic timber from art historical objects.” *Journal of Archaeological Science* 32 (2005): 261–271. Wazny, Tomasz (Gdansk / Baltic oak export, cited in Haneca). van Duivenvoorde and the KNOB bulletin literature on *wagenschot* / “De droechste waegescotten…”. Chinnery, *Oak Furniture: The British Tradition*. Macquoid, *A History of English Furniture*, Age of Oak. Bowett, “Furniture woods in London and provincial furniture 1700–1800” (Danzig oak at Gillow, 1740). USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (2010), ch. 4–5 and table 5–3a.
See: `english-oak-great-furniture`, `dutch-golden-age-shipping`, `navy-oak-reserves`, `quartersawn-arts-crafts`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: English oak and the great furniture
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# English oak and the great furniture
A joined stool in a parish church still does the job it was made for. Four legs, four rails, a seat that may have been replaced, and at each corner a mortise and tenon pinned with a draw-bored oak peg. The peg has lozenged in the hole. The shoulder is still tight. Victor Chinnery walked that joint until it stopped being a mystery and became manners — court cupboard, press, tester bed, the great chest with a till. Macquoid, opening the *Age of Oak* in 1904, treated this furniture as the first of four English timber ages and closed the age at 1660, when walnut veneer took the polite room. The kitchen did not read him. The church did not. The farm press did not. What changed in 1660 was fashion in a few rooms, not the fiber that held the house together.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
![Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.](../assets/grain-cuts/sawn-orientation.svg)
*Figure 3. Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.*
## Home oak, and what “English” hides
English furniture oak is *Quercus robur* and *Q. petraea*, the same pair the Baltic ports sold. The difference is the stand and the conversion. Home oak could be quicker grown, wider-ringed, used where a joiner could hide a wilder face — a stile, a back rail, the underside of a seat. Imported wainscot often took the show panels. “English oak furniture” is that sandwich more often than a gallery label wants to say. The joinery tradition is English, Netherlandish, and French. The fiber in a linenfold may have paid the Sound Toll. The Baltic draft takes that cargo. This one stays with the shop that assembled the house’s heavy furniture.
The USDA *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a) puts American white oak near 1,360 lbf Janka and specific gravity 0.68, northern red oak near 1,290 lbf and 0.63. European oak sits in the same neighborhood; a single FPL-equivalent number for *Q. robur* is still a library errand `[CITE NEEDED]`. Figure 4 is the scatter. Figure 3 is the cut: flatsawn cathedrals, quartersawn flake, rift stripe. English joined work of 1550–1660 prefers riven or radial stock for stiles and panels. A wedge follows the rays. The board is naturally quartered. That is why a thin panel can be wide and still stay quiet.
Ring-porous, tannic, hard enough to hold a pin. Iron and damp oak make black stains. Steam-bending is a historic use for boat frames and some chair bows; ash and hickory often took the extreme bends. Oak planes if the irons are sharp and the grain is straight. Quartersawn rays pick up. A wavy board tears no matter what the catalogue promised.
John Evelyn’s *Sylva* (1664) is a planting book written as the fashionable rooms were already turning toward walnut. He wanted oaks for the navy and for the kingdom’s future timber. Furniture shops lived on what the yards and the tanbarks did not take, and on the imported boards the navy did not want for knees. Albion’s *Forests and Sea Power* is the strategic pair; the navy draft takes the reserved forest. The great furniture is the civilian half of the same trees.
## Macquoid’s rooms, Chinnery’s joints
Percy Macquoid’s first volume is still the walk through the fashionable English house: blackened joined oak, linenfold, bulbous legs on a court cupboard, inlay of holly and bog oak on a Nonsuch chest. Treat it as a periodization, not a law. Provincial England kept cutting oak while London laid *Juglans regia* oysters on deal after 1660. Church benches, farm presses, kitchen tables — the Age of Oak did not end. It left the parlor.
Chinnery remains the construction book. The court cupboard is a display machine: open shelves, a closed cupboard below, heavy stiles, rails pinned through. The press is a clothes cupboard with doors on frame-and-panel. The tester bed is a four-post frame that must not rack; the joints are the architecture. The joined stool is the teaching piece because there is nowhere to hide a bad shoulder.
Inlay and carving sit on that structure. A Nonsuch chest with architectural marquetry is still an oak box with floating panels. Bog oak and holly are the dark and light strings. They are not a different furniture system. The system is the pinned frame.
Bowett’s later work on provincial woods matters even after 1700: Gillows could pay nearly mahogany prices for Danzig oak in 1740 because quartered Baltic was still a specified grade. English shops never forgot oak. They stopped showing it in the rooms Macquoid cared about.
## Joinery
Draw-bored mortise and tenon first. The hole in the tenon is offset toward the shoulder by a fraction. The pin, often riven oak, pulls as it drives. Chinnery’s photographs of lozenged pins are the aging proof. Do not confuse this with a later factory dowel glued in a bored hole. The offset is the whole trick.
Frame-and-panel is the carcase language. Stiles and rails mortised; panels grooved and free to shrink. Haunched tenons keep the mortise out of the end of a stile. A muntin splits a wide opening into two panels so no single board has to be heroic. Grooves are ploughed; a stuck moulding on the inner edge of a rail is cut in the solid, not planted, on better work.
The boarded chest is the other English grammar: six boards, nailed or pegged, sometimes a till, sometimes chip-carved. It is not a failed joined chest. It is a different contract — faster, cheaper, more willing to split along a board if the house dries. Both grammars run through the same century.
A table with trestle ends and a loose top is older than the joined frame table. The joined table — four legs, four rails, stretchers when the span asks, a top pegged or cleated — becomes the great dining board of the hall. Tops are often two or three boards, edge-jointed, sometimes with a breadboard that must not be glued across the end. If the pins in a breadboard are tight and the top is flatsawn, the next heating season splits the leaf. Figure 3 is why.
Floor-standing cupboards pick up hinges that split stiles if the screw or nail sits too near the edge. Replaced hinges are a common scar. Look for a second set of holes and an iron stain.
Wainscot as wall lining uses the same panel grammar as the chest, only taller. A room lined in Baltic boards and a chest made in the same shop can share a conversion habit. The furniture is the portable version of the room.
Pins are oak. Trenails in heavier work can be the same. Glue, when it appears, is hide glue on a shoulder that already has a mechanical lock. Glue alone is not the period trust.
## After 1660, the rooms that did not change
Walnut veneer took the polite London room. Oak stayed in the kitchen, the church, the farm, the college hall, the court cupboard that was already heirloom. Gothic Revival and Renaissance Revival in the nineteenth century hauled carved oak back into the dining room as a costume. Those suites are steam-sawn, often stained black-brown, sometimes competent, often louder than a 1620 press. The Arts and Crafts shops later asked for quartered oak again and meant it; that is another draft. The great furniture of 1500–1660 is the joined, pinned, tannic object that still sits in a nave or a farmhouse passage.
American joined oak exists in the seventeenth century — the so-called Pilgrim-century chests of New Haven and the Connecticut valley (Forman, *American Seating Furniture, 1630–1730*, is the seating half; the chests live in the same wood culture). Colonists also had pine, poplar, and walnut in quantity. English oak furniture is a joinery export as much as a timber export. The joint travelled. The Baltic board sometimes travelled with it. Home American oak did the rest.
## Conservation
Not CITES. Worm in sapwood is ordinary; heartwood holds. Iron stains at hinges are ordinary. A top that was a chest lid is ordinary. Strip a blackened church pew to “natural oak” and you have a 1960s taste, not a 1620 one. Original surfaces are thin oil, wax, soot, and hand. A thick polyurethane film is a different object.
Replacement seats on stools are expected. Look at the rails and pins to know the stool. A “Jacobean” suite from a 1920s factory has machine-cut mouldings, even pins, and a stain that sits in the pores. The lozenged pin is the tell that time, not a distressing wheel, did the work.
Repair a loose shoulder by drawing a new pin if the old one is gone; do not flood the joint with PVA and call it saved. Keep the panel floating. If a flatsawn replacement panel is the only board you have, leave it room in the groove.
## What to look for
Lozenged pins, a floating panel, ray flake on a thin face, iron stains, a till inside a chest, hinge scars, a seat rail that still has its original pegs. Macquoid’s corridor still works on the hand: blackened joined oak before the faded oyster walnut. Walk out of that corridor into the kitchen and the same joints are still there, only cleaner from soap and worse from cooks.
The great furniture is great because it is joined, not because it is courtly. A stool that still holds is the argument.
## Sources
Chinnery, *Oak Furniture: The British Tradition*. Macquoid, *A History of English Furniture*, Age of Oak (1904–08). Evelyn, *Sylva* (1664). Albion, *Forests and Sea Power* (naval context). Haneca et al., *JAS* 32 (2005), for the imported-panel problem. Bowett, provincial woods (Danzig oak at Gillow). Forman, *American Seating Furniture, 1630–1730*. USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a and ch. 4. Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*.
See: `baltic-oak-renaissance`, `navy-oak-reserves`, `walnut-baroque`, `quartersawn-arts-crafts`, `reclaimed-oak-beams`.

item.title: Dutch shipping and Golden Age timber
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Dutch shipping and Golden Age timber
Stand on the Zaan in the seventeenth century and the air is sawdust and tar. Wind-powered mills convert Baltic balks into boards. Timber auctions move oak and deal that never grew in Holland’s wet fields. Amsterdam’s warehouses hold *wagenschot* for local joiners and for re-export west. The Republic’s furniture — the great *kast*, the linen press, the boarded chest that went to a farm in Friesland — sits on a shipping economy, not on a native oak forest of English size. The Golden Age is a taste in pictures. It is also a quay.
![Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/trade-lanes.svg)
*Figure 2. Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.*
![Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/timeline.svg)
*Figure 1. Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.*
## A republic that imported its furniture wood
The Low Countries had oaks. They did not have enough slow-grown, radially useful furniture oak to feed a century of urban joinery and a shipbuilding industry at the same time. Baltic oak — *Quercus robur* and *Q. petraea* from the hinterlands of Gdansk, then Königsberg and Courland — filled the gap. Haneca and colleagues (2005) provenanced art-historical oak by ring width and pointed at that south-eastern Baltic. In 1565, they note, 85 percent of wainscots passing the Danish Sound shipped from Gdansk. Dutch buyers stood in that stream with the English and the Flemish. The KNOB bulletin literature on *wagenschot* — including the driest-boards instruction — is a Dutch-language half of the same specification.
Deal travelled the same sea: Scots pine (*Pinus sylvestris*) and spruce (*Picea abies*) as yellow, red, and white deal, sawn boards for floors, backs, and painted work. Bowett’s provincial-woods essays keep *wainscot* and *deal* from collapsing into moods. Different cargoes. Sometimes the same hull. Sound Toll registers and later timber-auction records at the Zaan and in London are the paper trail. Do not invent a named voyage or a price from a blank year. Ports in the ordinary timber literature include Riga, the Prussian quays, and the Norwegian outlets that fed the softwood side `[CITE NEEDED: pin a named cargo series to a year only with a register page]`.
Figure 2 puts the Baltic oak lane beside later mahogany and teak. Figure 1 is the milestone strip. For this hour the Baltic lane is the one a Dutch joiner lives on. Tropical woods appear in small work and in VOC-adjacent luxury — ebony stringing, later a tropical veneer — but the *kast* that holds the linen is oak, or oak show on a deal hide.
American white oak in the *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a) is the mechanical neighbor: Janka about 1,360 lbf, specific gravity 0.68. Northern red oak: 1,290 lbf, 0.63. European oak sits nearby; a single FPL Janka for *Q. robur* wants a bench citation `[CITE NEEDED]`. Eastern white pine, 380 lbf and SG 0.35, is not the Dutch furniture pine. The Republic’s softwood is Baltic *sylvestris* and spruce — harder in many northern grades than *P. strobus*, with a stronger ring. Furniture shops used the joinery grade. Masts and spars were another ticket (Albion’s naval book is the English strategic pair; Dutch yards had their own mast trade `[CITE NEEDED for a named Dutch mast-port series]`).
## What the Golden Age shop built
The Dutch *kast* is the object to stand beside. Tall, framed, often with heavy cornice and cushioned frieze, doors on floating panels, interior of deal or oak, sometimes ebonized mouldings that are stained fruitwood or true ebony in small section. It is a linen and plate cupboard for a merchant house. The wood is tannic, ring-porous, radial on the better doors. A cheaper *kast* can be painted or grained. Graining is a skill and a disguise.
Joined stools, gateleg tables, boarded chests, and wall panelling use the same grammar as English work because the shops shared a North Sea joinery culture. Distinctions are in proportion, in the profile of a moulding, in the hardware — not in a different physics. A Haarlem panel and a Southwark panel can be the same Gdansk hinterland tree.
After mid-century, French and Italian walnut taste and a veneer technology reach Amsterdam as they reach London. The walnut drafts take that hour. The Golden Age oak *kast* does not vanish. It becomes the conservative object in the same house that bought a veneered cabinet for the voorhuis.
Painted furniture of the farms — greens, reds, later the Frisian and North German cousins — is often deal. Identification on a painted antique is a scraped hidden edge and a resin-canal search. Do not scrape a museum piece.
## Joinery
Draw-bored mortise and tenon on the *kast* stiles. The pin pulls the shoulder. Oak likes a riven or quartered stile so the pin crushes along a predictable fiber. Frame-and-panel doors: groove deep enough for seasonal shrink, haunched tenons at the corners, a muntin if the door is wide. Raised panels appear; the raise is a bevel to a field, not a glued-on sheet.
Interior fittings — shelves on cleats, a hanging rail, small drawers — are often deal, nailed or pegged. A walnut-veneered cabinet of the next generation will still hide deal or oak. Open the door. The truth is pale.
Boarded chests for export and for farms: nailed six-board construction, iron straps, a lock plate. The fiber crushes around a nail and holds. Glue is secondary. A till inside is the same habit as an English chest.
Floor construction and stair joinery in a canal house use the same imported oak and deal. Furniture is the portable subset. A restorer who treats a *kast* as if it grew in a Utrecht coppice will buy the wrong repair board. Match ring width and cut, not a romantic “Dutch oak” label.
Veneer, when it arrives, is a different contract: hide glue, a ground of oak or deal, oysters and burls that check if the ground moves. That is the Baroque walnut hour. This draft stops at the solid *kast* and the quay that fed it.
Ship carpentry overlaps the furniture shop in tools and in timber grades, not in joints. A knee is a grown crook. A *kast* stile is a straight quartered balk. Albion’s English navy story and the Dutch admiralty yards both ate compass timber and straight oak; furniture took the leftovers and the joinery boards. Do not collapse a hull and a cupboard into one romance.
## Trade, war, and the end of an easy Baltic
The Sound Toll made Denmark a clerk on every Baltic board. Wars in the eastern Baltic and competition from English buyers shifted shares among Gdansk, Königsberg, Courland, and Riga (Haneca; Wazny). The Dutch were entrepôt merchants: buy, convert at the Zaan, sell on. A board in a London chest can have passed a Dutch mill. Dendrochronology names the forest. It does not always name the last ship.
Figure 1’s later milestones — mahogany after 1721, CITES in the twentieth century — are other clocks. The Golden Age clock is the Sound, the Zaan mill, and the *kast*. Tropical listings do not apply to *Quercus* or *Pinus sylvestris*. The conservation problem here is old-growth boreal and temperate oak, not an appendix number.
When the Republic’s great shipping hour tightens after 1672, the furniture trade does not stop. It changes suppliers and tastes. Walnut and later mahogany enter the polite room. Oak stays in the *kast* that already stood in the house. That is the same two-room story Macquoid told for England, told from a quay instead of a country-house corridor.
## Conservation
Boreal and Baltic forestry is a climate and old-growth argument. Antique *wagenschot* in a *kast* is reuse by definition. New “reclaimed Baltic oak” should have a story that is not a container of mixed hardwood. FSC and PEFC appear on Nordic pine for a reason; they are certificates, not a legal finding.
Lead in old paint on a Frisian cupboard is a health fact. Overpaint is a palimpsest. Stripping to “natural pine” is often a twentieth-century taste.
Repair a *kast* door with quartered oak of similar ring. A wide-ringed American red oak will take stain and still look like a patch: open pores, a different flake. White-group European or American oak is the closer neighbor. Tyloses and ray size still argue if the ring count is wrong.
## What to look for
A tall framed *kast* with floating panels, deal interiors, ebonized small mouldings, iron locks. Paint layers on a farm chest. A radial face on a door and a wilder ring on a hidden stile. A London bill that says wainscot or deal — the same words a Dutch auction used in another language.
The Golden Age picture on the wall may be a calm sea. The furniture in the room paid a mill on the Zaan and a clerk at Helsingør.
## Sources
Haneca et al., *Journal of Archaeological Science* 32 (2005). Wazny on Gdansk export oak. KNOB bulletin literature, “De droechste waegescotten…”. Bowett, furniture woods in London and the provinces (wainscot vs deal). Albion, *Forests and Sea Power* (strategic timber context). Macquoid, *Age of Oak* / *Age of Walnut* (English clock, for contrast). USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a. Chinnery, *Oak Furniture* (North Sea joinery grammar).
See: `baltic-oak-renaissance`, `navy-oak-reserves`, `walnut-baroque`, `white-pine-softwood-economy`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Navy oak and the reserved forest
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Navy oak and the reserved forest
A grown crook lies in a dockyard slip at Deptford or Portsmouth: a knee, the angle between a branch and a trunk that a sawyer cannot invent. Surveyors of the Woods marked such trees in the Forest of Dean and the New Forest. Straight balks for planks might come from the same English stands, or from the Baltic, or later from North American white oak. Robert G. Albion’s *Forests and Sea Power: The Timber Problem of the Royal Navy, 1652–1862* (Harvard, 1926) is the book that treats those marks as strategy. Furniture shops lived on what the yards did not take. A joined press and a seventy-four’s frame are not the same object. They are often the same genus in a fight over the same bole.
![Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/trade-lanes.svg)
*Figure 2. Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.*
![Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/timeline.svg)
*Figure 1. Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.*
## What the navy wanted that a chair does not
A ship wants compass timber — naturally crooked pieces for knees, futtocks, and stem parts — and long straight oak for planking and beams. Furniture wants straight, dry, often radial boards and stiles. The navy’s hunger for crooks left some straight furniture wood in the civilian market. Its hunger for straight oak of ship length did the opposite: it reserved forests and imported what England could not grow fast enough.
Albion’s dates, 1652–1862, run from the first Dutch wars through the ironclad. John Evelyn’s *Sylva* (1664) is the planting sermon in the middle of that span: sow oaks for a fleet your grandchildren will float. The fashionable London room was already turning toward walnut. The dockyard was not. Figure 1’s furniture milestones and Figure 2’s three lanes sit beside this third demand. Baltic oak fed wainscot *and* some ship planking. Atlantic mahogany later entered the Admiralty’s own buildings (Bowett on Thomas Ripley: mahogany cheaper than deal or wainscot if Navy ships brought it home, *Georgian Group Journal*, 1997). Indian Ocean teak became a dockyard wood in another draft. This one stays with oak and the reserved pine mast.
New England white pine (*Pinus strobus*) — Weymouth pine in English bills — was the mast tree. The Broad Arrow tradition and the Massachusetts charter of 1691 reserved large pines for the Crown (Albion; Manning’s Broad Arrow notes). The exact 1691 wording wants a charter page before a writer quotes it `[CITE NEEDED]`. Furniture shops used the smaller stems and the later cut-over. The white-pine drafts take that civilian half. Here the pine matters as the navy’s other reserved species: oak for the hull, pine for the stick that held the sail.
American white oak (*Quercus alba* and the white group) entered as colonial and then United States timber: tyloses, tight cooperage, ship planking. FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a: Janka about 1,360 lbf, specific gravity 0.68. Northern red oak: 1,290 lbf, 0.63 — open pores, less loved for wet work. European *Q. robur* / *Q. petraea* sit in the same hardness band `[CITE NEEDED for a single FPL-equivalent]`. Eastern white pine: 380 lbf, SG 0.35. A mast is not a hardness story. It is a length-and-taper story. A knee is not a Janka story. It is a grain-that-already-turns story.
## Reserved forests and imported balks
The Forest of Dean, the New Forest, and other Crown woods were not romantic leftovers. They were inventories. Surveyors marked trees. Enclosures and common rights fought the mark. Albion walks the politics: a navy that could not trust the next Baltic war to keep the Sound open had to plant, reserve, and buy abroad. Gdansk hinterland oak, already provenanced in furniture by Haneca et al. (2005), was also a naval store. Riga and the eastern ports sold ship timber and wainscot as related grades, not as one cargo with two names.
Home English oak built frames of ships and frames of presses. The conversion differed. A dockyard sawyer takes length and a grown angle. A joiner takes a dry radial face. A compass oak that makes a knee is a poor table top: wild grain, reaction wood, a plane that chatters. Furniture from “navy oak” in today’s salvage market is often a beam or a plank, not a knee. Name the part.
The Naval Stores Act of 1721 (in force 1722) is Bowett’s mahogany statute: duty off British West Indian timber. It belongs in the mahogany draft. It belongs here only as proof that the navy’s freight and the furniture trade shared ships and statutes. Ripley’s sentence — mahogany cheaper than deal or wainscot when carried freight-free — is an Admiralty accountant talking. Wainscot was still the comparison wood.
Do not invent a price per load or a named convoy. Albion and the port books are the place to read those numbers when a library copy is open. An invented ledger is worse than a gap.
## Joinery
Ship joinery and furniture joinery share the mortise and the trenail and almost nothing of the grammar.
A grown knee is bolted or trenail-fastened to a beam and a timber. The grain already turns. You do not draw-bore a knee the way Chinnery’s stool is draw-bored; you capture a crook that grew the angle. Treenails are oak or locust in later American practice `[CITE NEEDED for a dated Royal Navy trenail specification]`. Iron drifts stain tannic oak black — the same chemistry as a furniture clamp mark, at a larger scale.
Furniture from reserved-forest offcuts uses the ordinary English joints: draw-bored mortise and tenon, frame-and-panel, boarded chests. The wood may be quicker grown if the best crooks and the longest straights went to the yard. A wide, slow Baltic panel in a civilian chest can be better furniture wood than an English oak reserved for a futtock and then rejected.
Dockyard joiners also made chests, stools, and office furniture for the yards themselves. That work is oak or deal, nailed and pinned, not a distinct “navy style.” Look at the secondary wood and the tool marks, not at an anchor carved on a Victorian revival.
When old dockyard oak is reused as a table — a later salvage fashion — the joints are new. The beam may still hold a bolt hole, a drift stain, a shipwright’s mark. Those are evidence. A breadboard glued tight across a flatsawn naval plank will split the same as any oak. Frame the top or slot-screw it. The navy did not solve furniture movement. It solved a hull.
A mast pond is not a kiln. Mast pines sat in water. Furniture pine wants dry stock. Mixing the two stories without a moisture meter is how a “historic mast” table moves an inch the first winter in a heated house.
## What furniture shops actually got
Chinnery’s joined oak and Macquoid’s Age of Oak are the civilian record. Albion is the reason some of that oak was second choice. Tanbarks, charcoal, and house carpentry were other competitors. The great furniture did not wait for the navy to be satisfied. It used home oak, Baltic wainscot, and whatever the local mill had. After 1660 the polite room left oak; the dockyard did not. That split is the whole English timber politics of the late seventeenth century: Evelyn planting for a fleet, London veneering walnuts, a parish still sitting on joined stools.
American yards after independence used *Q. alba* and live oak (*Q. virginiana*) for specific naval parts `[CITE NEEDED before naming a particular frigate’s timber list]`. Furniture in the same ports used walnut, pine, and mahogany. The reserved-forest idea travelled as policy (Broad Arrow) more than as a furniture style.
## Conservation
Crown forests still exist as place-names and as working woods. Their furniture meaning is historic, not a permit category. *Quercus* in the American and European mains is not CITES-listed. Reclaimed “man-of-war oak” should be documented. A beam from a barn is not a ship because someone burned a rope mark into it.
Metal in dockyard salvage — bolts, drifts, copper — will ruin a saw. Scan. Old tannic stains around iron are stable if the metal is gone; if the metal remains, it keeps writing black.
Oak wilt and sudden oak death are living-forest facts `[CITE NEEDED for current range if counties are named]`. They are not a reason to strip a reserved ancient oak for a kitchen island. Plantation oak will not make a knee. Grown crooks take decades and a form of forestry few furniture mills practice.
## What to look for
On a period piece: ordinary English or Baltic oak joinery, not a hull joint. On a salvage table: bolt holes, drift stains, a shipwright’s mark that can be checked against a yard practice, or the absence of all three. On a “Broad Arrow” pine board: the mark is a naval-stores claim; ask for the object history. On a new English oak table: second-growth rings, a kiln ticket, no reserved-forest romance required.
Albion wrote a navy book. The press in the farmhouse is the other half of the inventory. A surveyor’s blaze on a Dean oak and a joiner’s pin in a stool are two claims on one genus. Only one of them floated.
## Sources
Albion, Robert G. *Forests and Sea Power: The Timber Problem of the Royal Navy, 1652–1862.* Harvard, 1926. Evelyn, *Sylva* (1664). Haneca et al., *JAS* 32 (2005). Bowett, “Thomas Ripley and the use of early mahogany,” *Georgian Group Journal* 7 (1997); Naval Stores Act notes. Manning on the Broad Arrow / 1691 charter `[verify wording]`. Chinnery, *Oak Furniture*. Macquoid, *Age of Oak*. USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a (white oak, red oak, eastern white pine).
See: `baltic-oak-renaissance`, `english-oak-great-furniture`, `dutch-golden-age-shipping`, `american-colonial-pine`, `white-pine-softwood-economy`.

item.title: American colonial pine
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# American colonial pine
A six-board chest in eastern white pine, painted oxblood, sits against a New England wall. Two sides, a bottom, a lid, a front and a back — nailed or pegged, often a till, light enough for one person to drag. It is not a failed oak chest. It is a different idea of furniture: cheap enough to own, soft enough to dent, honest about paint. Benno Forman’s *American Seating Furniture, 1630–1730* is the seating half of the same wood culture. Hurst and Prown’s *Southern Furniture 1680–1830* is the reminder that a Charleston parlor might show walnut or mahogany while the passage and the kitchen stayed pine. The colonies furnished more rooms in pine than in any hardwood the London books named.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
![Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/timeline.svg)
*Figure 1. Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.*
## Three pines, two coasts of a colony
Eastern white pine (*Pinus strobus*) — Weymouth pine in English bills — is the New England and later Great Lakes furniture pine. The USDA *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a) puts it at about specific gravity 0.35 and Janka 380 lbf at 12 percent moisture. Shrinkage green to ovendry is on the order of 2.1 percent radial, 6.1 percent tangential, 8.2 percent volumetric. Soft, even, low movement for a commercial wood, easy to work. Heartwood light brown with a red hint; it darkens in air. The handbook still lists furniture among its uses. Old-growth clears are a vanished ordinary grade. Second growth is knotty. Knots that hold are the tree. Knots that fall out are holes you plug or paint.
Southern yellow pines (*P. taeda*, *P. echinata*, and kin) are denser, with a loud latewood band. They appear in southern country furniture and as secondary wood under walnut. Longleaf heart pine (*P. palustris*) is a harder, resinous cousin — FPL about SG 0.59 and Janka 870 lbf — more floor and joist than chamber chest, though shops used what they had (Outland, *Tapping the Pines*; Earley, *Looking for Longleaf*). Do not call every pale southern board white pine. End grain shows the latewood jump.
Scots pine (*P. sylvestris*) is the European deal pine. It is not the colonial American default. A “pine” cupboard in Pennsylvania may also be yellow-poplar (*Liriodendron tulipifera*), greener and heavier. Basswood is even softer and more even. Resin canals tell pine from those hardwoods. Figure 4 places white pine at the soft, light end of the series anchors. Figure 1’s early milestones are Baltic oak and later mahogany; colonial pine is the American clock those London dates under-count.
The Broad Arrow reserved large white pines for masts (Albion, *Forests and Sea Power*; the Massachusetts charter tradition of 1691). The exact charter wording wants a page `[CITE NEEDED]`. Furniture shops used what the navy did not take: smaller stems, limbs, the later boards after a mast tree came down. A blanket chest is not a mast. It is the civilian remainder.
## Paint, and the rooms the histories skip
Painted pine is the furniture of people who had trees and brushes. New England blanket chests, Connecticut Valley cupboards, Pennsylvania work that is not all walnut, southern huntboards and pie safes that may be yellow pine or poplar or both. The Metropolitan and Winterthur hold the best of what survived. Most of it lived harder lives and did not.
Paint is linseed, milk, distemper — oxblood, blue, a green that goes black in the folds. Old layers may be lead. That is a health fact. Overpaint is a palimpsest. Stripping a cupboard to “natural pine” is often a 1960s taste, not an eighteenth-century one. Stain blotches on pine: earlywood drinks, latewood refuses. A “honey pine” finish is a later factory argument with the rings.
Shaker pine is a later, clearer subset — pale, chosen, maple and cherry beside it. Kassay and Rieman and Burks take that mix. The colonial chest is more willing to be red and dented.
Southern shops (Hurst and Prown) used yellow pine as a primary for painted and stained case work and as a secondary under walnut and mahogany. A Charleston parlor and a backcountry press are not one market. Forman’s seating survey shows turned chairs and joint stools that may mix maple, ash, oak, and pine in one object. Species follow the job: a post that must take a mortise, a seat that must take a turning, a panel that must take paint.
## Joinery
The six-board chest is the teaching piece. Nails hold because the fiber crushes and grips. Glue holds if resin is not on the surface. Pegs are older in some shops and better in a thin rail. A steel screw without a pilot — a later repair — splits. Battens across a lid, nailed or pegged, keep a wide board from cupping; if they are glued tight across a flatsawn top, the lid splits. Breadboard ends, when they appear on tables, must slot or pin in elongated holes.
Boarded construction is the colonial pine default for chests and many tables. Joined construction — mortise and tenon, frame-and-panel — appears when the shop has oak or when a pine cupboard wants doors that stay true. A pine panel in an oak frame is a North Sea habit translated: the panel floats, the frame is the grown-up wood. All-pine joined work exists; the tenons are fatter than a mahogany shop would cut, because 380 lbf is not 1,360.
Drawer work in better colonial case pieces may be pine sides with a walnut or maple front, or all pine, nailed or dovetailed. Early dovetails can be large and few. A plywood drawer bottom is a marriage. Hand-planed bottoms, bevelled into a groove, are the period contract.
Windsor production, already mixing species in the eighteenth century (Evans, *Windsor-Chair Making in America*), uses pine for some seats in later cheap work; elm is the seat that will not split. Do not assume a colonial “pine chair” is a Windsor. Turned post-and-rung chairs in maple and ash are Forman’s territory. Pine is more often the chest, the table top, the cupboard, the painted box.
A nailed six-board is allowed to be crude at the back and careful at the front. Look at the lid’s underside for plane tracks. A circular-saw skip is a nineteenth-century conversion or a later replacement.
## After the navy’s mark
Independence did not change the tree. It changed who could cut a mast pine without a Crown mark. The white-pine economy draft takes the later lumber hour: New England to the Lake States, clears for interiors, knotty grades for paint. Colonial furniture already shows the split: a clear boarded lid on a better chest, a knotty painted piece for the kitchen.
A southern pie safe with punched-tin panels is the humidity version of the same boarded idea. The case may be yellow pine or poplar; the tins keep air moving around pies and meat. Hurst and Prown teach the reader to look at the case species before the tin pattern. A Connecticut Valley cupboard with a bold grain-painted face is the northern cousin: the paint is architecture, the pine is the servant. Winterthur’s painted chests keep enough original film that a conservator can still sequence the colors. A house-owned safe that has been stripped to a gym-floor orange has lost the sequence. Leave a chip in the back if you need a resin-canal check. The show face is the document.
Macquoid’s English ages do not schedule this work. Figure 1 can be read without a colonial pine tick; that is a London map. A Winterthur blanket chest is still a 500-year furniture wood. Softwoods were never only poor. They were what a household could lift and paint.
## Conservation
*Pinus strobus* and the southern yellow pines are not CITES species. Old-growth white pine in commercial clears is scarce. Using remaining old-growth for a suburban table wastes a grade the seventeenth century already treated as building and mast material. Using managed and plantation pine for painted work is ordinary. The Lacey Act still applies if a container of “colonial pine” is imported mixed softwood. Ask for the country and the species.
Lead paint: do not sand a chest as if it were raw wood. Insect holes in sapwood are common. Active powder is a different problem from old flight holes.
Repair with *P. strobus* or a close northern pine. Southern yellow pine’s loud latewood shouts in a New England lid. The reverse is also true: a white-pine patch in a coastal yellow-pine safe reads as a pale stripe.
Arkansas shops work southern yellow pine more than *strobus*. A painted cupboard in that timber is a country object in the same boarded grammar. One sentence is enough.
## What to look for
Light weight, dents, paint layers, resin canals on an unseen end, a till, rose-head nails or later replacements, a lid that still has battens. A “mahogany” factory piece with a pine back is a later sandwich. A “Pilgrim” chest with machine distress is a Colonial Revival cartoon. Forman’s dates and Hurst and Prown’s rooms are the correctives.
Lift the chest. If two people are required, ask whether someone lined it with oak or filled it with lead paint. The first owner could move it.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (eastern white pine; southern pines; longleaf). Forman, *American Seating Furniture, 1630–1730*. Hurst and Prown, *Southern Furniture 1680–1830*. Albion, *Forests and Sea Power*. Evans, *Windsor-Chair Making in America*. Outland, *Tapping the Pines*; Earley, *Looking for Longleaf* (southern yellow-pine context). Kassay; Rieman and Burks (later Shaker pine). Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*. Winterthur collection practice.
See: `white-pine-softwood-economy`, `navy-oak-reserves`, `walnut-queen-anne`, `english-oak-great-furniture`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: White pine and the softwood economy
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# White pine and the softwood economy
A mast pond at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, held *Pinus strobus* that the Crown had already claimed with a Broad Arrow blaze. The tree was a taper of clear wood tall enough to step a ship. Albion’s *Forests and Sea Power* is the English strategic reading of that mark; the Massachusetts charter tradition of 1691 is the colonial statute half `[CITE NEEDED for the exact 1691 wording]`. Furniture never ate those sticks first. It ate the boards that came after the mast trade, then the lake-state clears that built interiors from Boston to Chicago, then the knotty seconds that twentieth-century dens called rustic. White pine is a softwood economy that sometimes made a chest. The chest is not the point of the tree. It is the remainder that still furnishes rooms.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## The handbook tree
Eastern white pine is the light, even, low-resin pine of the Northeast and the Great Lakes. FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a: specific gravity about 0.35, Janka about 380 lbf at 12 percent moisture. Shrinkage green to ovendry on the order of 2.1 percent radial, 6.1 percent tangential, 8.2 percent volumetric. Compared with white oak at 1,360 lbf and SG 0.68, or black walnut at 1,010 lbf and 0.55, it is the soft end of Figure 4. A buckle dents a tavern table. A dropped pot leaves a crescent. That is the species, not a defect label.
Heartwood is light brown with a red hint and darkens in air. Sapwood is paler and wide on second-growth trees. Old-growth clears — long, knot-free, slow enough to look like cream — were the interior-joinery grade: doors, wainscot in the American sense (wall boards, not Baltic oak), cupboard interiors, clock cases in New England that wanted light weight and a paint or veneer ground. The *Wood Handbook* still lists furniture among uses. The yard that can sell that clear today is selling a scarce remnant or a carefully graded modern piece, not 1850 ordinary stock.
Resin canals exist but are shy next to southern yellow pine. The latewood band is modest. The face can take a clear finish without the corrugated argument of *P. palustris*. Stain still blotches if you insist: earlywood drinks. Paint is the historic finish that understood the tree.
Michael Williams’s *Americans and Their Forests* is the geography book: the white-pine cut moved from New England inland and west as stands fell. Furniture factories in later decades used what the construction trade left. A Grand Rapids crate and a Boston chimney-breast can be the same species in different grades.
## Masts, boards, and the civilian remainder
England called the tree Weymouth pine. The navy wanted length and a clean taper. The Broad Arrow reserved the large stems. Smaller trees and the tops became boards. After independence the mark lost its Crown, not its mill. New England yards cut white pine for export and for domestic build. The colonial-pine draft is the painted chest of 1630–1780. This draft is the commodity: how a forest became dimension lumber, and how shops specified a furniture grade inside that flood.
Baltic deal — *P. sylvestris* and spruce — was Britain’s imported softwood. White pine was the North American answer to the same job: carcases, backs, painted rooms, the hide under a show wood. A London bill that says deal and a Boston bill that says pine are cousins in function. They are not the same ring. Repair an English dustboard with northern European pine; repair a Connecticut case with *strobus*. Southern yellow pine’s loud latewood is a third voice.
Do not invent a mast-price or a board-foot series. Albion and the customs books are where those figures live when a copy is open. The economy can be named without a fake invoice: reserved trees, then a lumber cut, then a furniture use on the grades that would not floor a mill or step a ship.
Clock shops liked white pine for cases because the movement is modest and the box is light on a wall. Case furniture in the Federal hour often hides pine or poplar behind mahogany or cherry. Open the drawer. The side that is pale and dented, with resin canals, is the economy talking.
## Joinery
Pine takes nails. That fact built more American rooms than dovetails did. The fiber crushes and grips. A rose-head nail in a boarded chest is period manners. Glue holds on a clean, low-resin face. Hide glue on a pine carcase under walnut veneer is the English and American sandwich of the walnut hour; the ground is often deal in London and white pine or poplar in the colonies.
Dovetails in pine must be cut fat. A slender mahogany tail in 380 lbf stock chips. Large, few tails on a colonial or country drawer are competence, not clumsiness. Later factory drawers in white pine can be machine-dovetailed and still correct for the wood.
Frame-and-panel in pine works if the panel floats. The wood moves less than oak, not zero. A wide flatsawn lid still cups. Battens, slot-screwed breadboards, and painted finishes that do not glue a film across a check are the old answers. A steel screw without a pilot splits a thin rail. Pegs are kinder.
Turned pine appears on cheap tables and some clock finials. It dents in the lathe if the tool is dull. Maple took the better turnings (Forman). Pine took the painted ones.
Interior joinery — doors, shutters, stair parts — uses the same mortise-and-tenon grammar as furniture, often with hide glue and a painted finish. A “furniture” table from house-joinery stock is a common afterlife. Look for hinge gains and a paint ghost.
Veneer on white pine is ordinary in the nineteenth century: a thin mahogany or walnut face on a light ground. The edge tells. A 12 mm pine core with a sliced face is a legal cabinet door if named. It is a slight if sold as a solid hardwood slab.
## The knotty century and the vanished clear
Twentieth-century American dens paneled in knotty pine made a fashion of the grade old-growth millers rejected for furniture. Colonial Revival factories added machine distress. Some of it is charming. Some of it is a cartoon of a six-board chest. Mid-century taste hid pine, then country taste brought it back. The clear old-growth door in a Federal house and the knotty rec-room panel are the same binomial. They are not the same material.
Lake-state logging left cut-over and second growth. Furniture from that second growth is knotty, wider-ringed, still 380 lbf, still willing to paint. Using remaining old-growth clears for a suburban dining table spends a structural and historic grade on a use pine already served in paint. Plantation and managed white pine for painted case work is the ordinary modern specification.
Walk a Saginaw or Muskegon mill town in the later nineteenth century and the product on the dock is dimension lumber first: boards for Chicago balloon frames, clears for doors, boxboards for freight. Williams maps that cut as a moving front. A furniture shop in the same town bought the grade that would not make a door stile — knots, pith, a waney edge — and painted it. A clockmaker in Boston or Connecticut still wanted the clear: light on a wall, stable enough that a painted or veneered case would not rack the movement. The two shops named the same tree and did not compete for the same board.
A counting-house interior in Salem or Boston — shutters, a desk, a railing — can be white pine throughout, painted or grained to look like oak. Graining is a skill. It is also how a softwood economy imitated a hardwood room without paying Baltic wainscot freight. Scrape a shutter’s bottom edge in a house you own. The cream wood and the shy resin canal are the tell. Leave a museum shutter alone.
Western pines enter later catalogues as “knotty pine” without a binomial. Ask. *P. strobus* is eastern. The handbook numbers above are for that species. A different pine is a different latewood.
## Conservation
Not CITES. Old-growth white pine in the East is a remnant ecology and a scarce lumber grade. Williams is the historical geography; living-forest policy is a separate literature `[CITE NEEDED before naming a particular remaining stand as a furniture source]`. Lacey still applies to imported “white pine” that may be mixed. Antique pine is reuse. New “reclaimed white pine” from a barn can be honest; a container of mixed softwood with a New England story is not.
Lead in old paint. Active powder-post in sapwood. A mast-pond history, if claimed, implies a waterlogged past; dry the board to the destination humidity before a glued joint.
## What to look for
Weight (low), dents, shy resin canals, a paint history, a carcase under a darker face, clock-case lightness, a clear door versus a knotty panel. A dealer’s “pumpkin pine” is a color word for old oxidized heartwood, not a species. End grain still has to be *strobus*.
The Broad Arrow was a navy claim. The blanket chest was what the household kept. Both were white pine. Only one of them was trying to be furniture. A mast pond in January and a painted cupboard in a heated parlor are the same species at two moisture contents. Dry the board to the room before you call it furniture stock.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a and species note (eastern white pine). Albion, *Forests and Sea Power*. Williams, *Americans and Their Forests*. Forman, *American Seating Furniture, 1630–1730*. Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*. Bowett, provincial woods (deal as the British functional cousin). Manning on the Broad Arrow / 1691 charter `[verify wording]`.
See: `american-colonial-pine`, `navy-oak-reserves`, `walnut-baroque`, `dutch-golden-age-shipping`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Walnut in the Baroque rooms
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Walnut in the Baroque rooms
When Charles II came back in 1660, a London chair changed color. Cane in the seat, scroll in the stretcher, and a thin skin of *Juglans regia* — grey-brown, streaked, sometimes an oyster of transverse slices — over a carcase of oak or deal.
