Macquoid later called the years to 1720 the Age of Walnut. French and Italian rooms had already been there. Dutch taste arrived with people and with prints. Adam Bowett’s *English Furniture 1660–1714: From Charles II to Queen Anne* is the construction-and-trade book that keeps the oysters attached to a shop, not to a mood. Open the drawer of a William-and-Mary card table. The sides are pale. The grain does not match the top. That is correct.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
![Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.](../assets/grain-cuts/sawn-orientation.svg)
*Figure 3. Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.*
## Two walnuts, one fashionable skin
*Juglans regia* is the European or “English” walnut — also Persian, French, Circassian, Italian, depending on the dealer’s poetry. Heartwood grey-brown to chocolate with dark streaks. Figure can be wild. The tree is smaller and more crotched than American black walnut; Restoration shops used it as veneer because the log asked for that. Solid *regia* exists on provincial pieces and on parts that had to take a joint — a leg, a stile. The show surfaces of polite London work are often a slice.
*Juglans nigra*, American black walnut, is a taller, straighter gift. The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a) puts it at specific gravity 0.55 and Janka 1,010 lbf at 12 percent moisture — softer than white oak (1,360 / 0.68), hard enough for a chair, friendly to tools. FPL’s species note still reads like a love letter: straight grain, easy to work, stable, takes a natural finish, much valued for furniture. About three-quarters of the commercial wood, the handbook said, comes from the Central States. In the Baroque hour *nigra* is not yet London’s fashion wood. It is already a colonial primary. The Queen Anne draft takes the American solid chair. This draft stays with the European skin.
Butternut (*J. cinerea*) is the pale cousin, used for carving and cheap imitation, now a canker story `[CITE NEEDED for a current USFS status note]`.
Walnut is semi-ring-porous. The face has a gentle grain, not oak’s trenches. It planes like a courtesy. It carves without coarse red oak’s crumbling. Burls and crotches are structural chaos and visual wealth. Oyster veneer — transverse slices laid like shells — used walnut, laburnum, and olive. The technique is of this moment; the monopoly is not. Figure 3 is why a veneer shop cares about cut: a transverse oyster is not a flatsawn cathedral and not a quartered flake. It is the log as a stack of coins.
Movement is moderate for a hardwood. It is not teak. A badly made pine or oak ground will still telegraph. Hide glue gone brittle will let a burl check. Cross-banding and a proper substrate are the quiet half of the fashion.
## Restoration, William and Mary, the court color
Restoration cane-back chairs, high-back scrolls, twist-turned legs, the first polite card tables, seaweed marquetry on olive and walnut grounds — the literature is thick because the rooms wanted to look like the court. Macquoid’s second volume is the gallery walk. Bowett 1660–1714 is the one that ties a cane chair to a joinery shop and a veneer merchant.
Dutch taste came with a Dutch king in 1689 and had been coming in objects before that. French taste came because France was the factory of fashion; André-Jacob Roubo’s *L’Art du menuisier* (1769–75) is later, but the Parisian veneer habit is earlier than Charles II. English trees and imported *regia* fed a trade that treated the figured log as a skin. Oak did not leave the kingdom. It left the rooms that wanted to look current.
Seaweed marquetry is a fine end-grain and veneer drawing in pale and dark woods, often on a walnut field. It is a different contract from Chinnery’s pinned oak. The panel may still float. The picture does not like a ground that cups. Figure 4 places walnut’s hardness among the anchors: carvable, not soft as pine, not trench-pored as oak.
Do not invent a royal commission or a price per foot of oyster. Named pieces live in museum records — Wallace Collection notes help for later French marquetry; English Restoration chairs live in V&A and country-house lists `[CITE NEEDED before attaching a specific inventory number to a claim]`. The type is secure. The invoice is not, unless you have it.
## Joinery
Veneer on an oak or deal carcase is the Baroque walnut contract. The carcase is joined: mortise-and-tenon frames, pinned or glued, drawer runners, a dustboard of deal. The show face is hide-glued. A bookmatched pair of crotch leaves on a cabinet door is a sawyer’s flitch opened like a page. Oysters are laid in a field, often framed with a stringing line of holly or box. The edge of the carcase, if honest, shows the pale ground.
Cane seats are a woven panel in a grooved frame. The frame is walnut, solid, with stretchers that may be scrolled or twisted. The twist is a lathe job on a square blank; walnut takes it. Oak did it earlier and thicker. The cane fails first. Replacement cane is expected. Look at the frame’s joints to date the chair.
Twist turning, scroll brackets, and a carved crest sit on solid walnut or on a walnut-faced construction. Draw-boring is less the religion than it was in oak; glue and a tight shoulder do more work in a smaller section. A loose Restoration chair is often a failed glue line at a stretcher, not a lozenged pin.
Cane fails in a predictable order: the weave at the front rail, then the holes worn oval. A restorer who recanes and then stains the new cane dark to “match 1680” is matching a tea advertisement. Period cane was paler. The frame’s oxidized walnut is the old color; the seat was a light grid. Look at the groove that holds the cane spline. A later tacked-on sheet of machine cane is a different joint. The Baroque chair is a grooved frame. Keep the groove.
Drawer dovetails in this hour can be fine. Sides are oak or deal. Bottoms are planed, bevelled into grooves. A plywood bottom is a later marriage. The Queen Anne highboy with an MDF dustboard is a warning from another century.
Table tops in solid walnut exist on provincial pieces. Polite London card tables are often veneered, with a deal or oak core, rule joints on later leaves, hinged flaps. If the ground moves and the veneer does not, the oysters check. Humidity in a 1690 house went up and down with the fire. Central heating is crueler.
Seaweed and arabesque marquetry want a stable ground and a toothing plane. The cutter leaves a keyed surface for hide glue. Sanding that surface off in a modern refinish is how a picture lifts.
## Finish and light
Old French polish on *regia* can look golden. The wood darkens, then some of the red and the gold leave in a south window and you get a flat brown. Oil goes deeper. A thick polyurethane film looks sealed-in, like furniture afraid of itself. Stain is rarely required on heartwood and often muddies the grain. Sapwood is the nuisance: pale, left visible on some period pieces, steamed away in modern mills. Disclose the steam on a new board. A 1690 oyster does not have it.
Iron and walnut are kinder than iron and oak, but water stains and sun fade are the daily enemies. A card-table leaf that lived closed is darker than the one that faced the window. That is a record, not a mismatch to “correct.”
## Conservation
Black walnut is a managed American hardwood, not a CITES appendix tree. *J. regia* in parts of its range has been pressured by veneer markets `[CITE NEEDED for a current IUCN or national status]`. Stolen backyard *nigra* in the last twenty years is a real crime file `[CITE NEEDED: named prosecutions]`. A cheap wide slab from an unnamed seller has a past. This hour’s objects are mostly *regia* veneer. The ethical buy of a new “Baroque walnut” suite is a binomial and an edge: solid, veneered, or printed.
Hide glue is reversible. PVA floods and stays. A restorer who wants the oysters to be removable later keeps the period adhesive. Brittle glue and a checking burl want humidity first, not a flood of finish.
Lead in later overpaint. Worm in deal grounds. A carcase that is later than its veneer is a common marriage.
## What to look for
Pale drawer sides, oysters or burl on the show face, cane in a grooved frame, twist legs, seaweed on a box, a deal dustboard. A 1970s “Mediterranean” suite with printed walnut grain is a poster. A 1690 table with a pine drawer is a shop telling the truth. Heart versus sap, solid versus a 2 mm jacket, European streak versus a later American chocolate — the edge still ends the argument.
Macquoid gave the age a name. The drawer still gives the construction.
## Sources
Bowett, *English Furniture 1660–1714: From Charles II to Queen Anne*. Macquoid, *A History of English Furniture*, Age of Walnut. Roubo, *L’Art du menuisier* (later French shop practice). USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a (black walnut; *regia* as imported neighbor `[CITE NEEDED if a handbook line is quoted]`). Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*. Chinnery, *Oak Furniture* (for the oak carcase under the skin). Edwards and Macquoid, *Dictionary of English Furniture*.
See: `walnut-queen-anne`, `english-oak-great-furniture`, `mahogany-chippendale`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Walnut and the Queen Anne chair
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Walnut and the Queen Anne chair
A cabriole leg ends in a pad foot. The knee may carry a shell. The splat is a solid vase, not yet the pierced lace of a *Director* plate. In London the show wood is still often *Juglans regia*, a veneer on oak or deal, or a solid leg joined to a veneered seat rail. In Philadelphia or the Virginia Piedmont the same silhouette can be *Juglans nigra* in the solid, sap streak and all. Queen Anne is an English reign (1702–1714) and an American style that runs later, into the 1750s. Bowett’s *English Furniture 1660–1714* and *Early Georgian Furniture 1715–1740* are the London books. Winterthur and Hurst and Prown are the American rooms. The chair is one fashion. The fiber is two continents.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
![Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.](../assets/grain-cuts/sawn-orientation.svg)
*Figure 3. Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.*
## The famine that will not sit still
Connoisseurs liked a tidy prelude to mahogany: frost, overcutting, a “walnut famine” in the 1720s, then the new wood. Bowett has been cautious. What the port books show after the Naval Stores Act of 1721 (in force 1722) is mahogany becoming cheap enough to carve in the solid. Walnut stays in provincial shops and in American ones. Fashion moved. Ledgers are messier than a famine story. Macquoid’s Age of Walnut ends at 1720 as a London clock. A Boston high chest in black walnut does not read that page.
*Juglans nigra*: FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a — specific gravity 0.55, Janka 1,010 lbf at 12 percent moisture. Softer than white oak (1,360 / 0.68), kinder than maple, strong enough in the right section for a cabriole that tapers to a pad. The handbook still calls it much valued for furniture. *J. regia* is the greyer, more streaked European cousin, often sliced. Figure 4 places *nigra* among the anchors. Figure 3 is the cut on a solid American leg: a cabriole wants rift or a careful selection so two faces do not flash a cathedral and two stay quiet. A veneered English seat rail can hide a deal core; the knee, if carved, wants solid wood.
Walnut planes, carves, and takes a moulding without oak’s trenches. A shell on a knee is a gouge job. The splat — vase, solid, sometimes a simple piercing later in the run — is thinner than an oak splat and thicker than a Chippendale interlaced back. R. W. Symonds argued that mahogany’s strength let chairmakers go more slender still. Bowett quotes him and complicates the credit. The Queen Anne splat is already a walnut idea: a flat, shaped board tenoned into a shoe and a crest, not a joined gothic tracery.
## London veneer, American solid
English Queen Anne and early Georgian case work continues the Baroque sandwich: walnut face, oak or deal hide. High chests, dressing tables, bureau-bookcases. Cross-banding, herringbone, a herringed edge on a top. The carcase joinery is the same family as 1690, the silhouette slighter, the turnings fewer, the cabriole the new line.
American shops in Philadelphia, New York, Newport, Charleston, and the backcountry built the silhouette in the woods they had. Black walnut was a primary, not a jacket. Cherry and maple took the same forms in New England and Pennsylvania. Southern shops used walnut beside cherry and southern pine (Hurst and Prown). A sap streak on a 1730 American rail is ordinary. Steaming to blend sap and heart is a later mill habit; do not demand it of a period piece.
Winterthur holds the high-style end: a Philadelphia walnut easy chair, a high chest with a broken arch, cabriole knees with shells. County museums hold the country cousins: a pad foot that is a pad, a splat that is a board, a rush seat. Forman’s earlier seating survey stops at 1730; the Queen Anne chair is the next grammar — less turned post-and-rung, more shaped solid.
An easy chair is a test of the knee joint under upholstery. The wings and the loose cushion hide a pine or poplar subframe; the show legs are *nigra*, carved, with a shell that must survive a vacuum cleaner for two centuries. Take the loose seat out if a curator will let you. The corner block, the tenon shoulders, and the secondary species are the shop. Newport’s related work can be finer in the ankle and more willing to drop stretchers. A backcountry Virginia chair keeps the stretcher and a thicker pad. Hurst and Prown’s plates are the place to see that range without collapsing it into one “southern Queen Anne.” The rush-seat cousin — a vase splat, a pad foot, a seat that was recaned or re-rushed twice — is the chair that actually furnished a room. High style is the archive. Rush is the census.
Do not invent a shop price. Chippendale’s *Director* (1754) is already a mahogany book for ambitious plates. Some “Queen Anne” chairs that now wear a London attribution are walnut because the shop still had it, or because the client was provincial. A lens on an unseen rail ends the species argument.
## Joinery
The cabriole is a shaped solid. The knee meets the seat rail in a joint that must take side load: a mortise in the rail, a tenon from the leg, often a glue block in the front corner. Stretchers return on country chairs and drop on high-style ones that trust the joint and the wood. When they drop, a failed glue line is a broken chair. Oak of 1620 would have pinned and stretched. Walnut of 1710 often glues and hopes. Surviving chairs are the ones whose blocks were fitted.
The splat sits in a shoe — a separate piece on better work — and in a crest-rail mortise. The crest may be carved; the ears are fragile. A repaired ear is common. The shoe hides the bottom tenon and gives the splat a finished start. A splat tenoned through the rear rail without a shoe is cheaper work or a later simplification.
Seat frames are mortised. Upholstered seats (drop-in or upholstered over) hide webbing and a pine or deal subframe. Slip seats in walnut-framed chairs can be pine. Rush seats appear on country pieces. A plywood drop-in is a replacement.
Case pieces: dovetailed drawers, deal or pine or yellow-poplar sides in America, oak or deal in England. Dustboards. A “Queen Anne” highboy with fiberboard dustboards was assembled after the form was already a reproduction style. Hand-planed bottoms, bevelled to a groove, are the period test.
Veneer on a cabriole chair is mostly on flat rails and on case work, not on the shaped leg. A carved knee in veneer is a later trick or a break. Solid *nigra* legs in America are the honest version of the line.
Rule-jointed leaves on tables still want room to shrink. Breadboards glued tight across a walnut top split it the same as oak. Buttons and slots at the aprons are the manners.
## Toward mahogany without a neat famine
After 1722 Jamaica wood enters the port books in quantity (Bowett’s thesis and the RFS Naval Stores Act notes). London high style can afford to carve mahogany in the solid. The splat gets thinner and more open. The Queen Anne vase remains in the country and in America, sometimes stained to look like the new wood. A walnut chair with a mahogany stain is a period possibility and a later one. A lens, not a label.
Provincial England kept walnut. So did the American interior, long after Macquoid turned his page. The Chippendale draft takes the statute and the splat. This draft stops at the pad foot and the two walnuts that wore it.
## Conservation
Neither *J. nigra* nor *J. regia* is the CITES problem mahogany became. High-grading of figured logs is the quiet harm. Stolen eastern walnut trees are a documented crime class `[CITE NEEDED: named prosecutions]`. A reproduction “Queen Anne” suite in steamed, even-colored walnut is a modern mill product. Name the steam. A 12 mm veneer on MDF is a kitchen door if sold as such.
Original finishes are thin: oil, wax, a spirit varnish. French polish on a 1710 American chair is often a later gift. Polyurethane is a different object. Sun fade on one leaf of a drop-leaf is a record. Matching it with dye is a choice; disclose it.
Hide glue at the knee block is reversible. A chair that racks wants the block refitted, not a metal bracket on the show face.
## What to look for
Pad foot, vase splat, a shoe, a glue block in the front corner, sap on an American rail, a deal or poplar drawer side, veneer on an English rail and solid on the knee. Stretchers present or absent. An ear that has been replaced. A *Director* piercing on a chair called Queen Anne — that chair has changed reigns.
The English reign was short. The American chair kept the name and the walnut tree that grew in the yard. A pad foot worn flat on the inner edge still points to how the sitter rose. That wear is a census mark. A replaced foot that does not wear is a restoration.
## Sources
Bowett, *English Furniture 1660–1714*; *Early Georgian Furniture 1715–1740*; *The English Mahogany Trade 1700–1793* (duty change vs famine). Macquoid, Age of Walnut. Hurst and Prown, *Southern Furniture 1680–1830*. Forman, *American Seating Furniture, 1630–1730* (the seating culture just before). Winterthur collection practice. USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a. Chippendale, *Director*, 1754/1762 (the next splat). Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*.
See: `walnut-baroque`, `mahogany-chippendale`, `american-colonial-pine`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Mahogany and the Chippendale shop
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Mahogany and the Chippendale shop
Thomas Ripley told the Admiralty that mahogany would be cheaper than deal or wainscot if Navy ships brought it home (Bowett, *Georgian Group Journal*, 1997). That sentence still surprises people raised on Macquoid’s luxury. The Naval Stores Act of 1721, in force 1722, stripped the duty from British West Indian timber. Jamaica wood that had not been worth the freight became, in the port books, a furniture wood you could carve in the solid. The splat of a mid-century London chair is a tax story, a sugar-island story, and only then a style story.
![Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/trade-lanes.svg)
*Figure 2. Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.*
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## What the statute changed
Adam Bowett’s thesis, *The English Mahogany Trade 1700–1793*, is the backbone. There is little hard evidence of a furniture trade in mahogany before 1700. The 1660 Book of Rates lists other West Indian woods — brazeletto, ebony, fustic, lignum vitae, sweetwood, speckled wood — and not mahogany. After 1722 the customs values jump: Bowett’s RFS lecture notes £695 in 1723, £3,121 in 1725, £4,060 in 1729. Macquoid’s date of 1733 and Cescinsky’s 1748 are connoisseur dates. The statute is the date.
Jamaica dominated the early furniture supply. Honduras “bay-wood” became a large, cheaper, often coarser supply later in the century. Cuban and Hispaniola woods had quality reputations and Spanish-imperial politics. Figure 2 puts that Atlantic lane beside Baltic oak and Indian Ocean teak. They are parallel, not a relay race.
Gillow of Lancaster bought Jamaica wood as a provincial firm in a port world, not only as a London satellite (Bowett, Jamaica/Gillow paper). Twenty to forty percent of mahogany after about 1730 entered through out-ports, unlike walnut, which had been a London monopoly. Mahogany was a leveller. Provincial chairmakers could get it.
Harewood House paid Thomas Chippendale with money that sat on West Indian estates — Bowett’s opening image. The chair and the plantation are the same economy. Enslaved labor logged and milled. That belongs in the caption, not in a footnote the reader can skip.
## The trees
*Swietenia mahagoni* — Cuban, Santo Domingo, West Indian — is the fine, often darker, tighter mahogany of the early trade. Commercial sizes were exhausted early. *S. macrophylla* — Honduran, big-leaf, later “genuine mahogany” — ranges from Mexico to the Amazon. The *Wood Handbook* describes American mahogany as pale pink to dark reddish brown, generally straighter than African *Khaya*, easy to dry, dimensionally stable, durable, easy to work, a premier veneer wood. Janka is commonly cited near 800 lbf, specific gravity near 0.45–0.50 (FPL imported-woods chapter / Kukachka FPL-125). Softer than white oak, kinder than maple, strong enough in the right section for a slender chair.
Figure 4 places that hardness among the series’ ten anchors. Mahogany is not the hard wood. It is the carvable, stable, moderately light wood that made a pierced splat possible without the crumbling of coarse oak or the glass fight of hard maple.
## Joinery: why the splat got thin
R. W. Symonds argued that mahogany’s strength let chairmakers draw legs, rails, and backs more slender, with more accentuated curves, than walnut allowed. Bowett quotes him and complicates the credit: the style did not wait for a new fiber the way a myth wants. Shops already knew how to make a splat. What they got after 1722 was a wood cheap enough to waste in carving, even enough to pierce, and stable enough that a thin member stayed a thin member through a London winter.
A Chippendale splat in the *Director* (1754; third edition 1762) is a carved, often interlaced, openwork back. The joint at the shoe, the crest rail tenons, the carved knee on a cabriole — these want a fiber that takes a gouge across the grain without crumbling and a chisel along the grain without tearing into a pore line the way oak does. Mahogany’s diffuse-to-semi-ring texture is that fiber. Walnut can do some of it. Oak does it as a thicker, simpler splat, or as a splat you do not pierce.
Seat rails in mahogany can be slighter than oak rails of the same span. The glue block in the front corner is still there; the wood is not magic. Stretchers return when the design asks for them (country cousins, some Gothic plates). The high-style London chair often trusts the joints and the wood.
Dining tables in two or three wide flatsawn leaves, rule-jointed, want the stability FPL still praises. The leaves still move. The rule joint is the period answer: a molded edge that hides a gap as the leaf shrinks. A later factory that glues a breadboard tight across a mahogany top will split it the same as oak.
Carcase work in this hour is often still oak or deal inside. The show wood is mahogany. Open a drawer. The truth is pale.
## Workability and finish
Mahogany planes, carves, and takes a moulding without oak’s trenches. Crotch and curl are the show veneers of the next hour (`mahogany-regency-empire`). Ribbon stripe appears when the grain interlocks and the board is quartered — more famous later in sapele than in all *Swietenia*.
It finishes like a gift: oil, wax, French polish, a film that looks deep. Old oxidized mahogany is brown. Refinishers who sand to pink and then dye fire-engine red are making a 1900s dining-room idea, not a 1760 one.
## What Chippendale’s book does not say
The *Director* is a pattern book. It assumes mahogany for the ambitious plates. It does not assume every provincial chair that now wears the name was made in St Martin’s Lane. Gillow and a hundred unnamed shops made “Chippendale” in the wood they could get. Some of it is walnut. Some of it is oak with a mahogany stain. A lens on an unseen rail ends the argument.
A carved knee on a cabriole is a cross-grain argument. The gouge works downhill on one side of the knee and uphill on the other. Mahogany forgives that more than oak’s pore line and more than maple’s hardness. The knee block — a glued-on piece that thickens the rail-to-leg meeting — is still there on many London chairs. It is a joint, not a carving flourish. Country cousins skip it and keep the rail thicker. The *Director* plate does not show the block. The underside does.
Pierced Gothic and Chinese plates in the third edition (1762) waste more wood than a solid splat. That waste is the duty cut made ordinary. A shop that could not afford to throw half a splat on the floor stayed with walnut or with a simpler back. When you see an openwork back in oak, look at the thickness. The member is usually fatter. The piercing is usually simpler. The fiber is the reason.
Chippendale’s own *Director* plates are not a species catalogue. Plate after plate names the form — a “French chair,” a “Gothic chair,” a “breakfast table” — and leaves the timber to the shop. That silence is useful. The book sold a language of ornament that any timber able to take a gouge could speak. Mahogany won because it spoke that language at less risk than walnut. The plates that show pierced Gothic backs assume a wood that will hold a cusp after the fretsaw has removed half the splat. White oak can do that work if the member stays fat. Cherry can. Pine cannot. The *Director* is a joinery filter disguised as fashion.
Country shops used the same imported boards for slats and stretchers without carving a leaf. Those chairs survive in greater numbers than the gilt pier tables, and they tell you more about how the timber actually entered ordinary rooms.
The Federal American hour is the same genus on a different coast, with yellow-poplar and pine as the servants. The Regency and Empire hour is crotch veneer and a darker, heavier taste. The splat and the statute are the English hinge. The later rooms change the finish, not the fiber.
## Conservation, already latent
Cuban *S. mahagoni* in commercial furniture sizes is a memory. *S. macrophylla* is CITES Appendix II for neotropical populations (in force 15 November 2003). The permit draft (`cites-swietenia-permits`) takes the annotation. A new “Chippendale mahogany dining set” from an unnamed exporter is a labeling problem before it is a style problem. A 1760 chair in a collection is the ethical supply of that look.
## What to look for
A carved splat in the solid, oxidized brown, secondary wood of oak or deal, a shoe that is a separate piece, a crest rail tenon you can feel from the back. On a Victorian “Chippendale”: redder finish, machine-cut piercing, maybe still *Swietenia*. On a 1960s suite: probably *Khaya* or a print. On a new table: the invoice binomial.
Arkansas does not grow *Swietenia*. A shop that wants that carved thinness in a domestic wood is looking at walnut or cherry, and at a splat that will not be as open as the *Director* plate. Name the wood. Do not name the island you did not pay for.
## Sources
Bowett, *The English Mahogany Trade 1700–1793*; “Thomas Ripley…,” *Georgian Group Journal* 7 (1997); Jamaica/Gillow paper; RFS Naval Stores Act notes. Chippendale, *Director*, 1754/1762. Macquoid, *Age of Mahogany* (periodization, not the duty date). USDA FPL imported woods; Kukachka FPL-125. CITES 2003 mahogany release.
See: `mahogany-federal-america`, `mahogany-regency-empire`, `cites-swietenia-permits`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Mahogany in Federal America
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Mahogany in Federal America
Duncan Phyfe’s New York shop, on the street that became Fulton, sold a shield-back chair whose splat is thinner than a Chippendale splat and quieter. The wood is still mahogany. The statute that made Jamaica logs cheap enough to carve in London — the Naval Stores Act of 1721, in force 1722 — is Adam Bowett’s English story (*The English Mahogany Trade 1700–1793*; *Georgian Group Journal*, 1997). Federal America inherited the fiber and the Atlantic lane, not the duty cut. After independence the same *Swietenia* came in under American customs, to shops that already knew yellow-poplar as a servant. The chair is a Hepplewhite plate in a New World carcase.
![Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/trade-lanes.svg)
*Figure 2. Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.*
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## The same genus, a different coast
Bowett killed Macquoid’s 1733 and Cescinsky’s 1748 as the dates mahogany “arrived.” The English furniture trade in the wood is thin before 1700; the 1660 Book of Rates names brazeletto, ebony, fustic, lignum vitae, and not mahogany. After 1722 the customs values jump — Bowett’s RFS notes give £695 in 1723, £3,121 in 1725, £4,060 in 1729 — because duty came off British West Indian timber and Navy ships could carry it freight-free. Thomas Ripley told the Admiralty it would undercut deal and wainscot. Jamaica dominated the early furniture supply. Honduras “bay-wood” grew as a cheaper, often coarser later stream. Twenty to forty percent of the English intake after about 1730 entered through out-ports. Gillow of Lancaster bought Jamaica wood as a provincial firm in a port world.
Figure 2 puts that Atlantic lane beside Baltic oak and Indian Ocean teak. They are parallel clocks. An American Federal chair sits on the Atlantic clock. It does not sit on Macquoid’s London staircase as a late Age of Mahogany leftover. Hepplewhite’s *Guide* (1788) and Sheraton’s *Drawing-Book* (1793) are the pattern books the coastal shops already owned or pirated. The wood in the chair is the wood Bowett tracked through Kingston and the out-ports, now billed in dollars at Philadelphia, New York, Boston, Newport, Charleston, Baltimore, and Salem.
What the early United States charged on that wood is a customs story I will not invent. The published American duty schedules of the 1790s treat West Indian timber; pin the exact line at publication `[CITE NEEDED: the 1789/1790/1794 tariff language on mahogany]`. The point for the shop is simpler. Coastal towns could get *Swietenia*. Inland towns used walnut and cherry because the log was local. A “Federal” high chest in the Ohio valley with no mahogany is not a failed Boston piece. It is a different forest.
Enslaved labor logged and milled on the islands that filled those bills. That belongs in the caption, as it does in the Chippendale hour. A Phyfe chair can be beautiful and still be a receipt.
## Two *Swietenia*, and the numbers that explain a tapered leg
*Swietenia mahagoni* — Cuban, Santo Domingo, West Indian — is the finer, often darker, tighter mahogany of the early trade. Kukachka (FPL-125, 1970) says *S. mahagoni* and *S. humilis* are generally heavier than the big-leaf species and, by his date, used almost entirely within their growth areas because volume was already limited. *S. macrophylla* — Honduran, big-leaf, later “genuine mahogany” — ranges from southern Mexico through Central America into the Amazon. It supplied the major commercial volume by the time FPL wrote the imported-woods chapter.
The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190, 2010) describes American mahogany as pale pink to dark reddish brown, generally straighter than African *Khaya*, easy to dry, dimensionally stable, durable, easy to work, a premier veneer wood. Janka is commonly cited near 800 lbf, specific gravity near 0.45–0.50 (imported-woods chapter / Kukachka FPL-125). Kukachka puts mahogany’s strength in the neighborhood of paper birch and black cherry. Figure 4 places that hardness among the series’ ten anchors. Softer than white oak (about 1,360 lbf, SG 0.68). Kinder than sugar maple. Strong enough, in the right section, for a square-tapered Federal leg that would look stingy in oak and glassy in hard maple.
Federal chairs are often still mahogany in the solid: legs, rails, splat, a shoe. Carcases are another contract. Open a Philadelphia or New York secretary of 1795. The show surfaces are mahogany. The drawer sides, dustboards, and backboards are frequently yellow-poplar — *Liriodendron tulipifera*, FPL-GTR-190 at SG 0.42 and Janka 540 lbf — or, in New England, eastern white pine (about 380 lbf, SG 0.35). Charleston mixed pine and sometimes cypress. Hurst and Prown’s *Southern Furniture 1680–1830* and the Winterthur catalogues make that geography an attribution tool. A “Salem” piece with tulip-streaked poplar sides wants an argument.
## Joinery: the splat thins, then the face becomes a leaf
The Chippendale splat was a carving problem. The Federal splat is a drawing problem. Shield, oval, and urn backs want a fiber that takes a fine piercing and a clean moulding without oak’s pore trenches. Mahogany’s diffuse-to-semi-ring texture is that fiber. Seat rails can be slighter than oak rails of the same span. The glue block in the front corner is still there. Stretchers often disappear on the high-style chair; they return on country cousins and on some painted Baltimore seating.
Inlay is the Federal tell that Chippendale shops used more sparingly. Holly and maple stringing, satinwood panels, ebony lines, bellflowers, eagle and urn paterae — a palette of pale and black against the red-brown ground. Much of that black is ebonized holly or a stained hardwood, not a bar of Gabon *Diospyros*. Look at a chip. The ebony draft in this series is the place for Boulle and piano keys. Here the black is usually a line a millimeter wide.
Veneer arrives in earnest on the larger surfaces. A card table with a book-matched mahogany top over a pine or poplar ground is already a sandwich. Hide glue, a hammer or a caul, the leaf sliced from a figured log that was too precious to waste as a solid slab. Late Federal and early American Empire push that sandwich into crotch. The flame figure of a crotch veneer on a yellow-poplar drawer front is a different contract from a solid Jamaica dining leaf. The poplar moves. The crotch wants to stay a picture. If the glue holds and the ground was dry, the picture lasts. If a later refinisher sands through the leaf, the green or purple tulip streak shows. That chip is the lesson.
A breadboard end glued tight across a solid mahogany top will split it the same as oak. The rule joint on a dining table is still the period answer for leaves that must meet and still move. Federal shops knew this. Some later revival factories forgot.
## Shops and plates
Phyfe is the name the market recites. The shop was larger than one pair of hands, and “Phyfe” on a label is not a species test. Charles-Honoré Lannuier’s New York work, with its French Empire grammar, already belongs to the next hour (`mahogany-regency-empire`). John and Thomas Seymour in Boston, Samuel McIntire’s carving in Salem, the Townsend-Goddard circle’s late Newport work, Philadelphia’s remaining high-chest shops, Baltimore’s painted and inlaid school — each town had a secondary-wood habit and a way of using the import.
Hepplewhite and Sheraton plates assume mahogany for the ambitious seating. They also assume satinwood and painted decoration. American shops used satinwood when they could import *Zanthoxylum flavum*; they used figured maple when they could not. A Connecticut piece with maple inlay is often a satinwood wish. Do not invent a particular Phyfe invoice or a royal commission. The Winterthur and MFA object records are the evidence; the splat and the drawer side are the residue.
Painted fancy chairs — Hitchcock and the factory line that follows — are a maple and beech story with a mahogany stain in the cheaper grades. The stain does not survive a worn arris. A lens on an unseen rail ends the argument.
## Workability and the brown that is not a dye
Mahogany planes and takes a bead without oak’s trenches. Interlock, when it appears, wants a scraper. Crotch and curl are show veneers; ribbon stripe is quieter in *Swietenia* than in later sapele. It finishes like a gift: oil, wax, a spirit varnish, later French polish. Old oxidized Federal mahogany is brown, sometimes with a golden cast in the early pieces. Refinishers who sand to pink and then dye a fire-engine red are making a 1900s dining-room idea, not a 1795 one.
Dust is milder than rosewood’s sensitizing dust. That is not a reason to skip collection. Glue is ordinary if the surface is clean.
## What the next hour does to the same tree
By 1815 the fashion darkens and thickens. Crotch veneer spreads over whole drawer fronts. Pillars, paw feet, gilt bronze, a heavier silhouette — English Regency and French Empire grammar on American poplar grounds. The Regency-Empire draft takes that hour. This one stops at the tapered leg and the stringing line.
By 1900 Cuban *S. mahagoni* in commercial furniture sizes is already a memory (the peak draft in this series). Honduran *S. macrophylla* keeps the name. Then *Khaya* and *Entandrophragma* borrow it.
## Paper, 2003, and a drawer you can open
Neotropical *S. macrophylla* went onto CITES Appendix II (decision 2002, in force 15 November 2003) for logs, sawn wood, veneer, and plywood (CITES press release, 11 November 2003). *S. mahagoni* and *S. humilis* are also listed. Finished furniture may fall outside that annotation; the sawn wood in the factory does not. Brazilian rosewood (*Dalbergia nigra*) is Appendix I — a different genus, a sharper brake — and the rest of *Dalbergia* followed onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15. Those dates belong on the same shop wall as Bowett’s 1722, because a new “Federal mahogany dining set” from an unnamed exporter is a labeling problem before it is a style problem.
The U.S. Lacey Act as amended in 2008, and APHIS Phase VII declarations (1 December 2024), make a binomial on an invoice part of the piece. A 1795 chair in a collection is the ethical supply of that look.
## What to look for
A shield or oval back in the solid, oxidized brown, square-tapered legs, holly or maple stringing, a shoe you can feel. Open a drawer: poplar in the Mid-Atlantic, pine in New England, a mix in the South. On a late piece, crotch veneer over that same pale ground. On a Victorian “Federal”: redder finish, machine-cut inlay, maybe still *Swietenia*. On a 1960s suite: probably *Khaya* or a print. On a new table: the invoice binomial.
Arkansas does not grow *Swietenia*. A shop that wants Federal thinness in a domestic wood is looking at walnut or cherry, and at a splat that will not take the same open piercing. Yellow-poplar is still the right servant for a veneered face. Name the wood. Do not name the island you did not pay for.
## Sources
Bowett, *The English Mahogany Trade 1700–1793*; “Thomas Ripley…,” *Georgian Group Journal* 7 (1997); Jamaica/Gillow paper; RFS Naval Stores Act notes. Hepplewhite, *Guide*, 1788. Sheraton, *Drawing-Book*, 1793. Winterthur furniture catalogues; Hurst and Prown, *Southern Furniture 1680–1830*. USDA FPL-GTR-190; Kukachka FPL-125. CITES 2003 mahogany release; CoP17 *Dalbergia*; Annotation #15. USDA APHIS Lacey Phase VII.
See: `mahogany-chippendale`, `mahogany-regency-empire`, `cites-swietenia-permits`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Mahogany in the Regency and Empire hours
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Mahogany in the Regency and Empire hours
A New York pier table of 1815 wears a crotch-mahogany face so loud the drawer front looks like a folded flame. Behind that leaf, if you chip a corner, the ground is yellow-poplar or pine. Charles-Honoré Lannuier brought Percier and Fontaine’s grammar across the Atlantic; Duncan Phyfe’s later shop learned the same heavier silhouette. English Regency and French Empire did not invent mahogany. They spent the figured log as a picture glued to a cheaper carcase. The Chippendale splat had been a tax story (Bowett’s 1721 Naval Stores Act, in force 1722). This hour is a veneer story.
![Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/trade-lanes.svg)
*Figure 2. Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.*
![Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).](../assets/cites-conservation/furniture-timber-listings.svg)
*Figure 5. Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).*
## Darker, heavier, still the same lane
Adam Bowett’s thesis remains the English backbone. There is little hard evidence of a furniture trade in mahogany before 1700. After the duty came off British West Indian timber, Jamaica wood that had not been worth the freight became a solid carving wood. Ripley told the Admiralty it would undercut deal and wainscot (*Georgian Group Journal*, 1997). Honduras bay-wood later filled volume. Figure 2 keeps that Atlantic lane beside Baltic oak and Indian Ocean teak. By 1800 the lane is older than the style. Cuban and Hispaniola woods still carried quality reputations and Spanish-imperial politics. Commercial sizes of *Swietenia mahagoni* were already tightening. *S. macrophylla* was becoming the volume tree.
Macquoid’s Age of Satinwood (from about 1770) is a pale English hour that overlaps this one and then loses the argument. Thomas Hope’s *Household Furniture and Interior Decoration* (1807) wants mahogany, rosewood, gilt, and a classical archaeology that does not apologize for weight. Percier and Fontaine’s *Recueil de décorations intérieures* (1801) is the French pattern book. English Regency shops — Gillow still among them, now a London and Lancaster house — made the same dark turn. American Empire factories, a decade later, industrialized the crotch.
Do not invent a particular voyage or a price per foot of crotch. The port books, the pattern books, and the surviving grounds are the evidence `[CITE NEEDED: a named Lannuier or Phyfe object record for one crotch pier table]`.
Enslaved labor still sits in the island end of the lane. A gilt-bronze mount does not wash that out.
## What crotch wants from a ground
Crotch is the junction of stem and limb, sliced into leaves that book-match as a plume or a flame. The figure is unstable in the solid: short grain, a tendency to check, a waste of the log if you try to make a drawer front from the fork itself. Veneer is the honest use. Hide glue on a yellow-poplar or deal ground is the historic sandwich. FPL-GTR-190 puts yellow-poplar at SG 0.42 and Janka 540 lbf — light, wide, paint-and-glue friendly, a hardwood that behaves like a well-brought-up softwood. Eastern white pine (about 380 lbf, SG 0.35) does the same job in New England. The mahogany face, if it is Honduran *S. macrophylla*, sits near 800 lbf and SG 0.45–0.50 (FPL imported-woods chapter / Kukachka FPL-125). Kukachka notes that *S. mahagoni* and *S. humilis* run heavier, and that by 1970 those two were used almost entirely at home.
The joinery implication is not a metaphor. A solid Jamaica dining leaf of 1760 moves as one board; the rule joint hides the gap. A crotch face on poplar is two species with two shrinkage rates, tied by a protein glue. If the ground was dry and the leaf was hammered or caulled flat, the picture lasts through a heated apartment better than a wide flatsawn solid of the same figure would. If a later shop glues a breadboard across the sandwich, or belts through the leaf, the contract breaks. The green tulip streak that shows in a chip is *Liriodendron*, not a defect in the mahogany.
Cross-banding at the edges — a ribbon of straight mahogany or rosewood around the crotch — is both a frame and a stress break. French polish or a spirit varnish wants that frame to stay put. A water spill at the edge lifts the band first.
Piano cases in this hour begin to matter. Broadwood in London, then the American makers, wanted a stable box that could wear a figured skin. Mahogany and rosewood both appear. The case is a carcase problem before it is a music problem: a wide surface, a lockboard, a fall that must not twist. Veneer on a softwood or poplar ground is how you get a flame without a checking slab. The Victorian rosewood draft takes the later parlor piano. Here the point is that Empire shops already knew the sandwich.
Boulle work — brass and turtle against ebony, André-Charles Boulle’s Paris technique, revived under the Empire and the Restauration — is a different sandwich on a different ground. It belongs in the ebony draft. Empire mahogany sometimes wears gilt bronze that *looks* like Boulle from across a room. It is not. Look at the inlay line. If the “brass” is a mount screwed on, you have Empire furniture. If the brass is a leaf sawn with the turtle, you have a Paris luxury the mahogany shop is quoting.
## The silhouette
English Regency chairs can still be mahogany in the solid: saber legs, a scrolled tablet, a cane seat, a lightness that Hope’s heavier plates do not always share. French Empire seating is more often a dark show wood with gilt and a rectangular logic. American Empire goes thick: pillars with carved pineapple or acanthus, paw feet, a sofa with a rolled arm that wants a lot of wood or a lot of veneer. The secondary woods tell the town the way they did in the Federal hour. Open the drawer.
Sheraton’s *Cabinet Dictionary* (1803) is late enough to see the turn. The *Drawing-Book* of 1793 still has the tapered Federal leg. Twenty years later the fashionable New York shop is selling a pier table that would look overdressed in a 1790 dining room. Style changed. The genus did not.
Rosewood banding and rosewood chairs appear beside the mahogany. *Dalbergia nigra* is already a show veneer in this hour; the Victorian draft is when the parlor and the piano eat it in quantity. Do not collapse the two hours. A Regency sofa table with rosewood cross-banding on a mahogany skin is a palette, not a substitution.
## Workability when the figure fights the plane
Straight mahogany still planes like a gift. Crotch does not. Short grain around the plume tears. A scraper and a cabinetmaker’s scraper plane are the period tools; a later belt sander is how the leaf gets thin. Interlock in some *Swietenia*, and later in sapele sold as mahogany, wants the same scraper. Kukachka’s warning about tension wood — fuzzy or torn grain in planing — is a shop fact, not a period complaint.
Finish in this hour is darker on purpose. Spirit varnish, oil, then French polish; ormolu mounts that want a brown ground, not a pink one. Old oxidized Empire mahogany can go almost black in the recesses. Refinishers who “bring back the red” are arguing with the hour.
Movement is still modest for the density (FPL’s praise of mahogany’s stability). Wide solids still need to float. The veneered carcase moves less across the face and more at the edges if the ground was flatsawn poplar. Frame-and-panel interiors remain manners for a wide board. The industrial version of that manners is plywood, a century later. The plywood draft in this series is the place for Eames and Aalto. The ancestor is this sandwich.
## Exhaustion, already visible
Kukachka, writing in 1970, treats *S. macrophylla* as the commercial mahogany and the West Indian species as local woods. The exhaustion began earlier. By 1900 Cuban mahogany in commercial furniture sizes is a memory (the peak draft). Empire shops of 1820 were already taking what the islands and the Bay would send. Honduras wood can be coarser; Cuban, when you can still find it on a period piece, is often tighter. A lens and a weight test help. They do not replace a binomial on a new invoice.
African *Khaya* is not this hour. It is the 20th-century name-theft. A “Empire mahogany” suite of 1925 may be *Khaya* with a crotch print. Look at the edge.
French Restauration and Charles X shops kept the dark field and sometimes brought back lighter woods as a relief. English Regency can still surprise you with a cane seat and a saber leg that is mahogany in the solid, a lighter object than the New York pier table. American factory Empire of the 1820s–40s is the hour that floods the inland parlor: pillars turned by the hundred, crotch leaves matched by the dozen, poplar carcases stacked in a drying shed. The secondary wood remains the dating tool. A “New York” Empire bureau with tulip-streaked drawer sides is doing the Mid-Atlantic job. A New England cousin with white-pine interiors is doing the other job. Do not attribute by the flame alone.
Gilt bronze and gilt composition tell on each other. A Lannuier-quality mount has weight and a back that was meant to be seen by a workman. A later factory “ormolu” can be a stamped sheet or a composition that has lost its leaf. That is not a species test. It is a shop test sitting on the same crotch face.
## Figure 5 and the permits
Figure 5 is the later map. Neotropical *S. macrophylla* entered CITES Appendix II in 2003, in force 15 November 2003, typically for logs, sawn wood, veneer, and plywood. *S. mahagoni* and *S. humilis* are listed. Brazilian rosewood (*D. nigra*) is Appendix I. The rest of *Dalbergia* went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15 as later revised so finished musical instruments and small finished products would not freeze the concert hall. An Empire pier table already in the country is usually legal to own. Shipping it across a border is a Management Authority question. A new “crotch mahogany” slab from an unnamed exporter is a permit question before it is a decorating question.
The U.S. Lacey Act as amended in 2008, and APHIS Phase VII (1 December 2024), sit on top. Species+ is the living page.
## What to look for
A flame on a drawer, a poplar or pine interior, pillars, paw feet, gilt that is a mount and not a Boulle leaf, a cross-band that has lifted at a water ring. On an English Regency chair: saber legs, maybe still solid mahogany. On an American Empire sofa: veneer, a lot of it, and a ground you can see in a chip. On a Victorian revival: redder, louder, sometimes still *Swietenia*. On a 1960s “Empire” dining room: probably not.
Arkansas does not grow *Swietenia*. A shop that wants this hour’s picture in a domestic wood is looking at walnut crotch — a real figure, a different color — on the same poplar ground the 1815 shop used. Name the face. Name the ground. The flame is a leaf, not a miracle.
## Sources
Bowett, *The English Mahogany Trade 1700–1793*; Ripley, *Georgian Group Journal* 7 (1997). Hope, *Household Furniture*, 1807. Percier and Fontaine, *Recueil*, 1801. Sheraton, *Cabinet Dictionary*, 1803. USDA FPL-GTR-190; Kukachka FPL-125. CITES 2003 mahogany release; CoP17 *Dalbergia*; Annotation #15. Winterthur / Lannuier literature.
See: `mahogany-federal-america`, `mahogany-chippendale`, `rosewood-victorian`, `plywood-and-core-stock`, `cites-swietenia-permits`.

item.title: Rosewood in the Victorian parlor
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Rosewood in the Victorian parlor
A parlor piano from about 1880 with a Brazilian rosewood case is a legal object in a living room and a paperwork object if you ship it across a border. *Dalbergia nigra* — jacaranda da Bahia — is the dark, fragrant, violet-brown wood of that case, of rococo-revival parlor sets, and of a forest in the Brazilian Atlantic that Warren Dean wrote as a destruction story (*With Broadax and Firebrand*). B. F. Kukachka, writing for the Forest Products Laboratory in 1970 (FPL-125), said something a furniture writer should keep on the bench: amazingly, there are no technical data for this species. Its early acceptance by the makers of classic furniture “mitigated against the need for a thorough academic study.” The piano came first. The Janka number came later, from compilations, not from Kukachka’s table.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
![Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.](../assets/grain-cuts/sawn-orientation.svg)
*Figure 3. Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.*
## What Kukachka could say without a test machine
He could say the range: eastern forests of Bahia to Rio de Janeiro, nowhere abundant after centuries of cutting. Color variable — brown, red, violet, irregularly streaked with black — with local names for the prevailing hue. Texture coarse, commonly overlooked because the color does the talking. Grain generally straight. Heartwood oily or waxy to the hand, odor fragrant and distinctive. Thoroughly air-dry wood “just barely floatable in water,” which is a shop way of saying the specific gravity sits near 1.0. Hardness “exceeds by far any of the native hardwood species used in the furniture and veneer field.” Machines and veneers well; glue if you take the oily-wood precautions. Excellent reputation for durability against fungus and insects, including termites, though furniture is not a termite test. Primary use in 1970: veneer for decorative plywood. Solids for cutlery handles, brush backs, cue butts, fancy turnery. Shortages already bringing in *Machaerium* — caviuna — of similar color and finer texture.
Compiled Janka figures for *D. nigra* are commonly given near 2,790 lbf, with specific gravity in the 0.8–0.95 band (Wood Database, citing the usual FPL-adjacent sources). Mark those as compilations beside Kukachka’s empty table. Figure 4 will not plot a number he refused to invent. Indian rosewood (*D. latifolia*), which Kukachka *did* weigh, averages about 53 pounds per cubic foot; compiled Janka near 2,440 lbf, SG near 0.83. The Victorian parlor used both. The name on a London or New York bill is often just “rosewood.” A lens and a smell in a fresh kerf help. They do not replace a binomial.
Mahogany, for scale, sits near 800 lbf and SG 0.45–0.50 (FPL imported-woods / Kukachka). White oak near 1,360 lbf and 0.68. Rosewood is the hard, oily, fragrant outlier in the parlor, not a darker mahogany.
## How the parlor ate a forest
English Regency and French Empire already used rosewood as a show veneer and as banding on mahogany. The Victorian hour industrializes the appetite. Rococo-revival suites — laminated and carved backs, marble-top tables, étagères, whatnots — wanted a wood that took a high polish and read as luxury under gaslight. John Henry Belter’s New York patent of 1858 (the V&A plywood history flags it) is a moulded-laminate rosewood back: several leaves in a mould, carved after, produced in batches. That is plywood thinking inside a Victorian costume. The plywood draft in this series returns to Belter as a process. Here he is a consumer of *Dalbergia*.
Pianos ate more. Broadwood, Steinway, Chickering, a hundred provincial makers: a case is a large, stable box that must wear a figured skin and take a finish that looks like furniture, not like a crate. Rosewood veneer on a softwood or poplar ground is the standard sandwich. Hide glue, later animal-glue variants, then early synthetics. The fallboard and the lockboard are the places a restorer sees the leaf thickness. Do not belt through it. The finish is part of the object’s legal and market identity. Stripping an Appendix I case to “brighten the rosewood” is how a living-room piano becomes a lesser thing.
Solid rosewood seating exists — small chairs, some sofa frames — but the weight and the cost of the log pushed shops toward veneer. A dining table that is truly solid *D. nigra* in the wide top is heavy in the hand and loud in the paper now. Most “rosewood” tables are leaves on pine or poplar. Open the underside.
Dean’s Atlantic-forest history is the ecological background. Colonial extraction is the supply story. Enslaved and coerced labor sits in parts of that history as it does in mahogany. Do not tell the piano as a European object only. Do not invent a price per log or a particular imperial commission. The forest, the case, and the later appendix are enough.
East Indian *D. latifolia* — Kukachka’s purplish-brown with blackish growth-zone streaks, narrowly interlocked, a central core that often carries shakes — entered the same shops when Bahia wood tightened. The Indian-export draft takes that lane. Victorian London and New York mixed the two without always writing the coast.
## Joinery: an oily leaf on a pale ground
Figure 3 is the cut geometry. Rosewood veneer is usually sliced, not rotary: crown-cut cathedrals or a quieter stripe, book-matched on a fallboard. Rotary would waste the figure and widen the pore. The ground is flatsawn poplar or pine more often than not. Tangential movement in that ground is the large number in FPL-GTR-190, chapter 4. The leaf is thin enough that it follows the ground if the glue holds. If the ground cups, the figure cocks. If you glue a solid rosewood breadboard across a veneered top, you have misunderstood the sandwich.
Carving on Belter-type backs is carving after lamination. The gouge meets end grain and face grain in the same curve. Rosewood takes it because it is hard and fine enough in the right log; it also chips if the glue line is proud. A solid mahogany Chippendale splat is a different fiber problem (Bowett’s cheap Jamaica wood after 1722). Do not use the Chippendale hour as a gloss on a Victorian laminate.
Pore filler is part of the Victorian polish. Kukachka says filling is desirable if you want a very smooth surface on Indian rosewood; Brazilian’s coarse texture wants the same habit. French polish on a filled ground is the high parlor look. Oil alone leaves the pore open and the color quieter. Neither finish is a 1760 mahogany brown. Victorian rosewood is meant to look like stone with a smell.
Dust is a sensitizer. Kukachka’s cocobolo note — dermatitis like ivy, a collecting system essential — is the family warning. *D. nigra* and *D. latifolia* deserve the same hygiene. Some people do not get a second chance at a first exposure `[CITE NEEDED: a named occupational-health note]`.
Glue: wipe the oil, then glue, then clamp longer than your mahogany habit. A scraper often beats a plane.
## Substitutes already in the shop
Walnut can look like a tired rosewood in a dark room. Stained mahogany, ebonized beech, printed grain on later suites. *Machaerium* as Kukachka warned. Bubinga (*Guibourtia*; some species later listed with Annotation #15) as a 20th-century stand-in. The eye is easy to fool under a parlor lamp. Weight, pore, and a fresh-scratch smell help.
Bowett’s mahogany story is the earlier Atlantic luxury. By 1850 mahogany is still in the dining room; rosewood has taken the piano and the show parlor. They are not a relay. They sit in the same house.
The factory multiplied the leaf. A London or New York cabinet shop of 1840 might veneer a single étagère with care. A Grand Rapids or High Wycombe plant of 1880 could put a rosewood photograph — still a real leaf, then later a print — on a carcase that left the line every hour. Marble tops, casters, tufted seats, a whatnot that is more air than wood: the silhouette is Victorian even when the face is a millimeter. Open the back. If the secondary is poplar or pine and the glue blocks are machine-cut, you are in the factory hour. If the secondary is oak and the blocks are hand-shaped, you may be earlier, or you may be a shop that kept older manners.
Rococo-revival carving on a laminated back is not the same as carving on a solid Chippendale splat. Belter’s gouge meets a stack. A slip of the tool can pop a glue line. Repairs that inject hide glue and clamp in a mould are conservation. Repairs that screw a plywood patch behind a broken rose are a different object. Name the patch.
## The law that the 1880 piano did not know
*D. nigra* sits on CITES Appendix I. Commercial trade in wild specimens is effectively shut. The rest of *Dalbergia* went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15 — first with a 10 kg non-commercial shipment exemption, later revised (CoP18, in force 26 November 2019) so finished musical instruments, parts, and accessories are exempt, and small finished products sit under a weight cap on the listed wood. Furniture, especially new furniture in sawn rosewood, is why the genus was listed. A dining table is not a jewelry box. A piano is a musical instrument under the later annotation; verify the current text on Species+ before you ship. This draft is not a permit.
Neotropical *Swietenia macrophylla* entered Appendix II on 15 November 2003. A Victorian house can hold both woods. The papers are not the same.
The U.S. Lacey Act as amended in 2008, and APHIS Phase VII (1 December 2024), sit on top. Antique *Dalbergia* already in the country is usually legal to own. Export is the sharp question.
## What to look for
Smell in a kerf, weight, a violet streak, a veneer line at the lockboard, poplar or pine inside, a Belter-type laminated back that is several leaves, not a solid slab. On an ebonized Victorian suite: often a finish on a paler hardwood, not ebony and not rosewood. On a new “rosewood parlor set” from an unnamed exporter: walk away unless the papers are boringly complete.
Arkansas does not grow *Dalbergia*. The local dark hard woods are walnut and locust. They will not be rosewood. They do not need to be. The series includes this hour so a buyer can enjoy an old piano and not commission a new one from a genus that is now a legal third rail.
## Sources
Kukachka, FPL-125 (1970), *Dalbergia nigra* and *D. latifolia* entries. USDA FPL-GTR-190. Dean, *With Broadax and Firebrand*. V&A plywood history (Belter 1858). CITES App. I *D. nigra*; CoP17 *Dalbergia* App. II, 2 January 2017, Annotation #15 (CoP18 revision). CITES 2003 mahogany release. Bowett on the earlier mahogany lane. USDA APHIS Lacey Phase VII.
See: `rosewood-gothic-revival`, `brazilian-rosewood-midcentury`, `indian-rosewood-exports`, `ebony-inlay-keys`, `cites-dalbergia-2017`.

item.title: Rosewood and the Gothic Revival parlor
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Rosewood and the Gothic Revival parlor
A. W. N. Pugin wanted oak. Church furniture, the Houses of Parliament fittings, the moral argument that a pointed arch should sit in a northern hardwood — that is the English Gothic Revival most people can name. Walk into an American parlor of 1848 and the pointed arch is often rosewood. J. and J. W. Meeks, Alexander Roux, a dozen New York and Philadelphia shops carved quatrefoils and clustered colonnettes in *Dalbergia* veneer on pine or yellow-poplar. The wood is the same Bahia or East Indian rosewood the rococo parlor used. The silhouette is a cathedral quoted in a dark, oily leaf. Oak stayed in the hall and the church. Rosewood took the front room.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
![Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).](../assets/cites-conservation/furniture-timber-listings.svg)
*Figure 5. Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).*
## Two Gothics, one genus
English ecclesiastical Gothic is a riven-and-sawn oak story: Pugin, the Cambridge Camden men, later Scott. American architectural Gothic — Alexander Jackson Davis, Downing’s cottage books — could live in painted pine. The furniture that filled those cottages and the city row houses next door split. Hall chairs and bookcases sometimes followed Pugin into oak. Parlor chairs, étagères, and center tables followed the luxury market into rosewood and mahogany.
The Meeks firm’s labeled Gothic suites (the type associated with houses such as Stanton Hall in Natchez) are the object to keep in your head: pointed-arch chair backs, crockets, a dark polish, a marble top on the table. Roux’s New York shop worked in the same vocabulary and also in the Louis XV revival. A single maker could sell you Gothic on Tuesday and rococo on Thursday. Both might be rosewood. The difference is the piercing, not the tree.
Do not invent a royal commission or a price for a Meeks suite. Museum labels and the surviving secondary woods are the evidence. Winterthur and the Met open-access records are the place to start `[CITE NEEDED: pin a specific Meeks object accession at publication]`.
John Henry Belter’s laminated rosewood (patent 1858) is usually rococo, not Gothic — compound curves, roses, not quatrefoils. The V&A plywood history uses Belter as a moulded-ply milestone. A Gothic Revival chair is more often a joined or doweled frame with applied tracery and a veneered splat. If the back is several leaves in a mould, you may have a Belter-type process wearing pointed ornament. Look at the edge of the back. Laminate shows as layers. A solid splat shows as one thickness.
## The tree does not know it is Gothic
*Dalbergia nigra* is Kukachka’s species without a test table (FPL-125): Bahia to Rio, oily, fragrant, barely floatable when dry, harder than the native furniture woods, used mainly as veneer. Compiled Janka near 2,790 lbf; treat that as a compilation beside his empty column. *D. latifolia*, which he did describe, averages about 53 pounds per cubic foot, purplish-brown with blackish growth-zone streaks, narrowly interlocked, a shake-prone core; compiled Janka near 2,440 lbf, SG near 0.83. Figure 4 places hardness among the series’ anchors. Rosewood is not mahogany (about 800 lbf, SG 0.45–0.50). It is not oak (white oak about 1,360 lbf, SG 0.68). A pointed arch carved in oak is a pore-and-ray problem. A pointed arch veneered in rosewood is a leaf-and-ground problem.
Yellow-poplar grounds (FPL-GTR-190: SG 0.42, Janka 540 lbf) and pine grounds are the servants, as they were for Empire crotch mahogany. Hide glue, a sliced leaf, cross-banding around a Gothic panel that is trying to look like stone tracery. The joinery implication is the same sandwich with a different picture. Crotch mahogany on poplar is a flame. Rosewood Gothic on poplar is a window. Both fail when the glue line lets go at a water ring or when a belt sander meets the leaf.
Applied crockets and colonnettes are often separate turnings or carvings, glued or pinned to the veneered frame. They snap. Repair with the same species is now a permit question if the scrap is imported. Repair with dyed walnut or pear is how shops have always faked a missing crocket. Name the repair.
Mahogany Gothic exists. Bowett’s Jamaica-to-London lane (Naval Stores Act 1721, in force 1722) had already made *Swietenia* the default show wood of the previous century. A Gothic Revival library in mahogany is a real object. The parlor fashion of the 1840s–60s still preferred the darker, oilier *Dalbergia* when the client would pay. They are not substitutes for each other. They are two luxuries in the same revival.
## Why a pointed arch in an oily wood
Fashion, not theology. Downing and the pattern books made Gothic a domestic style: a cottage, a villa, a chair that announced taste. Rosewood announced money. Put them together and you get a chair that quotes a cathedral and smells like a jewelry box when you open a door. Oak would have been the Pugin-correct choice. Oak was also the hall-chair wood, the church-screen wood, the wood that read as old even when the suit was new. Rosewood read as now.
Eastlake, later in the century, pulls the dark parlor back toward oak and ebonized finishes and a flatter, incised ornament. That is a different hour. Do not call every pointed chair Eastlake. Eastlake is a book (1872 in America) and a factory look. Gothic Revival rosewood is earlier and glossier.
English shops made Gothic rosewood too — not only oak. A London chair with clustered columns and a palisander face is not a failed Pugin. It is a parlor object. Continental Gothic Revival has its own oak-and-softwood habits. This draft stays with the rosewood parlor because that is the species hour.
A bookcase with clustered columns and a pointed-arch glazed door is the large object in this vocabulary. The stiles may be solid mahogany or a cheaper hardwood, veneered. The tracery in the glass is often a separate fret, pinned or glued to the sash. Rosewood on the door face, oak or pine in the carcase, a dustboard of poplar: the piece is a map of what the shop would spend. Castellation along a cornice is applied. It snaps in a move. Do not invent a Davis drawing for a particular bookcase unless the object record says so. The geometry is enough.
Southern American houses that bought New York Gothic — Natchez, the river towns, Charleston parlors that could afford the freight — used the same Meeks-and-Roux language in rooms that also held Empire crotch mahogany. The woods sit together. The hours overlap. A house is not a museum label.
## Workability when the ornament is applied
Rosewood dulls tools. Calcareous deposits in some *D. latifolia*, Kukachka notes, blunt edges rapidly. A 25-degree cutting angle helped him get a smooth plane surface on the Indian wood. Gothic piercing in a veneered splat is often fret-sawn through the leaf and the ground together, then filed. If the ground is poplar, the file meets a soft wood under a hard skin. The arris crumbles on the poplar side first. That is why so many Gothic chair backs show pale wounds at the points of the tracery.
Finish is a high polish: filler in the coarse pore, French polish or a spirit varnish, a look like wet stone. Old pieces oxidize toward brown. The violet that catalogues praise is easier to see on a fresh scrape than on a hundred-year film. Do not sand a listed wood to find it.
A side chair in this vocabulary is a light object with a heavy name. The back looks like a window. The seat is often a slip, upholstered, on a frame that is mahogany or a cheaper hardwood with a rosewood face on the show rails. Turn the chair. If the side rails are pale under the seat, you have the sandwich. If the legs are solid rosewood, the chair will surprise you when you lift it. Most parlor Gothic chairs are not that surprise. They are a picture of a cathedral glued to a pine idea of a chair.
Dust collection is not optional. Sensitizing dust is a family trait of *Dalbergia*.
## Figure 5, Appendix I, and the church that is not the problem
Figure 5 is the later map. *D. nigra* is CITES Appendix I. Commercial new trade from the wild is not a furniture plan. The rest of *Dalbergia* went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15 as revised at CoP18 (finished musical instruments exempt; small finished products under a weight cap on the listed wood). A Gothic Revival chair is not a guitar. Sawn wood and veneer for a factory are not a casual import. Neotropical *Swietenia macrophylla* entered Appendix II on 15 November 2003 — relevant if the “Gothic” library is mahogany, not rosewood.
Pugin’s oak is not listed. That is not a moral ranking. It is a genus fact. A new oak Gothic chair can be a specification: *Quercus alba*, United States, quartersawn. A new rosewood Gothic chair is a paperwork object before it is a style object.
Antique pieces already in the country are usually legal to own. Export wants the Management Authority. The U.S. Lacey Act (2008 amendment) and APHIS Phase VII (1 December 2024) sit on top of the appendix.
Dean’s Atlantic-forest account still sits under the Bahia wood. Indian *D. latifolia* has its own colonial extraction story (the export draft). Do not tell the quatrefoil as a New York idea only.
## What to look for
Pointed arches and quatrefoils in a dark, oily face; a veneer line; poplar or pine inside; applied crockets that have snapped and been glued; pale wounds at the fret points. On a Pugin-type church chair: oak, often, and a different moral. On a Belter-type parlor chair: laminate, roses, not Gothic. On an Eastlake factory chair: flatter ornament, often oak or ebonized. On a new “Gothic rosewood” suite: the invoice binomial and the permit, or a walk away.
Arkansas grows oak that will take a pointed arch honestly. It does not grow *Dalbergia*. A shop that wants this hour’s silhouette without the appendix is looking at quartersawn white oak, or at walnut, and at ornament that does not pretend to be Bahia.
## Sources
Kukachka, FPL-125, *D. nigra* and *D. latifolia*. USDA FPL-GTR-190. Pugin’s oak argument (treat as the English ecclesiastical pole). Downing; Meeks / Roux object literature `[CITE NEEDED: specific accession]`. V&A plywood history (Belter, by contrast). Dean, *With Broadax and Firebrand*. Bowett on the mahogany lane that Gothic mahogany still uses. CITES App. I *D. nigra*; *Dalbergia* App. II, 2 January 2017, Annotation #15; *S. macrophylla* App. II, 15 November 2003.
See: `rosewood-victorian`, `brazilian-rosewood-midcentury`, `english-oak-great-furniture`, `cites-dalbergia-2017`.

item.title: Teak in the colonial dockyards
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Teak in the colonial dockyards
HMS *Trincomalee* left the Bombay Dockyard in 1817 as a 46-gun frigate of Malabar teak. The Wadia yard had already sent *Salsette* (1807) and the seventy-four *Minden* (1810) into Admiralty service. Home oak was short; teak did not splinter like English oak under shot, and it did not eat iron the way oak tannin does (Albion, *Forests and Sea Power*; the Bombay experiment after 1802). The same heartwood that framed a hull lined a campaign chest: oily, siliceous, indifferent to a hold. Furniture inherited a dockyard wood. It did not invent one.
![Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/trade-lanes.svg)
*Figure 2. Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.*
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## A ring-porous tree on three clocks
*Tectona grandis* is a ring-porous tree of India, Burma (Myanmar), Thailand, and the old East Indies. The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190, imported-woods chapter) describes the heartwood as yellow-brown to golden brown, aging richer, coarse, usually straight, with excellent dimensional stability and a very high natural durability. Silica in the fiber dulls tools. Workability is moderate for that reason. Density sits on the order of American oak; compiled Janka is commonly given near 1,070 lbf, specific gravity near 0.55, plantation stock sometimes lighter and oil-poor. Figure 4 puts that hardness among the series’ ten anchors. Teak is not the hard wood. It is the oily, stable, outdoor-and-hold wood that a navy and a campaign joiner could both name.
Figure 2 puts the Indian Ocean lane beside Baltic oak and Atlantic mahogany. They are parallel, not a relay race. Macquoid’s London clock never ran this timber. A Bombay keel, a Rangoon export boom, and a Java plantation are a different clock.
Indian shipwrights used Malabar and Canara teak long before the East India Company tried to monopolize it. The Company annexed Malabar, set up a crude forest management on that coast in 1802, and proclaimed a timber monopoly over teak and other specified trees in 1807. The well-organized Malabar merchant trade resisted the monopoly the way it had resisted the pepper monopoly (relinquished 1793). The dockyard still got logs. The forest department became a principal branch of public service because the yard could not live on hope [CITE NEEDED: Mann’s Malabar timber essay is the modern account; pin the archive citation at publication].
## Bombay, then Rangoon and Moulmein
The Napoleonic emergency is the documentary hinge. Oak in the home yards was a known shortage (Albion). Officers had reported favorably on teak-built ships in action. A first teak-constructed ship sailed up the Thames in 1795; the Bombay Marine’s *Cornwallis* impressed the Admiralty enough that they bought her and then asked for a ship of the line and a frigate a year from Bombay. The stock of timber and plank at the Presidency, collected since the 1802 order to build men-of-war, was said to equal three years’ consumption, replenished from Canara and Malabar `[CITE NEEDED: the Admiralty or Bombay yard minute that states the three-year figure]`. Do not invent a price per load. The species, the yard, and the statute-and-contract paper are enough.
Parsi Wadia master builders — Lowjee the founder of the yard, later Jamsetjee Bomanjee and his line — built the Admiralty teak ships. *Trincomalee*’s keel went down in the upper old dock on 25 April 1816, after *Amphitrite* and the Company ship *Buckinghamshire* floated out. She is still afloat as a museum hull. That longevity is the furniture argument in naval clothes: heartwood that does not sulk in salt and weather.
Burma became the later export engine. The 1911 *Encyclopaedia Britannica* teak article, still a useful period snapshot, puts the chief European export on the Burma coast, principally Rangoon and Moulmein. Between 1786 and 1825, 111 European vessels were built at Rangoon, aggregating 35,000 tons, teak the chief timber. Moulmein became British after the first Burmese war (1826); from 1829 to 1841 more than 50,000 loads of teak left, and 68 vessels were built there.
