When the British took the country in 1852, teak was already the chief article of export. The forests that first fed Moulmein sat on the Attaran, a feeder of the Salween; by 1841 more distant forests were coming down-river. Bangkok sent quantities to Europe after 1882. Java exported a little. The furniture trade later inherited those ports as names on a grade: Burma teak, Siam teak, Java teak. A grade is not a permit.
Extraction is a political and military story as well as a forest one. Later sanctions and logging bans belong in a buying note, not in a romance of the deck `[CITE NEEDED: a dated Myanmar export-ban / sanctions instrument at publication]`. Enslaved and conscripted labor sit in other imperial timber records; Burmese teak labor is its own archive. Do not flatten it into a caption about “craft.”
## Campaign knockdown, brass, and a hold
Campaign furniture is a military-administrative style: brass corners, flush handles, a chest that splits into two stacking cases, fittings that let a piece come apart for a march or a ship. Mahogany did a lot of this work in the Atlantic world. Teak did it on the Indian Ocean stations because the wood was already in the dockyard and because it would not sulk in a hold the way an under-dried oak or a soft deal carcase would. The knockdown is the joinery, not the romance. Screws, bolts, hooks, and interlocking battens — not glue as the primary contract — so a clerk or a batman could take the piece down without a bench. Recessed brass keeps the faces from tearing each other in a crate. A secret drawer is a period taste. A flush hinge is a survival habit.
Nicholas Brawer’s survey of British campaign furniture is the modern catalogue habit `[CITE NEEDED: confirm edition and the teak-versus-mahogany split in the plates]`. Morgan & Sanders and later campaign shops sold the form to officers who were already living in a teak climate. Some chests are mahogany with teak slats; some are teak throughout; some are camphor or *Cedrela* cousins sold under a cedar word. A lens on an unseen rail ends the argument. The dockyard wood and the parlor wood share a binomial. They do not share a finish schedule.
Deck work taught the same manners. Teak planks on a weather deck are caulked: oakum driven into the seam with a caulking iron, then paid with pitch or marine glue. The oil in the heartwood and the silica that dulls a plane are the same facts that keep a seam from rotting out as fast as a softwood deck. The furniture chapter that follows (`teak-deck-and-garden`) takes the grey bench and the patio. The yard and the chest that left it are this hour’s objects.
## Java planted; China used; London barely named it
Dutch colonial furniture in Java used teak because the tree was there, and because the Dutch planted it. The plantation story is the later slug (`sustainable-teak-plantations`). The colonial fact is older: a VOC and then a Netherlands-India administration that treated *Tectona* as a state timber, the way Britain treated Malabar and Burma. Chinese shops in Southeast Asia used teak for chests and tables that never saw a Copenhagen oil can. The furniture is older than Danish modern. Danish modern is why most buyers can spell the word.
English fashionable shops in Macquoid’s mahogany and satinwood hours did not make teak their show wood. A London bill of the 1780s that says teak is worth a second look; it may be a dockyard leftover, a curiosity, or a later mis-label `[CITE NEEDED: a named London cabinet-maker’s bill that specifies teak before 1850]`. Provincial and colonial shops are where to look. Anglo-Indian furniture — the caned chairs, the carved Bombay blackwood cousins, the teak tables with turned legs that look a little too thick for Hepplewhite — sits in that provincial-imperial room. Do not call it Chippendale because the splat is pierced.
## At the bench: silica, oil, iron
A plane iron that just finished a cherry job will feel tired after twenty feet of teak. That is the shop tax FPL names. Carbide helps. So does accepting that teak is not mahogany under the iron. Wipe the oil back before glue. Stainless or bronze fasteners if the piece will see weather or a damp hold; teak and cheap steel can still make stains even if the wood is kinder than oak. Sanding dust is an irritant for some people. So is the oil.
Ring-porous brown plus a greasy feel plus a blunted iron is the working ID. Smell is milder than juniper, not the kitchen-spice of eastern redcedar. Weight is oak’s neighbor, not western redcedar’s. A plantation board with wide rings is still *Tectona* if the anatomy agrees; it is not “Burma grade” because the tag says so. Iroko (*Milicia*) is the later African lookalike, sold as “African teak,” not this tree. Afrormosia (*Pericopsis elata*) is a closer visual cousin and already CITES Appendix II. White oak is the domestic outdoor furniture wood of the tyloses story. It does not look like teak.
## What to look for
A campaign chest with brass corners and knockdown screws, a teak smell in a fresh scratch, secondary wood that may be deal or a local tropical. A Bombay or Rangoon ship-carpenter’s box that migrated into a house. A Dutch-Javanese kast in teak, heavy, architectural. A Victorian Anglo-Indian table with turned legs and a coarse pore. On a 1960s sideboard: you have left this chapter. On a crate that says only “teak”: Lacey wants the binomial and the harvest country. *Tectona grandis* is not a CITES appendix species in the rosewood sense; some populations and some export regimes are tightly controlled.
Arkansas does not grow teak. A designer who wants the dockyard manners in a domestic hardwood is looking at white oak, not at a stain. The campaign chest and the Wadia frigate share a species. They do not share a century, a port, or a finish. Name the tree. Then decide whether the job is a hull, a knockdown case, or a wish.
## Sources
Albion, *Forests and Sea Power*. USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (teak / imported woods). Kukachka FPL-125. 1911 *Encyclopaedia Britannica*, “Teak” (Rangoon / Moulmein export snapshot). Mann, Malabar timber trade / EIC monopoly notes `[CITE NEEDED: full citation]`. Wadia / Bombay Dockyard accounts; *Trincomalee* museum history. Campaign-furniture catalogues `[CITE NEEDED]`. CITES (negative: not listed as *Dalbergia* is).
See: `teak-deck-and-garden`, `sustainable-teak-plantations`, `navy-oak-reserves`, `mahogany-chippendale`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Teak on the deck and in the garden
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Teak on the deck and in the garden
A teak weather deck is a joinery problem before it is a luxury. Planks are laid with a seam, oakum is driven into that seam with a caulking iron, and the seam is paid with pitch or a later marine compound. The heartwood’s oil and the silica that dulls a plane are the same facts that keep the seam from rotting out as fast as a softwood deck. Leave the same wood in a garden without a film and it goes silver. Oil is a look, not a duty. The grey bench in the rain is doing what the wood does.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
![Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/trade-lanes.svg)
*Figure 2. Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.*
## The same numbers, a different job
*Tectona grandis* is still the ring-porous tree of the dockyard chapter. The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190) still gives excellent dimensional stability and a very high natural durability. Compiled Janka sits near 1,070 lbf, specific gravity near 0.55 — oak’s neighbor, not maple’s. Figure 4 places that hardness among the series’ ten anchors. Outdoor furniture does not need a higher number. It needs heartwood, a joint that drains, and fasteners that will not stain.
Figure 2 keeps the Indian Ocean lane in view. The garden bench of 1985 and the Bombay frigate of 1817 share a species and a port geography. They do not share a finish, a shop, or a labor system. Plantation teak from Africa and Latin America is a later supply on that same map (FPL already noted plantations). The plantation slug takes the papers. This draft takes the wet face.
Old Burma teak is the folklore grade: tight rings, dark, greasy. Plantation boards can be lighter, paler, wider-ringed, less oily. Both are *Tectona* if the anatomy agrees. Neither is “yacht grade” because a catalogue said so. Sapwood on a garden rail is the cheap cut; it will not last like heart. Look at the end grain. A wide pale band is a specification, not a surprise.
## Caulking, camber, and a bench that holds water
Deck caulking is the period outdoor joint. The plank edges are slightly beveled or left square depending on the yard; the seam is a controlled gap, not a hairline glue line. Oakum — hemp fiber, historically tarred — is driven in layers with a caulking iron and a mallet until the seam is tight. Paying (pitch, later butyl or polysulfide compounds) keeps water from sitting in the fiber. Teak’s stability is why the seam stays a seam through a season of sun and spray. A glued teak “deck” on a yacht interior is a different contract: veneer or thin stock on a stable ground, no oakum, a look. Do not restore one as if it were the other.
Garden furniture borrowed the durability and dropped the caulking. Mortise-and-tenon slats, through-tenons wedged, sometimes knockdown hardware so a steamer chair packs. The failure is almost never the heartwood. It is a joint that traps water against end grain, a steel screw that stains, a flat seat that ponds, a cushion that keeps the slats wet. Design that drains will outlive a finish schedule. Design that holds a puddle will fail in teak as surely as in oak.
Stainless or bronze fasteners outdoors. Teak is kinder to iron than oak is — the tannin story is not teak’s — but cheap steel still makes black halos and rust streaks. Washers that hold water against the face are a small cruelty. Predrill; the wood is hard enough to split a thin slat if you drive blind.
## Indoor honey, outdoor silver
After 1945, Danish and other Scandinavian shops used teak for dining chairs, sideboards, and low tables. Finn Juhl, Arne Vodder, a hundred factories. Indoor teak in the 1950s was oiled to stay honey. That oil can is a maintenance habit, the way a cutting board is a maintenance habit. A thick polyurethane on a 1958 sideboard is a different object. Some of the best Danish work is solid; much is veneer on cheaper cores. The Danish-modern chapter in this series returns to the mix with oak and rosewood. Teak was the tropical member of that triad.
American suburban “teak” of the 1960s includes true *Tectona*, and also print, and also other brown ring-porous woods. A lens on an unseen rail. A 1958 sideboard with an oiled face and a teak smell in a fresh scratch is one object. A 1968 suite with a printed grain that dies at the edge is another. Do not strip the first and paint it without a long thought. The finish and the wood were a pair.
Late-century garden furniture made plantation teak a patio staple. The grey bench is not neglected. It is the outdoor specification. Owners who want the honey color outdoors are choosing oil and a cloth, forever. Owners who want silver are choosing the weather. Both are honest if named. A film finish on a garden table will crack and hold water in the cracks. That is a finish failure, not a species failure.
Steamer chairs and plantation chairs of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries sit between the campaign chest and the patio set. A steamer chair is a knockdown: slats, a sliding footrest, hardware that lets the piece fold for a deck. Some are teak, some are mahogany, some are painted beech pretending. The joint that matters is the pivot and the stop, not a glued carcase. Look at the hinge metal. Look at whether the slats can drain. A 1920s P&O-deck romance in a catalogue is not a named ship; it is a form. Do not invent a liner.
Gluing and finishing may need the oil wiped back. Solvent on the joint faces, then the glue the shop trusts — often epoxy outdoors, hide or PVA indoors if the oil is cut. Silica still dulls edges. Sharp carbide. Collection of dust is not optional in a small shop. A caulking iron does not belong on a furniture seam unless you are actually laying a deck. Paying a garden-table joint with pitch is a confusion of contracts. Leave the furniture joints as joints. Leave the deck seams as seams.
## Lookalikes on the patio
Iroko (*Milicia*) is the African wood sold as “African teak.” Ring-porous, durable, a Janka often cited near 1,260 lbf. It is not *Tectona*. The pore and the color rhyme; the oil and the smell do not quite. Afrormosia (*Pericopsis elata*) is a closer visual cousin and already CITES Appendix II. Cumaru, ipe, and the South American deck woods are harder, heavier, more iron than oil. They make furniture that feels like a deck. Fine if wanted. Robinia (black locust) is a temperate outdoor hardwood, yellow-green when fresh, a true alternative for benches, not a teak clone. White oak is the domestic outdoor furniture wood of the tyloses story. It does not look like teak. It lasts if designed to drain.
Rubberwood (*Hevea*) with a toner is an indoor plantation wood. It is not outdoor teak. A “teak finish” on a big-box chair is a stain. The crate that says only “teak” fails Lacey the same way a crate that says only “mahogany” fails it. The binomial and the harvest country are the specification.
Kitchen worktops in European shops used teak and then iroko for the same oil-and-water story. An oiled teak counter next to a sink will stain and go grey in the wet zone if you let it. That is not a defect. A film-finished teak counter that delaminates at the sink is a finish and a substrate problem. Ask whether the top is solid, a thick laminate, or a veneer on a board that will swell. Outdoor manners indoors still want a drain and a cloth.
*Tectona grandis* is not a CITES appendix species in the rosewood sense. Some populations and some export regimes are tightly controlled, and illegal logging in Southeast Asia is documented `[CITE NEEDED: a named TRAFFIC or national-export note at publication]`. “Burma teak” as a sales name should come with a legal path or be treated as a story. FSC and national export papers matter. The plantation draft takes that paper trail at length.
## What the wet face tells you
At the bench, ring-porous brown plus a greasy feel plus a blunted iron is still the working ID. Outdoors the color goes toward silver-grey; a fresh cut or a sanded patch shows the old gold. Weight is oak’s neighbor. Smell is milder than juniper. A plantation board with wide rings will still weather; it may check more and hold less oil. Standing-dead or poorly stickered stock cups like any ring-porous hardwood. Teak’s stability is excellent, not magic.
On a yacht: look at the seam. Real caulking has a compound line and a thickness of plank. A printed teak floor in a condo has neither. On a garden bench: look at the end grain of the slats, the fastener metal, whether the seat can drain. On a 1950s dining chair: oil, a honey that has gone toward brown, joints that were made for a room. On a 1990s patio set: plantation rings, stainless screws, a price that may or may not match the papers.
Arkansas does not grow teak. A designer who wants the outdoor manners in a domestic hardwood is looking at white oak or cypress, not at a stain. A designer who wants the 1960s interior color is looking at a named *Tectona* with papers, or at walnut, or at an honest iroko. The caulked deck and the grey bench share a species with the campaign chest. They share a wet-face habit. They do not share a century. Name the tree. Then decide whether the job is a seam, a slat, or a wish.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (teak). Kukachka FPL-125. Traditional caulking practice (oakum / paying) `[CITE NEEDED: a named boatbuilding manual if quoting a compound]`. Danish modern surveys (Fiell; museum collections). Iroko / afrormosia notes in the lookalike chapter. CITES (negative for *Tectona*; Appendix II for *Pericopsis elata*). USDA APHIS Lacey binomial rule.
See: `teak-colonial-dockyards`, `sustainable-teak-plantations`, `iroko-teak-lookalikes`, `danish-modern-woods`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Ebony, inlay, and the piano key
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Ebony, inlay, and the piano key
André-Charles Boulle’s cabinets in the Wallace Collection are brass and turtle cut as one picture, the black ground a *Diospyros* that takes a polish like stone. The name *ébéniste* comes from this wood. Most of the job, by the time Riesener was shading a flower in kingwood, was a tropical palette that was not ebony. The black that people mean when they say the word is still a small, heavy, fine-textured heartwood used for lines, keys, and the counterpart to brass — not for dining tables. Kukachka (FPL-125) put African commercial ebony at about 63 pounds per cubic foot and Ceylon *D. ebenum* at about 73. A solid Gabon chest would be a monster of weight. A piano’s sharp keys, when they were wood, were this genus in strips.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
![Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).](../assets/cites-conservation/furniture-timber-listings.svg)
*Figure 5. Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).*
## Several blacks, one trade name
African ebony of commerce, Kukachka writes, is believed to be *Diospyros crassiflora* and *D. piscatoria* — small trees, West Africa, color from patchy to a uniform black, the best jet attributed to *D. crassiflora*. Very fine texture, very hard, about 63 pounds per cubic foot. Seasons rapidly in small sizes, tends to split or distort. Best worked with metal-working equipment. Specialty uses: small parts of musical instruments, carvings, turnery.
East Indian and Ceylon ebonies: *D. melanoxylon*, *D. ebenum*, Andaman *D. marmorata*. Ceylon ebony extremely heavy, fine, even, black, with irregular light-brown streaks less loud than in most East Indian woods; about 73 pounds per cubic foot. The black portions of *D. ebenum* develop long, fine, deep cracks if you try to season large dimensions. Convert small, store under cover. *D. melanoxylon* is the species some older notes say to girdle and stand before felling `[CITE NEEDED: confirm Kukachka’s girdling report against a forest-department source]`. Macassar (*D. celebica*) and Andaman woods are the striped brown-black that Art Deco treated as a modern luxury. Compiled Janka for Gabon-type ebony is commonly given near 3,080 lbf; Ceylon and Macassar compilations sit in the same brutal neighborhood. Figure 4 will not make ebony look like mahogany (about 800 lbf, SG 0.45–0.50). It is off the scatter’s polite cluster.
American persimmon (*D. virginiana*) is the temperate cousin: golf-club heads, shuttles, a pale wood with a dark heart when it has one. It is not a piano-key ebony. Do not sell it as one.
African blackwood is *Dalbergia melanoxylon* — Kukachka’s 70 pounds per cubic foot at 6 percent moisture, a clarinet wood. The genus is rosewood. The color is black. The name fools buyers. Keep the binomials apart.
## Boulle, stringing, and the black that is a finish
Boulle work is a sandwich: brass and turtle (and sometimes pewter) sawn together, laid into or onto an ebony or ebonized ground, the première-partie and contre-partie reversing which material is the field. The Wallace Collection’s notes are the place to see it without a romance. The ground must be stable and black through or black enough that a chip does not flash pear. Some period “ebony” grounds are ebonized pear, maple, or a softwood with a film. That is a historic finish, not a fraud, if named. A lab test is what a customs officer may want. A chip is what a restorer can get.
Federal American inlay used ebony stringing — or a black line that wants to be ebony. Holly and maple are the pale partners; satinwood the yellow; mahogany the field (Bowett’s Atlantic *Swietenia* after 1721/1722, now in New York and Philadelphia shops). A line a millimeter wide does not need a Gabon log. It needs a dense black that will not crumble under the scratch stock. Boxwood is the pale opposite number in many English lines. The boxwood draft in this series is that millimeter. This draft is the black one.
Empire furniture sometimes quotes Boulle with gilt-bronze mounts on crotch mahogany. The mounts are screwed. Boulle is sawn. The Regency-Empire draft makes that distinction. Do not flatten them.
Victorian ebonized suites — Eastlake and the factory cousins — are often beech or a pale hardwood under black varnish. Look at a worn arris. If the brown shows, you have a finish. If the black goes through a dense, fine pore and the piece weighs like a stone fragment, you may have *Diospyros*. Most parlor “ebony” is the finish.
## Piano keys and the piano case
The case and the keys are different contracts. A Victorian parlor piano may wear a Brazilian rosewood case (*D. nigra*, Appendix I) on a pine or poplar ground — the rosewood-Victorian draft. The keys, when they were wood and ivory, were ivory naturals and ebony sharps, or later celluloid and a stained hardwood. Kukachka’s “small parts of musical instruments” is the sharp key, the tailpiece, the frog, the fitting — not the case. The case is a carcase. The key is a strip.
Ivory is its own appendix story. This draft will not invent a date for the plastic takeover of the natural key `[CITE NEEDED: a dated industry shift from ivory/ebony to celluloid and later plastics]`. What a restorer can still say: a sharp that is *Diospyros* is a small, legal-in-place antique part and a paperwork part if you ship a set of raw key blanks. A sharp that is stained maple is a finish. Look at the end grain of a loose key.
The piano case in rosewood or mahogany is veneer on a ground, as crotch mahogany on yellow-poplar was in the Empire hour. Ebony as a case wood is rare and usually a skin or a stringing, not a slab. When Art Deco uses Macassar, it is a sliced face on a cheap core: a cabinet, a clock, a radio, a picture of stripe. The plywood draft is the industrial version of that skin.
Stringed-instrument fittings — tailpieces, frogs, tuning pegs, chinrests — are Kukachka’s “small parts” in another shop. A cello peg is a turning problem in a brittle, fine wood. A piano sharp is a planing problem in a short strip. Neither is a furniture carcase. The cabinet shop that keeps a bar of Gabon for stringing is closer to the ébéniste than to the piano factory. The scratch stock that cuts a one-millimeter groove in a mahogany rail is the Federal tool. The black line glued into that groove is this chapter. If the line is stained holly, say so on the repair ticket.
Antwerp and Paris ebony cabinets of the 17th century — architectural pieces with ripple mouldings, often with painted or pietre-dure panels — are the large objects that seem to contradict the “no dining table” rule. Look again. Much of the black is veneer or a thin solid on a softwood carcase. The weight is still ugly. The show is a skin. Ripple mouldings are a separate small-wood problem, often in ebony or an ebonized fruitwood, cut against a rocking moulding plane or a dedicated engine. Do not invent a particular cabinet’s invoice. The Rijksmuseum and the V&A object records are the place to start.
## Workability: metal tools, chatter, a fine dust
Kukachka is blunt. African ebony: metal-working equipment. East Indian ebonies: extremely hard by hand and machine, considerable dulling, brittle, harsh cut, fine sawdust. Hold the work firmly in the planer or it chatters. A very smooth finish is possible. The cabinet trade used it primarily for inlay. That sentence should govern new design. You are not making a tabletop.
Seasoning cracks in Ceylon black are why furniture-sized boards are a bad idea even before the law. Convert small. Store covered. Do not start with a wide flatsawn plank and hope.
Glue is possible on a clean, fresh surface. Oil is less a teak problem than a finish-contamination problem. Dust collection is hygiene. The sawdust is fine enough to float.
## Figure 5 and the listings
Madagascar *Diospyros* populations have been listed (CoP16 and after) after documented illegal trade. Check Species+; annotations change. African and Asian ebonies sit in a mix of appendix and national-law controls that this draft will not pretend to freeze. Figure 5 is illustrative. Confirm at publication.
Brazilian rosewood (*Dalbergia nigra*) is Appendix I — the piano-case wood, not the key wood. The rest of *Dalbergia* went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15. Neotropical *Swietenia macrophylla* entered Appendix II on 15 November 2003. A single instrument can hold all three papers: rosewood case, mahogany veneer elsewhere, ebony sharps. The owner who ships the piano learns this the hard way.
The U.S. Lacey Act (2008 amendment) and APHIS Phase VII (1 December 2024) sit on top. Antique inlay already in the country is usually legal to own. A bag of new Gabon blanks from an unnamed seller is a different object.
## Substitutes the shop has always used
Ebonized pear, maple, holly, beech. Dyed walnut. Polymer keys. Macassar prints on lauan. The honest sentence is the finish name or the binomial. “Ebony piano” without a look at the keys and the case is two guesses.
Bowett’s mahogany lane taught Europe to spend a tropical hardwood in the solid. Ebony never got that hour at dining-table scale. It stayed a millimeter, a key, a ground for brass. That is not a lesser job. It is the job the density allows.
A restorer replacing a lost Federal stringing line should document the scrap. New Gabon is a permit question. Dyed holly is the old shop answer and the honest one if named. A restorer replacing a set of sharp keys on an 1880 piano is in the instrument trade, not the furniture trade, and should read the current annotation before ordering blanks. The case may be Appendix I rosewood. The keys may be a different paper. Treat them as two objects that happen to share a stand.
## What to look for
A Boulle field that is black through, or a film on pear. A Federal stringing line. A sharp key’s end grain. A Macassar stripe that stops at a ply edge. An ebonized Eastlake chair with brown in the wear. Weight that surprises you in a small box.
Arkansas does not grow furniture ebony. Persimmon grows; it is not a key wood in the Gabon sense. A shop that wants a black line can ebonize holly or maple and say so. The Wallace cabinet is the museum supply of the other look.
## Sources
Kukachka, FPL-125, African and East Indian *Diospyros*; *D. melanoxylon* for the name trap. USDA FPL-GTR-190. Wallace Collection Boulle notes. Roubo, *L’Art du menuisier* (shop context). Bowett on mahogany (the solid-tropical contrast). CITES Madagascar *Diospyros*; App. I *D. nigra*; *Dalbergia* App. II, 2 January 2017, Annotation #15; *S. macrophylla* App. II, 15 November 2003. USDA APHIS Lacey Phase VII.
See: `rosewood-victorian`, `boxwood-inlay`, `cites-ebony-africa`, `mahogany-regency-empire`.

item.title: Birdseye maple and the factory pale
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Birdseye maple and the factory pale
A mill in the Great Lakes belt opens a sugar-maple log and finds a constellation. The leaves go to a veneer dryer, then to a factory that will glue them onto a cheaper ground for a Federal-revival card table, a radio cabinet, a 1940s bedroom suite whose catalogue says “maple” and means a color. The same genus turns a Windsor leg that takes a crisp bead, and it floors a bowling alley because the Janka number is 1,450 lbf and the fiber does not fuzz under feet. Figure is not a species. Factory pale is not a forest.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
![Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.](../assets/grain-cuts/sawn-orientation.svg)
*Figure 3. Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.*
## Hard, soft, and the English “sycamore”
Hard maple is *Acer saccharum* (sugar, rock) and *A. nigrum* (black). The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a) gives sugar maple specific gravity 0.63 and Janka 1,450 lbf at 12 percent moisture — among the hardest of the ordinary American furniture woods, in a class with white oak and above cherry and walnut. Figure 4 places that hardness among the series’ ten anchors. Heartwood is light reddish brown; sapwood is wide and white. Texture is fine and even. Grain is usually straight until it is not.
Soft maple is mostly *A. rubrum* (red) and *A. saccharinum* (silver). Red maple: SG 0.54, Janka 950 lbf — cherry’s neighbor. It machines well and takes paint and stain. It is not a failed hard maple. It is a different ticket. Factory “maple” bedroom suites of the Colonial Revival years were often a red-orange stain on whichever pale hardwood the plant had, soft maple among them. A lens on an unseen rail. End grain: diffuse pores, no oak vessels, no pine resin canals. Weight surprises people who thought pale meant pine.
European furniture “sycamore” is *Acer pseudoplatanus*, a maple. Quartered, it can be pale and ray-flecked. Dyed grey it became harewood for Hepplewhite and Sheraton inlay. American sycamore is *Platanus occidentalis*, a different family. The word is a trap already named in this series. Bigleaf maple (*A. macrophyllum*) on the Pacific coast has its own figured trade. Regional, not a substitute binomial for sugar maple.
## Figure is a cut and a defect, not a tree
Birdseye, curly (fiddleback), quilted, blistered — grain deviations, more common in hard maple, not exclusive to it. A shop pays for figure by the leaf. Catalogues that say “tiger maple” are selling curl. The Federal inlay tradition used the pale sap and the figure as a stand-in for satinwood when satinwood was a ship away. A Connecticut cherry chest with maple inlay is a conversation among species, not a single-wood object. The satinwood draft returns to that wish.
Figure 3 is the cut geometry. Birdseye reads on a flatsawn face as small circular disruptions; it is not a ray flake and not a cathedral. Curl shows as a washboard across the grain, louder on a quartered or rift face when the fiber undulates. Quilt is a rarer topographic figure, more a Pacific and a specialty-log story. A kitchen island in plain hard maple is still hard maple. It is allowed to be boring and hard.
Tear-out on curl is sharp blades and light cuts, a scraper, sometimes a back-bevel. Filling birdseye so it does not pit takes patience and a finish that does not shrink out of the eyes. The surface photographs like water. Veneer factories sliced the best logs because a solid birdseye board wide enough for a table is a trophy and a movement risk. Hide glue on a deal or yellow-poplar ground is the historic sandwich. A plywood ground is the later sandwich. A paper foil on particleboard is a photograph of birdseye. The edge tells you which contract you bought.
## Chairs, Shakers, and a wood that mostly refuses the steam box
Nancy Goyne Evans keeps finding maple in the turned members of American Windsors even when the seat is elm or pine and the bow is oak. That is a job list, not a species patriotism. Hard maple turns a crisp bead and wears like a tool. Chair shops in Philadelphia, New York, and New England bought it by the wagon from the seventeenth century on. It does not steam-bend like ash or beech. The fiber is hard and short-tempered in the box; shops that need a hoop use ash, oak, or hickory. Maple takes the lathe. Beech takes Thonet’s radius. Do not credit maple with the café chair.
Shaker work at Hancock, Sabbathday Lake, and Pleasant Hill uses maple where a piece must stay true: chairs, stands, sometimes peg rails, the understructure of tables (Kassay; Rieman and Burks). The slat-back with a tape seat and a pommel finial is often maple. Tape — cotton or wool, later a synthetic — weaves through holes in the seat rails. The holes want a wood that will not crumble. Maple is that wood. The oval box is the mixed-wood cousin: maple sides, steamed and fingered in a swallow-tail, copper tacks, a pine top and bottom. The maple takes a gentler bend than a Windsor hoop; the fingers and the tacks are the visible fasteners. A box in sapele from a weekend class is a shape. The cherry draft takes the face wood that darkens. This draft keeps the pale members.
Hard maple and nails are a fight. Predrill. Screws too. The wood has no tyloses story and no teak oil story. It does not like weather. Ambrosia streaks — beetle wound response — are a color fashion of the last twenty years, not a separate tree and not an antique grade.
## Factory blonde, gym floors, and the word on the tag
The twentieth century split the name. School furniture and bowling alleys and gym floors kept using hard maple because the Janka number is not a metaphor. Factory catalogues used “maple” as a color. Colonial Revival suites pushed a red-orange toner. Mid-century blonde was often a clear finish on sapwood, sometimes a light toner — the pale dining room next to the teak that got the magazine covers. Blotch in stain is worse on soft maple. Dye and a finish that does not pretend the wood is walnut will treat you better.
The white sapwood yellows in UV. A “white maple” kitchen in a south window will cream. Water-white finishes slow this; they do not repeal it. Thermal darkening is a cherry trick more than a maple one; maple’s drama is figure and stain, not russet.
Biedermeier used maple when birch was not the local tree. French *érable* appears in provincial work. English satinwood-age furniture used harewood as a grey field. None of these are the Great Lakes veneer mill, and all of them are the same genus doing a pale job.
Sugar maple is a managed northern hardwood. FPL still centers commercial lumber in the Middle Atlantic and Great Lakes, about two-thirds of the cut. Climate and sugar-bush economics affect the furniture log. Soft maple is abundant in many eastern stands. Neither is CITES. The fashion for wide live-edge slabs asks a sugar maple for a shape it does not want to give. That is ordinary forestry, not an appendix.
Factory conversion is the other half of birdseye’s life. Rotary and sliced veneer mills paid for the eyes. A leaf a millimeter thick on a yellow-poplar or basswood ground is how a 1920s radio cabinet and a 1940s suite got a constellation they could not have afforded in the solid. The glue line is the tell. Solid birdseye in a drawer front is a small-shop or a high-style choice. Solid birdseye in an eight-foot table is a trophy and a cupping risk; flatsawn figure still moves on the tangential number. Quartersawn curl (fiddleback) is the instrument-maker’s cut: stripe across the width, less width-movement than a flatsawn eye board. Figure 3 is that argument. A mill that sells “figured maple” as a mixed bundle is telling you to specify eyes or curl if you care which photograph you bought.
School desks and gym floors kept the plain hard maple because denting is a use, not a fashion. The factory bedroom used the name because pale hardwood was cheap and stain was cheaper. Those two objects share a binomial and nothing else in the room. A bowling alley is a wear surface. A Colonial Revival headboard is a color. Say which job. Inlay stringing in maple is the cheap pale line the boxwood draft will name as a substitute; it works on a Federal apron if you accept a softer fingernail test. Maple will not take Thonet’s café radius. It will take a gentle oval-box bend. Keep the jobs apart.
## What to look for
End grain first. Diffuse pores. Weight. Figure across the light — eyes, curl, or plain. On a Windsor: a turned leg that takes a bead. On a Shaker chair: tape holes that have not crumbled, a pommel that is crisp, not fat. On a Federal card table: birdseye or curl as a satinwood wish, often veneer. On a 1940s suite: a color called maple that chips to a different wood. On a gym floor: the real thing, dented, still pale.
Arkansas is not Vermont. Hard maple is a northern commercial center; soft maple and scattered hard maple still enter southern shops. A designer specifying maple in the South is often specifying shipped stock. Bradley Brand works that shipped hard maple when a pale, dent-resistant top is the job — the same *Acer saccharum*, not a local sugar bush. Say hard or soft. Say figured or plain. The word alone is fog.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (hard and soft maple; table 5–3a). Evans, *Windsor-Chair Making in America*. Kassay; Rieman and Burks (Shaker). Sheraton / Hepplewhite plates (harewood). Hoadley (figure, blotch, cut).
See: `cherry-shaker`, `satinwood-adam-style`, `yew-medieval-turnery`, `glossary-grain-and-cut`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Cherry in the Shaker room
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Cherry in the Shaker room
Leave a newly planed board of American black cherry in a sunny shop for a month, half of it under a scrap of plywood. Take the scrap off. The exposed wood has gone toward russet. The masked wood is still the color of a peeled stick. Clients call the dark “cherry.” They mean the sunburn. Shaker communities put that wood on the pieces that faced the room: stands, some case fronts, the meetinghouse color that maple would not become. John Kassay’s measured plates and Rieman and Burks’s catalogue are the furniture fact. The theology of simplicity has been written to death.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## The short list
The United Society of Believers furnished rooms the way they furnished theology: a short list, repeated until it became a vocabulary. Maple for the parts that must stay true and take a turning. Cherry for the face that will darken in the window. Pine for the broad, painted or clear boards that do not need to be heroes. Occasional butternut, occasional walnut, a little figured maple. Mount Lebanon, New York — the central ministry — ran a chair industry that sold to “the world.” Hancock, Massachusetts, Sabbathday Lake, Maine, Canterbury, New Hampshire, Enfield, Connecticut, sat in the white-pine and hard-maple forest. Kentucky’s Pleasant Hill sat in a different mix: more walnut, more cherry, more southern secondary woods. The Shakers bought and sold timber. They were not only forest hermits.
*Prunus serotina* is the furniture cherry of North America. The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a) lists black cherry at specific gravity 0.50 and Janka 950 lbf — walnut’s neighbor, softer than hard maple, harder than poplar. Figure 4 places that hardness among the series’ ten anchors. Machining is “very good.” Shrinkage is moderately high, but the wood is “very dimensionally stable after drying.” Cabinetmakers forgive the gum streaks for that clause. Heartwood is light to dark reddish brown with a luster. Sapwood is nearly white, narrow in old trees, wide in second growth. Production, FPL notes, has been centered in the Middle Atlantic States; the range runs from southeastern Canada through the eastern United States.
Hard maple (*Acer saccharum*): SG 0.63, Janka 1,450 lbf. The chair wood. Eastern white pine (*Pinus strobus*): SG about 0.35, Janka about 380 lbf. The cupboard wood. European cherry (*P. avium* — cerisier, Kirsche, gean) is the kitchen and Biedermeier cousin, often a bit paler and pinker in fresh stock. English fashionable shops in the eighteenth century did not make it their mahogany. Neither species is the ornamental flowering cherry of lawns, which is useless as timber.
## Tape, swallow-tails, and thin legs
The Mount Lebanon slat-back with a tape seat and a pommel finial is the commercial object. Chair tape — cotton or wool, later a synthetic — weaves through holes in the seat rails, over and under, a seat you can renew without re-caning. The holes want maple. A 20th-century factory “Shaker” is often a stain and a tape seat on mixed hardwoods: some decent maple, some beech or birch from a hotel-chair plant. Look at the turning. Look at the underside. A pommel that is fat and vague is not a Mount Lebanon pommel. Kassay’s plates are the comparison. Numbers stamped or written under a slat — a #7 rocking chair as the famous size — are commercial marks, not monastery poetry. Communities sold chairs by the dozen.
The oval box is the mixed-wood object that sits beside the Windsor in this series. Maple sides, steamed and fingered in a swallow-tail, copper tacks, a pine top and bottom. The swallow-tail is a finger joint cut so the overlapping ends lock like a bird’s tail; the tacks are the fasteners you can see. The maple takes a gentler steam bend than an ash hoop — a radius the thin side will accept without splitting if the grain is straight and the fingers land on sound wood. A steel nail in place of a copper tack is a different object. A box in all walnut is a different community or a later fancy. Hide glue is the historic adhesive for a lot of the case work. Ask before you soak a joint.
A Hancock-quality cherry stand has thin, exact legs and a top that moved and was allowed to. The historic stands are lighter than the reproduction houses want them. A thick leg is the tell of a factory that insured itself against freight damage. Peg rails are not a decorative row. They are how a chair leaves the floor so the floor can be cleaned. Look at the wear on the peg and at the hole in the chair finial. A cupboard interior is as careful as the face: shelves that fit, a pin that holds, no slush of leftover stain.
Mahogany appears when they made goods for “the world” or when a piece is not as Shaker as the dealer hopes. Heavy Renaissance Revival walnut is not their hour. Tropical inlay is not their hour. The absence is a specification.
## Inland Federal, gum, and the runner’s pale ring
Cherry is also the show wood of a certain American house that was never Shaker: Connecticut, Pennsylvania, western Massachusetts, later Ohio. High-style coastal shops preferred mahogany when they could get it (Bowett’s statute story belongs in the Chippendale draft). Inland shops had cherry. A Lancaster County chest of drawers can be as exact in its inlay as a Philadelphia mahogany piece, with maple and holly instead of satinwood. Hepplewhite sideboards, Pembroke tables, tall clocks with white-pine or poplar works-boxes and cherry hoods — the type fills Winterthur and a hundred town historical societies. The piece is polite. It never saw a Jamaica wharf.
Gum pockets and pitch flecks are handwriting, not rot. A shop that fills every one with color-matched putty is making a different product from a shop that leaves them. Second-growth sapwood is wide. A sap streak on the edge of a contemporary board is ordinary. Cherry and steel make marks if you leave a damp chisel. It is not oak’s tannin black. It is enough to curse. Secondary wood in cherry case pieces is often pine or poplar. A cherry drawer side is a luxury or a small-shop choice.
Blotch is the finishing quarrel, shared with pine and sometimes maple (Hoadley). A washcoat, a dye chosen for evenness, or an oil-varnish that does not shove pigment into the soft stripes: each is a school. The other school waits. Light and oxygen will do more than a pad of Van Dyke brown, and they will do it in the direction the wood already wants to go. UV finishes slow the darkening. A kitchen of even pink is a choice. A buyer who wants the twelve-year color should be told to keep objects off the top for the first seasons or to accept pale rings forever. Two leaves of a table that do not match are often a runner and a window, not two logs. Thermal darkening — heat and light boxes — works, and it can go too far toward brown-black. Tell the client before the box does.
The orange “Shaker finish” of late reproductions is often a toner the historic piece did not wear. Cherry was allowed to darken. Maple was allowed to stay pale. Pine was painted or left, depending on the room. Milk paint, distemper, later industrial paints, clear varnish, oil. Do not distress. The originals wore.
## Factory red and the 1990s dining room
American Colonial Revival factories stamped “cherry” on suites that were gum, birch, or maple under a red finish. Sweetgum (*Liquidambar*) has been a stand-in: interlocked, more movement, a different anatomy under a lens. An unseen edge ends the argument. Late-century trade names — “Oregon cherry” and the rest — need binomials. Orchard trees for fruit are not a timber supply.
The 1990s made a cherry decade in American dining rooms: reddish tables, clear finishes, a reaction to oak kitchens. Those tops are now in their oxidation middle age. South-window pieces and apartment-blind pieces no longer look like the same wood. Reproductions still push a red dye that sits in the grain and does not match the inside of the drawer. Look there.
French provincial armoires in cherry are a tourist sentence that happens to be true. German Biedermeier used cherry beside birch and pear when a warmer pale was wanted. Alpine painted furniture sometimes hides cherry and more often hides pine. Do not trust color. Southern shops used cherry where it grew. It was never the coast’s defining wood the way walnut and heart pine were (Hurst and Prown). It shows up. It does not brand the tidewater.
Black cherry is a commercial U.S. hardwood, not a CITES species. Clear wide stock from a tree that also has mast and wildlife value is ordinary pressure. Black knot and gum are grading issues. *P. avium* in Europe is managed and planted; it can still be stolen from hedgerows. Provenance is a habit. The species is not mahogany’s emergency.
## What to look for
Gum flecks. Fine diffuse pores. A luster under oil. On a Shaker stand: thin legs, a top that was allowed to move, cherry that darkened without a red toner. On a Mount Lebanon chair: maple, tape, a crisp pommel, a number under a slat. On an oval box: swallow-tail fingers, copper tacks, pine lid. On a Federal chest: holly or maple stringing, poplar or pine inside. On a reproduction: thick legs, orange finish, a tape seat on beech.
Arkansas grows cherry in the Ozarks, not in the volumes of Pennsylvania, but the species is the same *P. serotina*. Bradley Brand works that Ozark cherry when the log is there — a Federal wood that never needed a port. The sun will still finish the job after the truck leaves.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (black cherry; table 5–3a). Kassay, *The Book of Shaker Furniture*, 1980. Rieman and Burks, *The Complete Book of Shaker Furniture*, 1993. Hoadley (blotch). Winterthur / Federal furniture literature. Hurst and Prown (southern context).
See: `maple-birdseye-factory`, `satinwood-adam-style`, `ash-sporting-chairs`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Yew on the pole lathe
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Yew on the pole lathe
A medieval turned cup in yew is a small orange object with a cream rim if the turner left the sap. The pole lathe — spring pole, cord, a hook tool — is how a lot of that small work was made: bowls, cups, treen, the occasional fine box, a knob that feels like stone. The English longbow is the famous yew object. The furniture objects are closer to the ground. *Taxus baccata* is a conifer that behaves like a hard, elastic hardwood. Tight rings. No vessels. A shop that only knows oak and elm will miss it.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## Softwood numbers, hardwood manners
Closed grain, no pores. It is a conifer. Hardness in secondary compilations sits high for a “softwood,” around 1,500 lbf Janka `[CITE NEEDED: confirm a primary FPL or equivalent number; FPL-GTR-190 does not treat yew as a commercial furniture lumber in the domestic tables]`. Density is high. Figure 4 will not give you a handbook row for yew among the ten anchors; the wood sits off the commercial scatter and still belongs in the room. Heartwood is orange to russet, sometimes with a purple hint. Sapwood is sharply pale. That two-tone is the furniture look: a Windsor bow with a ribbon of cream sap, a slab stool with a white edge, a turned cup that keeps the sap as a lip.
It planes to a glass surface and tears where the grain swirls around knots — and yew is knots. It turns. It scrapes. It takes a polish that looks like a hard varnish even under oil. Dry yew moves less than its hardness suggests. Knots check. Design for the defects. They are the tree. The foliage and seed (not the red aril) are poisonous to livestock. The wood in a chair is not a poison story for sitters. Old churchyard logs hide metal and grit. Cut slowly.
Do not confuse yew with osage-orange (*Maclura pomifera*), another orange bow wood, American, a ring-porous hardwood. Osage shows up in rustic work and tool handles. Anatomy decides: vessels versus none. Do not confuse it with the hotel “yew” of the 1980s — burl veneer on a cheaper ground, a golden slice that is not a stick chair.
## The lathe before the parlor
Medieval and early modern England used yew for small joined work, for inlay, and for the occasional fine box. Treen — the household woodenware that rarely survives — is the volume that museums under-represent. A turned cup, a salt, a pulley, a needle case: the tree’s small diameter is a specification, not a disappointment. English garden and churchyard yew took a century to make a billet. The turner used what the tree offered. Wide flats do not exist. Anyone selling a “yew” dining top without a glue line is selling a veneer or a different tree.
Italian *tasso* appears in inlay. French and Alpine work used yew in small doses. It was never mahogany. Inlay slips of yew in a walnut or oak ground are the small high-style use: a warm line, not a field. Boxwood is the pale cousin of that line; yew is the orange one. The boxwood draft takes the stringing rebate. This draft keeps the turn and the bend.
Pacific yew (*T. brevifolia*) is a different history — a bow wood, a tool wood, then a taxol-bark story that had nothing to do with chairs. It was never a case-work supply. American furniture rarely shows *T. baccata*. A catalogue “yew” dining table is likely European yew veneer, or a stained impostor. Look at the edge.
## Steam-bend radii, the Windsor hoop, the Welsh arm
Bending is the bowyer’s art and the chairmaker’s. Steam or heat, a form, a restraint. The elasticity that made a war bow makes a Windsor hoop that comes back. English Windsors used yew when the shop could get it; ash did the same bending job more often. Not every Thames-valley or High Wycombe shop had churchyard thinnings and limestone-hill stools in the rack. Vernacular chair books are the right shelf. Chinnery’s oak volume is the wrong one. Cotton, Jenkins, and Dunn on Welsh and country seating are the names restorers reach for `[CITE NEEDED: pin the chair monograph you have on the bench]`.
A Windsor bow in yew wants a clean steam and a form that matches the stick, not a fight against a knot that will open on the outside of the bend. The usable steam-bend radius is kinder than maple’s and tighter than a clumsy oak flatsawn hoop — closer to ash when the grain is straight, worse than ash when a knot sits on the extrados `[CITE NEEDED: a bending-wood table that actually lists Taxus]`. Thickness still governs: a thin long span will snap where a new ash bow would complain first. Standing-dead churchyard wood can be brittle. Tap a dry stick. The good bow-grade rings. Bend with caution.
Welsh stick chairs used yew for arms and occasional sticks when the tree was local. Collectors pay for the color now out of proportion to the farmhouse status the chair had when it was new. That price is a modern taste. The original was a country seat. Ash, elm, and oak did more of the English seating volume. Yew is the minority that photographs well.
Churchyard trees and outdoor gates used the durability of the heart. Local felling rules and sentiment are the real limits. *T. baccata* is not a typical CITES furniture listing. Old trees are cultural monuments. Furniture should come from windthrows and managed cuts, not from a raid on a medieval yard. Pacific yew was pressured by the taxol harvest before synthesis. It was never a furniture supply.
## Two later objects that are not the cup
The main furniture tradition after the medieval turnery is country seating from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries: the yew-wood Windsor, prized now, vernacular then. The late twentieth century made a third object: yew burl veneer on boardroom desks and hotel case goods in Britain, a golden sliced surface that is not a stick chair and not a pole-lathe cup. That veneer can be handsome. It is a different object. Do not restore a 1980s pedestal desk as if it were a Welsh armchair.
Fashion was always a minority taste. Price now is a collector’s taste. The romance of the churchyard tree is real and also a hazard. A 17th-century English table with yew inlay is using the tree correctly: a line or a small panel, not a field. A “yew suite” from a catalogue is using the word.
The pole lathe is worth a paragraph because the furniture word “turnery” is not a factory lathe. A spring pole above, a cord around the work, a hook or a gouge in the rest: the work spins toward the tool on the downstroke and idles back. Green wood turns cleaner. Yew can be turned drier than alder or birch because it is dense and oily enough to take a polish off the tool. Medieval and early modern turners made the cups and the knobs this way; later wheel-lathes and then industrial lathes took the volume. A yew chessman or a Windsor pommel from a nineteenth-century shop may be wheel-lathe work. A museum cup with a hook-tool facet may be earlier. Do not date a piece by the wood alone. Date it by the tool mark if you can see one `[CITE NEEDED: a named treen or lathe monograph — MacGregor, or Cotton on chairs]`.
At the bench the dust is fine. The polish is the historic point; a thick plastic film is a different object. Glue is ordinary hide or PVA on clean, dry heart. Knots want to be accepted or cut out, not filled and forgotten. A finish slows the fade from orange toward brown. Owners who want the two-tone should keep the piece out of a south blast, or accept the fade. Inlay stringing in yew is possible and rare; boxwood did more of that linear job because it is paler and more even. Yew’s inlay credit is a warm slip, not a trellis.
## What to look for
Orange heart, white sap, tiny rings, a turned cup or knob that feels like stone, a bent bow, a Welsh arm, a hotel desk with yew burl veneer. Weight. A polish like stone. On a cheap “yew” suite: the edge. On a southern bench: you are probably looking at an antique or a veneer, not an Arkansas log. The local elastic hardwoods for a bend are hickory and ash. Different color. Same job if the part must come back to shape.
If the invoice says yew and the panel is eighteen inches wide without a glue line, look again. The tree does not offer that board. If the invoice says yew and the end grain shows vessels, you are holding osage or a stained hardwood. If the invoice says yew and the face is a photographic burl on particleboard, you are holding a 1980s hotel. The pole-lathe cup, the Windsor hoop, and the veneered desk can share a showroom wall. They should not share a caption.
English longbow literature is useful for the fiber and dangerous for the furniture caption. A war bow wants a specific sap-and-heart cut — the cream sap in tension, the orange heart in compression. A Windsor bow wants a stick that will take a steam-bend radius without opening a knot. Those are related selections, not the same object. Do not hang a chair on Agincourt. Hang it on High Wycombe or a Welsh kitchen, and on the form the stick actually went around. A turned cup with a cream lip is the medieval object this slug started on. Keep it in the room when the collector only wants the hoop.
## Sources
Hoadley (softwood anatomy). English vernacular chair literature `[CITE NEEDED]`. Bowyer literature for mechanical comparisons. Wood Database compilations for hardness (secondary). Chinnery (limited). V&A / museum treen notes `[CITE NEEDED]`.
See: `ash-sporting-chairs`, `beech-bentwood-thonet`, `boxwood-inlay`, `maple-birdseye-factory`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Satinwood in the Adam room
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Satinwood in the Adam room
Macquoid’s fourth age, from about 1770, is named for a yellow wood that takes a polish like dry silk. A Hepplewhite or Sheraton card table — satinwood veneer, perhaps a harewood border, painted swags on a golden ground — is the object that taught English fashionable rooms to go pale after mahogany’s brown decades. Robert Adam’s interiors wanted classical light. Satinwood did what gilding did, with grain. Hepplewhite’s *Guide* (1788) and Sheraton’s *Drawing-Book* (1793) assume the color. Two trees, not one, carried the name.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
![Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.](../assets/grain-cuts/sawn-orientation.svg)
*Figure 3. Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.*
## *Zanthoxylum* and *Chloroxylon*
West Indian satinwood (*Zanthoxylum flavum*) was the earlier prize, a Caribbean citrus-family wood that was cut until it became a rumor. East Indian satinwood (*Chloroxylon swietenia*), from southern India and Sri Lanka, took the trade in the nineteenth century. They are not the same genus. They both sit in Rutaceae. They are both hard, lustrous, and yellow when the finish is kind. They were used mostly as veneer because the logs were not American-walnut generous.
Eric Meier’s Wood Database comparison (secondary, but careful) notes similar pore sizes and a useful tell: East Indian satinwood often shows ripple marks from storied rays; West Indian does not, and looks slightly freckled. Hardness is in the maple-and-above class `[CITE NEEDED: FPL or Kukachka numbers for both species]`. Figure 4 will not give you a handbook row among the ten anchors; the wood sits with the imported specialists. They work with a brittle, sometimes interlocked grain. They take a polish that is the point of the fashion.
Figure 3 is why the face looks the way it does. A quartered leaf can show the ripple in *Chloroxylon* more clearly. A flatsawn leaf of *Zanthoxylum* reads as a quieter yellow with that freckle. Ribbon and cathedral are not oak’s here; the cut still decides whether you see stripe or a broader wash. Veneer factories sliced for figure and for yield. A whole commode in satinwood veneer is a luxury of the 1780s–1810s. Solid satinwood in wide members is scarce then and scarcer now.
*Chloroxylon swietenia* is IUCN Vulnerable (Asian Regional Workshop, 1998, still widely cited). *Z. flavum* is scarce in commercial sizes. Neither is a kitchen-island wood.
## Stringing, harewood, and a painted swag
Inlay stringing is the linear art of the same pale room. A rebate is cut in the ground — mahogany, satinwood, or a dyed sycamore field — and a slip of boxwood, holly, or satinwood itself is glued in and scraped flush. The line can be a millimeter wide. Boxwood is the hard pale; holly is the Federal white; satinwood stringing is a yellow line in a darker neighbor. Rosewood sat as the dark banding. Harewood — *Acer pseudoplatanus* dyed grey-green — sat as the cool field. The marquetry chapter in this series is the picture-making version of that palette. A trellis of stringing on a Sheraton table is a drawing. Do not sand through a painted Sheraton panel to “find the satinwood.” The paint is the design.
Adam’s interiors — plaster, pale paint, classical ornament — made a room in which a golden card table could look inevitable. The brothers did not invent the wood. They invented a demand for light after the brown mahogany decades. Gillow and a hundred unnamed shops made “Adam” and “Sheraton” in the woods they could get. Some of it is satinwood. Some of it is figured maple. Some of it is painted beech. A lens on an unseen rail.
French taste used lighter woods in the late Louis XVI and Directoire years; satinwood appears, and so do other yellows. American Federal shops used satinwood when they could import it, and figured maple when they could not. A Connecticut piece with maple inlay is often a satinwood wish. That wish is a complete design history. It does not require a Vulnerable log. The maple draft takes the birdseye factory. This draft keeps the imported yellow.
Victorian and Edwardian revivals brought satinwood back in display cabinets and Sheraton-revival desks. Some of that is *Chloroxylon*. Some is a dyed pale hardwood. A 1905 display cabinet may still be East Indian veneer over a deal or oak carcase. A 1930s bedroom in the same yellow is likelier avodiré or a toner. The date on the piece is half the identification. The other half is the ray ripple under a raking light.
## Ports, islands, and the plywood-age crowd
West Indian satinwood came from the same Caribbean basin that sent mahogany, in smaller quantities and for a different fashion. Do not invent a particular packet or a price. The species and the islands are the facts; a named customs line that separates *Zanthoxylum* from *Swietenia* is still a research note `[CITE NEEDED]`. East Indian satinwood rode the later imperial timber trade from southern India and Ceylon (Sri Lanka) into Victorian and Edwardian shops that wanted a Sheraton revival and had exhausted the island prize.
Avodiré (*Turraeanthus*), movingui (*Distemonanthus*), limba, obeche, even yellow birch with a toner — the twentieth century sold “satinwood” as a color. Meier’s “Sorting Out Satinwoods” is the practical key. If the piece is not at least mid-nineteenth-century and of quality, East Indian is the likelier true wood; if it is 1785 and English court-quality, West Indian is the romance and sometimes the fact. Density of the true satinwoods is high relative to that plywood-age crowd.
Check CITES and IUCN at publication; listings move. New satinwood furniture is a specialist and permit question. Antique satinwood is the ethical supply for anyone who is not a museum. Lacey still wants the name on a new import. “Satinwood” is not a binomial.
At the bench the wood is brittle compared with mahogany. Thin old veneer chips. Sun fades the yellow toward a sad maple. Keep a card table out of the blast, or accept the fade. A polish that looks like dry silk is the historic point; a thick plastic film is a different object. Hide glue on a deal or oak ground is the historic sandwich. A paper foil on particleboard is a photograph of yellow.
Stringing repair is a small-shop job that punishes haste. The old slip is often brittle. A new boxwood or holly line must match thickness and color; satinwood stringing yellows differently from holly. Cut the rebate clean, do not undercut the ground veneer, glue, scrape, stop. A filler stripe of pale putty is a confession. Painted decoration on a satinwood ground — swags, husks, a medallion — is a different layer: gesso or a thin paint on the veneer, sometimes with a black ink line. The Adam room wanted that drawing. A restorer who strips to “original wood” has destroyed the object the plate book asked for.
Card tables are the teaching form. Rule-jointed leaves, a hinge that hides, a top that may be satinwood on one face and mahogany or oak on the other. Open it. The underside is the truth: deal, oak, or a later plywood patch. Concertina-action frames exist on better tables; a simple pivot is commoner. The wood of the frame is often not the wood of the face. That is not a fraud. It is how a pale luxury was built on a cheaper carcase, the same contract walnut veneer had used a century earlier.
## Federal maple and the sentence for a designer
American Federal shops solved the pale-room problem with what they had. Figured maple — tiger, birdseye, a quiet curl — did the satinwood job in Connecticut, Massachusetts, and the Mid-Atlantic when the imported leaf was scarce or dear. Holly and a little imported exotic turned up as inlay. The object is still Federal. The wood is not a failed satinwood. It is the continental answer.
Biedermeier shops in the German-speaking lands made a virtue of pale birch, pear, and cherry after the Napoleonic wars. That is another pale-room tradition, not Macquoid’s Age of Satinwood, and it has its own chapter. A designer who likes classical light has more than one tree.
Arkansas has no satinwood tree. The Federal substitute on this continent was always maple. Specify *Acer saccharum*, or an antique *Chloroxylon* piece already in the country, or a named modern yellow — avodiré, maple, a dyed pear — with the name on the invoice. A new “satinwood” kitchen from an unnamed mill is a color. Ask which genus. Then look at the ripple, the freckle, or the missing both.
Painted Adam-style furniture on cheaper woods — beech, birch, pine — is the volume that outsold the satinwood commode. The pale room was a color scheme before it was a timber scheme. Sheraton’s plates assume satinwood for the ambitious pieces; they do not assume every provincial chair that now wears the name was built in a yellow veneer. Gillow bought what the ports sent. A painted fancy chair is not a failed satinwood. It is the seat that had to be sold in quantity, the same sentence the beech draft will use for a different factory. Harewood and satinwood on the same table are a pair, not a substitute. The grey field makes the yellow read. If the harewood has gone brown, the pair is broken and the satinwood looks louder than Sheraton drew it.
## What to look for
Yellow lustre, ripple or freckle, a 1790 card table, painted decoration, harewood beside it, stringing a millimeter wide. A Sheraton-revival cabinet of 1905: maybe *Chloroxylon*. A 1930s “satinwood” bedroom: maybe avodiré. A Connecticut Federal table with curl maple: the wish, completed. On a new yellow veneer: the edge, the binomial, the papers.
## Sources
Macquoid, *Age of Satinwood*. Hepplewhite, *Guide*, 1788. Sheraton, *Drawing-Book*, 1793. Wood Database, “Sorting Out Satinwoods”; *Chloroxylon* / *Zanthoxylum* pages. IUCN *C. swietenia*. Federal furniture literature (maple as substitute). Adam interior literature `[CITE NEEDED: a named monograph if quoting a particular room]`.
See: `maple-birdseye-factory`, `boxwood-inlay`, `mahogany-chippendale`, `cherry-shaker`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Beech, steam, and the No. 14
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Beech, steam, and the No. 14
In 1859 the Gebrüder Thonet put a café chair on the market that was six pieces of steamed beech, ten screws, two nuts, and a cane seat. The V&A’s early example (W.31-2011) is thin and exact; later No. 14s grew thicker. Philadelphia Museum of Art notes the shipping arithmetic: thirty-six dismantled chairs to a crate. Some fifty million are said to have been made by 1930 (V&A texts). The chair is famous. The wood is why the chair exists. *Fagus sylvatica* in Moravian and Austrian forests bent in iron moulds after a steam bath, dried, and packed flat. Oak would not have done this at that price. Walnut would not have grown in those stands. Beech did.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## The wood that takes a radius
European beech and American beech (*F. grandifolia*) are close cousins in the shop. The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190) calls American beech heavy, hard, strong, high in shock resistance, “highly suitable for steam bending.” It shrinks a lot and must be dried with care. It machines smoothly, turns, wears. Color runs from nearly white sap to reddish-brown heart, sometimes without a clear line. Little figure. Uniform texture. Janka about 1,300 lbf, specific gravity about 0.64 at 12 percent moisture — maple-and-oak country. Figure 4 places that hardness among the series’ ten anchors. Greatest lumber production, FPL notes, in the Central and Middle Atlantic States. European beech is the larger furniture story because the factories were there.
Rays on a quartered beech face are a small, even fleck — not oak’s mirrors. The wood looks dull until a finish wakes the pink. It has almost no outdoor durability. A bench left in weather is a short story. It moves. A wide panel is a risk. Frame-and-panel, or laminate, or stay narrow. Dry it thoroughly and let it sit at house humidity before glue-up. It will move after you think you are done. Glue holds. Nails hold if you predrill; the wood is hard.
Steam-bend radii are the industrial secret in plain sight. A straight-grained, defect-free stick, steamed until plastic, pulled around an iron mould, clamped, dried in the mould. Popular accounts of the No. 14 give factory times — steam, moulds, about twenty hours drying around 70 °C `[CITE NEEDED: pin Ostergard or a factory manual for the temperature and hours]`. Thickness governs the tightest radius: shops talk in multiples of thickness, and beech will take a tighter loop than flatsawn oak and a far tighter loop than hard maple, which mostly refuses the box. The No. 14’s back is two loops; the legs are also bends. The usable radius is why the chair can be six pieces instead of a joined walnut carcass. A small shop can bend a chair part. A small shop cannot pretend a flatsawn beech slab will stay flat in a steam-heated room.
Michael Thonet began with laminated veneer bends in Boppard, then moved to solid steam-bent beech and to Koritschan in Moravia. Competitors (Kohn and others) used the same stands. Café chairs from Lisbon to Chicago are beech objects with local stains. Alvar Aalto’s laminates are birch. The idea of a bent seat is cousin to Thonet, not the same mill. The Finnish chapter takes that. What belongs here is the species credit: European beech made the café century possible.
## Before the café, and under the stain
Before the café chair, beech was already in the shop as a toolmaker’s wood: moulding-plane bodies, workbench parts, mallets, anything that must wear smooth and take a precise cut. Medieval and early modern Europe used it for trenchers, bowls, cheap furniture, the insides of things. English shops in the eighteenth century put it under paint — the cheaper Sheraton and Hepplewhite lines, then the fancy-chair factories. It is not Macquoid’s oak and not his mahogany. It is the seat that had to be sold in quantity.
American beech never became a high-style show wood. Floors, tool parts, furniture frames, food-related wood (little taste). Some Windsor shops used it. It was never elm’s equal as a seat in the English sense, nor maple’s equal as a New England turning wood. Thonet is not a maple story. Maple would have turned some parts; it was not the steam-bent price point in Moravian forests.
Beech takes stain too well. Factory “walnut,” “mahogany,” and “cherry” chairs from the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries are often beech underneath. The Thonet red-brown is a finish, not a heartwood, and it is honest because the form is honest. A carved “Renaissance” parlor chair in stained beech is a costume. Chip the finish. The pore is not oak’s. The weight and the even texture remain.
The cane seat in the No. 14 ring is a different contract from a Shaker tape seat. Cane is woven through holes in a steamed beech hoop; tape weaves through maple rails. Both are seats you can renew. A later plywood or pressed-seat No. 14 is a factory revision. Look at the ring. The V&A early example is the thin type; hotel stock grew thicker because freight and abuse punish a slender bend.
The six pieces of an early No. 14 are worth naming because the count is the design. A circular seat ring; a front-leg hoop that is also the front rail; a rear-leg and back-loop assembly (or two loops, depending how you count the continuous bends); stretchers that are themselves bent sticks; cane in the ring. Later catalogues vary the count. The V&A object record is the place to look before you argue with a dealer `[CITE NEEDED: confirm the exact part list on W.31-2011 if you quote it as six]`. Screws through the bends replace the mortise. The radius of the back loops is the dimension that made the chair cheap: one mould, many sticks, no carved splat. Maple would have turned a pommel. It would not have given that loop at that price in those forests.
## Knockdown as industry, not campaign
Thonet’s screws and nuts are a knockdown, but not a campaign knockdown. Campaign fittings — brass corners, flush handles, interlocking chests — are a military-administrative style in mahogany and teak (the dockyard draft). Thonet’s knockdown is a shipping style: thirty-six chairs in a crate, assembled at the café with a screwdriver. The joint is a screwed socket, not a draw-bored mortise. The wood makes it possible because the bend replaced the joint. That is the industrial sentence. A restorer who glues a No. 14’s screwed joints as if they were eighteenth-century chairs has misunderstood the object.
Beech stayed the European chair wood through school seating, dining sets, pale postwar German and Czech factories, kitchen tables in a thousand flats. Some Danish work used it when oak was not the point. American taste called it “cheap imported chair.” That snobbery missed the Thonet achievement and the tool-wood quality. It correctly identified a lot of stained hotel furniture.
Steaming wants straight grain, no defects, adequate time — a bending-wood protocol, not a slab-table fantasy. A flatsawn beech stick with a cathedral on the face will break toward the bark side on a tight radius. Rift or a near-quartered stick is the bending stock. The glossary’s cut diagram is the same argument in a café factory. Beech is not CITES. European forests are managed; mast years and climate affect increment. American beech has beech bark disease in parts of the range `[CITE NEEDED: USFS current map]`. Neither is a rosewood emergency. Both can be exhausted locally if factories want only the large, clear stems.
Tool-wood beech — the plane body, the mallet, the workbench dog — is the other life that never got a café. It wears smooth. It takes a precise cut. It is why a restorer who only knows Thonet still meets *Fagus* in a moulding plane. Food-related wood (little taste) is a third life: bowls, spoons, a butcher’s block in some European shops, though maple took more of that American job. The species is a utility that fashion occasionally noticed. The No. 14 is the notice that stuck.
## What to look for
Even texture, small rays, a pink-brown, stain that chips to pale. On a café chair: the bend, the screw, the cane, a radius that oak would not have given for the money. On an early No. 14: thin members, V&A’s W.31-2011 as the comparison. On a later hotel chair: thicker bends, the same screws. On a “walnut” parlor chair: pale wood under the chip. On a plane body: the right species in the right job.
Arkansas grows little commercial beech. A southern shop meets *F. grandifolia* as a tool wood or a shipped chair part, not as a Moravian forest. The chair most people in modern cities have sat on, without knowing, was this one. Name the tree. Then decide whether the job is a radius, a stain costume, or a wish.
Repairing a broken bend is not a mortise repair. The fiber is already plastic-set in a curve; a scarf in the middle of a loop is a visible confession unless you hide it under a later stain. Better to replace the stick and steam a new one to the old mould, or to a tracing of the surviving mate. Hide glue in a screwed Thonet socket is a misunderstanding. The screw is the joint. Cane replacement is ordinary: soak, weave, peg or glue the ends as the ring requires. Tape is the Shaker seat, not this one. Keep the seats on their woods. A No. 14 that has lost its cane and gained a plywood disc is a factory or a kitchen revision. Name it. Do not call the disc original 1859.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (American beech; table 5–3a). V&A W.31-2011; V&A text on No. 14 production numbers. Philadelphia Museum of Art, Model No. 14. Ostergard, *Bent Wood and Metal Furniture*. Hoadley.
See: `ash-sporting-chairs`, `maple-birdseye-factory`, `teak-colonial-dockyards`, `yew-medieval-turnery`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Ash, the hoop, and the sporting chair
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Ash, the hoop, and the sporting chair
A Windsor bow coming off a form is ash doing the work fashion used to ignore. The piece was in the steam box until the fibers would move. It was pulled around iron or timber, clamped, and left to set. The same long fiber made tennis frames, tool handles, wagon gear, and the white-ash baseball bat until maple and aluminum took shares. Furniture treated ash as a servant until Mission shops and later pale interiors noticed the open grain. Then a beetle from Asia arrived in Michigan in 2002 and the servant’s tree began to die in streets and woodlots across the eastern United States.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## Handle grade and a quiet oak face
White ash (*Fraxinus americana*) sits at specific gravity 0.60 and Janka 1,320 lbf in the *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a) — oak’s neighbor in hardness, a little lighter. Figure 4 places that hardness among the series’ ten anchors. Ring-porous: a bold earlywood pore line, a face like a quieter oak. Heartwood light brown; sapwood wide and nearly white. That pale sap is the restaurant-table ash of the 2010s. Black ash (*F. nigra*) is lighter (basic SG in the 0.45–0.48 range, FPL), a basket-splint and swamp wood, not handle grade.
