European *F. excelsior* is the English and continental chair ash, never abandoned by designers who needed a pale, tough bend.
Ash has no tyloses. You do not build a barrel from it. Durability in the ground is poor. Durability in a stretcher is excellent. Springy long fiber survives rungs that snap in a short-fiber species. Chair shops and bat factories used to buy from the same grade stories. Tap a board. Handle-grade rings. Kiln-dried stock from standing-dead trees can be brittle. Bend with caution.
Ash planes well, with pore-edge tear if you rush. Dark stain hits the earlywood first and makes a striped, oak-revival face. Clear finish on pale sapwood is the later taste: Scandinavian-adjacent interiors, the “white oak” look for people who wanted more bounce in the grain. Open pores want filler if you want glass. Most shops now leave them. Rays are finer than oak’s. The flake will not flash. Red oak’s open pores resemble ash; quartered red oak still shows an oak ray if you look. The tyloses test still separates white oak from this tree.
## Steam-bend radii: the hoop, not the café loop
Evans’s American Windsor research and the English vernacular literature agree on the job: bend and toughness. English country chairs — ash and elm in the Midlands and the Thames valley — are older than Macquoid’s parlor ages. High-style eighteenth-century London did not make ash its mahogany. Painted Hepplewhite-style chairs sometimes used beech or birch; ash shows up in the cheaper painted seat. Provincial work is where to look. A continuous-arm bow in ash is the American sentence. Oak will bow too; quartersawn oak was used; hickory will bow and come back like a tool. Maple mostly refuses the box. Beech takes Thonet’s tight café radius in Moravian volume. Ash takes the Windsor hoop and the sporting frame.
Steam-bend radius still follows thickness and grain. A straight-grained ash bow, steamed and pulled around a form, will take the hoop radii High Wycombe and New England shops needed — tighter than a clumsy flatsawn oak, not as tight as the smallest Thonet beech loops on a café back `[CITE NEEDED: a bending-wood table that lists Fraxinus next to Fagus]`. A knot on the outside of the bend will open. A standing-dead urban log after the beetle may snap where a green handle-grade stick would complain first. The sporting-goods shop knew this before the furniture shop wrote it down. Tennis frames, hockey sticks, the bat: the same selection. A chair back that must flex and return is that selection in a parlor.
Mission and Arts and Crafts shops used ash when oak was dear or when a paler open grain was wanted. Some American factory “oak” of the golden-oak years is ash under a stain. A lens on the end grain. Mid-century bent-plywood ash faces and pale dining furniture were a fashion return, not a new species. European designers never left *F. excelsior* for chairs.
The sporting chair is not only a metaphor. Club chairs and porch rockers in ash, gymnasium seating, the pale restaurant chair of the 2010s, the tennis-club bench: shops specified ash because it flexes and shows a grain that reads as honest. A tennis frame of laminated ash, before graphite, is the same selection as a Windsor bow — long fiber, a radius, a return. Baseball bats were white ash until maple (the hard, dense *Acer saccharum* of the birdseye draft) and aluminum took shares. The bat factories and the furniture shops bought from the same grade stories. That is a purchasing fact, not a romance of sport.
Shaker tape seats are usually maple rails, not ash; the oval-box swallow-tail is maple. Ash’s joinery credit is the hoop and the stretcher, not the tape hole. Campaign knockdown fittings are a teak and mahogany habit. Ash knockdown is a Windsor you can ship in parts, or a later factory chair with screws. Do not confuse the contracts. A through-tenon on a Mission ash arm, pinned, is the visible joint that style wanted. A steam-bent continuous arm is the joint the fiber wanted. Both are ash chairs. They are not the same chair.
## 2002, and the other thinning
Emerald ash borer (*Agrilus planipennis*) was identified in the Detroit area in 2002 (USDA / APHIS and Forest Service timelines). It has since killed ash across a huge part of the species’ North American range. The furniture implication is not that ash has left the earth. It is uneven salvage, a question over future clear wide stock, and a warning to designers who treated ash as infinite pale oak. Urban and woodland salvage has flooded some markets with dead standing timber of uneven quality. Metal in street trees ruins saws. Ask how long the tree stood dead, and whether anyone ran a detector.
Europe has its own ash disaster: *Hymenoscyphus fraxineus*, ash dieback, a different organism, a similar thinning of *F. excelsior* (noted as a parallel introduced-pathogen story in the chestnut-blight review literature). English chair woods are not what they were. Use what is already down. Dry it. Do not sell stained poplar as ash. Planting and breeding programs exist. They are not a catalogue grade yet.
*Fraxinus* species are not CITES furniture woods in the mahogany sense. The conservation issue is pest and disease. Street-tree furniture is a reasonable use if the wood is identified and dried. A pale ash table from domestic hardwood is still one of the more readable American buys: no appendix, anatomy you can see, a history in chairs that does not need a tropical port. The beetle makes that sentence sadder than it was in 1999. It does not make it false.
Salvage drying is the shop problem the extension bulletins underplay. Standing-dead ash can be dry on the outside and wet at the core, or the reverse, or checked so a steam bend is a gamble. Sticker it. Weigh it. Bend a sample. A board that rings like handle grade may still have a hidden shake. Urban nails and fences are the other tax. A detector pass is cheaper than a saw. The furniture that comes out of that pile can be honest and beautiful. It cannot be specified as if the 1999 forest still stood.
High Wycombe’s chair woods were a shop list, not a patriotism: ash for bows, beech for turned members in some lines, elm for seats, occasionally yew when the stick was pretty. Evans’s American list is maple for turnings, oak or ash for bows, elm or pine for seats. The sporting-goods list is ash until the material changes. Three lists, one genus in the bending job. A designer who specifies “ash chair” without saying hoop, splat, or restaurant slab has specified a color. Say the part. Then say whether the log was living or standing dead, and how it was dried. The Janka number will not save a brittle bend.
Through-tenons and pinned stretchers in Mission ash want the spring and the open pore. A tight glue-only stretcher in a short-fiber species snaps; ash complains first and often holds. Predrill for pins. The earlywood will take stain in stripes if you darken the piece — the golden-oak costume. A clear finish on sapwood will yellow a little, like maple sap, less dramatically than cherry. That pale restaurant table of 2014 is now in its cream middle age. Leave it, or accept a refinish that will not stay white. A steam-bent arm that was forced past its radius will show a raised grain on the extrados; that is the fiber talking, not a finish fault.
## What to look for
Ring-porous, no big oak rays, spring in a thin member, a bend without a break. On a Windsor: the bow. On a 1900 “oak” rocker: maybe ash. On a 2010s table: sapwood that will yellow a little. On a tennis frame or a bat: handle grade, the same tree. On a new wide slab: the standing-dead question. On a stained factory chair: the end grain, not the catalogue word.
Arkansas is ash country in the same way it is oak country — mixed hardwood stands, white ash in the better soils. A shop that works it now is working a wood whose living future is being argued in extension bulletins. The boards already in stick are still boards. The hoop, the stretcher, and the sporting frame share a fiber. They do not share a century. Name the tree. Then decide whether the job is a radius, a pale top, or a salvage.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (white and black ash; table 5–3a). USDA / NISIC and APHIS on emerald ash borer, 2002. European ash dieback: Gross et al. cited in *Cryphonectria* reviews. Evans, *Windsor-Chair Making in America*. Hoadley.
See: `beech-bentwood-thonet`, `yew-medieval-turnery`, `maple-birdseye-factory`, `cherry-shaker`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Cedar linings and the moth chest
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Cedar linings and the moth chest
Open a late-nineteenth-century Pennsylvania or Shenandoah Valley chest in January and the first fact is smell. Eastern redcedar heartwood carries a kitchen-spice note shops still sell as moth insurance. “Cedar” on a furniture label is a family reunion that invited strangers. The Pennsylvania moth chest is usually *Juniperus virginiana*, a juniper with purple heartwood. A Spanish colonial chest or a cigar-box lining may be *Cedrela odorata*, Spanish cedar, a Meliaceae cousin of mahogany. A Pacific blanket chest may be western redcedar, *Thuja plicata*, a true thuja, light, durable, not a parlor show wood. Three genera. One English word. Keep them in separate drawers.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## Eastern redcedar: the lining wood
The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a) lists eastern redcedar around specific gravity 0.47 and Janka 900 lbf at 12 percent moisture — harder than you think for a “cedar,” cherry’s neighborhood, not pine’s. Figure 4 places that hardness among the series’ ten anchors. Heartwood is dull red to purple-red; sapwood is cream and sharp. That hardness is why a lid can take a sitting child and why a knot, left proud, will print a shirt.
Whether the volatiles still deter moths in a forty-year-old chest with a worn surface is a question shops over-claim `[CITE NEEDED: a current entomology note]`. Fresh heartwood is the traditional belief. A film finish inside a chest is a decision against that habit. Owners who want the smell leave the interior unfinished. Owners who want a coffee-table top from a recycled chest should accept brown: the purple fades in sun.
The wood is knotty. Clear grades are small. It is used for chests, closet lining, small boxes, pencils (the pencil trade also used incense-cedar, *Calocedrus decurrens*). It works easily, takes a polish, and will stain a damp shirt if the finish is thin. The shirt test is crude and useful: a damp cotton rag rubbed on unfinished juniper heart will often pick up color. Hoadley’s anatomy pages will show you a juniper, not a mahogany: no vessels, a distinct heart, a smell you can still get off a fresh shaving.
American furniture: the cedar chest as a nineteenth- and twentieth-century factory object (Lane and others, Altavista, Virginia, and the catalogues that followed) is a cultural form — dowry, storage, a smell. Earlier, small southern and Mid-Atlantic boxes. Not a Chippendale wood. Chippendale never asked for it. A joiner making a small box in 1840 did. Closet lining nailed over pine studs is the same genus in a cheaper contract: aromatic slats, often knotty, a smell that fades.
Knots are not defects in this wood; they are the tree. Eastern redcedar on glades and old fields is often limby. Clear cuttings are short. A shop that wants a clean lid glue-up is selecting, not milling a forest sawlog. Shrinkage numbers in the handbook are modest for a wood of its density; the practical movement problem is not a table top — it is a lid that was flatsawn through a knot and then hung over a heat register `[CITE NEEDED: the exact radial/tangential pair from FPL table 4–3 or 5–3 if you quote them]`.
## *Cedrela*: the mahogany cousin in the lining
Kukachka’s imported-woods paper (FPL-125) and the *Wood Handbook*’s imported chapter treat *Cedrela odorata* as a light, fragrant utility hardwood, not as a structural oak. Compiled Janka figures sit well below Honduran mahogany’s commonly cited 800 lbf; specific gravity is often given in the high 0.3s `[CITE NEEDED: the exact FPL or Kukachka row for C. odorata]`. It machines like a mild *Swietenia*. Watch the softness on arrises. The fragrance is a selling point and a finishing complication; some film finishes trap it, some owners want it. It is not teak-durable in every grade. Interior work is the honest job: humidor linings, cigar boxes, drawer bottoms and sides in tropical and colonial furniture, the secondary wood that smells when you open the piece.
Colonial Spanish and Portuguese furniture in the Caribbean and Brazil used *Cedrela* and related woods because they grew in the same empires as mahogany. English fashionable shops used it less as a show face. When it appears in a London or Philadelphia piece it is often a drawer lining, a cigar cabinet, or a later repair. Ports that handled it sat on the same sugar-and-log routes Bowett mapped for *Swietenia*. Do not invent a particular ship. The customs category is the evidence, and a named port-book line that separates *Cedrela* from mahogany is still a research note `[CITE NEEDED]`.
*Cedrela* listings have moved. Populations have sat on Appendix III and have been the subject of later uplisting proposals. Species+ at publication is the living page. A Missouri redcedar mill and a furniture importer of tropical *Cedrela* do not share a legal file. Lacey wants the binomial. “Cedar” is not enough.
At the bench, *Cedrela* versus *Swietenia* is smell, softness, and a slightly more open, cedar-family fragrance rather than the flatter mahogany odor. A humidor that smells right and a dining table sold as “Spanish cedar” are not the same specification. Treat *Cedrela* as a secondary mahogany. Sharp tools, modest feed, a finish chosen for the job (oil if you want smell; a film if you want a box that wipes clean). Watch end-grain checking on thin box sides. The wood will take a stain that makes it look more like *Swietenia* than it is. Refuse that trick on a piece you will later have to name.
## *Thuja* and the other “cedars”
Western redcedar (*Thuja plicata*): specific gravity about 0.32, Janka about 350 lbf — a true light, durable, outdoor and shingle wood. Furniture use is porch, garden, the occasional chest, contemporary outdoor benches. The odor is different from juniper. The hardness is not a table-top hardness unless you like dents. Heartwood durability is a tropolone story in the wood-science literature — thujaplicins and related extractives that discourage fungi `[CITE NEEDED: the FPL durability class row and a named extractives paper]`. That chemistry is why a shingle lasts and why a garden bench can be left unfinished to go silver. It is not a reason to build a dining table and then be surprised by dents. Fasteners should be stainless or bronze if the piece lives in weather. End grain drinks finish; the flats can look dry a week later. That is the wood, not a failed product.
Old-growth *Thuja* on the British Columbia and Washington coasts is a conservation argument with its own literature. Second-growth and certified stock exist. A crate that says only “cedar” on an import invoice fails Lacey the same way a crate that says only “mahogany” fails it.
White cedar (*Thuja occidentalis*) is canoe-and-fence in the Northeast, almost no furniture. Port-Orford-cedar (*Chamaecyparis lawsoniana*) is a Pacific specialty, a Japanese-export wood, a boat wood, a mill rarity after root disease cut the commercial forest `[CITE NEEDED: a dated note on Phytophthora lateralis and the Port-Orford trade]`. Yellow-cedar (*Callitropsis nootkatensis*) is another Pacific specialty. Incense-cedar belongs in the pencil trade more than in the furniture rack. None of these should be sold as the Pennsylvania moth chest. A shop that lumps them on a sales tag is selling a smell.
## Linings, lids, and the joints that belong
A cedar lining is a secondary-wood contract. Thin slats or a veneer of juniper or *Cedrela* are nailed, glued, or slipped into a pine, poplar, or mahogany carcase. The lining is not structural. The carcase is. Tongue-and-groove aromatic slats, often run vertically in a closet or horizontally in a chest, are the factory lining joint: they can shrink and still cover. A flush-fitted lining board that was glued tight across a wide pine lid will split or buckle. Leave a gap. The smell does not require a glue-up. Do not restore a Lane chest as if the aromatic interior were the show face; the factory already decided which side faced the room. Campaign knockdown fittings — brass corners, split chests — turn up on travel trunks that may be lined with *Cedrela* or camphor cousins; they are not a juniper habit. Deck caulking is a teak habit. Do not caulk a moth chest.
Humidor work is *Cedrela*’s specialist shop. Spanish cedar linings in a mahogany or walnut box, sometimes a whole *Cedrela* box, a lid that seals, a gauge. The wood’s job is humidity buffer and smell. A film finish on the inside fights both. Oil or nothing on the lining; a finish on the show face. Cigar factories in Cuba and elsewhere kept the binomial for that reason, not for a parlor fashion `[CITE NEEDED: a named cigar-industry wood note]`. A dining table sold as Spanish cedar is using the lining word for a show-wood job. Ask why.
Juniper: glue is ordinary hide or PVA on clean, dry heart; knots want to be accepted or cut out, not filled and forgotten. Dust and splinters irritate some people. *Cedrela*: watch the softness. *Thuja*: design that holds water against end grain will fail. Do not put a western redcedar outdoor-bench finish on a juniper linen chest. Different jobs.
Eastern redcedar is a pasture invader in parts of the Midwest and a timber tree in others — not scarce. Spanish cedar is a tropical hardwood with a genuine harvest and permit story. Western redcedar old-growth is a Pacific conservation fight. The word “cedar” on an import invoice is not enough.
## What to look for
Smell, purple versus mahogany-tan versus chocolate-weathered grey. Knots in juniper. A cigar box. A Lane chest. A porch bench that is too light to be oak. A “cedar” dining table: ask which genus, then sit down. Arkansas grows *Juniperus virginiana* on glades and old fields. A chest from that wood is a local object. It is not Spanish cedar and does not need to be. The moth chest, the Havana box, and the porch bench can share a showroom wall. They should not share a species line.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (eastern redcedar; western redcedar; imported *Cedrela* notes). Kukachka FPL-125. CITES Species+ (*Cedrela*). Hoadley. Cigar and humidor trade practice. Lane factory history `[CITE NEEDED]`.
See: `boxwood-inlay`, `teak-colonial-dockyards`, `mahogany-chippendale`, `cherry-shaker`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Boxwood stringing and the pale line
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Boxwood stringing and the pale line
A boxwood rule does not wear out in a hurry. Folding rules from the nineteenth-century tool trades — boxwood with brass joints — outlived the men who carried them in an apron. Thomas Bewick made end-grain box the ordinary wood-engraving block; the press then made it industrial. Furniture uses *Buxus sempervirens* the way a jeweler uses gold: stringing, banding, knobs, chessmen, the pale line in a dark walnut veneer. Nobody makes a press cupboard of box. The tree does not make the board. The line is the job.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## A shrub-tree, not a timber
*Buxus sempervirens* is a shrub-tree of tiny rings. Specific gravity can exceed 0.9. Secondary hardness tables put Janka near or above 2,800 lbf `[CITE NEEDED: a primary mechanical test; FPL-GTR-190 does not table European box as a commercial American lumber]`. Figure 4 will not give you a handbook row among the ten anchors; the wood sits off the commercial scatter and still draws the furniture. Pale yellow, closed, almost no visible pore on the face, a silky end grain. Diffuse-porous, so dense some pieces sink. Wide flats do not exist. Anyone selling a “boxwood” table top is selling a veneer or a different tree.
European box from the Mediterranean and the Caucasus, English garden box that took a century to make a billet, later East London “box” that was often *Buxus* from the Black Sea trade. African box (*B. macowanii*) and other hard pale woods filled the engraving trade when Turkish and European box ran short `[CITE NEEDED: 19th-c. engraving-trade supply notes]`. It turns like ivory’s cousin. Files, scrapers, a polish with its own dust. Hand planes can do small faces if the iron is sharp; the wood is abrasive in a fine way. It moves less than its density might scare you into thinking, in small sections. In a humid swing, a wide glue-up of box would still be a mistake. There are no wide glue-ups. There is no stock. Finish is often wax or oil or nothing. The wood is already a finish.
Do not confuse boxwood with “box elder” (*Acer negundo*), a soft maple with red stain streaks. The names share a syllable and nothing else. Holly (*Ilex*) is the other Federal inlay white; it is not as hard. Maple stringing is the cheap pale line. Box is the line that survives a fingernail.
## Stringing: the rebate, the slip, the scrape
Inlay stringing is the furniture joint this slug is for. A rebate — a shallow groove — is cut in the ground, following a line the designer drew. A slip of boxwood is planed thin, sometimes as little as a millimeter in section, glued into the rebate, and scraped flush. Hide glue is the historic adhesive. The ground may be walnut, mahogany, ebony, or a dyed harewood field. The line is a highlight the way a drawing uses a white stroke. William-and-Mary and later walnut furniture uses box lines that way. French ébénistes used it with ebony and brass. Roubo and the Wallace Collection marquetry notes put pale *Buxus* in the same kit as dyed greens and the dark woods. A seventeenth-century English table with box inlay is using the tree correctly: a line, not a field.
Sheraton and Hepplewhite plates assume stringing as part of the pale classical room. Satinwood can be the field; box or holly can be the line; rosewood the dark neighbor. Adam interiors wanted that drawing. A Baltimore Federal table with holly stringing is the continental cousin — often holly because box was an imported specialist and holly grew. The satinwood draft takes the yellow field. This draft keeps the pale hard line.
Parquetry and pictorial marquetry multiply the same idea: a saw, a knife, a bundle of dyed and natural veneers, hot sand for a shadow. The pale piece in a flower or a trellis is often box or holly. When the wood-engraving trade collapsed, the furniture inlay trade did not take up the slack. It had already moved to other whites. Fashion: always a minor wood by volume, a major wood by eye.
A wood-engraving block is cut on the end grain so the tool meets a field of tiny rings, not a long fiber. Bewick’s school and the later London trade depended on that cut. Furniture stringing is the long-grain cousin. The same density that held a thousand impressions on a press holds a fingernail on a drawer front. Chessmen, rule joints, turned knobs and finials, musical-instrument fittings (a recorder beak, a guitar bridge pin), textile printing blocks — boxwood’s main life was not seating. Keep the objects in scale.
Banding is stringing’s wider cousin: a ribbon of box, sometimes with a dark neighbor, set into a broader rebate. Parquetry floors and table tops used the pale hard wood for the light square. A boxwood knob on a mahogany drawer is the turning shop’s share — a piece you can feel as stone, a screw or a tang into the drawer front. Do not replace it with a maple knob and call the job done. The hardness is the specification. Federal shops that could not get box used holly for the line and maple for a knob. That is honest if named. A laser-cut “boxwood inlay” from a gift shop is often maple or a print. The edge and a fingernail end the argument.
Stringing around a curved Sheraton apron wants a slip that will take a gentle bend. Box will accept a large radius if the slip is thin and the grain is straight; it will snap on a tight cabriole knee. Shops steamed or kerfed, or they used holly, or they painted the line. Steam-bend radii here are jewelry radii, not Thonet’s café loops. Do not put a box slip into a steam box and expect beech manners. Heat, a form, a light restraint, or a kerf on the back of the slip: the small-work protocol. A broken line filled with putty is the tell of a repair that rushed.
## Neighbors on the appendix, box off it
*Dalbergia* — rosewood, the dark neighbor of so much stringing — went onto CITES Appendix II on 2 January 2017 (the whole genus; *D. nigra* was already Appendix I). Brazilian rosewood, East Indian rosewood, the banding woods that sat next to box on a Sheraton table: those are the listed neighbors. *Buxus* is not a CITES furniture listing. The pale line and the dark band do not share a legal file. That is the conservation sentence for this slug. Confirm Species+ at publication; listings move. Do not write a rosewood permit for a boxwood slip. Do not treat an unlisted *Buxus* knob as a free pass to ship a *Dalbergia* table.
*Buxus sempervirens* in European gardens has been hit by box blight and box-tree moth in recent decades — an ornamental crisis, not a CITES furniture listing `[CITE NEEDED: current CABI or forestry notes]`. Wild box in the Mediterranean and Caucasus has been pressured by historic trade. Buy small, old, or clearly garden-salvage stock. Do not specify box for surfaces that holly or maple stringing can do. A forestry monograph on the historic *Buxus* trade belongs on the source shelf when you can put a hand on it `[CITE NEEDED]`.
American furniture used imported box for the same inlay jobs because the tree is not an American forest species. Substitute pale woods did the cheap stringing. Garden box from a ripped-out hedge is full of dirt at the collar and small in diameter. Use it for what it is. Old engraving blocks are historical objects; do not cut them for knobs. Box dust is fine and can irritate.
Ebony inlay — the black key, the dark string — is the other specialist line in this series (`ebony-inlay-keys`). Box is the pale answer. Together they draw the furniture. Neither is a table wood.
## What to look for
A pale hard line in walnut or ebony. A turned knob that feels like stone. An engraving block, end-grain, nineteenth century. A folding rule with brass joints. A Sheraton table with stringing a millimeter wide. A “boxwood” large table: a lie or a veneer. On a Federal piece: maybe holly, not box — look at the hardness with a fingernail. On a new “inlay” from a gift shop: even, dead, often laser-cut maple or a print.
Arkansas does not grow *Buxus* as timber. A southern shop meets it as inlay stock. The local pale hard wood is maple. Different scale. Related job. The rule, the block, and the stringing line share a genus. They do not share a century. Name the tree. Then decide whether the job is a line, a knob, or a wish.
Repairing a missing line is a small, slow job. Match the species if you can: box to box, holly to holly. A maple patch in a boxwood trellis will dent first and yellow differently. Cut the rebate to the old depth; do not widen it to make the work easier. Scrape, do not sand through the neighboring veneer. On a William-and-Mary oyster or a seaweed-marquetry box the pale line is part of a picture; replacing it with a fat commercial stringing from a catalogue is a different drawing. Keep the scale. A millimeter was the point.
CITES officers meet boxwood’s neighbors more often than they meet box. A Sheraton table with rosewood banding and box stringing can need a *Dalbergia* paper to move across a border and no paper for the pale line. That asymmetry is the law, not a shop preference. Antique pieces already in the country are usually legal to own. They can be complicated to export if the dark neighbor is listed. Ask before you crate the table. The boxwood knob in your pocket is not the problem. The banding is.
## Sources
Hoadley. Bewick and wood-engraving histories. Roubo; Wallace Collection marquetry notes. Sheraton / Hepplewhite plates (stringing). Wood Database (secondary hardness). CITES CoP17 *Dalbergia* (neighbors, not *Buxus*). `[CITE NEEDED: a forestry monograph on Buxus trade]`.
See: `satinwood-adam-style`, `ebony-inlay-keys`, `maple-birdseye-factory`, `cites-dalbergia-2017`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Padauk as a modernist accent
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Padauk as a modernist accent
African padauk arrives in the shop as an argument about color. Fresh heartwood of *Pterocarpus soyauxii* is a deep, almost unreasonable red. Kukachka (FPL-125) called it striking, the sapwood grayish-white and up to eight inches thick, sharply defined. Then light and time pull the red toward brown, the way cherry pulls toward a deeper red-brown, only louder. Modernists who used it as a stripe, a door, a pull, or a chair that was meant to be a flame were borrowing a dye-wood’s manners for furniture. The tree is not a mahogany and not a rosewood. The invoices that called it both were selling a hue.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
![Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).](../assets/cites-conservation/furniture-timber-listings.svg)
*Figure 5. Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).*
## What Kukachka measured
*P. soyauxii*: Nigeria, Cameroon, French Equatorial Africa, the Congo. Texture coarse and somewhat uneven; pore lines conspicuous. Grain straight or, more often, interlocking, with a narrow stripe on the quarter. About 44 pounds per cubic foot. Machines remarkably well; finishes and glues easily. Low total shrinkage; little movement in service. In the United States of 1970, utilized only as veneer for decorative purposes.
Compiled Janka for African padauk is commonly given near 1,970 lbf, specific gravity near 0.67–0.75 (Wood Database beside FPL/Kukachka). Figure 4 places that hardness above mahogany (about 800 lbf, SG 0.45–0.50) and in the neighborhood of a hard maple, below the rosewoods (Indian *D. latifolia* compiled near 2,440 lbf; Brazilian *D. nigra* a compilation near 2,790, and Kukachka’s empty table). White oak sits near 1,360 lbf and SG 0.68. Padauk is the hard, stable, coarse-pored red, not the oily palisander and not the carvable *Swietenia* of Bowett’s 1722 lane.
Narra (*P. indicus*) is the Pacific cousin: yellow and red forms, aromatic when fresh, interlocked, ring-porous, a local furniture prestige wood, veneer-grade logs costly on the quarter (Kukachka). Andaman padauk (*P. dalbergioides*) is another trade name in the older English books. Camwood and barwood (*P. tinctorius* and related) are dye woods first. Kosso, *P. erinaceus*, rode into the 2010s as “African rosewood” and onto CITES Appendix II — a different species, a furniture-and-china trade, not this accent wood. Keep the binomials. Figure 5 is the later map; *P. soyauxii* has generally sat outside the rosewood listings `[CITE NEEDED: confirm Species+ status for P. soyauxii at publication]`. *P. santalinus* (red sandalwood) and *P. erinaceus* have not.
## Accent, not carcase — until someone tries
A dye-wood genus tempts a designer to use the heart as a signal: a through-tenon wedge, a door in a pale oak case, a laminated stripe in a table top, a chair that is all one red until it isn’t. That is a modernist habit, not an 18th-century one. Chippendale shops spent Jamaica mahogany in the solid because the Naval Stores Act made it cheap enough to carve (Bowett). They did not stripe it into oak for a color shock. Biedermeier and the pale northern shops used local birch and cherry. Padauk as a flash is a 20th-century idea: aniline was already teaching the eye to want a pure hue, and here was a hue that grew.
I will not invent a particular Gerrit Rietveld or De Stijl commission in padauk. Pin named objects at publication `[CITE NEEDED: a documented modernist piece in Pterocarpus, museum accession]`. What the shop can still say: the wood shows up in studio furniture, in inlay, in mid-century and later pieces that want a red the cherry will not give, and in a lot of turning and knife handles. Kukachka’s “veneer only in the U.S.” is a 1970 trade note, not a law of nature. Solids exist. They are heavy for their size and they will brown.
The browning is the design problem. A padauk accent next to a white maple interior is a different object in year ten. Finish slows the shift; it does not cancel light. Some shops seal the red under a UV-filtering film and still lose the argument near a window. If you want a red that stays, you are in pigment, not in *Pterocarpus*. If you want a wood that starts loud and settles, say so to the client.
## Joinery: a stable, coarse, interlocked member
Low movement is the gift. A padauk door in an oak frame will still move — every hardwood does — but Kukachka’s “little movement in service” is why people try floating panels less carefully than they should. Do not glue a padauk panel tight in a groove. Frame-and-panel remains manners.
Interlock tears under a plane on the quartered stripe. A scraper. Coarse pores drink filler if you want a glass top; they look honest if you oil and leave them open. Glue is friendly for the density class, he says, which is a relief after rosewood’s oil. Dust is still dust; some *Pterocarpus* dusts are irritants `[CITE NEEDED: a named occupational-health note]`. Collect it.
As a wedge or a key in a through tenon, padauk is a hard, visible lock. As a face on plywood, it is a sliced leaf on a core — the same sandwich as crotch mahogany on yellow-poplar, louder. As a molded-ply shell it is rare; birch and the Eames-Aalto line own that hour. A padauk stripe in a laminated bench is a color layer in a structural stack. Name the glue. Count the plies.
A whole chair in padauk is possible and usually a mistake of weight and of color change. The coarse pore will read as oak-loud under a stain someone used to “calm” the red. Let it be padauk or pick another wood. A table top that is a padauk field with maple breadboards is a movement problem dressed as a stripe problem: the field is stable for its density, the maple is not the same species, and the breadboard still needs elongated fasteners. Low movement is not no movement. Hoadley’s geometry still applies.
Piano cases are rosewood and mahogany stories. Boulle is ebony and brass. Padauk does not belong in those contracts except as a later repair someone’s uncle tried. Name that too.
## The name traps
“African rosewood” in the last twenty years often means *P. erinaceus* (kosso), listed, a different trade. “Vermilion” and “padauk” trade across *Pterocarpus* species. “Coralwood” and “mutenye” wander in. Mahogany it is not: no *Swietenia* anatomy, no Bowett statute, a harder, coarser, redder wood. Rosewood it is not: not *Dalbergia*, not the oily Bahia smell, not Appendix I. A stained padauk trying to be palisander is a waste of a red.
Narra in the Philippines and the old East Indies is a prestige furniture wood with its own colonial ledger. Do not flatten it into African padauk because both are *Pterocarpus*. The Pacific tree and the West African tree shared a genus and a dye reputation, not a shop.
Studio furniture after 1970 is where American shops actually met padauk as a solid: a box lid, a banded table top, a turned bowl that was never meant to stay red. The wood machines cleanly enough that a weekend maker treats it as friendly. Then the window does its work. A banded top that was maple-and-flame in year one is maple-and-brown in year twelve, unless someone kept it in a drawer. That is not a defect. It is the species. If the band is a through-stripe, the glue lines will telegraph slightly as the padauk and the maple move their small, different amounts. Kukachka’s low-movement note is comparative, not zero.
Inlay as a modernist accent — a padauk disc in an oak door, a dovetail of red in a pale carcase — wants the same scratch-stock manners as Federal ebony stringing, in a louder hue. Route shallow. Glue clean. Do not let a proud padauk inlay stand above a soft pine ground; the pine will wear, the red will become a ridge, then a snag.
## Law, without pretending this is jacaranda
*D. nigra* is Appendix I. *Dalbergia* spp. went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15. Neotropical *S. macrophylla* entered Appendix II on 15 November 2003. Those are the papers in the next bin in the yard. *P. soyauxii* has been the unlisted bright red that shops reached for when they wanted color without a rosewood permit. That can change. Figure 5 and Species+ are the check, not this sentence. *P. erinaceus*, *P. tinctorius*, and *P. santalinus* already demonstrate that the genus is not a free-for-all.
Lacey (2008 amendment) and APHIS Phase VII (1 December 2024) still want a binomial and a country. “Padauk” on a crate is a color. *Pterocarpus soyauxii*, Cameroon, is a specification.
## What to look for
A red that has gone brown in the sun and stayed red inside a cupboard; coarse pores; a stripe on the quarter; a veneer line; an accent in a pale case. On a piece sold as rosewood: weigh it, smell it, look at the pore — padauk is a different contract. On a piece sold as mahogany: too hard, too red, too coarse. On a new “African rosewood” dining table: ask which *Pterocarpus*, and whether it is the listed one.
Arkansas does not grow *Pterocarpus*. Cherry will give you a red-brown that moves with the years and a Janka near 950 lbf (FPL). It will not give you the first-year flame. That is an honest difference. Use padauk as an accent if the papers are clean and the client will live with the brown. Do not use it as a false name for a genus that is already on an appendix.
A turning blank of padauk is how most American shops first meet the wood: a bowl, a handle, a finial. The coarse pore throws tear-out on the end grain of a bowl if the gouge is dull. The red dust stains a bench and will pink a maple board left on top of it. Wipe the bench before you plane the pale wood. That is not a conservation note. It is an ordinary Tuesday in a small shop.
## Sources
Kukachka, FPL-125, *P. soyauxii* and *P. indicus*. USDA FPL-GTR-190. Wood Database compilations for Janka (named as compilations). CITES: App. I *D. nigra*; *Dalbergia* App. II, 2 January 2017, Annotation #15; *S. macrophylla* App. II, 15 November 2003; check *Pterocarpus* listings on Species+. Bowett on mahogany (contrast). USDA APHIS Lacey Phase VII.
See: `brazilian-rosewood-midcentury`, `mahogany-chippendale`, `cites-dalbergia-2017`, `workability-hand-tools`.

item.title: The 1973 Convention and a furniture crate
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# The 1973 Convention and a furniture crate
On 3 March 1973, in Washington, eighty-odd delegations signed a trade convention that did not mention Chippendale, a dining leaf, or a piano case. The instrument is the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora. Article XXII set entry into force at ninety days after the tenth ratification. That date is 1 July 1975. The United States had already ratified, on 14 January 1974; for the first ten Parties, including the U.S., the Convention bound them on the same July morning. A crate of sawn wood that cleared a dock in June 1975 and a crate of the same species that cleared in August 1975 are not the same legal object if the species had been placed on an appendix. This draft walks that paper. It is not a permit. It will not issue one. Species+ and the national Management Authority are the living pages.
![Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).](../assets/cites-conservation/furniture-timber-listings.svg)
*Figure 5. Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).*
![Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/timeline.svg)
*Figure 1. Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.*
## What the Convention actually is
CITES is a trade convention among Parties. It is not a forestry code and not a furniture statute. Article II splits listed species into three appendices. Appendix I is species threatened with extinction that are or may be affected by trade; commercial trade in wild specimens is not a furniture plan. Appendix II is species that may become threatened unless trade is regulated, plus look-alikes that customs cannot tell apart; trade is allowed with permits and a non-detriment finding. Appendix III is a species a Party asks others to help control. The text lives at cites.org. The lookup for a binomial on an invoice is Species+.
Each Party names a Management Authority and a Scientific Authority. In the United States the Fish and Wildlife Service holds the management seat for most CITES timber. The Scientific Authority is the one that must be able to say, in writing, that a proposed export will not be detrimental to the survival of the species. That sentence is the non-detriment finding. A factory in High Point cannot write it. A designer in Arkansas cannot write it. A magazine chapter cannot write it.
Annotations are the fine print that decide whether a finished chair is a specimen. Some listings cover the whole animal or the whole tree. Timber listings often name commodities: logs, sawn wood, veneer sheets, plywood. Annotation #6, which later attached to neotropical *Swietenia macrophylla*, is that list. Annotation #15, which later attached to *Dalbergia* (except *D. nigra*), is a different list with exemptions. The Convention of 1973 did not invent those numbers. Conferences of the Parties added them as furniture and musical-instrument trade forced the text to get specific. Figure 5 is a schematic of origin regions, not a current appendix. Confirm at publication.
Figure 1 puts 1973 and 1975 on the same timeline as Baltic oak, Jamaica mahogany after 1722, and the later listing years. The Convention is a hinge, not a beginning. The trees were already in the shops.
## A crate, a code, and a binomial
Picture a crate on a Savannah or Long Beach dock in 1976. The packing list says “wood furniture” or “mahogany lumber.” The Harmonized System as we now use it did not yet rule every invoice; the point is the same. Customs needs a name. The Convention needs a species. “Mahogany” is a color word. *Swietenia macrophylla*, *Khaya ivorensis*, and a rotary face of *Shorea* are three different objects. CITES does not grade the chair. It asks whether the specimen in the crate is a listed taxon, from a listed population, in a listed form.
If the answer is Appendix I, commercial import of a new wild specimen is the wrong plan. Brazilian rosewood, *Dalbergia nigra*, went onto Appendix I later (CoP8, in force 11 June 1992). If the answer is Appendix II, the exporting Party’s Management Authority must have issued an export permit, backed by a non-detriment finding. Some Appendix I movements also need an import permit on the receiving side. If the answer is “not listed,” CITES is quiet. Other laws may not be. The U.S. Lacey Act as amended in 2008, Food, Conservation, and Energy Act §8204, makes illegally harvested plant product a crime whether or not the tree sits on an appendix. APHIS Phase VII declarations, 1 December 2024, reach more furniture HTS codes. Those instruments are later drafts. They sit on top of 1975, they do not replace it.
A pre-Convention certificate exists for specimens acquired before the listing bound the Parties. Antique annotations exist in some later texts. Neither is a postcard you write yourself. USFWS will tell you. A dealer’s shrug will not.
## What 1973 did not settle
The Washington text did not list big-leaf mahogany. It did not list the rosewood genus. It did not list Madagascar ebony. *Swietenia humilis* appears on Appendix II from the Convention’s own first day, 1 July 1975, with a parts annotation that has since been revised `[CITE NEEDED: original 1975 annotation wording versus current #4]`. *S. mahagoni* waited until 1992. Neotropical populations of *S. macrophylla* went onto Appendix II at CoP12 (Santiago, 2002), in force 15 November 2003, Annotation #6: logs, sawn wood, veneer sheets, plywood. The whole genus *Dalbergia* (except *D. nigra*, already I) went onto Appendix II at CoP17, in force 2 January 2017, Annotation #15, revised at CoP18 in 2019 so finished musical instruments and small finished products — wood of the listed species up to 10 kg per shipment — would not freeze concerts and jewelry boxes. Madagascar populations of *Diospyros* went onto Appendix II at CoP16, in force 12 June 2013, Annotation #5.
Those dates belong in the later slugs. The 1973 draft exists so a reader can see the machine before the species fall into it. Conferences of the Parties amend appendices. Reservations exist. A Party can enter a reservation and be treated, for that listing, as a non-Party, with the paperwork that implies. India entered a reservation on the 2017 *Dalbergia* genus listing `[CITE NEEDED: current status of that reservation]`. The Convention still runs.
National implementing statutes are where a crate actually stops. CITES “does not take the place of national laws,” the Secretariat’s own explainer says. It is a framework. The U.S. Endangered Species Act and the implementing regulations at 50 C.F.R. part 23 are the American teeth. A shop that treats a CITES.org printout as a license has misread both documents.
## Furniture language for the three appendices
Appendix I, said as furniture: do not commission a new dining table in a wild Appendix I timber. *Dalbergia nigra* is the famous case. Own the 1880 piano if it is already in the country. Ask before you export it. A new “Brazilian rosewood suite” from an unnamed mill is a fantasy or a crime.
Appendix II, said as furniture: trade is a permit path, not a ban. The mill that imports sawn *S. macrophylla* from a neotropical range state needs the export permit and the finding. The designer who specifies *Dalbergia latifolia* for a sideboard that weighs eighty kilograms of listed wood has written a permit problem, not a jewelry-box exemption. Finished furniture may sit outside a timber annotation. The sawn wood in the factory does not. Read the annotation, not the hangtag.
Appendix III, said as furniture: one country asked for help. Some cedars and other woods have sat here. The listing can be narrower than a genus. Always look up the current appendix. This chapter will not update itself when CoP20 moves a line.
Look-alike listings matter in a warehouse. Customs officers are not wood anatomists. The 2017 *Dalbergia* genus listing exists in part because a crate labelled “rosewood” could be any of dozens of species, and a look-alike rule is how you stop the laundering. TRAFFIC and Chatham House’s five-taxa paper is the trade-analysis neighbor of that decision. It is not a permit.
## A shop file that would have made sense in 1976 and still does
Keep the binomial. Keep the country of harvest. Keep the date you looked the taxon up, and the page you looked it up on. If you import, keep the permit or the declaration. If you do not import, keep the mill’s chain-of-custody sheet anyway. An edge that matches the name is the object-level check: tyloses in white oak, the oily pore of teak, the tight diffuse face of maple, the printed cathedral that does not turn the corner.
A crate that says only “wood” is a refusal. A salesperson who says “it’s all mahogany” is a refusal. A funny price on a listed genus is a refusal.
Arkansas white oak, walnut, cherry, and pine do not sit on the furniture-timber appendices this series cares about. That is a practical fact, not a halo. Stolen walnut trees exist. Lacey reaches domestic plants taken in violation of state or foreign law. The Convention of 1973 is silent on a Boone County log that never crossed a border. The 2008 amendment is not.
## How to look at a piece that predates the paper
A 1760 Jamaica chair is older than the Convention by two centuries. It is usually legal to own in the United States. It can be complicated to export. The same is true of a 1962 Danish rosewood credenza, which is younger than the Convention and older than the 2017 genus listing. Pre-Convention and antique rules are real. They are administered, not assumed. Photograph the grain. Keep the invoice. If the piece later wants to go to London, the file starts in the living room, not at the airport.
A new table claiming an old name is the opposite case. The invoice binomial is the first question. The harvest country is the second. The annotation is the third. Fashion without that file is how *Swietenia* and *Dalbergia* arrived at the appendices. The 1973 text did not cause the logging. It built a gate after the ships had already sailed for three hundred years.
Arkansas white oak is a specification a 1973 delegate would have understood without an appendix: *Quercus alba*, United States. The Convention was written for the other crate — the one whose name was a color and whose origin was a shrug.
Look at the dock date and the binomial. That is the Convention in a shop. The later drafts — `cites-swietenia-permits`, `cites-dalbergia-2017`, `cites-ebony-africa`, `conservation-today` — put particular trees through the same gate. This page is the gate.
## Sources
CITES text, signed Washington 3 March 1973; Art. XXII; entry into force 1 July 1975 (cites.org; UNTS 993, I-14537). U.S. ratification 14 January 1974. Species+. USFWS timber / 50 C.F.R. 23. CITES 2003 mahogany release; CoP12 *S. macrophylla*. CoP17 *Dalbergia* (in force 2 Jan. 2017); CoP18 Annotation #15 revision (2019). CoP8 *D. nigra* (11 June 1992). CoP16 Madagascar *Diospyros* (12 June 2013). USDA APHIS Lacey; 2008 §8204; Phase VII (1 Dec. 2024); Federal Register 31 May 2024. TRAFFIC / Chatham House five-taxa paper.
See: `cites-swietenia-permits`, `cites-dalbergia-2017`, `cites-ebony-africa`, `conservation-today`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Dalbergia, 2 January 2017
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Dalbergia, 2 January 2017
A rosewood dining table is not a jewelry box. That sentence is the whole of Annotation #15, said as furniture. On 2 January 2017 the genus *Dalbergia* — every rosewood and palisander except the one already on Appendix I — entered CITES Appendix II. The decision was CoP17, Johannesburg, 2016. The annotation that came with it was #15. CoP18, Geneva, 2019, revised #15 so that finished musical instruments, finished instrument parts and accessories, and finished products up to 10 kg of wood of the listed species per shipment would not freeze concerts and small boxes. A sideboard that holds eighty kilograms of *D. latifolia* is not in that sentence. This draft is the genus listing and the annotation. It is not a permit.
![Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).](../assets/cites-conservation/furniture-timber-listings.svg)
*Figure 5. Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).*
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## The tree that was already shut
*Dalbergia nigra* — jacaranda da Bahia, Brazilian rosewood — went onto Appendix I at CoP8, in force 11 June 1992. TRAFFIC called it the first tree species on Appendix I. Commercial trade in wild specimens is not a furniture plan. Warren Dean’s *With Broadax and Firebrand* is the Atlantic-forest history behind the piano cases. An 1880 parlor piano with a *D. nigra* case is a legal object in an American living room and a paperwork object if you ship it across a border. A new dining table in wild *D. nigra* is a fantasy or a crime.
The rest of the genus kept moving. East Indian rosewood (*D. latifolia*), cocobolo (*D. retusa*), Honduras rosewood (*D. stevensonii*), Siamese rosewood (*D. cochinchinensis*), the Madagascar rosewoods, kingwood and tulipwood — a palette of dense, oily, fragrant hardwoods that Victorian pianos, French ébénisterie, and mid-century Danish sideboards all wanted. Some species sat on Appendix II or III before 2017, often limited to logs, sawn wood, and veneer. Customs still faced a crate labelled “rosewood.” Officers are not wood anatomists. CoP17 Prop. 55 said the quiet part: they are unlikely to tell the species apart. The genus listing is a look-alike rule as much as a biology rule.
Figure 5 is a schematic of origin regions. Confirm the appendix at publication. Figure 4 places hardness and density among the series’ ten anchors. *Dalbergia* sits off the right-hand edge of that scatter: Janka numbers commonly cited well above 2,000 lbf for *D. nigra*, specific gravities often 0.8–1.0 (Wood Database compilations; check FPL imported-woods notes before treating a single figure as law). They are the heavy, oily woods. They are why a “solid rosewood suite” that ships cheap is not rosewood.
## What 2 January 2017 changed in a shop
From that morning, *Dalbergia* spp. except *D. nigra* sat on Appendix II with Annotation #15. The first text of #15 included all parts and derivatives except leaves, flowers, pollen, fruits, and seeds; a non-commercial export cap of 10 kg per shipment; and special rules that pointed *D. cochinchinensis* at Annotation #4 and Mexican *Dalbergia* at Annotation #6 (CITES PC23 documents). Guitar companies and orchestras learned the first version the hard way. Taylor Guitars’ public CITES note is a clear industry walkthrough. Verify it against Species+. Furniture companies have less excuse. A dining table was never going to hide under a 10 kg non-commercial line.
CoP18, August 2019, revised #15. The text that entered into force on 26 November 2019 reads, in furniture English: all parts and derivatives except (a) leaves, flowers, pollen, fruits, and seeds; (b) finished products to a maximum weight of wood of the listed species of up to 10 kg per shipment; (c) finished musical instruments, finished musical instrument parts, and finished musical instrument accessories; (d) parts and derivatives of *D. cochinchinensis*, covered by #4; (e) parts and derivatives of *Dalbergia* spp. originating and exported from Mexico, covered by #6. The Interpretation section defines the instrument terms against Harmonized System Chapter 92, and defines “10 kg per shipment” as the weight of the listed wood in each item, not the gross weight of the crate (CITES PC25 Doc. 36). A jewelry box may pass. A guitar may pass. A rosewood dining table does not pass.
Three *Guibourtia* species — *G. demeusei*, *G. pellegriniana*, *G. tessmannii*, the bubingas — carry the same annotation. A “rosewood look” in bubinga is not a way around the paper.
India entered a reservation on the 2017 genus listing (CITES Notification 2017/010). Reservations are not a shop license in a Party that did not enter one. Check the current notice. This draft will not update itself.
## A sideboard at the airport
A 1962 Danish credenza in *D. latifolia*, bought in Milwaukee in 1998, is usually legal to own in the United States. It became more complicated to export after 2 January 2017. Owners who want to sell it to London need a permit path, not a dealer’s shrug. Photograph the grain. Keep the invoice. Pre-Convention certificates exist for specimens acquired before the listing bound the Parties. They are administered by the Management Authority. USFWS is the American office. A magazine chapter is not.
A new “rosewood suite” from an unnamed exporter is the opposite object. If the price is funny, the wood is funny. If the hangtag says rosewood and the piece is light, you are looking at stained walnut, printed foil, or a hope. Weight, pore, and a fresh-scratch smell help. Many *Dalbergia* are fragrant when cut. They do not replace a binomial on an invoice. A lab test is what a customs officer may want.
Sawn wood and veneer for a furniture factory are not a casual import. Annotation #15 as revised still covers those commodities. The mill that wants *D. latifolia* leaves for a run of doors needs the export permit and the non-detriment finding from the country of harvest. Finished furniture that is mostly rosewood is a permit problem unless it fits the 10 kg finished-product line — and a dining table does not.
## How the wood behaves, since the listing did not change the fiber
Rosewoods are hard, dense, and often oily. They dull edges. They can starve a glue joint if you treat them like mahogany. Dust is a sensitizer; some people do not get a second chance at a first exposure `[CITE NEEDED: a named occupational-health note]`. A scraper often beats a plane on interlock. The polish looks like stone. Victorian shops used them as veneer more than as solid tops, except in small work and in some mid-century Danish pieces. Solid *Dalbergia* dining tables that are truly the genus are heavy, expensive, and now legally loud.
Figure 4’s scatter is the contrast. Honduran mahogany sits near 800 lbf and SG 0.45–0.50. White oak near 1,360 lbf and 0.68. *Dalbergia* is the other end of the rack: you lift a drawer and the drawer argues. That is useful when you are trying to decide whether a dark brown suite is rosewood or a photograph.
Repair with the same species is a permit question when the patch is imported. Repair with walnut or dyed pear is how shops have always faked a missing moulding. Name the repair. Do not strip an Appendix I piano case over a weekend to “brighten the rosewood.” The finish is part of the object’s market and legal identity.
## Lacey on top
The U.S. Lacey Act (16 U.S.C. §3371 et seq.), amended by the Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008 §8204, makes it illegal to trade plants taken in violation of U.S. or foreign law. It does not care whether the crate is also a CITES specimen. A rosewood log illegal in the source country is illegal here. APHIS Phase VII, 1 December 2024 (Federal Register 31 May 2024), extends declarations to remaining plant-product HTS codes that are not 100 percent composite, including more furniture. Due care is the standard. A certificate on a website is not automatically due care. FSC is a useful risk tool. It is not a finding that Lacey has been met.
Stolen walnut trees exist. Domestic wood is not automatically innocent. *Dalbergia* does not grow in Arkansas. The local dark hard woods are walnut and locust. They will not be rosewood. They do not need to be.
## What to write on a specification
*Dalbergia latifolia*, country of harvest, permit number, Annotation #15 read and filed. Or: *Juglans nigra*, United States, quartersawn. Or: vintage *Dalbergia*, already in the country, invoice and photographs in the project file, export not contemplated. Those are three different objects. “Rosewood dining set” is not a specification.
Species+ is the lookup. The annotation text is the fine print. This series will not issue a permit. It will not update itself when CoP20 changes a kilogram line. It will say: a guitar is a Chapter 92 object; a jewelry box may be a 10 kg object; a dining table is a furniture object. The 2017 listing exists because the genus was a furniture and flooring trade, not because a concert hall needed a new tax.
Look at the weight and the invoice. If the crate is a table, do not quote the instrument exemption. If the crate is a guitar, read Taylor’s note and then read Species+. If the crate is an 1880 piano in *D. nigra*, you are on Appendix I and the living-room rule is not the airport rule.
## A factory leaf and a concert guitar
The 2017 listing hit two trades that had shared a genus and not a paperwork culture. Guitar shops already knew *D. nigra* as Appendix I. They did not all know that *D. latifolia* fingerboards and *D. retusa* bridges would become Appendix II specimens on 2 January. The first year of #15 produced a pile of industry notes and a pile of seized or delayed shipments. CoP18’s instrument exemption was the political answer to that pile. Furniture factories had less of a lobby and less of an exemption. A sliced rosewood leaf for a High Point door run is still sawn wood or veneer in annotation English. It is not a Chapter 92 object. It is not 10 kg of listed wood in a finished box. It is why the genus was listed.
Kingwood and tulipwood — *D. cearensis*, *D. decipularis*, the ébéniste’s small woods — sit in the same genus and the same 2017 net. A banding line on a French commode already in a museum is not a new import. A new banding stock from an unnamed supplier is.
The smell in a fresh kerf is a pleasure. The permit is the price of that pleasure crossing a border. This page does not sell either.
## Sources
CITES CoP17 *Dalbergia* spp. App. II, in force 2 January 2017; Annotation #15. CoP18 (2019) revision of #15, in force 26 November 2019; PC25 Doc. 36 (definitions of 10 kg and finished instruments). CoP8 *D. nigra* App. I, 11 June 1992. TRAFFIC, *Trade in Dalbergia nigra and the European Union*. CITES Notification 2017/010 (reservations). Species+. USFWS timber pages. Taylor Guitars CITES note (industry; verify). Dean, *With Broadax and Firebrand*. USDA APHIS Lacey; 2008 §8204; Phase VII (1 Dec. 2024). FPL imported woods / Wood Database (hardness; treat as compilation).
See: `cites-1973-convention`, `cites-swietenia-permits`, `rosewood-victorian`, `brazilian-rosewood-midcentury`, `conservation-today`.

item.title: Swietenia, Annotation 6, and the mill permit
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Swietenia, Annotation 6, and the mill permit
A dining table in “genuine mahogany” and a bundle of sawn *Swietenia macrophylla* on a mill floor are not the same CITES object. Neotropical populations of big-leaf mahogany entered Appendix II at CoP12 (Santiago, 2002), in force 15 November 2003. The annotation is #6: logs, sawn wood, veneer sheets, and plywood. Finished furniture may sit outside that list. The mill that imported the boards does not. The CITES press release of 11 November 2003 is the dated public notice. This draft is the permit path for the genus the Chippendale shop already used. It is not a permit. It will not issue one.
![Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).](../assets/cites-conservation/furniture-timber-listings.svg)
*Figure 5. Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).*
![Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/trade-lanes.svg)
*Figure 2. Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.*
## Three *Swietenia*, three clocks
*Swietenia humilis*, the Pacific-dry-forest mahogany, sits on Appendix II from the Convention’s first morning, 1 July 1975. The parts annotation has been revised; current text is not the 1975 text `[CITE NEEDED: original annotation versus current #4]`. *S. mahagoni* — Cuban, Santo Domingo, West Indian, the fine early furniture mahogany — went onto Appendix II in 1992 (in force 11 June 1992, with *D. nigra*’s Appendix I day). Commercial sizes of *S. mahagoni* were already a memory in the shops. *S. macrophylla* — Honduran, big-leaf, the “genuine mahogany” of the later trade — ranges from Mexico to the Amazon. Range states put populations on Appendix III from 16 November 1995 (logs, sawn wood, veneer). CoP12 moved neotropical populations to Appendix II and added plywood to the commodity list. Fifteen November 2003 is the furniture date.
Populations outside the Neotropics — plantation *S. macrophylla* in Fiji, Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, the Philippines — sit outside that Appendix II listing. Kew’s *CITES and Timber* says so in one sentence. Species+ is the check. A plantation board from Fiji and a wild board from a Central American forest are the same binomial and different paper. Do not treat the Fiji board as a loophole you invented. Treat it as a harvest-country fact you can show.
Figure 5 is origin regions, illustrative. Figure 2 puts the Atlantic mahogany lane beside Baltic oak and Indian Ocean teak. Bowett’s Jamaica wood after the Naval Stores Act of 1721 (in force 1722) is the furniture beginning of that lane. The 2003 listing is the permit end of the wild neotropical run. They belong on the same wall.
## What Annotation #6 covers, in mill English
#6 designates logs, sawn wood, veneer sheets, and plywood. Resolution Conf. 10.13 (timber definitions) points those words at Harmonized System codes: logs as wood in the rough (HS 44.03); sawn wood normally thicker than 6 mm (HS 44.06, 44.07); veneer sheets usually 6 mm or less (HS 44.08). Plywood was the late add. The Plants Committee, August 2003, accepted the HS 44.12 definition as an interim: three or more sheets glued and pressed, grains of successive layers generally at an angle (PC14 Doc. 7.5.1). Preferred unit on a plywood permit: square metres.
A rough-sawn flitch of *S. macrophylla* from Guatemala is a #6 specimen. A sliced crown-cut face 0.6 mm thick is a #6 specimen. A five-ply sheet with a mahogany face and a mahogany core is a #6 specimen if the listed wood is what the annotation names. A finished dining table, already a piece of furniture with legs and a finish, may fall outside #6. The boards that became the table did not. The factory that imported the sawn wood needed the export permit from the range-state Management Authority and a non-detriment finding from that Party’s Scientific Authority. A High Point warehouse that buys the finished table still has Lacey due care. It may not have a CITES import permit for the table if the annotation truly excludes finished furniture. That “may” is why you read Species+ and USFWS, not this paragraph, before you ship.
This draft is not a permit. Annotations move. CoP20 can rewrite #6. The living page wins.
## The permit, said as a file
The exporting Party issues the export permit. The Scientific Authority must find the export non-detrimental. The Management Authority must be satisfied the specimen was legally obtained. For Appendix II timber, the importing Party does not always need a matching import permit; national rules differ, and the EU is stricter than the Convention’s floor `[CITE NEEDED: current EU Annex B mahogany import practice]`. In the United States, USFWS is the office. 50 C.F.R. part 23 is the regulation. A shop that wants new neotropical *S. macrophylla* in the solid or as veneer is buying a file: binomial, harvest country, permit number, finding date, quantity, and the annotation that applied on the day of export.
Re-exports need their own paper, tracing back to the original export. A bundle that lost its number in a kiln shed is a problem, not a story. Pre-Convention certificates exist for wood acquired before 15 November 2003 (or before the relevant earlier listing). They are not a shrug. They are a form.
TRAFFIC and Chatham House’s five-taxa paper tracked mahogany among other listed timbers. Illegal wild *S. macrophylla* exists beside legal plantation wood. A certificate on a website is not automatically due care. FSC is a risk tool. It is not a CITES finding and not a Lacey finding. APHIS and FSC both say versions of this.
## Lacey, 2008, and the crate that says MAHOGANY
The Lacey Act (16 U.S.C. §3371 et seq.), amended by the Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008 §8204, makes it illegal to trade plants taken in violation of U.S. or foreign law. A mahogany log illegal in Peru is illegal in Savannah. The declaration — scientific name, country of harvest, quantity, value — is the import stamp. Phase VII, 1 December 2024 (Federal Register 31 May 2024), extends that stamp to remaining plant-product HTS codes that are not 100 percent composite, including more furniture. A crate that says only MAHOGANY fails the declaration the way a crate that says only CEDAR fails it. *Swietenia macrophylla*, Guatemala, is a line. *Khaya ivorensis*, Ghana, is a different line. *Shorea* spp. as a rotary face is a third line. “Genuine mahogany” is an ad.
Some furniture HTS codes were omitted from the first Phase VII list (APHIS noted 9403409040, 9403409060, 9403409080 and promised a later notice with six months’ lead). Check the current APHIS page. This chapter will not update itself.
## What the wood still is
The *Wood Handbook* describes American mahogany as pale pink to dark reddish brown, generally straighter than African *Khaya*, easy to dry, dimensionally stable, durable, easy to work, a premier veneer wood. Janka is commonly cited near 800 lbf, specific gravity near 0.45–0.50 (FPL imported-woods chapter / Kukachka FPL-125). Softer than white oak, kinder than maple, strong enough in section for a slender splat. The 2003 listing did not change the fiber. It changed the invoice.
Wide flatsawn leaves still move. The rule joint on an 18th-century dining table is still the period answer. A factory that glues a breadboard tight across a new mahogany top will split it the same as oak. Floating panels, slotted screws, and a plywood ground are still the manners. The permit does not float the panel.
*Khaya* and *Entandrophragma* (sapele, utile, sipo) filled the name after Cuban *S. mahagoni* ran out of commercial sizes. They are Meliaceae. They are not *Swietenia*. A ribbon-striped quartered sapele door is one of the best furniture faces of the last hundred years. It is a substitute name when the invoice says mahogany. Santos mahogany is *Myroxylon*. Philippine mahogany was lauan. The Chippendale draft (`mahogany-chippendale`) is the splat and the 1721 statute. This draft is the 2003 permit.
## How to specify, and how to look
Write *Swietenia macrophylla*, neotropical, permit path in the file — or *S. macrophylla*, plantation, country outside the Neotropics, papers that show it — or *Khaya ivorensis*, named, or *Juglans nigra*, United States. A 1760 Jamaica chair in a collection is the ethical supply of that look. A new “Chippendale mahogany dining set” from an unnamed exporter is a labeling problem before it is a style problem.
On the piece: oxidized brown on an 18th-century splat, oak or deal secondary wood, a shoe that is a separate piece. On a Victorian table: redder finish, maybe still *Swietenia*. On a 1960s suite: probably *Khaya* or a print. On a new table: the invoice binomial and the harvest country. Ribbon that looks like sapele: read the sapele chapter.
Arkansas does not grow *Swietenia*. A shop that wants that carved thinness in a domestic wood is looking at walnut or cherry, and at a splat that will not be as open as the *Director* plate. Name the wood. Do not name the island you did not pay for.
## A permit that names plywood
PC14 Doc. 7.5.1 is a dull file and a useful one. After CoP12 added plywood to the mahogany annotation, the Plants Committee had to say what plywood was. Three or more sheets, glued and pressed, grains of successive layers generally at an angle: HS 44.12. Square metres on the permit, not a furniture sketch. A five-ply door skin with a *S. macrophylla* face and a *S. macrophylla* core is that object. A five-ply door skin with a *S. macrophylla* face and a *Shorea* core is a mixed specimen; the listed face is still a veneer sheet under #6 if the leaf is what the annotation names. Do not invent a fraction. Ask USFWS. The mill that peels the leaf in a range state needed the finding before the knife hit the log.
Non-detriment findings for mahogany have a working-group history. The Bigleaf Mahogany Working Group, kept alive at CoP12 as Decision 12.21, is the paper trail of range states trying to make Appendix II mean something other than a stamp. TRAFFIC’s later five-taxa work is the outside audit. A finding that is a form letter is a finding a Scientific Authority may still have signed. Due care on the American side is not satisfied by assuming they meant it. Keep the document. Keep the quantity. Keep the date.
A 1760 Jamaica chair does not have that file. It has a collection record and a secondary wood. A 2004 bundle of Honduran sawn wood does have that file, or it should. Those are the two objects this series will not conflate.
Look at the mill ticket, not the hangtag. If the ticket is sawn wood from a neotropical range state, you want Annotation #6 paper dated after 15 November 2003, or a pre-Convention story that USFWS will accept. If the ticket is a finished table, you still want Lacey due care and a binomial. This page will not stamp either document.
## Sources
CITES press release, 11 November 2003; CoP12 Prop. 50; PC14 Doc. 7.5.1 (plywood definition). Annotation #6; Res. Conf. 10.13 timber definitions. Species+; Kew, *CITES and Timber* (plantation populations). *S. humilis* App. II 1 July 1975; *S. mahagoni* App. II 1992; App. III *S. macrophylla* 16 November 1995. USFWS 50 C.F.R. 23. USDA FPL imported woods; Kukachka FPL-125. Bowett, *The English Mahogany Trade 1700–1793*. USDA APHIS Lacey; 2008 §8204; Phase VII (1 Dec. 2024); FR 31 May 2024. TRAFFIC / Chatham House five-taxa paper.
See: `mahogany-chippendale`, `cites-1973-convention`, `cites-dalbergia-2017`, `conservation-today`.

item.title: African ebony and the listed black
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# African ebony and the listed black
A piano key that is truly Gabon ebony is a small, dense, jet object, and a crate of the same wood is a customs argument. True ebonies are *Diospyros*. The furniture black of 17th-century Antwerp cabinets, of Boulle’s counterpart to brass, of piano sharps when the sharps were wood, and of Art Deco accents is this genus — or it is a stain on pear. Madagascar’s populations of *Diospyros* went onto CITES Appendix II at CoP16 (Bangkok, 2013), in force 12 June 2013, Annotation #5: logs, sawn wood, and veneer sheets. Gabon ebony, *Diospyros crassiflora*, is a West and Central African tree, IUCN Endangered, and a different listing question. Check Species+ the morning you specify it. This draft is the African black in shops and the paper that sometimes follows it. It is not a permit.
![Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).](../assets/cites-conservation/furniture-timber-listings.svg)
*Figure 5. Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).*
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## Two Africas, one word
Madagascar is an African island with its own *Diospyros* flora — dozens of species, many poorly separated on a dock. In March 2010 Madagascar decreed a ban on cutting, exploiting, and exporting *Dalbergia* and *Diospyros* (CITES Notification 2013/039). In 2011 it listed those genera’ Malagasy species on Appendix III. CoP16 moved the Madagascar populations of both genera to Appendix II, annotated #5. The listing took effect 12 June 2013. The Secretariat spent the following years asking Parties to check shipments, because illegal rosewood and ebony kept leaving the island (SC65 Doc. 48.1). The Action Plan attached to Decision 16.152 is the paper trail of that failure. A container of “ebony” from Toamasina after June 2013 is a #5 question if it is logs, sawn wood, or veneer.
Gabon ebony — *D. crassiflora* (trade also says African ebony, Nigerian ebony) — grows in Cameroon, Gabon, the Republic of the Congo, the Central African Republic, and neighbors `[CITE NEEDED: current range-state list from a flora]`. It is the jet-black heartwood of the piano-key and inlay trade. It is not a Madagascar species. A CoP16 proposal synonym that looks like *D. crassiflora* is a Malagasy name now treated as *D. mcphersonii* (CoP16 Prop. 58). Do not conflate them. *D. crassiflora* has sat off the appendices while the Madagascar populations sat on them. That can change at a Conference of the Parties. Species+ is the living page. IUCN Endangered is not a CITES appendix. It is a conservation status. Both belong on a specification, and they are not the same stamp.
Ceylon ebony (*D. ebenum*) and Macassar (*D. celebica*, striped brown-black) are Asian trades. They appear here only so a reader does not call every black key Gabon. Figure 5 lumps origin regions as a schematic. Confirm.
## Weight, hardness, and a key
Ebony is why Figure 4’s scatter has an empty upper-right corner in this series’ ten anchors. Wood Database compilations put Gabon ebony’s Janka near 3,000 lbf and specific gravity near or above 1.0 — the piece sinks, or nearly does. Treat those figures as compilations until you have an FPL row. The shop fact does not need a decimal. A solid Gabon ebony chest would be a monster of weight and money. Furniture used the wood as stringing, as a key, as a banding, as a clock-case accent, as the black in a Boulle pair. Antwerp and Paris cabinets of the 17th century are the luxury objects. Victorian ebonized furniture is often a finish on pear, maple, or beech. Look at a chip. If the black is a skin, you have a stain. If the black goes through a dense, fine pore and the piece weighs like stone, you may have *Diospyros*. A lab test is what a customs officer may want.
The *Wood Handbook* is thin on African ebony as a structural furniture species because shops did not build tables from it. Hoadley will tell you it is hard, fine, and punishing to edges. It turns. It engraves. It does not forgive a dull gouge. Dust is nasty; collection is not optional `[CITE NEEDED: a named occupational-health note for *Diospyros* dust]`. Glue is ordinary if the surface is clean and not polished to a seal before the joint.
A piano with wooden sharps is a dated object. Later pianos went to plastic. Repair of an old key with true Gabon is now a supply and a paper problem. Repair with dyed hornbeam or a polymer is how most shops keep a keyboard even. Name the repair.
## Illegal trade, named as a crate
The Madagascar story after 2010 is not a sermon. It is a Standing Committee file. Notification 2013/039 asked Parties to inspect timber leaving the island. SC65 recorded “numerous reports of suspected illegal exports” after the 12 June 2013 listing.
