EIA and other NGOs published container-level accounts; treat those as advocacy documents and check the CITES notices before you quote a tonnage `[CITE NEEDED: a dated CITES or TRAFFIC tonnage you are willing to stand behind]`. The Chinese market for Hongmu and for black furniture woods is part of the demand side `[CITE NEEDED: a named trade-statistics paper, not a headline]`. A shop in Arkansas does not need the geopolitics. It needs to know that “Madagascar ebony” on an invoice after 2013 is a listed population, and that a funny price is a refusal.
West and Central African *D. crassiflora* has its own illegal-logging file. IUCN Endangered is the status. National harvest and export rules in Gabon and Cameroon exist and change `[CITE NEEDED: current Gabon / Cameroon export rule for ebony]`. Lacey does not wait for an appendix. The U.S. Lacey Act as amended in 2008, Food, Conservation, and Energy Act §8204, makes a plant illegal here if it was taken in violation of foreign law. APHIS Phase VII, 1 December 2024, reaches more furniture HTS codes. A crate of inlay stock that was illegal to cut in the source country is a Lacey crate whether or not Species+ shows an appendix.
The 1973 Convention (signed 3 March, in force 1 July 1975) is the machine. *Dalbergia nigra* went onto Appendix I on 11 June 1992. The *Dalbergia* genus went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15 revised at CoP18 in 2019 (musical instruments / 10 kg). Neotropical *Swietenia macrophylla* went onto Appendix II on 15 November 2003, Annotation #6. Madagascar *Diospyros* is the ebony date on that same wall: 12 June 2013, #5. Do not borrow the rosewood 10 kg exemption for a sawn ebony flitch. Different annotation. Different genus.
## Ebonized versus ebony, in a room
Victorian “ebony” suites are usually stained. The fashion was a black parlor, not a *Diospyros* forest. French polish over a black ground, or a spirit stain on pear, reads as ebony at ten feet and as a finish at a chip. Art Deco used Macassar and other striped ebonies as a modern luxury: a cabinet face, a clock, an accent, not a farm table. English Regency and French Empire used rosewood as the dark show veneer more often than solid ebony. Boulle’s brass-and-turtle cabinets at the Wallace Collection are the place to see the black as a counterpart, not as a table top.
Inlay and stringing are the honest furniture uses. A 1 mm line of Gabon in a satinwood panel is a historic craft. A new dining table advertised as solid African ebony is a weight and money claim that should make you pick up a corner. If the corner is light, the advertisement is a stain. If the corner is heavy and the invoice lacks a binomial and a harvest country, put the corner down.
## Shop file
Binomial. Harvest country. Date you checked Species+. If the wood is Madagascar *Diospyros* in logs, sawn wood, or veneer, you want Appendix II paper under Annotation #5, or a refusal. If the wood is *D. crassiflora*, you want the current appendix (or the absence of one) plus Lacey due care plus the range-state export rule. If the wood is a stain, write “ebonized pear” or “ebonized maple.” Do not write ebony.
Repair patches imported as sawn stock follow the annotation. A gram of inlay in a traveler’s pocket is not a dining table; it can still be a specimen if the listing covers that form. This draft will not draw that line for you. USFWS will.
Arkansas does not grow *Diospyros* of the jet furniture kind. Persimmon (*D. virginiana*) is a pale, hard, domestic cousin used for golf-club heads and some textile shuttles, not for Boulle. It will not be Gabon. It does not need to be. A dark domestic hardwood in the same shop is walnut. Name it.
## Keys, stringing, and a Boulle pair
Piano sharps were a volume market. A single keyboard is a handful of grams of jet heartwood, sawn, dyed if the sap streaked, glued to a pine or basswood carcass. Factories in the late 19th century ate *D. crassiflora* in those grams. They did not eat it as tables. When plastics took the sharps, the furniture and inlay trades remained the excuse to cut the tree. A 1 mm stringing line in a satinwood panel is the honest leftover of that trade. A “solid ebony console” on a website in 2024 is usually a stain, a hope, or a Lacey problem.
Boulle’s counterpart to brass is turtle and ebony in the same Paris luxury. The Wallace Collection pieces are the place to see the black as a line, not as a slab. English Restoration cabinets used ebony as a ground for japanning and as a banding. Dutch and Antwerp ebony cabinets of the 17th century are a different, heavier claim; some of that black is stained pear even there. A lens on an unseen edge ends the argument better than a catalogue.
Macassar (*D. celebica*) is striped and Indonesian. It is the Art Deco face people mean when they say “ebony” and show brown lightning. It is not Gabon and not Madagascar. Do not file it under Annotation #5. Do not file Gabon under #5 either unless Species+ has moved. The 2013 listing is a population listing: Madagascar. The word ebony is not a population.
Look at a chip and a scale. A skin of black on a light wood is a finish. A jet heartwood that sinks in the back of the mind is *Diospyros* or a hope. The invoice decides which. The 2013 Madagascar listing and the 1975 Convention are the paper. This page is not a stamp on that paper.
## Sources
CITES Notification 2013/039; CoP16 Prop. 58; Decision 16.152 and Action Plan; SC65 Doc. 48.1 (illegal export reports after 12 June 2013). Annotation #5. Species+. IUCN Red List, *Diospyros crassiflora* (check date). Wallace Collection / Boulle context. Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*. USDA FPL (limited ebony rows; Wood Database compilations for Janka — treat as such). Lacey Act 16 U.S.C. §3371 et seq.; 2008 §8204; APHIS Phase VII (1 Dec. 2024). CITES 1973/1975; *D. nigra* 11 June 1992; *S. macrophylla* 15 Nov. 2003 #6; *Dalbergia* 2 Jan. 2017 #15, CoP18 2019.
See: `ebony-inlay-keys`, `cites-1973-convention`, `cites-dalbergia-2017`, `conservation-today`.

item.title: Plantation teak and the papers
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Plantation teak and the papers
A plantation board of *Tectona grandis* can be *Tectona* and still disappoint a buyer who paid for a Burma story. Wide rings, paler heart, less oil, a specific gravity that sits at the light end of the handbook range. The anatomy is the same ring-porous brown. The folklore grade — tight, dark, greasy — is a different growing year and a different forest politics. “Sustainable” on a hang-tag is not a binomial and not a permit. The papers are the piece.
![Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/trade-lanes.svg)
*Figure 2. Three parallel supply chains — Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany, and Indian Ocean teak — with documentary milestone years.*
![Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).](../assets/cites-conservation/furniture-timber-listings.svg)
*Figure 5. Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).*
## What the tree still is
The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190) already treated teak as an imported furniture and decking wood with properties “generally on par with those of U.S. oaks,” excellent stability, very high natural durability, silica as the shop tax. Compiled Janka near 1,070 lbf, specific gravity near 0.55. Plantation stock can run lighter. That is a grading fact, not a moral one. Figure 2 keeps the Indian Ocean lane next to Baltic oak and Atlantic mahogany. Plantations in Africa and Latin America are later dots on that map, not a new species.
*Tectona grandis* is not a CITES appendix species in the rosewood sense. Figure 5 is the contrast: *Dalbergia*, *Swietenia macrophylla* (neotropical populations, Appendix II in force 15 November 2003), African ebony annotations — the listed neighbors. Teak’s legal life is national export law, bilateral sanctions, Lacey declarations, and whatever certificate a mill bought. Confirm Species+ and the national instrument at publication. Listings move. A hang-tag does not.
Dutch Java planted teak because the tree was already a state timber in the East Indies. That planting is older than the late-twentieth-century patio boom and older than FSC. The VOC and then the Netherlands-India forest service treated *Tectona* as a crop with a rotation, not only as a wild log `[CITE NEEDED: a named Java teak-plantation monograph — Boomgaard or a forestry-service history]`. British India and Burma ran reservations and a forest department that mixed conservation language with a dockyard appetite (the colonial-dockyard draft). A plantation is not automatically a virtue. It is a land use. Whose land, whose labor, what rotation, what chemical, what mill — those are the questions a certificate is supposed to answer and sometimes does not.
West African and Central American farms of the late twentieth century were a response to Asian export controls and to a patio fashion that had outrun the folklore grade. FPL already noted plantations as a real supply. The rings on those boards are the evidence a shop can see without a certificate. The certificate is the evidence a customs officer can see without a board. Both belong on the piece.
## Rings, oil, and the folklore grade
Old-growth or long-rotation teak from the Burma and Siam folklore is tight-ringed because the tree grew slowly. Heartwood is darker, oilier, the face that restorers still call “greasy.” Plantation rotations in Indonesia, West Africa, Central and South America, and later farms in Central America and Brazil can be twenty to thirty years or a little more `[CITE NEEDED: a named plantation-rotation survey, not a vendor blog]`. Wider rings. More sapwood in the log. Less extractive in some stems. The wood still weathers silver outdoors. It still dulls a plane. It may check more, glue a little easier (less oil), and look paler under the same oil can.
A shop that pretends plantation and Burma are the same product is selling a story. A shop that pretends plantation is not teak is selling a different story. Both are *Tectona* if the pore and the silica agree. Specify rotation and origin the way you specify quartersawn. The board will tell you the rings. The invoice must tell you the country.
Indoor Danish-modern teak of the 1950s and 1960s was often the older supply — Burmese and Thai logs into Copenhagen factories — and also, as the years went on, whatever the mills could get. Some of the best is solid; much is veneer. The garden furniture of the 1980s–2000s is the plantation object most buyers now own. Do not restore a patio armchair as if it were a Juhl. Do not oil a grey bench and call it a sideboard.
## Papers, not poetry
The U.S. Lacey Act as amended in 2008, and APHIS Phase VII declarations (1 December 2024), make a binomial on an invoice part of the piece. “Teak” is not enough. *Tectona grandis*, harvest country, and the rest of the declaration fields are the specification. A crate that says only “teak” fails the same way a crate that says only “mahogany” fails.
FSC and PEFC chain-of-custody are private certificates. They are not a legal finding and not a CITES permit. They can be useful. They can be bought and gamed. Read the certificate number. Ask whether the claim is forest-management or mixed-credit. A mixed-credit sofa can be mostly something else with a teak face. That is honest if the invoice says so.
National export regimes matter more than a magazine adjective. Myanmar’s teak export rules have tightened, loosened, and been sanctioned in cycles `[CITE NEEDED: dated instrument — ban, partial ban, or sanctions list at publication]`. Indonesia’s plantation export is a different paper. Ghana, Côte d’Ivoire, Tanzania, Panama, Costa Rica, Brazil — each has a forest law and a mill culture. Illegal logging in mainland Southeast Asia is documented by TRAFFIC and others `[CITE NEEDED: a named report year]`. “Burma teak” as a sales name without a legal path is a story. Treat it as one.
CITES is the wrong panic and the right habit. Teak is not *Dalbergia*. Afrormosia (*Pericopsis elata*), the closer visual cousin, is Appendix II. Iroko (*Milicia*) is the African lookalike, not listed like rosewood, still a Lacey name problem if the crate says teak. A specifier who writes “sustainable teak” and means iroko has written a false binomial. A specifier who writes *Tectona* and attaches country plus certificate has written a sentence a customs officer can read.
## What a plantation shop can and cannot do
Silica still dulls. Oil still wants wiping before glue, even when there is less of it. Outdoor design still fails if it ponds. Stainless or bronze still belong in weather. The plantation board does not repeal the dockyard manners. It changes the color, the oil, and the politics.
Wide plantation flatsawns will move like other ring-porous hardwoods. Teak’s stability is excellent, not magic. A glued-up table top still wants a finish on both faces and a base that lets it shrink. Breadboard ends still need slotted screws. Campaign knockdown fittings still make sense for a piece that will travel; they are not a green badge. Deck caulking still wants heartwood and a seam, not a plantation veneer on a yacht-interior plywood. A “sustainable teak deck” that is a 3 mm face on a foam core is a photograph of a deck. Name the core.
Plantation sawyers often slab for yield. You get more wide boards by flatsawing. The cathedrals on a plantation table are a cut, not a grade. Quartersawn plantation teak exists; it is quieter and dearer, the same geometry the glossary already explained for oak. Specify the cut if the face matters. Specify heartwood if the weather matters. Sapwood on a plantation rail is common because the rotations are short. A wide pale band on the end grain is the mill leaving money in the board.
Substitutes belong on the invoice. Rubberwood (*Hevea*) with a toner is an indoor plantation wood, often a retired rubber tree, useful and honest if named. It is not outdoor teak. White oak is the domestic outdoor furniture wood. Robinia is the temperate bench wood. Neither looks like teak. Both last if designed to drain. A designer who wants the honey interior color without tropical papers is looking at walnut, or at an antique *Tectona* already in the country, or at a named veneer with a core you can see.
Reclaimed dock and warehouse teak — demolition beams, old decking — is a third supply that vendors fold into the sustainability sentence. Some of it is the folklore grade. Some of it is painted, nailed, and oily in ways that fight glue. Metal in old decks ruins saws. A detector pass and a named demolition, not a mood. Reclaimed is not plantation and not a CITES workaround. It is a used board. Say so. A “reclaimed Burma teak” coffee table at a funny price may be new plantation with a wire-brush. Look at the fastener holes. Look at whether they go through or stop at the face.
## How to read a tag
Look at the rings. Count them on the end grain if the mill left you an end. Look at the oil in a fresh scratch. Look at the sapwood band. Then look at the paper: binomial, country, certificate, and whether the claim is solid, veneer, or mixed. Figure 5 will not show teak in a CITES color. That absence is information. It is not a free pass.
On a 1960 Copenhagen sideboard: older supply, oil, a honey that has gone brown; papers may be a later reconstruction. On a 1995 patio set: plantation, stainless screws, a grey face if anyone left it out. On a new “Burma teak” dining table at a funny price: ask which forest, which year, which permit. On a crate of “sustainable outdoor furniture”: open the declaration. Arkansas does not grow teak. The local outdoor ethic is white oak or cypress. The plantation ethic, if you want this tree, is a named farm and a paper trail, not a mood.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (teak; plantation mention). Kukachka FPL-125. CITES Species+ (negative for *Tectona*; *Pericopsis*, *Dalbergia*, *Swietenia* for contrast). USDA APHIS Lacey Phase VII. FSC / PEFC chain-of-custody (private, not law). TRAFFIC / national Myanmar–Indonesia export notes `[CITE NEEDED]`. Dutch Java plantation history `[CITE NEEDED: a named forestry monograph]`.
See: `teak-colonial-dockyards`, `teak-deck-and-garden`, `cites-dalbergia-2017`, `cites-swietenia-permits`, `conservation-today`, `iroko-teak-lookalikes`.

item.title: Reclaimed oak beams
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Reclaimed oak beams
A tithe-barn tie beam lands on a bandsaw. The first cut shows a square nail, then a black ring where the nail’s iron met tannin, then a mortise that once held a brace with a draw-bored pin. The mill is not making a beam. It is making a table top from a joint that already had a life. Reclaimed oak is a real furniture wood. It is also a salvage claim that can be a barn, a mill, a warehouse, or a container of mixed hardwood with a story stapled to it. Chinnery’s joined furniture and Albion’s naval oak are the earlier lives some of these balks actually had. Most barn beams in the American market are nineteenth-century house and farm carpentry: *Quercus alba* or a red-group cousin, pegged and notched, not a 1565 wainscot and not a man-of-war knee.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
![Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/timeline.svg)
*Figure 1. Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.*
## What the handbook still says after a century in a roof
White oak: Janka about 1,360 lbf, specific gravity 0.68 at 12 percent moisture (FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a). Northern red oak: 1,290 lbf, 0.63. European *Q. robur* / *Q. petraea* sit in the same band `[CITE NEEDED for a single FPL-equivalent]`. A beam that sat dry in a roof for a hundred years is not a different species. It is a different moisture history. The *Wood Handbook* (ch. 4) still owns the movement: tangential shrinkage larger than radial; a flatsawn face cups; a quartered face stays quieter. Figure 4 is the hardness scatter. Figure 1 is the long trade strip. Reclaimed stock is not on that strip as a milestone. It is a second use of woods the strip already named.
Tyloses in white-oak heartwood still plug pores. A water drop sits. Red oak still drinks. The test works on a freshly cut end if finish has not sealed it. Barn paint and linseed on the old surface will lie. Cut a hidden end.
Ring width tells the stand, not the romance. Slow, even rings can be an old-field American oak or a European import. Wide rings are second growth or a fast site. Dendrochronology can provenance a beam the way Haneca et al. (2005) provenanced art-historical panels. A hang-tag that says “European castle oak” without a ring study is a story. Some beams are European. Some are Ohio. The mortise does not speak Latin.
Metal is the shop fact that overrides romance. Square nails, wire nails, spikes, bolts, plaster keys, a wagon staple, a bullet. Scan or cut slowly. A bandsaw blade that finds a drift becomes a lesson. Iron stains in tannic oak are black and deep; they will not sand out to a clean blonde without taking the face with them. Leave them, or site the cut so they become an edge, not a lake in the middle of a dining leaf.
## Where the beams came from
American barn and mill frames of the nineteenth century are the common supply: white oak and chestnut in some regions (chestnut is a blight story after 1904; a wormy chestnut beam is a different chapter), pine in others. English and Low Countries barns can be *Q. robur*, sometimes with earlier reused ship or house timber in the same frame. Albion’s dockyard oak appears in the salvage market with a frequency that should make a buyer suspicious. A bolt hole and a shipwright’s mark that can be checked are evidence. A burned-in fouled anchor is not.
Heart-pine joists are often sold next to oak beams in the same warehouse. They are *Pinus palustris* or another yellow pine, FPL longleaf about 870 lbf and SG 0.59 — not oak. Loud latewood, resin, orange heart. Name them separately (Outland; Earley). A “reclaimed hardwood beam” pile that mixes the two is a pile, not a specification.
Do not invent a demolition date or a price per board foot. Documented salvage has a building address and a photo of the frame before it came down. Undocumented salvage has a truck.
A warehouse walk is the practical education. Meter the beam: a weathered top face can read several points wetter than the boxed heart after a rain week. Stickers between flitches, a month in the shop’s humidity, then a second reading. Glue on the first reading and the leaf will move after delivery. Smell creosote; if it is there, you are in a sleeper pile, not a barn pile. Sight down a mortise: a clean, unused mortise on all four faces of a “beam” is a machine decoration. An original mortise has crushed fibers, a peg stain, and a direction that made sense in a frame. Photograph it before you slice. The photograph is the provenance the hang-tag will not be.
Furniture use is a late fashion: dining tables from joists, mantel beams that never held a roof, “live-edge” slabs from boxed hearts that still want to check. Some of it is honest reuse. A mortise in the underside of a table is a good tell. Some of it is new oak stained with tea and iron to fake the tannin stain. End grain and a moisture meter end that argument faster than a story.
## Joinery
The beam’s original joints are carpentry: mortise and tenon with a peg, sometimes draw-bored; lap dovetails at a plate; a birdsmouth; a scarf. Those joints are large. They were cut for a load and a building movement, not for a dining chair. When you slice the beam into furniture, you cut through that grammar. The peg hole becomes a void in a table top. Fill it with an oak plug of similar ring, leave it as a witness, or site the leaf so the hole is off the plate. Do not fill it with epoxy tinted as “character” if you are claiming a clean furniture face — or do, and say so.
New furniture joints in reclaimed oak are ordinary joints in a harder, often more brittle material. Old heart can snap where a new kiln-dried board would bend. Predrill for screws. Draw-bore a new mortise and tenon if you want the old manners; the fiber still crushes, but a dry, case-hardened surface can split if the offset is greedy.
Frame-and-panel remains the polite way to use unstable flatsawn slices from a boxed heart. A slab table from a whole beam is a bet against the cut geometry in the glossary: the boxed heart wants to check along the pith. Many “beam tables” keep the pith and then act surprised. Cut the heart out, or live with the check, or spline it and admit the spline.
Breadboard ends on a reclaimed leaf must slot. The beam may have a moisture gradient from a weathered face to a protected heart. Let the stock sit at the destination humidity. A barn in January and a kitchen in July are not the same kiln.
Veneering a slice of beam face onto a stable ground is a way to keep the iron stain and the peg witness without a 40 mm cupping slab. Name the ground. A beam photograph on MDF is not reclaimed oak.
Through-tenons and visible pegs on a new base under a reclaimed top are a choice. They are not proof the top is old. Stickley’s visible pin is an Arts and Crafts religion; a barn peg is a carpentry leftover. Do not confuse them on a hang-tag.
## Conservation
Taking a listed barn apart for dining tables is a loss of a building. Taking a collapsed barn apart after a survey is reuse. The difference is paperwork and a photograph, not a finish. Oak as a species is not CITES-listed in the American and European mains. Lacey still applies to imported “reclaimed oak” that may be mixed tropical or undocumented hardwood. Ask for the country, the species, and the building if the price depends on the story.
Insect holes: old flight holes in sapwood are common. Active powder is a pile of dust on the warehouse floor. Heartwood is less tasty. Do not buy a beam that is still raining frass.
Lead paint on a mill beam. Creosote on a railway sleeper sold as a “beam” — a different chemistry, a poor indoor furniture wood, a health problem. Sleepers are not barns.
Oak wilt and sudden oak death affect living trees `[CITE NEEDED for current range if you name counties]`. They do not make a dry beam safer or more valuable.
Arkansas white oak still quarters from new logs. A shop that wants flake without a barn story can buy kiln-dried quartered stock and skip the nail. That is the quieter local sentence.
## What to look for
Mortises, pegs, iron stains, a weathered face versus a protected one, metal on a scan, ring width, tyloses on a fresh end, a documented address. A perfectly even “aged” color on all four faces of a beam is a stain. A moisture reading above the room’s equilibrium is a wait, not a glue-up.
Haneca’s method can still be applied to a panel sliced from a European beam. A castle on the invoice cannot.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a and ch. 4. Haneca et al., *JAS* 32 (2005), for provenance method. Chinnery, *Oak Furniture* (the joints the beams sometimes reused). Albion, *Forests and Sea Power* (dockyard claims). Outland; Earley (heart pine mixed into the same warehouses). Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*. Williams, *Americans and Their Forests* (barn and farm timber geography).
See: `english-oak-great-furniture`, `navy-oak-reserves`, `quartersawn-arts-crafts`, `baltic-oak-renaissance`, `conservation-today`.

item.title: Quartersawn oak and Arts and Crafts
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Quartersawn oak and Arts and Crafts
Gustav Stickley’s Craftsman Workshops at Eastwood, on the edge of Syracuse, hung white oak in a tent with aqueous ammonia. The tree’s tannin went brown in the fiber, not only in the pore. Ray flake — the silver grain English joiners already knew from riven wainscot — went darker or lighter than the ground, depending on the board. *The Craftsman* (1901–1916) published the settle and the library table as if the reader already knew the tent. William Morris, in *Hopes and Fears for Art* (1882) and in the practice of Morris & Co., had already set oak and the visible joint against ebonized mahogany pretence. The fashion of 1900 is a sawing choice and a chemistry choice. Figure 3 is the sawing. The tent is the chemistry.
![Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.](../assets/grain-cuts/sawn-orientation.svg)
*Figure 3. Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.*
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## Why oak, why that face
They wanted a northern hardwood that was not mahogany’s empire and not walnut’s Victorian parlor. Oak was local or could be, tannic, visible in the grain, and old in the English floor. Quartersawn stock shows the medullary rays as flake and moves less in width than a flatsawn board (FPL-GTR-190, ch. 4: tangential shrinkage commonly about one and a half to two times radial). Settles and library tables wanted wide, quiet faces. Flatsawn Mission exists. It was the cheaper line. Collectors still sort by flake.
White oak (*Quercus alba* and the white group): specific gravity about 0.68, Janka about 1,360 lbf at 12 percent (FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a). Tyloses plug the heartwood pores. That is why tight cooperage attaches to white oak, and why a fume has tannin to react with. Northern red oak (*Q. rubra*): SG about 0.63, Janka about 1,290 lbf. Open pores. You can blow through a straight red-oak end grain. Stain floods. Fuming is less dramatic. The shops that cared specified white. Figure 4 places both among the anchors. European *Q. robur* and *Q. petraea* have the same ray anatomy; a single FPL Janka wants a bench citation `[CITE NEEDED]`. Slow-grown English or Baltic oak is often finer than a wide-ringed second-growth American board. The binomial does not tell you the ring count.
Maple will not fume the same way. A “fumed” maple is a stain. Ash will take a brown; it is not oak’s tannin story.
Haneca et al. (2005) and the Gdansk wainscot trade explain why a radial oak face was already dear in 1565. Gillows could pay nearly mahogany prices for Danzig oak in 1740 (Bowett, provincial woods). Stickley did not invent quartering. He made the flake the badge of a factory that wanted to look like a guild.
## Eastwood, Sapperton, East Aurora
Eastwood made the American object most people mean by Mission: a settle or a library table in quartersawn white oak, through-tenons with visible pins, corbels under a top, a brown that photographed well. The mill was not a cottage. The catalogues are the proof: models, prices, a finish called fumed.
In the Cotswolds, Ernest Gimson and Sidney and Ernest Barnsley at Sapperton were closer to Morris and farther from a mail-order settle. English oak, visible joints, a finish that was not always a fume. C. F. A. Voysey’s designs — the owl suite is the postcard — used oak as a northern moral wood. Charles Limbert’s factory in Grand Rapids and then Holland, Michigan, cut cutouts into oak that was sometimes lighter, sometimes more Mackintosh than Eastwood. Elbert Hubbard’s Roycroft shops at East Aurora, New York, made a heavier, more hammered oak. The Prairie school overlapped: oak interiors that were architecture. Lesser Mission factories from Indiana to the Pacific coast flooded the catalogues after 1905. Collectors still sort by flake, by hardware, by the red decal on a drawer.
Golden oak of the 1890s — often quartersawn, often a yellow-brown varnish, pores filled — is a cousin, more factory, more Renaissance-revival leftover. Do not collapse it into Stickley. A filled golden-oak sideboard and a fumed 1910 settle are both oak. They are not the same finish religion.
Museum holdings — the Art Institute of Chicago, the Dallas Museum of Art, Winterthur’s Mission pieces — are where an unstripped surface still teaches. A dealer’s “refinished Stickley” is often a darker, thicker thing than Eastwood shipped.
Do not invent a catalogue price. *The Craftsman* printed them; quote a plate only with the issue in hand `[CITE NEEDED for any dollar figure]`.
## Joinery
Through-tenons with visible pins are the American Craftsman signature. Draw-boring is older than Stickley; Chinnery’s oak stools already pulled a shoulder with an offset pin. Eastwood made the pin a show face. The pin can be oak or a darker walnut. A steel dowel with a wood cap is a later cheat unless named. Historic tenons often sit flush or a hair proud. A tenon that looks like a hat is a reproduction flourish. Proud tenons get knocked.
Corbels under a top are brackets, often through-tenoned or screwed from above. The top itself must still move. Buttons, slots, or a cleat that does not glue across a wide quartered leaf — quartered moves less, not zero. A library table with a top screwed tight around the perimeter will split on a heating season the same as a Jacobean board.
Frame-and-panel doors on sideboards: groove, floating panel, often a quartered panel so the flake is the door. Raised panels are less the Mission language than a flat field and a square edge. Limbert’s cutouts are pierced flats; they want even, quartered or rift stock so the void does not wander across a cathedral.
Seat frames and settle rails are mortised. Glue blocks hide in corners. Hardness at 1,360 lbf lets a slender Mission rail span farther than a pine rail; it does not excuse a missing stretcher on a cheap factory cousin.
Hardware: hammered copper and iron on American pieces; quieter iron on many English ones. A bright brass knob on a 1910 settle is usually a replacement.
Fumed finish is not a joint, but it is shop work. Ammonia vapor, a tent or a chamber, color that keeps changing after the tent comes down. Sunlight still moves the brown. Clients who want a 1905 settle matched to a new leaf must be told that the next two years are part of the finish. Ammonia is dangerous. Ventilation is not a suggestion. Test boards from the same tree if you can. The latewood and the ray will not go the same brown. That is the point.
A morning in that tent is a chemistry shift you can smell before you can see. Boards hung on edge, a tray of aqueous ammonia, a wait measured in hours, not a wipe of pigment. When the flaps open, the oak is already brown and still not finished changing. Gimson’s bench at Sapperton was a quieter room: a visible mortise, a finish that might be oil, a piece that did not need a mail-order photograph. Both rooms used the radial face Figure 3 names. One broadcast it. One sat with it.
## The scratch test and the pore
Not every brown oak chair is fumed. Many were stained and shellacked. A true fume has color in the wood. A scratch that stays pale is a stain. A scratch that stays brown is in the fiber — or a deep dye. Original finishes are thin. Restoration that pours polyurethane on a 1905 settle is a different object. The pore Stickley left open is a 1910 idea, against the filled golden-oak pore of 1892.
Red oak pretending to be the 1905 catalogue is a common floor. The pore argues. The ray is quieter. The water-drop test on an unseen end still sits on white and sinks on red if the finish has not sealed the question.
Printed “Mission oak” on a fiber core has no end-grain rings. Figure 3 cannot be faked by a photograph.
## Conservation
Oak is not a CITES appendix tree in these mains. The living-forest pressures are high-grading of wide clears, oak wilt and sudden oak death in some regions `[CITE NEEDED for a range map if counties are named]`, and a second-growth ring that will not look like Baltic wainscot. Specify quartered. Specify white. Specify ring if you care.
A 1910 settle is the ethical supply of that look. A new “Stickley” in mixed red oak, stained, is a finish. Arkansas white oak still quarters; the flake is the same anatomy Eastwood wanted, on a wider ring. One sentence is enough.
If you fume now, tell the client the color will keep moving. If you do not fume, do not call the stain a fume.
## What to look for
Flake on a radial face, through-tenons, a pin that is wood, a brown that survives a scratch, thin original film, hammered hardware, a decal, a filled golden-oak cousin that is not the same religion. Morris supplied the English sentence. Stickley supplied the American mill. The ray was already in the tree when a Gdansk splitter sold wainscot. The tent made it a catalogue.
## Sources
Stickley, *The Craftsman*, 1901–1916; *Craftsman Homes*, 1909. Morris, *Hopes and Fears for Art*, 1882. Chinnery, *Oak Furniture* (older draw-bore). Bowett, provincial woods (Danzig oak, 1740). Haneca et al., *JAS* 32 (2005). USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190, ch. 4 and table 5–3a. Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*. Museum holdings: Art Institute of Chicago; Dallas Museum of Art; Winterthur Mission pieces.
See: `english-oak-great-furniture`, `baltic-oak-renaissance`, `reclaimed-oak-beams`, `walnut-baroque`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Flatsawn cathedrals and the floating panel
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Flatsawn cathedrals and the floating panel
A dining-room door that split down a glued-up cathedral in January is a flatsawn lesson. The rings on the end grain run parallel to the face. The width of the door is mostly tangential grain. Tangential shrinkage is the large number in the *Wood Handbook* tables (FPL-GTR-190, ch. 4). The shop that glued the panel into a tight groove, or glued a breadboard across the whole end, asked the wood to be plywood. It is not. Frame-and-panel is not a style. It is manners for a wide board. This draft is the cathedral face: how you get it, what it does in a heated room, and why a panel that can shrink is the old answer.
![Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.](../assets/grain-cuts/sawn-orientation.svg)
*Figure 3. Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.*
## The cut
Flatsawn — plain-sawn, slash-sawn, through-and-through — means the saw runs tangent to the rings. On the face you get arches. Oak and ash make the loudest cathedrals because they are ring-porous; you can count years with a thumbnail. Maple and cherry make quieter ones. Mahogany in the 18th-century solid, Bowett’s cheap Jamaica wood after the Naval Stores Act of 1721 (in force 1722), was often flatsawn because the logs were huge and the shops wanted width for dining tables. A two-board top with matching cathedrals opening away from a glue line is a flatsaw trophy. You can still see the pair on drop-leaf tables in museum collections: the arches are the middle of the tree, split and opened.
Figure 3 is the geometry. Quartersawn boards put the rings nearly perpendicular to the face; the face is radial; oak shows flake. Riftsawn sits at about 30 to 60 degrees: straight stripe, fewer flakes. This chapter is the tangent. The rift and moisture drafts take the other two faces and the numbers.
When pitsaws and later water-powered sash mills took over from riving, flatsawing won on yield. You get more wide boards by slabbing the log. A 16th-century linenfold panel that started as a riven, naturally quartered board can be thin, wide, and stable in a way a cheap 19th-century oak sideboard is not. Baltic wainscot, the *wagenschot* of the Gdansk trade, was typically cleft or sawn to keep the face radial (Haneca et al. 2005). Buyers paid for that. Fashion and thrift later aligned on the cathedral. The circular saw left skip marks on backboards. Rotary veneer is the flatsawn idea taken to a lathe: the log turns, the knife peels a continuous sheet, and the cathedrals repeat at the circumference. That is how a 1950s bedroom suite can have the same arch every eighteen inches. Nature does not clone a ray every foot. A mill does.
## Movement, named as a door
FPL chapter 4 treats tangential shrinkage as commonly about 1.5 to 2 times radial for many hardwoods. White oak’s published green-to-ovendry figures sit near 10.5 percent tangential and 5.6 percent radial (FPL-GTR-190, tables in ch. 4 / species notes). Red oak is quieter on the tangential number and still a problem in a wide door. Hard maple, black walnut, black cherry — each has its own pair. Longitudinal change is a rounding error, on the order of 0.1 to 0.2 percent. You do not design for length. You design for width.
Shrinkage happens below fiber saturation, commonly near 30 percent moisture content. A board at 12 percent, the handbook’s mechanical-test moisture, still has travel left if the room goes to 6 percent in a January apartment. Equilibrium moisture content tracks relative humidity and temperature; FPL’s EMC tables are the shop reference. Period furniture was built for rooms that went cold at night. Central heating and air conditioning reset the average. A flatsawn oak leaf glued up in 1780 at a higher average humidity will shrink across the grain and may split along a glue line or open a rule joint. The door that split in January is that math in paint-grade pine or in show oak.
Cup is the other flatsawn habit. The rings try to flatten. The bark-side face becomes convex as the board dries, in the usual telling; Hoadley walks the geometry in *Understanding Wood*. Chair seats that were flatsawn cup toward the bark side. A table top without battens or breadboards will dish. That is not a defect in the tree. It is the cylinder remembering it was a cylinder.
## Joinery that assumes a cathedral
The groove in a frame-and-panel door is deep enough that a flatsawn oak panel can lose width and still sit. The panel is not glued around the perimeter. A spot of hide glue at the top center, or no glue at all, is the historic habit: the panel can move in the groove, and the show face stays centered. The stiles and rails are often closer to quartered so the frame stays true next to glass or a door edge. If you glue the panel in, you have made a wide flatsawn board with a stiff frame around it. The panel splits, or the frame rackets, or the door goes diamond. The split door in the lede is usually that mistake, or the cousin mistake: a breadboard glued across the whole end.
A breadboard end across a flatsawn top must slot-screw or pin in elongated holes. The center pin or screw can be tight. The outboard fasteners must ride. If the pins are tight at the ends, the top splits. If the breadboard is glued across the whole end, the top splits. Eighteenth-century shops knew this. Some nineteenth-century factories forgot. Some twenty-first-century box stores never learned. Look at the underside. Elongated holes and screws that can slide are evidence. A tight glue line at the breadboard shoulder and a crack in the top are evidence of the other school.
Buttons, table clips, and slotted metal fasteners are the same idea in a carcase: the top is held down and allowed to grow and shrink across its width. Pocket screws in a rigid pattern across a wide flatsawn top are a split waiting for February. Hide glue on a historic joint can be reversed with heat and moisture. Urea-formaldehyde on a factory edge cannot. If you must glue a wide top, glue long-grain to long-grain along the joints and fasten the assembly as if it were still a moving board — because it is.
Draw-boring in oak likes riven or quartered stiles. A flatsawn stile will still take a pin. The cathedral in a door stile is a visual problem more than a joint problem: the arch runs off the edge and the pair of doors will not match. Chair shops that want matching legs buy rift. Door shops that want matching stiles do the same, and they let the panel be the cathedral if the client wants figure.
## Fashion for the arch
Matching cathedrals on a mahogany dining leaf were a pride mark. The two boards came from one flitch, opened like a book. Walnut oyster veneer is a different conversion: end-grain slices, not a flatsawn face, but the same appetite for a picture the tree did not draw as a quartered stripe. Golden-oak factory sideboards of the 1890s often showed loud flatsawn figure under a yellow varnish, pores filled. Stickley’s catalogues wanted the other face — flake — and charged for it. A flatsawn Mission chair is a cheaper cousin. Collectors still sort by the arch versus the ray.
Paint hides species and cut. A pine cupboard with cathedrals under milk paint is still a flatsawn object; the panel still wants to float. Country shops knew. Some reproduction shops glue the panel “so it won’t rattle.” It will not rattle. It will split.
Rotary-cut lauan and printed foil are the industrial cathedral. The repeat gives them away. A 1970 oak suite with the same arch every eighteen inches and no end-grain rings is a photograph. Look at the edge.
## How to see it on a piece you did not make
End grain: rings running across the thickness, parallel to the face, mean flatsawn. If you cannot see the end, look at the face. Cathedrals versus straight stripe plus flake (oak) or ribbon (interlocked tropicals). Wear: cup toward the bark side on a seat; a breadboard whose pins elongated into slots; a door panel that has shrunk and left a line of raw wood in the groove in winter, or swollen and stuck in August.
Period: a 1600 joined chest with ray flake is doing a different job. A 1760 two-board mahogany top with matching arches is this chapter. A 1905 flatsawn oak sideboard is a factory yield choice. A 1970 print is a factory costume.
Cost: flatsawing wastes less of the log than quartering. That is why it won. A true quartersawn white-oak dining table still costs more per foot than a flatsawn one from the same kiln charge. Designers who want the arch should say flatsawn and then say how the width will move. Designers who write “solid oak” and get a cathedral they did not expect have not specified a cut.
Arkansas white oak flatsaws into loud earlywood pores and a stain problem if you wanted quiet. It also flatsaws into a handsome kitchen table if the breadboard is slotted and the finish is honest. The cut is a choice. The split door is what happens when the choice is the face without the manners.
## A glue line that was the middle of the tree
Matching cathedrals are a book-match in the solid. The sawyer opened a flitch and the two faces that had been neighbors became a pair of arches opening left and right. Hide glue along that long-grain joint is the right glue if the piece should come apart. UF along that joint is a factory habit. Either glue will hold the pair as one panel. Neither glue will stop the pair from shrinking as one panel. The split that follows the glue line in January is often the joint starving as the two boards pull. The split that ignores the glue line and runs down an arch is the board itself, usually a too-wet core or a fastener that pinned the width.
Rule joints on drop-leaf tables are the period answer for a flatsawn leaf that will shrink: a molded edge that hides a gap. A later factory that drops a straight butt and a metal hinge on a mahogany leaf will show a light line in winter. The 18th-century shop was not more moral. It had already lost arguments with heated rooms that were less dry than ours.
Look at the groove. If the panel can move, the cathedral can stay. If the panel is a prisoner, the rings will open a crack and tell you so. Figure 3 is the picture. Keep it in your head when a catalogue says “solid oak” and the edge is 0.6 mm of something on a fiber core.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190, ch. 4 (moisture, shrinkage, EMC) and ch. 5 (species notes). Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*. Haneca et al. 2005. Bowett, *The English Mahogany Trade 1700–1793*; provincial woods paper. Chinnery, *Oak Furniture*. Stickley, *The Craftsman* (quartered as the other fashion).
See: `glossary-grain-and-cut`, `rift-cut-flooring`, `moisture-wood-movement`, `quartersawn-arts-crafts`, `veneer-versus-solid`.

item.title: Rift cut, matching legs, and a floor
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Rift cut, matching legs, and a floor
A run of dining-chair legs that do not match is usually a flatsawn run. Two faces show cathedrals. Two faces show something quieter. The set looks like leftovers. Rift cut — rings at about 30 to 60 degrees to the face — gives a straight stripe on all four sides, or close enough that a shop can sell twelve chairs. Yield is worse than slabbing the log. Complaints are fewer. Floors that want a quiet, linear oak without flake are the same cut in a longer piece. This draft is the compromise face: furniture first, then the floor that borrowed the name.
![Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.](../assets/grain-cuts/sawn-orientation.svg)
*Figure 3. Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.*
## The geometry, without poetry
Figure 3 is the cylinder. Flatsawn is tangent: arches, maximum tangential width, the large shrinkage number. Quartersawn is radial: rings on end in the thickness, oak flake, the smaller shrinkage number. Rift is the sector between. Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*, is the shop book. Mills disagree about the exact degrees. Thirty to sixty is the useful band. Below about 30 you start picking up cathedral. Above about 60 you start picking up ray flake in oak. A mill that sells “quartered and rift” as a mixed bundle is telling you to specify flake if you want flake, and to specify rift if you want a run of doors to match.
True quartering wastes the log. Rift wastes less than honest quartering and more than through-and-through. You get narrower boards and more offcuts than a flatsawn pile from the same diameter. That is why Baltic wainscot was dear, why Gillows in Lancaster could pay nearly mahogany prices for Danzig oak in 1740 (Bowett, provincial woods paper), and why rift white-oak flooring still costs more per foot than a plainsawn grade from the same kiln charge. The money is the waste and the extra handling. The product is a stripe that does not argue with its neighbor.
White oak (*Quercus alba* and the white group) is the American furniture and floor wood that made rift famous in catalogues. European oak (*Q. robur*, *Q. petraea*) has the same anatomy. Red oak will rift; the flake you are avoiding is smaller anyway, and the pores are more open. A designer who wants Stickley’s silver grain and writes “rift oak” will get a quiet stripe and a disappointed client. A designer who wants a hotel corridor without flake and writes “QS oak” may get flake in the middle of the run. Say the face.
## Chair legs, door stiles, table aprons
Chair shops like rift for legs that must match. A flatsawn leg is a different picture on adjacent faces. Turned legs show the problem in the round: the rings walk around the cylinder and the turning goes from cathedral to stripe every ninety degrees. Rift stock, chosen so the rings sit on the diagonal of the square, keeps a more even stripe through the turning. You still read the end grain. You still reject a blank that is flatsawn dressed up as rift.
Door stiles in a run of kitchen or cabinet doors are the architectural version. One cathedral in the middle of a set of fifteen is the complaint. Rift stiles and rails, flatsawn or quartered panels if you want figure in the field, is a coherent specification. All-rift doors are quieter. All-flatsawn doors are a cathedral gallery. Mixed “Q&R” from the mill is a lottery.
Table aprons and bed rails want the same evenness if they show. Breadboard ends on a flatsawn top are often rift or quartered so the end cap stays straight while the top moves. The fasteners still need slots. A rift breadboard glued tight across a flatsawn top will split the top the same as a flatsawn breadboard glued tight. Cut does not repeal chapter 4.
FPL-GTR-190, chapter 4, gives the shrinkage ratio — tangential about one and a half to two times radial for many hardwoods. Rift sits between. It is not quartersawn stability and it is not flatsawn travel. A wide rift oak table still moves. Fasten it as if it will. Floating panels, slotted screws, buttons under a top: the manners do not change because the stripe is straight.
## The floor that took the name
“Rift and quartered oak flooring” is a mill grade and a sales phrase. Architects mean: straight grain, minimal flake, or a controlled amount of flake, depending on the sentence. Some specs want rift only — no flake. Some want quartered — flake as a feature. Some accept the mixed bundle and then reject boards on site. Write the face. Write the allowed percentage of cathedral. Write the allowed flake. A flooring bundle labelled Q&R that arrives half plainsawn is a purchasing failure, not a surprise of nature.
Floors move less in service than a wide door because the strips are narrow. A 2¼-inch rift oak strip has little tangential width to argue with. A 7-inch flatsawn plank has a lot. Wide-plank floors in heated apartments cup and gape for the same reason dining tables cup and gape. Species and cut still matter. So does moisture at installation. FPL’s EMC tables and the floor’s own installation instructions (a dated NWFA or mill sheet, not a memory) are the documents. This draft is not an installation manual.
Historic floors were often flatsawn because yield won. Heart-pine floors in the South show loud latewood bands and cathedrals. Quartersawn oak strip of the late 19th and early 20th centuries — the tight, straight, sometimes slightly rayed corridors of better houses — is the cousin of Arts and Crafts furniture. Stickley’s rooms and a rift-cut floor are the same fashion in two planes. Golden-oak factory floors with filled pores are the louder cousin.
Engineered floors with a 2 or 3 mm rift-sliced face on a plywood core are a veneer story. The face can be honest rift oak. The core is the movement control. A 0.6 mm face on MDF is a photograph of rift. Look at the edge. The veneer draft takes that sandwich.
## How mills actually cut it
A sawyer who wants rift can take boards from the sectors of the log that sit between the quartered pie and the flatsawn slab. Some mills quarter the log first and then saw each quarter at an angle. Some use a circular mill and sort after the fact. Some saw-and-sort operations call anything without a loud cathedral “rift.” The ticket should say how the mill defines the word. A 10× lens on the end grain ends the argument: rings at a slant, not parallel to the face, not square-on.
Before the circular saw, riven oak followed the rays and gave you quartered stock, not rift. Rift is a sawn idea. You do not split a log at 45 degrees with a wedge and get a furniture blank. You saw it. That is why rift furniture is a mill-age and factory-age product more than a 1600 joined-chest product. The chest wanted ray. The hotel corridor wants stripe.
Sapele and some *Swietenia* show ribbon when quartered — interlocked grain reversing, not oak flake. “Rift sapele” in a door shop often means a quieter stripe with less ribbon flash. Say what you want. You cannot get oak flake from *Entandrophragma*. You cannot get sapele ribbon from *Quercus*.
## A room, a set, a specification
Walk a dining room. If the chair legs match on all four faces and the table top is a two-board cathedral, someone specified two cuts and paid for both. If the chair legs are a jumble of arches and stripes, someone bought “oak” and hoped. If the floor under them is a straight, quiet oak without flake, it is probably rift or a mixed Q&R that was sorted. If the floor is a cathedral every board, it is plainsawn and cheaper, and it will cup more in a dry season if the boards are wide.
Arkansas white oak rifts well. The rays are there if you quarter; they stay shy if you rift. The same forests that filled American shops in 1800 still yield both cuts, second-growth rings and kiln schedules aside. Specify the face. Specify white if you want tannin and a quieter pore than red. The 1740 Danzig price Bowett recorded was a freight and dryness price as much as a cut price. The modern premium is the waste.
## Nail, tongue, and a dry apartment
Strip flooring hides some of the cut argument because the piece is narrow. It does not hide a moisture argument. Install at the destination EMC. A rift oak floor laid at 12 percent in a shop and moved into a 6 percent apartment will gape. The gaps will be even if the cut is even; they will still be gaps. Wide-plank rift is not a repeal. A 7-inch rift plank has less tangential travel than a 7-inch flatsawn plank and more than a 2¼-inch strip. Fasten it as a moving board: cleats, a floating engineered core, or a nail pattern the mill’s dated sheet allows. Glue-down of a solid wide plank on a concrete slab is a split-door idea in another plane.
Chair legs next to that floor should match each other, not the floor. A rift floor and flatsawn legs is a coherent room if you meant it. A mixed bundle in both is a room that happened. Specify twice.
A factory that grades rift by the face photograph, without an end-grain check, will ship you a flatsawn board whose cathedral is shy. Reject it on the dock. The 10× lens is cheaper than the callback. Hoadley’s cylinder does not care about the grade stamp.
Look at the end of a leg and the end of a floorboard. Rings on the diagonal: rift. Rings parallel to the face: flat. Rings through the thickness: quartered. No rings, only a photograph: factory. Figure 3 is the picture. The moisture draft is the numbers. This page is why a set of chairs and a corridor cost more when they match.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190, ch. 4–5. Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*. Bowett, “Furniture woods in London and provincial furniture 1700–1800.” Haneca et al. 2005 (radial wainscot as the other historic premium). Stickley catalogues (flake versus the quiet stripe). NWFA / mill installation sheets (floors; verify the dated sheet you use).
See: `glossary-grain-and-cut`, `flatsawn-panel-figure`, `quartersawn-arts-crafts`, `moisture-wood-movement`, `veneer-versus-solid`.

item.title: Moisture, movement, and a stuck door
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Moisture, movement, and a stuck door
A door that sticks in August and shows a line of raw wood in the groove in January is chapter 4 of the *Wood Handbook* hung on hinges. Wood is a sponge with a grain. Below the fiber saturation point — commonly near 30 percent moisture content — loss or gain of bound water changes the dimensions across the grain. Tangential change is the large number. Radial is smaller, often by a factor of 1.5 to 2. Longitudinal change is a rounding error, 0.1 to 0.2 percent (FPL-GTR-190, ch. 4). The door is flatsawn in the panel and closer to quartered in the stiles if the shop was paying attention. If the shop glued the panel in, the door is a split waiting for the heating season. This draft is the moisture math and the joinery that assumes it.
![Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.](../assets/grain-cuts/sawn-orientation.svg)
*Figure 3. Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.*
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## What FPL chapter 4 actually says
Green wood can hold more water than its ovendry weight. Free water sits in the cell cavities. Bound water sits in the cell walls. Fiber saturation is the point where the cavities are empty and the walls are still saturated. Shrinkage and swelling, for practical shop work, begin there. The handbook’s mechanical tables — Janka, modulus, the numbers on Figure 4 — are reported at 12 percent moisture, a convention, not a magic room. A bone-dry antique pine table can feel harder than a damp oak board. Moisture first, then species.
Equilibrium moisture content is the moisture the wood will approach in a given relative humidity and temperature. FPL’s EMC tables are the reference. A shop at 70 °F and 50 percent RH is looking at something near 9 percent EMC `[CITE NEEDED: exact FPL table row if you quote a single pair]`. A January apartment with forced air and no humidifier can run much drier. A coastal August can run wetter. Period houses went cold at night and the average moisture in a chest sat higher than in a 2010 condominium. A flatsawn oak leaf glued up in 1780 will shrink across the grain in that condominium. It may split along a glue line or open a rule joint. Quartersawn leaves suffer less cup, not zero movement.
Published green-to-ovendry shrinkages, from the handbook’s species notes, are the working table:
| Species | Radial % | Tangential % | | --- | --- | --- | | White oak | 5.6 | 10.5 | | Red oak | 4.0 | 8.6 | | Sugar maple | 4.8 | 9.9 | | Black walnut | 5.5 | 7.8 | | Black cherry | 3.7 | 7.1 | | Eastern white pine | 2.1 | 7.4 | | Honduran mahogany | ~3.7 | ~5.1 |
Mahogany’s pair is the imported-woods / Kukachka tradition (FPL-125 and later handbook notes). Treat a single decimal as a mean, not your board. The ratio is the lesson. Flatsawn white oak is a wide traveler. Quartersawn white oak is a narrower traveler. Mahogany in the solid was prized in part because the pair is modest for a furniture hardwood. Wide tables still need to float. Figure 3 is why the cut multiplies whatever the species already wants to do.
Dimensional-change coefficients in chapter 4 let you estimate movement between two moisture contents without going all the way to ovendry. The shop version: a 24-inch flatsawn white-oak panel changing 4 percent moisture can move on the order of a quarter inch `[CITE NEEDED: show the handbook coefficient arithmetic if you publish a single fraction]`. That is a groove depth, or a split.
## Joinery that treats moisture as a fact
Frame-and-panel: the groove is deep enough that the panel can lose width and still sit. A spot of hide glue at the top center, or no glue, keeps the show face centered. Glue around the perimeter and you have invented a split door. The stiles and rails, closer to quartered, stay truer next to glass.
Breadboard ends: center fastener tight, outboard fasteners in elongated holes. Glue the tongue at the middle if you must. Glue the whole end and the top splits. Look at the underside of a 1790 table. Slots are evidence of manners. A crack in line with a tight pin is evidence of the other school.
Slotted screws through battens or pocket-screw patterns that all point the same way across a wide top are a factory shortcut that sometimes works and sometimes waits for February. Buttons and table clips are the cabinetmaker’s version: hold-down with travel.
Hide glue on a historic carcase can be taken apart with heat and moisture. The joint is a reversible contract. Urea-formaldehyde on a factory edge is not. A hide-glue mahogany chair can be repaired. A UF-glued breadboard that split the top is a different object. Choose the glue for the life you want, then design the joint for the moisture you will get.
Veneer assumes a ground. Hide glue on deal or yellow-poplar is the historic sandwich. If the ground moves and the glue goes brittle, the face checks — crotch mahogany on poplar in American Empire is the textbook failure. A plywood ground is the 20th-century sandwich: cross-bands cancel movement. A paper foil on particleboard is a photograph. The veneer draft takes the sandwich. This draft is why the sandwich was invented.
## Heat, air conditioning, and a finish
Finish slows moisture exchange. It does not stop it. A film on one face only — a table finished on top and raw underneath — is a cupping machine. Finish both sides. Hoadley says so. Old shops that waxed the underside were not being precious.
A finish that seals the end grain more than the face will still lose the argument at the ends first if the board was wet. End-grain sealer at the mill is a drying practice. It is not a substitute for acclimation. Let the wood sit at the humidity of the destination before you glue a wide panel. The 18th-century shop did this by having the boards in the building. The modern shop does it with a meter and a calendar. A pin meter in the middle of a 12/4 oak balk can lie if the shell is dry and the core is not. Read the core.
Kiln schedules exist because air-drying to furniture moisture takes time and still leaves a gradient. Second-growth Arkansas oak with wide rings dries differently from tight Baltic wainscot. The handbook’s species notes give starting points, not a recipe for your charge.
## Species on Figure 4, read as movers
Figure 4 is hardness and density, not shrinkage. Density and movement are related but they are not the same graph. Mahogany is moderately light and a modest mover. White oak is heavier and a large tangential mover. Ebony and rosewood are heavy and still move across the grain; they just do it as small objects. Pine is light; eastern white pine’s tangential number is not small (7.4 percent green to ovendry). A wide pine cupboard door is a traveler. Paint does not stop it. The panel still floats.
Interlocked tropicals (sapele, some elm) add tearout to the moisture story. The board may be stable enough on the quarter and still chatter under a plane. Workability is the next draft. Moisture is why you do not glue the panel even when the plane is happy.
## A walk around the stuck door
August: the flatsawn panel has swollen. The groove was not deep enough, or a bead of paint locked the edge, or the shop glued the panel. The door rubs the jamb. January: the panel has shrunk. A line of unfinished wood shows in the groove, or a split has opened down a cathedral, or a breadboard has torn the top. End grain on the panel: rings parallel to the face. End grain on a well-chosen stile: rings more nearly through the thickness. That is Figure 3 on a hinge.
Look at tabletops with breadboards. If the pins elongated into slots, someone understood tangential movement. If the breadboard split the top, someone did not. Look at a 2010 condominium dining table with pocket screws every four inches across a 42-inch flatsawn oak top. Look for the crack.
Arkansas shops send furniture into houses with air conditioning. The destination EMC is the design number, not the mill’s 12 percent sticker. Oak and walnut still move. Domestic is not a repeal of chapter 4. Specify cut, specify acclimation, specify the joint that travels. The Convention of 1973 will not float your panel. Neither will a Janka number.
## Hide glue, UF, and a panel that should rattle
A floating panel that rattles in January is doing its job. A bead of hide glue at the top center is enough to stop the rattle in a show door without imprisoning the width. A bead of UF around four sides is a split. The glue is a tool. Hoadley will say the joint is a moisture joint first. Conservators prefer hide on objects that should come apart. Factories prefer UF because the clamp time is short and the joint is “forever.” Forever on a wide flatsawn panel is a crack.
Veneer grounds are the other moisture object. A yellow-poplar drawer front moves. A crotch leaf on it does not want to. Cross-banding under the face — a historic ébéniste habit and later a factory habit — is a thin plywood idea before plywood. If you skip the cross-band and glue a leaf to a flatsawn solid ground, you are betting the hide glue will creep enough. Sometimes it does. Sometimes you get the Empire check.
Look at the groove and the slots. If they have room, the door will stick less and split less. If they do not, January will write the rest of this chapter on the face. FPL chapter 4 is the text. The door is the problem set.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (2010), ch. 4 (moisture, FSP, EMC, shrinkage, coefficients); ch. 5 species notes; imported-woods / Kukachka FPL-125 (mahogany pair). FPL-GTR-282 (2021) where it supersedes. Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*. Bowett (mahogany tables as wide flatsawn leaves). Chinnery, *Oak Furniture* (frame-and-panel as manners).
See: `glossary-grain-and-cut`, `flatsawn-panel-figure`, `rift-cut-flooring`, `janka-hardness-explained`, `veneer-versus-solid`.

item.title: Janka hardness, a steel ball, 12 percent
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Janka hardness, a steel ball, 12 percent
A pine tavern table dents under a buckle. A sugar-maple counter does not. The laboratory version of that observation is a steel ball, 0.444 inch in diameter, pressed into the side of a specimen to half its diameter. The load, in pounds-force, is the Janka side hardness. The USDA Forest Products Laboratory reports it at 12 percent moisture content (*Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190, tables 5–3a and following; Green, Begel, and Nelson, FPL-RN-0303, on nonstandard specimens). The number is an average. Your board is a sample of one. This draft is what the ball measures, what it does not, and why a dining table and a floor cite the same test for different reasons.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## Side hardness, not a moral ranking
The test is a dent test. It is not modulus of rupture, not shear, not “strength” in the beam sense. A wood can be hard and brittle, or softer and tough. Elm is the furniture reminder: not the hardest seat, but a seat that will not split out to the rim when you drive a tapered leg (Evans, *Windsor-Chair Making in America*). Janka does not tell you that. Specific gravity does not fully tell you that. The job does.
FPL’s convention is side hardness at 12 percent MC. End hardness is a different, usually higher number; shops that quote one figure almost always mean side. Moisture moves the number. A wet board dents easier. A bone-dry antique pine table can feel harder than a damp oak board. The moisture draft is the first chapter. This one assumes 12 percent because that is how the tables were built.
Green, Begel, and Nelson (FPL-RP-643) showed you can estimate Janka from specific gravity for many species. The scatter is real. Figure 4 is that scatter for ten anchors in this series. Density and hardness travel together. They are not the same point.
Working means, from FPL tables and the imported-woods / Kukachka tradition, as the series has already used them:
| Species | Janka (lbf, side, 12% MC) | SG (approx.) | | --- | --- | --- | | Eastern white pine | 380 | 0.35 | | Yellow-poplar | 540 | 0.42 | | Honduran mahogany | ~800 | 0.45–0.50 | | Black cherry | 950 | 0.50 | | Black walnut | 1,010 | 0.55 | | White oak | 1,360 | 0.68 | | White ash | 1,320 | 0.60 | | Sugar maple | 1,450 | 0.63 | | Shagbark hickory | 1,820 | 0.72 | | Teak (imported notes) | ~1,070 | ~0.55–0.66 |
Treat imported figures as handbook-or-compilation means. Brazilian rosewood and Gabon ebony sit off the right of Figure 4 — Janka compilations well above 2,000 and 3,000 lbf — and they are not structural table woods in the way oak is. A fingernail into an underside arris is crude and useful: pine yields, maple barely does, teak is oily and confusing, old finish lies.
## What a furniture shop does with the number
Dent resistance on a show top and a floor is the honest use. A maple butcher block and a pine blanket chest are different objects. A client who wants a dining table that takes a laptop and a belt buckle without a gallery of dents is asking for a number north of cherry, or for a finish that can be revived, or for a habit of using mats. The number does not choose. It ranks.
Chair stretchers and legs care more about section and grain than about a hundred Janka points. Mahogany at ~800 lbf made a slender splat possible not because it is hard but because the fiber is even enough to pierce and stable enough to stay thin (Symonds, quoted and complicated by Bowett). Hard maple at 1,450 will take a turned bead and fight a gouge. Soft maple is a different row. “Maple” on an invoice without hard or soft is a hardness problem.
Floors cite Janka more aggressively than furniture shops. A 2,000-lbf exotic and a 1,360-lbf white oak are sold as a ranking. Wide-plank flatsawn oak at 1,360 will still dent under a stiletto if the finish is thin and the heel is small. The test ball is larger than a heel point. Localized denting is not the table mean. Species with large earlywood pores (red oak, ash) can crush in the pore band even when the latewood is hard. The ball averages a small circle. A floor averages years of chairs.
Workability is not Janka. Silica in teak dulls edges on a wood that is only moderately hard. Interlocked sapele at a Janka near 1,410 (Wood Database compilation; check FPL before treating it as law) chatters under a plane. Hoadley is the shop book for that. The workability draft takes the tools. Hardness is why a pine plane shaving is easy and a hickory one is work. It is not why the sapele tears.
## History did not use the ball
Macquoid did not rank Ages by Janka. Shops ranked by the tool in hand and the dent in service. Oak for joined chests. Walnut for veneer and for American solids. Mahogany after 1722 because it was cheap enough to carve in the solid, not because a laboratory existed. Beech for Thonet because it steam-bends, with a Janka near 1,300 that nobody in 1859 wrote down. The ball is a 20th-century way to put a number on a 16th-century observation: some woods mark, some woods don’t.
Secondary woods are the other ranking. Yellow-poplar at 540 lbf lined Philadelphia drawers because it was cheap, stable enough, and light. You lift the drawer. Solid oak drawer sides make a chest that fights you. Janka predicts the dent on the arris. Density predicts the lift. Both belong on the specification.
## Limits, and a dent you can see
The test is on clear, straight-grained specimens when the handbook means what it says. Your knot, your interlock, your juvenile wood, your 8 percent or 14 percent moisture, your flatsawn face with a pore band — those are not the specimen. Green, Begel, and Nelson’s nonstandard-specimen note exists because people keep testing flooring scraps and small pieces. The correlation holds in the large. A single shop test with a homemade ball is a story, not a table.
Finish changes the felt hardness. A thick film hides a soft face until the film breaks. Oil on pine does not. A 1980s stain can make maple look like walnut; it does not make it dent like walnut. Fumed oak is a color reaction, not a hardness change.
CITES does not care about Janka. *Dalbergia* on Appendix II (2 January 2017, Annotation #15 revised 2019) and *Swietenia macrophylla* on Appendix II (15 November 2003, Annotation #6) are permit woods whether they dent or not. Lacey 2008 §8204 and APHIS Phase VII (1 December 2024) want a binomial, not a ball test. Hardness will not get a crate through Savannah.
## How to use Figure 4 in a room
Stand a pine tavern table next to a maple counter. Press a thumbnail into an unseen arris. That is the test without the machine. Then look at the job. A show top that must stay clean: maple, oak, hickory, or a finish you will renew. A carved splat: mahogany or walnut, and a section that forgives the gouge. A Windsor seat: elm, for split resistance you cannot read on Figure 4. A blanket chest: pine, and an honest expectation of dents.
Arkansas white oak, maple, hickory, cherry, and walnut cover most of the table. The number on the wall is FPL’s, at 12 percent, side hardness. Your board will vary. Specify the species and the job. Do not specify “hardwood” and hope the ball is on your side.
## Floors, counters, and a number that got advertised
Flooring catalogues made Janka a consumer word. Furniture catalogues mostly did not. That is why a client now asks whether a cherry table is “hard enough” and expects a single integer. Cherry at 950 lbf is a fine dining top if the house will accept a few marks and a finish that can be cut back. It is a poor shipping counter. Maple at 1,450 is a shipping counter that will still mark under a dropped can, because the ball is not a can edge. Hickory at 1,820 is the domestic top of Figure 4 and a wood that fights a plane. Specify the abuse, then pick the row.
End hardness, when FPL reports it, runs higher than side hardness. A chair leg’s end grain on a dirt floor is not the dining-table face. Do not borrow the end number to sell a top. Green, Begel, and Nelson’s nonstandard-specimen note exists because flooring scraps keep getting tested as if they were the handbook’s clear side-grain block. The correlation is good enough for a mill. It is not a certificate for your plank.
Moisture at test is 12 percent. A floor at 6 percent in January will dent a little less and gape a little more. A floor at 14 percent in a wet crawlspace will dent more and cup. The Janka table does not replace the moisture draft. Read both.
A pine tavern table at 380 lbf and a maple counter at 1,450 are the two ends of a room people already know by touch. The ball is how a mill writes that touch down. It is not how a shop chooses elm for a Windsor seat, or mahogany for a splat, or hide glue for a chair that should come apart. Use the number for dents. Use the species chapter for the rest.
Look at the dent that is already there. A buckle mark in pine is the species doing its job. A crushed earlywood pore in red oak is the anatomy doing its job. A maple top with no marks after ten years is either a careful house or a hard row on the table. Figure 4 is the map. The ball is 0.444 inch. The room is larger.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190, ch. 5 tables 5–3a ff.; imported-woods chapter. Green, Begel, and Nelson, FPL-RN-0303; FPL-RP-643. Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*. Evans, *Windsor-Chair Making in America*. Bowett / Symonds on mahogany and the splat. Wood Database compilations for tropicals not in the FPL domestic tables — cite as compilations.
See: `density-weight-shipping`, `moisture-wood-movement`, `workability-hand-tools`, `intro-500-year-timber`.

item.title: Density, freight, and a crate that argues
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Density, freight, and a crate that argues
A cubic foot of eastern white pine at handbook specific gravity 0.35 weighs on the order of 22 pounds at 12 percent moisture. A cubic foot of white oak at SG 0.68 weighs on the order of 47. A cubic foot of Gabon ebony, specific gravity near or above 1.0 in the compilations, is a crate that argues with the longshoreman and with the scale. Freight has always been part of furniture fashion. Thomas Ripley told the Admiralty that mahogany would be cheaper than deal or wainscot if Navy ships brought it home (Bowett, *Georgian Group Journal*, 1997). The wood was light enough, once the duty was gone, to carve in the solid. This draft is density as a shop number and as a shipping number. Figure 4 is the scatter. Figure 1 is the long trade that paid for the weight.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
![Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/timeline.svg)
*Figure 1. Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.*
## What the handbook means by specific gravity
FPL reports specific gravity on an ovendry-mass / volume-at-stated-moisture basis. The furniture tables commonly use volume at 12 percent. Basic specific gravity uses green volume. They are not interchangeable. A designer who writes “density 0.68” without saying which basis has written a muddle. The series follows the handbook’s 12 percent convention unless a note says basic SG.
Pounds per cubic foot at 12 percent is roughly SG × 62.4 × (a moisture adjustment). Shop shorthand: multiply SG by 62 and you are close enough to lift a board in your head. White pine ~22 lb/ft³. Yellow-poplar ~26. Mahogany ~28–31. Cherry ~31. Walnut ~34. White oak ~42–47. Hickory ~45–50. Those are means. Your balk varies. Heartwood versus sap, ring width, moisture above or below 12 percent — the scale will tell you.
Janka travels with density on Figure 4. Green, Begel, and Nelson (FPL-RP-643) estimated hardness from specific gravity. The scatter is why we still print both axes. Mahogany is the useful outlier in furniture history: moderately light, moderately hard, carvable. Ebony and rosewood are the other end: heavy, hard, used as small objects and veneers because a solid table is a freight and money problem.
