Moisture changes the weight more obviously than it changes the SG basis. A green oak balk can hold more water than its ovendry mass. Ship green and you pay for water. The Baltic wainscot trade paid for dryness as well as for the radial cut (Haneca et al. 2005; KNOB “driest wainscots” literature). That is a density story: water is dense. A kiln schedule is a freight schedule.
## Freight as style
English oak furniture of 1550 is not simply English oak. Gdansk wainscot moved west because the boards were worth the Sound toll: slow-grown, radially converted, dry enough. Weight per useful face was the product. Deal from the Baltic was the light, cheap cousin — pine and spruce for backs, painted furniture, and the insides of finer things. Ripley’s mahogany sentence is the Atlantic version. Jamaica wood after the Naval Stores Act of 1721 (in force 1722) rode Navy freight and a duty cut. A wood that is too heavy for its price stays a curiosity. Lignum vitae, already in the 1660 Book of Rates, made sheaves and mallets, not dining tables.
Rosewood pianos and ebony cabinets are luxury because the wood is scarce and because a little of it goes a long way by weight. A solid *Dalbergia* dining table that is truly the genus is heavy in the room and loud at the border after 2 January 2017. A solid Gabon ebony chest would be a monster. Veneer is how you ship the picture without shipping the cubic foot.
Thonet’s No. 14 (V&A W.31-2011) is six pieces of steamed beech. Beech is not light. The chair is light because the sections are small. Aalto’s birch laminate and the Eames plywood seats are density managed by thickness and by glue. Particleboard is dense in the wrong way: heavy, cheap, a kitchen wall that fights you when you move house. The engineered chapter takes the panel. This chapter is why the panel feels like a bag of cement.
## A crate on a dock, weighed
Picture two crates of equal outside volume. One is eastern white pine drawer stuff. One is white oak flooring. The oak crate can be double the pine on the scale. Ocean freight and now container weight limits care. So does a stair. So does a floor joist under a solid-oak library. Architects who specify solid rift-oak casework on a fourth floor without asking the structural engineer have written a density problem.
CITES and Lacey do not weigh the crate for biology, but the declaration asks for quantity. APHIS Phase VII (1 December 2024) wants scientific name, country of harvest, quantity, value. Quantity is often in kilograms or cubic metres. A crate that says “wood furniture” without a mass is the old habit. A crate of *Swietenia macrophylla* sawn wood after 15 November 2003 is an Annotation #6 specimen with a volume. A crate of *Dalbergia* after 2 January 2017 is an Annotation #15 problem if it is a dining table, and a 10 kg conversation only if it is a small finished object. Weight is legal language now, not only freight language.
Hide glue adds ounces. Urea-formaldehyde in a particleboard core adds pounds and a chemistry. The density of the tree is not the density of the object. Count the core.
## Shop uses of the number
Lift the drawer. Yellow-poplar and pine secondary wood make a tall chest possible. That is why Philadelphia high chests exist in the rooms they exist in. Solid oak sides would have changed the joinery and the market.
Weigh a “rosewood” suite. If it is light, it is not *Dalbergia*. If it is heavy and cheap, it is a problem. Weigh an “ebony” box. If it is light, it is ebonized pear. The Janka draft is the dent. This draft is the lift.
Shipping finished furniture inland: a solid-oak dining table, 1¼-inch top, 42 × 84, is on the order of a hundred pounds in the top alone before legs `[CITE NEEDED: show the arithmetic with your actual SG and thickness if you publish a single pound figure]`. A walnut table of the same size is less. A mahogany table less again. A veneered ply table is a different, often lighter object with a heavier carbon story in the glue. Specify the object, not the wood word.
Arkansas oak, walnut, cherry, and pine cover a useful density band without an ocean. That is a shorter haul and a binomial you can spell, not a halo. Stolen walnut still has a density. Lacey 2008 §8204 still applies if the log crossed a line.
## How to read a piece by lift
A 1760 mahogany chair is lighter than its oak country cousin of the same size. That is the fiber and the section. A 1962 Danish rosewood credenza is heavier than a teak one of the same outline. That is *Dalbergia* versus *Tectona*. A 2012 foil-wrapped dresser is heavy in the particleboard way and light in the face-veneer way. Lift, then look at the edge.
Figure 4 places the ten anchors. Figure 1 places the ships. Density is why pine painted furniture could be tall, why mahogany could be thin, why rosewood became a piano case and a permit, and why a crate of ebony is a scale event.
## Navy freight, a Sound toll, and a container limit
Ripley’s mahogany was a freight argument before it was a style argument. Navy ships already crossed. The duty cut of 1721 made the cubic foot worth carving. Baltic wainscot had paid the Sound toll for two centuries on a different cubic foot: oak, radial, dry. Albion’s *Forests and Sea Power* is the navy-oak neighbor of that sentence — masts and hulls, not dining tables, but the same scale. A wood that is heavy and cheap stays home. A wood that is light and dutied stays home. A wood that is heavy and precious travels as veneer or as a small object.
Modern containers have a payload limit. A factory that fills a box with solid white-oak casework hits the limit before it hits the volume. The same box filled with pine painted furniture hits the volume first. That arithmetic is why veneered MDF suites can be a wall of storage that still ships, and why a solid-oak library is a local mill’s job. Figure 1’s late years include the CITES cluster. Those years also include a freight market that made cheap tropical rotary faces cheaper than domestic solids for a generation. Density did not cause that. The price of a cubic foot on a ship did.
A specifier who writes a solid rift-oak reception desk, 2-inch top, 16 feet long, has written a hoist as well as a cut. Ask the stair. Ask the elevator. Ask the joist. The Janka number will not lift the desk. Write the thickness and the species on the shipping ticket. “Wood table” is how a crate gets reweighed at the dock and refused. Phase VII wants a mass and a binomial anyway. The scale and the appendix arrived in the same decade for a reason. Weight was always money. After 1 December 2024 it is also a line on a declaration.
Look at the bill of lading and the corner of the piece. If they disagree, believe the scale.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190, ch. 4–5 (SG bases, 12% tables). Kukachka FPL-125. Green et al., FPL-RP-643. Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*. Bowett, Ripley 1997; *The English Mahogany Trade 1700–1793*. Haneca et al. 2005. V&A Thonet W.31-2011. CITES *S. macrophylla* 15 Nov. 2003 #6; *Dalbergia* 2 Jan. 2017 #15. Lacey 2008 §8204; APHIS Phase VII 1 Dec. 2024. Wood Database compilations for ebony SG — treat as compilations.
See: `janka-hardness-explained`, `intro-500-year-timber`, `cites-ebony-africa`, `veneer-versus-solid`, `workability-hand-tools`.

item.title: Workability, Hoadley, and the plane that chatters
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Workability, Hoadley, and the plane that chatters
The plane chatters on interlocked sapele. That is a shop observation, not a metaphor. R. Bruce Hoadley’s *Understanding Wood* is the book that puts a reason under the chatter: grain direction reversing in successive bands, a cutting angle that lifts instead of severs, an edge that was sharp enough for mahogany and is not sharp enough now. Janka on Figure 4 will tell you sapele is harder than *Swietenia*. It will not tell you the scraper is the next tool. This draft is workability as the furniture shop knows it — edge, glue, and the joint that assumes the fiber — not as a catalogue adjective.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
![Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.](../assets/grain-cuts/sawn-orientation.svg)
*Figure 3. Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.*
## What Hoadley puts on the bench
Hoadley treats wood as a material you cut, not as a finish photograph. Cutting angle, sharpness, moisture, and grain direction are the four variables that decide whether a plane leaves a surface or a tear. A high effective cutting angle — a tight mouth, a back-bevel, a scraper’s hook — handles interlock and figured faces. A low angle on a block plane loves end grain on a clean pine or mahogany. The same low angle on quartered sapele ribbon is a tearout machine. Figure 3 matters here: a flatsawn cathedral changes direction on one face. You plane “up the hill” of the arch and then you turn the board, or you scrape.
Silica and other inclusions dull edges. Teak is the famous furniture case. The Janka is only moderate (~1,070 in imported notes). The edge dies anyway. Hone more often. Carbide on the machine side; a dedicated iron on the bench side. Oak tannin rusts planes if you leave the shavings. Cherry is kind until a gum pocket. Maple is fine-textured and hard; the plane must be sharp or the surface fuzzes and then polishes into blotch later. Mahogany, the *Wood Handbook*’s premier furniture tropical, planes, carves, and takes a moulding without oak’s trenches. That is why the splat got thin after 1722, once the duty was off (Bowett). The tool and the statute are the same story.
Moisture is a tool variable. Green wood cuts easier and then moves. Furniture-dry wood at 6 to 8 percent in a winter shop can crumble on end grain and burn on a saw. FPL chapter 4 is the moisture text. Hoadley is the reminder that the iron sees the moisture you actually have, not the 12 percent in the Janka table.
## Species as tool problems
Ring-porous oaks and ashes: the earlywood is a trench. A moulding plane leaves a dotted line unless you fill or you accept the dotted line. Quartersawn oak is easier to keep flat under the plane; the ray flake can chip if the iron is steep and dull. Rift is the even stripe (Figure 3) and a friend to a run of legs.
Diffuse-porous cherry, maple, yellow-poplar, true mahogany: the plane can leave a surface that looks like light under glass. Interlock, when it appears in *Swietenia* or more often in *Khaya* and sapele, ends that gift. Scraper. Then a cabinet scraper. Then a sanding sequence that does not dish the ribbon.
Softwoods: resin in pine gums the iron. Southern yellow pine’s latewood is a hard band that the plane rides up onto; the surface goes wavy. Eastern white pine is the opposite gift — 380 lbf on Figure 4, a joiner’s wood, dents under a buckle.
Rosewoods and ebonies: hard, often oily, dust that sensitizes. Do not machine *Dalbergia* without collection. Some people do not get a second chance at a first exposure `[CITE NEEDED: a named occupational-health note]`. Wipe oily faces before glue. A scraper often beats a plane. After 2 January 2017 the genus is Appendix II; after 11 June 1992 *D. nigra* is Appendix I. The tool problem is older than the appendix. The appendix is why you may be scraping walnut instead.
Beech takes a turning gouge and a steam bend (Thonet No. 14, V&A W.31-2011). Elm takes a seat boring and a wedge, not a draw-bore. Boxwood takes a stringing plane a millimeter wide. Lime (basswood) takes a carver’s gouge across the grain without crumbling. Each of those sentences is a tool choosing a tree.
## Glue is a tool
Hide glue — animal collagen, hot or liquid — is the historic furniture adhesive. It tacks. It creeps a little. It reverses with heat and moisture. A 1760 mahogany chair can come apart for repair because the glue was designed to. Hoadley and every conservator you trust will say some version of this. Hide glue on a veneer ground is the historic sandwich. It fails when the ground moves and the glue goes brittle: crotch mahogany on yellow-poplar, American Empire, the face checks.
Urea-formaldehyde is the 20th-century interior-furniture glue: cheap, gap-intolerant in the wrong way, not reversible. Klim’s 1990 WAG paper is the conservator’s timeline: protein, then casein (Aalto’s cold bends), then phenolics for wet work, then cheap ureas. A UF-glued breadboard that was glued across a flatsawn top has made a permanent split. Phenol-formaldehyde, the dark line of exterior ply, is a different chemistry: better wet behavior, still not a hide-glue repair culture.
Yellow PVA is the small-shop default. It creeps less than hide, reverses poorly, and grabs faster than a beginner wants on a complicated clamp-up. Choose the glue for the life of the joint. Then design the joint for movement: floating panels, slotted screws, buttons under a top. Glue will not repeal chapter 4. A perfect iron and a glued-in panel still give you a split door.
## Joinery as workability
Draw-bored mortise and tenon in riven oak holds because the pin, driven slightly offset, pulls the shoulder tight as the oak moves (Chinnery, *Oak Furniture*). You need a wood that crushes in a predictable direction. Interlocked elm does not get that pin in a seat; it gets a tapered leg and a wedge from above (Evans).
A mahogany splat takes a gouge across the grain without crumbling and a chisel along the grain without tearing into a pore line the way oak does. Hard maple will hold a bead and fight the same gouge. Sapele will chatter. Specify the wood for the tool in the plate, not only for the color in the plate.
Slotted screws in a breadboard or a table top are workability of a different kind: the screwdriver is the tool, the elongated hole is the joint. If you drive them tight at the ends of a wide flatsawn top, you have used the tool well and the design badly.
Hand-cut dovetails in pine are easy and look like it if you are careless. In oak they want sharp marking and a mallet. In maple they want patience. In plywood they want a different conversation: you are cutting veneers and glue lines. The veneer draft takes that sandwich.
## Machines, and what they hide
A wide-belt sander will flatten chatter and also flatten the conversation. You can sand sapele into submission and then watch the ribbon blotch under stain because the torn fibers and the dense bands drink differently. A sharp scraper and a plane, used first, leave a surface that finishes more evenly. Hoadley is not nostalgic about this. He is describing the fiber.
CNC routers like MDF and even-textured hardwoods. They do not like silica, voids, or a knife that has already died on teak. Carbide helps. Dust collection is not optional on rosewood, on MDF, or on western redcedar. The machine does not repeal the material.
Arkansas oak, walnut, cherry, maple, and pine cover a useful workability band. Interlock is rare. Tannin in oak will still rust a plane. Cherry will still blotch if you skip a conditioner or a scraper. Domestic is not a synonym for easy. It is a synonym for a known iron.
## A gouge, a scraper, and a glued panel
Chippendale’s splat is a gouge problem. Mahogany’s diffuse texture lets the tool cross the grain without the crumbling oak gives you in a thin piercing. Walnut can do some of it. Hard maple will hold the arris and fight the same cut. Sapele will chatter in the ribbon and then take a scraper to a finish that looks like the *Director* plate if you are patient. The plate does not name the iron. The wood does.
A cabinet scraper, sprung, is Hoadley’s answer to figure. It is also the answer to a tearout you already made. You are cutting a dust, not a shave. The surface can burnish. Stop before the polish seals the pore if you still have to glue. Hide glue wants a clean, slightly open surface. UF wants fit and clamp. Neither glue wants a surface you just waxed to see the color.
The split door returns here because workability includes the joint you chose after the plane was happy. A perfect sapele panel, scraped, oiled, and glued into a tight groove, is a January crack. Floating panels and slotted screws are tool work: a plow plane or a slot in a breadboard, a screwdriver that stops before it pins the width. The iron and the fastener are the same chapter.
Look at the surface under raking light. Tearout is interlock or a dull iron or a cathedral planed the wrong way. A dotted moulding is oak earlywood. A polished, slightly wavy pine board is latewood bands. A checked crotch veneer is a ground that moved under hide glue that went glass. Figure 4 is hardness. Figure 3 is cut. The iron is the third axis. Hoadley is the text. The split door is what happens when the iron was fine and the panel was glued.
## Sources
Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*, 2nd ed. (2000). USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190, ch. 4–5. Klim, WAG 1990 (adhesive timeline). Bowett, mahogany and the splat. Chinnery, *Oak Furniture*. Evans, *Windsor-Chair Making in America*. V&A Thonet W.31-2011. CITES *Dalbergia* dates as in the conservation drafts.
See: `janka-hardness-explained`, `moisture-wood-movement`, `veneer-versus-solid`, `glossary-grain-and-cut`, `mahogany-chippendale`.

item.title: Veneer, solid, and the ground that moved
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Veneer, solid, and the ground that moved
A crotch-mahogany face on a yellow-poplar drawer front, American Empire, that has checked into a thousand hairlines is a veneer lesson. The leaf wanted to stay put. The ground moved across the grain. The hide glue went brittle. The picture of the tree opened. Solid wood would have moved as one piece — cupped, shrunk, maybe split along a glue line — but it would not have been a skin riding a different species. Veneer is not a sin. It is a contract: a thin face, a ground, an adhesive, and a weather. This draft is that contract, from oyster walnut to foil on particleboard.
![Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.](../assets/grain-cuts/sawn-orientation.svg)
*Figure 3. Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.*
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## Two conversions of the same log
Solid furniture is a board thick enough to hold a joint: a splat, a dovetail, a mortise. Veneer is a leaf, historically sawn, later sliced or rotary-peeled, glued to a cheaper or more stable ground. Walnut after 1660 in England is the fashion that made the leaf ordinary: oyster and burl, seaweed marquetry, a deal or oak carcase. The log was too precious and too figured to quarter into solids for every surface. Mahogany after 1722 went the other way — cheap enough, after the Naval Stores Act, to carve in the solid (Bowett). Then Empire and the factories swung back to crotch veneer over pine and poplar. The fiber did not change. The price of the face did.
Figure 3 is the cut of a solid board. Veneer has its own geometry. Sliced crown-cut repeats a cathedral more politely than rotary. Rotary, the log on a lathe, peels a continuous sheet: wild arches, cheap, the 1950s dresser side. Quarter-sliced oak shows flake; rift-sliced oak shows stripe. A 1910 Stickley door with ray flake is usually sliced, not peeled. Look at the repeat. Nature does not clone a ray every foot.
Hoadley’s veneer pages still teach the difference between a leaf and a board. Thickness matters. A 3 mm sawn veneer on a historic piece behaves more like a thin board. A 0.6 mm sliced face is a skin. A paper foil is a photograph. The edge tells you which contract you bought.
## The ground is the furniture
Hide glue on deal or yellow-poplar is the historic sandwich. The ground moves as FPL chapter 4 says it will: more tangentially than radially, below fiber saturation, toward the room’s EMC. If the leaf’s grain does not run with the ground’s grain, the leaf is a cross-band by accident and will try to split or check. If the grains run together, they move together until the glue fails. Hide glue reverses with heat and moisture; it also goes glass-brittle with age and central heating. The Empire crotch that checked is that failure. Conservators relay the leaf. A belt sander is not a relay.
Plywood as a ground is the 20th-century answer. Cross-bands cancel movement. A walnut face on a birch core is a stable door in January and in July. The 18th-century frame-and-panel was the old answer to the same physics: the panel floats, the frame stays. Plywood is the industrial floating panel, except the “panel” is the whole slab. An Eames LCW can be a shaped seat without the splits you would expect from a solid flatsawn slab steamed into a compound curve (V&A plywood history; Engelbrecht on the 1946 chair).
Particleboard and MDF as grounds stay flatter still and die in water. A walnut-veneered MDF kitchen door is a respectable object if the invoice says so. A paper-foil “walnut” on chip is a costume. Formaldehyde in old ureas is an indoor-air specification (CARB / TSCA Title VI), not a harvest stamp. You want both conversations.
Urea-formaldehyde as the veneer adhesive is the factory default for interior work. It does not reverse. A delaminated 1950s dresser with protein glue can sometimes be reclamped. A UF bubble under a casserole is a different repair, often a replacement leaf. Phenol-formaldehyde, the dark line, belongs to exterior and aircraft ply (Klim 1990). Name the glue when you can.
## Solid manners that veneer does not need — and some it still does
A solid flatsawn oak door needs a floating panel or it splits. A veneered MDF door does not float; it is a rectangle. Do not apply solid-wood manners to a stable panel and call it honesty, and do not apply panel manners to a solid top and call it modern. Buttons, slotted screws, and breadboards with elongated holes are for solids that move. A veneered-ply top can be screwed more rigidly. A veneered-ply top with a solid-wood breadboard glued across the end has invented a new split: the solid cap moves, the ply does not.
Solid edges on a veneered top — a lipping — are a good shop habit. They take the dent (Figure 4: the face may be walnut at 1,010 lbf, the core yellow-poplar at 540). They also take the moisture at the end grain. Finish the lipping and the underside. A finish on one face only is a cupping machine even on ply, less so than on solid, still real on cheap cores.
Matching — book, slip, radial — is a design choice as old as the 17th-century ébéniste. The Wallace Collection’s Riesener notes are the handmade version. Factories automated matching and then abandoned it for random rotary. A pair of doors that book-match are a specification. A pair that do not are a price.
## Law on a thin face
Decorative faces in rosewood and mahogany sit under CITES when the species does. Neotropical *Swietenia macrophylla* went onto Appendix II on 15 November 2003, Annotation #6: logs, sawn wood, veneer sheets, plywood. The leaf is named. *Dalbergia* went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15, revised at CoP18 in 2019 (finished musical instruments; finished products up to 10 kg of listed wood per shipment). A rosewood-faced sideboard is not a jewelry box. *D. nigra* is Appendix I (11 June 1992). Madagascar *Diospyros* veneer after 12 June 2013 is Annotation #5. Lacey 2008 §8204 and APHIS Phase VII (1 December 2024) want the face species and, when you can know it, the core species. A lauan core has a forest. This draft is not a permit.
## How to look, and what to specify
Look at the edge. A leaf that turns the corner with the grain is veneer or solid. A photograph that dies at a 0.4 mm ABS is foil. A void behind a 0.6 mm face is cheap ply. Thin dark lines, many of them, are ply. Homogeneous brown fuzz is MDF. Chips in pale glue are particleboard. End-grain rings through a thick top are solid; rings that stop at a glue line under a skin are a sandwich.
Look at the failure. Checks in a crotch that follow no board joint: veneer on a moving ground. A split down a cathedral in a thick top: solid, probably flatsawn, probably fastened tight. A bubble under a hot dish: foil or a failed urea. A panel that has shrunk in a groove: solid, and the shop that let it float was right.
Specify: face species, cut of the face (crown, quarter, rift, rotary), thickness of the leaf, core species, glue, and whether the edges are solid. Or: solid *Quercus alba*, flatsawn, floating panels, slotted screws in the breadboard, hide glue if the piece should come apart in a hundred years. Those are different objects. “Walnut dining table” is not a specification.
Arkansas shops meet veneer as imported faces on imported cores, and as domestic walnut and oak leaves on domestic ply or on yellow-poplar for paint-grade work. The solid side of that rack is the older contract. The useful sentence is the long one. The Eames DCM and a printed suburban suite share a century. They do not share a glue, a mould, or a noun.
## Oyster, crotch, and a foil that blistered
Oyster veneer — end-grain slices of walnut or laburnum, laid like overlapping coins — is a 17th-century conversion that wastes less of a small, figured stem than a solid board would. The ground is still deal or oak. The glue is still hide. Movement in the oysters is a different geometry (end grain, not a long face), and the failure is lifting at the edges, not a cathedral split. Seaweed marquetry is the cousin: two woods, a knife, a ground. The Wallace Collection and the walnut-baroque draft take the pictures. This chapter only needs the contract: leaf, ground, hide, weather.
Crotch and burl are the show leaves of the next hours. They are unstable as solids. They are why veneer exists. A solid crotch slab is a conversation piece and a movement problem. A crotch leaf on ply is a conversation piece that stays a rectangle. A crotch leaf on flatsawn poplar is the Empire check.
Foil under a casserole blisters. There is no plane that fixes a bubble. A solid top would have a white ring you might revive. Choose the life before you choose the leaf. Hide glue on a historic leaf can be reversed. UF on a factory leaf cannot. Floating panels belong to solids. Slotted screws belong to solids. A veneered-ply top screwed rigid is acceptable physics. A solid top screwed rigid is a split.
Look at the edge and the check. If the picture of the tree has opened and the core is a different color, you are in this chapter. If the whole thickness opened along a glue line, you are in the flatsawn and moisture chapters. Figure 3 is the solid cut. Figure 4 is why a poplar ground dents and a maple lipping does not. Hide glue is the old contract. UF is the factory contract. Neither will save a specification that says only wood.
## Sources
Hoadley, *Understanding Wood* (veneer, glue, movement). USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190, ch. 4–5. Klim, WAG 1990. V&A plywood history; Engelbrecht on Eames 1946. Bowett (solid mahogany after 1722; walnut as the veneer hour). Wallace Collection / Riesener. CITES #6 (15 Nov. 2003); *Dalbergia* #15 (2 Jan. 2017; CoP18 2019); *D. nigra* App. I 11 June 1992. Lacey 2008 §8204; APHIS Phase VII 1 Dec. 2024.
See: `flatsawn-panel-figure`, `moisture-wood-movement`, `workability-hand-tools`, `plywood-and-core-stock`, `glossary-grain-and-cut`.

item.title: Brazilian rosewood in the mid-century shop
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Brazilian rosewood in the mid-century shop
A Copenhagen sideboard of 1962 with a rosewood face is a smaller, sharper luxury than the teak dining set in the same catalogue. The magazines flattened Danish modern to a honey brown. The shops did not. Oak, teak, walnut, and rosewood were four different prices of the same grammar: visible joinery, a thin oil or a thin film, a case that shows the leaf. *Dalbergia nigra* — jacaranda da Bahia, Appendix I — is the name Americans recite. Much of the rosewood that actually left Danish factories was East Indian *D. latifolia* and related stock. Still a listed genus. Still a forest with a colonial ledger. The binomial on a vintage piece is often a guess until someone looks.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
![Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).](../assets/cites-conservation/furniture-timber-listings.svg)
*Figure 5. Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).*
## Bahia wood in a teak decade
Kukachka (FPL-125, 1970) wrote *D. nigra* while the mid-century trade was still moving. He had no mechanical table. Early furniture use, he said, had excused the academy from measuring it. He could still say the facts that matter to a specifier: eastern Brazil, Bahia toward Rio, nowhere abundant, color in brown-red-violet with black streaks, oily or waxy, fragrant, barely floatable dry, harder than native furniture hardwoods, veneer first, solids for small work, *Machaerium* already in the shipments as a lookalike. Compiled Janka near 2,790 lbf, SG in the high 0.8s to near 1.0, is the later compilation. Figure 4 will not pretend Kukachka plotted that point.
*D. latifolia*, which he did weigh at about 53 pounds per cubic foot, is the other historic furniture rosewood: purplish-brown, blackish growth-zone streaks, narrowly interlocked, shake in the core, veneer in the United States, compiled Janka near 2,440 lbf, SG near 0.83. Danish buyers took both when they could. Brazilian wood had the older prestige and the tighter supply. Indian and Indonesian (sonokeling) wood had volume. A 1960s label that says only “rosewood” is a color word. The Indian-export draft takes *D. latifolia* as a lane. This draft stays with *D. nigra* as the name that became the legal third rail, and with the furniture that wore either wood as if they were one fashion.
Mahogany, for scale, remains the carvable mid-density wood of Bowett’s 18th-century Atlantic lane — about 800 lbf, SG 0.45–0.50 (FPL / Kukachka). Mid-century shops still used *Swietenia* and *Khaya*. They did not confuse them with palisander except in advertising. Teak (compiled Janka near 1,070 lbf, SG near 0.55) was the export look. Rosewood was the third luxury: darker, heavier, rarer, a sideboard meant to look scarce.
## Who used it, and how the joint changed
Finn Juhl’s sculptural chairs are often teak or walnut; some production and some specials took rosewood. Arne Vodder’s cases, Ib Kofod-Larsen’s seating, a long list of factory sideboards from the Copenhagen and provincial plants — the rosewood pieces are the ones estate sales still photograph first. Hans Wegner’s named chairs are more often oak or walnut; rosewood appears in some production and in the market’s wish. Do not invent a particular Juhl invoice. Object records and the Guild exhibition catalogues are the evidence `[CITE NEEDED: pin one Guild-exhibition rosewood lot at publication]`.
Solid versus veneer is the joinery split. A solid rosewood chair seat or arm is a dense, oily member that wants sharp tools, a scraper, and a glue surface wiped of extractives. It moves less in width than a flatsawn oak seat of the same dimension, and it weighs more than the client expects when they lift the chair. A veneered case — the common sideboard — is a sliced face on a cheaper core: teak, oak, particleboard in the later cheaper lines, or a plywood that the catalogue hoped you would not ask about. The 18th-century ancestor of that sandwich is crotch mahogany on yellow-poplar (the Empire draft). The mid-century version may be a true *Dalbergia* leaf on a lauan or birch core. Look at the edge. Count plies. Weigh the door.
Molded ply versus solid is the other split. The V&A plywood history and the Eames DCM sit in the plywood draft; Aalto’s Paimio birch is not rosewood. Mid-century rosewood is rarely a compound-curved shell. It is a flat face or a solid sculpted member. Grete Jalk’s 1963 molded-ply chair (V&A exhibition lists) can wear a rosewood face; the structure is still laminate. Do not call a flat-faced Vodder sideboard an Eames problem. Call it a leaf-and-core problem.
Oil is the honest mid-century finish on these pieces. A thick film that looks like a piano is a later “restoration.” Victorian rosewood *wanted* that piano polish (the Victorian draft). Danish rosewood wanted grain you could still feel. The two hours share a genus and fight about sheen.
## Workability in a factory that also ran teak
Rosewood dulls knives. Dust sensitizes. Kukachka’s cocobolo dermatitis note is the family warning; collect the dust. Glue wants the oil wiped back; clamp longer than the teak habit. A scraper beats a plane on interlock and on the polish the wood will take if you let it. Calcareous deposits in some Indian boards blunt edges (Kukachka on *D. latifolia*). Brazilian boards, when you still meet them as offcuts in a repair shop, are the oily, fragrant ones that barely float.
Screws hold if you pre-drill. The wood is hard enough to split a rail that a teak rail would forgive. Dowels and mortise-and-tenon in solid members are the Copenhagen habit. Cam locks in a later veneered case are the factory habit. Look underneath.
A sliding-door sideboard is the characteristic large object. The door is a veneered panel in a groove, or a panel hanging from a fiber or metal track. Rosewood on a core that has gone out of flat will bind in January and rattle in July if the core was cheap particle. A decent ply core stays a rectangle. The pull is often a routed finger or a small metal bar; a rosewood pull that is a solid sticking is a nicer shop. Drawer sides in the better plants are teak or oak, not the face genus. That is honest if you can see it. A face of palisander and a side of lauan with a stain is the cheaper plant.
Upholstered seating in rosewood — a frame that shows at the arm, a loose cushion — is a sculptor’s use of the solid. The rail is thick because the wood is brittle compared with ash. You do not steam-bend *Dalbergia* the way Thonet steamed beech. You cut the curve from the solid or you laminate a few leaves for a gentle bow. The plywood draft is the place for compound shells. This hour’s famous chairs are still mostly cut and joined.
Bowett’s mahogany statute (1721/1722) is not this supply. The Bahia forest and the Malabar-to-Java *Dalbergia* lane are. Enslaved and coerced labor sits in the older Brazilian extraction the way it sits in mahogany. Mid-century invoices are quieter about that. Dean’s Atlantic-forest book is still the background for *D. nigra*. Do not tell the sideboard as a Scandinavian object only.
American and Italian factories ran the same darker luxury in the same years: a rosewood wall unit, a headboard, a dining table with a leaf that is too wide to be a honest solid without a price the catalogue would not print. Much of that is veneer on particleboard. The Copenhagen Guild pieces are the high end of a broader habit. A suburban “rosewood” suite of 1968 is more often the print or the cheap leaf. The mid-century draft in this series is not a license to baptize every brown wall unit *D. nigra*.
## Figure 5: Appendix I is not a style note
*D. nigra* is CITES Appendix I. Commercial trade in wild specimens is effectively shut. You do not specify new Brazilian rosewood furniture. You enjoy old pieces already in the country, or you specify another wood.
The rest of *Dalbergia* went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15 — in force with the CoP17 listing, later revised at CoP18 so finished musical instruments, parts, and accessories are exempt, and small finished products sit under a weight cap on the listed wood. A dining table is not a jewelry box. A 1962 sideboard being sold abroad is a permit conversation. Neotropical *Swietenia macrophylla* entered Appendix II on 15 November 2003; relevant if the same room holds a “mahogany” case that is actually big-leaf.
Figure 5 is the map. Species+ is the living page. The U.S. Lacey Act (2008 amendment) and APHIS Phase VII (1 December 2024) sit on top. This draft is not a permit.
Repair with the same species is a permit question when the patch is imported. Repair with walnut or dyed pear is the old shop fake. Name it.
## Substitutes the 1960s already knew
Walnut can impersonate a tired palisander. Teak with a dark toner. Printed foil on particleboard. Bubinga and other *Guibourtia* (some later listed under Annotation #15). *Machaerium*. A 1970s “rosewood wall unit” is often a photograph. A lens on an unseen edge ends the argument.
New work that wants this hour’s sharpness without the appendix: American black walnut (FPL: SG 0.55, Janka 1,010 lbf), smoked oak, a named plantation teak with papers. None of these is jacaranda. They do not need to be.
## What to look for
A dark, streaked face with an oily look; weight in a solid member; a veneer line on a case; an oil finish that has worn to pale at the pulls; a Copenhagen or provincial factory mark. Ask whether the wood is *D. nigra* or *D. latifolia* before you ship. On a print: no pore, no smell, a core that swells. On a new “Brazilian rosewood” suite: walk away.
Arkansas does not grow *Dalbergia*. Oak, walnut, and cherry will do the mid-century grammar of visible joints and a thin finish without borrowing a Bahia name. The point of this hour is to say what the vintage piece is, and what a new commission cannot be.
## Sources
Kukachka, FPL-125, *D. nigra* and *D. latifolia*. USDA FPL-GTR-190. Dean, *With Broadax and Firebrand*. Copenhagen Cabinetmakers’ Guild exhibition literature; Fiell, *Scandinavian Design*. V&A plywood history (Jalk / Eames contrast). CITES App. I *D. nigra*; *Dalbergia* App. II, 2 January 2017, Annotation #15; *S. macrophylla* App. II, 15 November 2003. USDA APHIS Lacey Phase VII. Bowett on the earlier mahogany lane (contrast).
See: `indian-rosewood-exports`, `rosewood-victorian`, `danish-modern-woods`, `cites-dalbergia-2017`, `plywood-and-core-stock`.

item.title: Indian rosewood and the export lane
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Indian rosewood and the export lane
Kukachka’s FPL-125 entry on *Dalbergia latifolia* starts in the provinces. Native to most of India except the Northwest. Heartwood dark purplish-brown, denser blackish streaks terminating the growth zones, an attractive figure on flatsawn surfaces. Average weight about 53 pounds per cubic foot. Texture uniform and moderately coarse; grain narrowly interlocked, an inconspicuous stripe on the quarter, punched up by the dark zones. Similar in look to Brazilian and Honduras rosewood. That paragraph is a furniture specification written as a forest note. The export lane — Malabar, Bombay, later Java as sonokeling — made it a world wood. CITES made it a permit wood on 2 January 2017.
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
![Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/timeline.svg)
*Figure 1. Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.*
## What the handbook could measure
Unlike *D. nigra*, which Kukachka had to describe without a test table, Indian rosewood came with shop manners. It air-dries fairly rapidly with little degrade if you protect it; slight surface and end checking, shakes that lengthen, a central core that very commonly contains numerous shakes. Moderately refractory. Kiln-dries well but slowly; color said to improve in the kiln. Heavy, high strength, particularly hard for its weight once seasoned. Moderately hard to work by hand; fair resistance on machines. Calcareous deposits blunt tools. A 25-degree cutting angle gave him a smooth plane surface. Turns well; high screw-holding. Fill the pores if you want a glass top. In the United States of 1970, used primarily as veneer. “High-class furniture and cabinet work” is his phrase for the decorative job.
Compiled Janka is commonly given near 2,440 lbf, specific gravity near 0.83 at 12 percent (Wood Database beside FPL/Kukachka). Figure 4 places that hardness among the series’ anchors. White oak sits near 1,360 lbf and SG 0.68; Honduran mahogany near 800 lbf and 0.45–0.50; yellow-poplar, the historic American ground, near 540 lbf and 0.42. *D. latifolia* is the hard, oily, interlocked cousin of Bahia jacaranda, not a darker teak (teak compiled near 1,070 lbf, SG near 0.55).
Honduras rosewood and cocobolo (*D. retusa*) sit in the same genus palette. African blackwood (*D. melanoxylon*) — Kukachka’s 70 pounds per cubic foot at 6 percent moisture, a woodwind wood — is a *Dalbergia* that furniture shops almost never saw as a carcase. Do not collapse the genus into one parlor color.
## Ports, plantations, and a colonial ledger
Indian joiners used *D. latifolia* at home long before London wrote “rosewood” on a Regency invoice. The export is the European and later American and Danish appetite: veneer for case goods, solids for small work, then mid-century factory furniture that wanted a darker luxury than teak. Java and other Indonesian growth — sonokeling — entered the same trade name. The trees are not a single forest. The invoice often treated them as one.
Do not invent a price per ton at Bombay or a particular Company monopoly clause for rosewood the way teak had one. Teak’s Malabar monopoly (1807) is a documented dockyard story (the teak draft). Rosewood rode the same imperial shipping without the same navy excuse. Pin a dated export-statistic series at publication `[CITE NEEDED: a named Indian forest-department or customs series for D. latifolia]`. Figure 1 is the long clock: Baltic oak, Atlantic mahogany (Bowett’s 1721/1722 duty cut), tropical peak around 1900, then the CITES years. Indian rosewood sits on that clock as a 19th-century parlor wood and a 20th-century export, not as Macquoid’s London age.
Enslaved and coerced labor is louder in the Bahia and West Indian stories. Indian forest labor under Company and Raj administration is a different, still extractive, ledger. Do not tell a Copenhagen sideboard as a wood that appeared from nowhere.
Musical instruments took the species as seriously as furniture did. Sitars and related instruments at home; guitar backs and sides in the 20th-century West. Annotation #15’s later musical-instrument exemption is a concert-hall clause written after factories and guitar shops discovered they had been listed. Furniture is why the genus went on the appendix. A dining table is not a guitar.
## Joinery: shakes in the core, a leaf on a ground
The shake-prone core is a conversion fact. A sawyer who tries to get wide solid tops from the heart will write checks into the panel. Veneer from the outer, sounder wood is the historic furniture use Kukachka already recorded for the U.S. trade. A solid chair arm or a turned pull is a different, smaller contract.
Interlock means the plane will tear on the quartered stripe. Scraper. The 25-degree angle is his machine note; a hand plane with a tight mouth and a steep chipbreaker is the bench version. Calcareous specks — the “petrified” white flecks some boards show — are where a plane iron dies. Feel for them before you take a long finishing cut.
As a face on a case, *D. latifolia* wants the same sandwich the Empire shop used for crotch mahogany: a sliced leaf on yellow-poplar, pine, or, later, plywood or particleboard. Hide glue, then synthetics. The leaf follows the ground. If the ground is a cheap void-core, the figure telegraphs. If the ground is Baltic birch or a decent hardwood ply, the door stays a rectangle. Molded ply versus solid is not this species’ famous hour — that is birch and the Eames-Aalto line — but a rosewood face can ride a molded shell (Jalk and others). The structure is still the laminate. The name on the catalogue is still the face.
Piano cases in the Victorian hour used both rosewoods. Indian wood appears on instruments that are not Bahia-colored enough for the romantic caption. Smell and streak, not a dealer’s country, decide. Boulle work is ebony and brass, not this chapter.
Bowett’s mahogany — Jamaica logs after 1722, cheaper than deal when the Navy carried them — is the Atlantic supply that taught Europe to carve a tropical hardwood in the solid. Indian rosewood rarely got that solid-carving hour in London. It arrived as a veneer luxury into a shop that already knew how to glue a leaf. That is why so much “rosewood furniture” is a picture on a pale carcase. Open the door.
Colonial and later Indian workshops used the same species for furniture that never left the subcontinent: carved chairs, carved screens, a box with a brass mount. Some of that work was made for export as “Bombay blackwood” or under other trade names that wander between *D. latifolia* and other dark hardwoods. Shisham in the north is often *D. sissoo*, a different species, a different furniture habit, now also inside the genus listing. Do not flatten every Indian “rosewood” bed into Malabar palisander. Look at the pore and the streak. Pin a named trade-name paper at publication `[CITE NEEDED: a furniture-trade note separating sissoo, latifolia, and blackwood in export lists]`.
Sonokeling from Java is *D. latifolia* grown and converted in a different forest administration. Mid-century European buyers took it as Indian rosewood. The papers, when they exist, should say the country of harvest. After 2017 that sentence is not pedantry.
## Workability and dust
Pore filler if you want the Victorian glass look. Oil if you want the mid-century feel. Neither will make this wood into teak. Silica is teak’s tax; calcium is sometimes this wood’s tax. Dust is a sensitizer across *Dalbergia*. Collect it. Some people do not get a second chance `[CITE NEEDED: named occupational-health note]`.
A dining table in exported Indian rosewood is usually a veneered top on a hardwood or ply ground, with solid edges if the shop was proud. A solid top from the shake-prone core is a future crack. Breadboard ends on that solid are the same geometry lesson as oak: slot-screw or watch it split. The mid-century oil finish wants renewal, not a later film that traps the oil and looks like a failed piano. Victorian London wanted the piano. Copenhagen wanted the grain. Same species, two sheens, two hours.
Glue: wipe, then glue, then wait. Screw-holding is high once you pre-drill. The wood will split a thin rail that oak would only bruise.
## 2017, Annotation #15, and the other appendix
*D. nigra* was already Appendix I. The rest of *Dalbergia* — including *D. latifolia* — went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15. CoP18 revised the annotation (in force 26 November 2019): finished musical instruments, parts, and accessories exempt; small finished products under a weight cap on the listed wood per shipment. Sawn wood and veneer for furniture factories are not a casual import. Neotropical *Swietenia macrophylla* entered Appendix II on 15 November 2003. A room can hold both papers. They are not interchangeable.
Figure 1’s last marks are those dates. Species+ is the living page. The U.S. Lacey Act (2008 amendment) and APHIS Phase VII (1 December 2024) sit on top. Vintage Indian-rosewood furniture already in the country is usually legal to own. Export is the question Danish-modern owners learned after 2017. This draft is not a permit.
New specification: another wood, or *D. latifolia* only with the permit path in the file and a named country of harvest. “East Indian rosewood” without a binomial is an ad.
Guitar shops learned the 2017 listing in public; furniture shops have less excuse. A crate of sawn *D. latifolia* for a factory is the object the annotation was written to catch. A finished sitar crossing a border may sit under the later instrument exemption. Verify. Do not guess from a blog. Species+ and the Management Authority are the living references.
## What to look for
Purplish-brown with blackish zone lines, weight, an oily feel, interlock tear-out on a quartered edge, shakes if someone used the core as a top, a veneer line on a case. On a sitar or a guitar: the instrument annotation, still verify. On a 1960s Danish sideboard: maybe this species, maybe *D. nigra*, maybe a print — look. On a new suite at a funny price: walk away.
Arkansas does not grow *Dalbergia*. Walnut will do a dark, hard furniture wood with papers you can read. It will not smell like a Malabar kerf. That is an honest loss.
## Sources
Kukachka, FPL-125, *D. latifolia* (and *D. nigra*, *D. melanoxylon* for contrast). USDA FPL-GTR-190. CITES CoP17 *Dalbergia* App. II, 2 January 2017, Annotation #15 (CoP18 revision). CITES App. I *D. nigra*; *S. macrophylla* App. II, 15 November 2003. Bowett on the mahogany lane (contrast). Dean on the Bahia forest (contrast). USDA APHIS Lacey Phase VII.
See: `brazilian-rosewood-midcentury`, `rosewood-victorian`, `tropical-hardwood-peak-1900`, `cites-dalbergia-2017`.

item.title: Plywood and the core
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Plywood and the core
The V&A’s short history of plywood in ten-ish objects opens with a correction. It has always been assumed that the history of plywood was mainly that of the flat board. That is not the case. Between about 1850 and 1890 moulded plywood was the common innovative form, and furniture design drove it. John Henry Belter’s New York patent of 1858 moulded chair backs in batches of eight. Charles and Ray Eames’s 1942 US Navy leg splint taught compound curves that became the DCM. Alvar Aalto’s Paimio seat is a birch scroll between two frames. The face can be walnut, teak, rosewood, or birch. The core can be a tree the catalogue hoped you would not name. This draft is the sandwich: what the layers do that a solid board will not, and what they hide.
![Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.](../assets/grain-cuts/sawn-orientation.svg)
*Figure 3. Tangential, radial, and rift cuts through a log and the face-grain patterns they produce in finished boards.*
![Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/timeline.svg)
*Figure 1. Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.*
## Before the mould: a leaf on a ground
Cross-banded veneer is older than the factory. An Empire pier table with a crotch-mahogany face on yellow-poplar is already a two-species contract. Hide glue, a hammer or a caul, a flame figure that would check if you tried to use the fork as a solid drawer front. FPL-GTR-190 puts yellow-poplar at SG 0.42 and Janka 540 lbf — wide, glue-friendly, the Mid-Atlantic servant under Federal and Empire mahogany (Bowett’s Atlantic *Swietenia*, the same genus the 1721/1722 duty cut had made cheap enough to carve in the solid). The leaf follows the ground. If the ground cups, the picture cocks. Plywood is that idea with the grain of each inner leaf run the other way so the cup argues with itself.
Figure 3 is why. A flatsawn solid is mostly tangential grain; tangential shrinkage is the large number in the *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190, ch. 4). A quartersawn solid moves less in width. A three-ply or seven-ply sheet cancels the width change by stacking contradictions. The 18th-century frame-and-panel was manners for a wide board. The cross-band is industrial manners for a wide sheet.
Rotary veneer — a log on a lathe, peeled like a paper towel — makes the cheap cathedrals of a 1950s dresser side. Sliced veneer makes the crown-cut and quarter-cut faces that want to look like show wood. Furniture that wants to look like a solid uses sliced faces. Furniture that wants to be cheap uses rotary faces. Furniture that wants to be honest modern sometimes shows the ply edge.
## 1850–1890: the mould before the badge
Belter’s technique, the V&A notes, increased speed and cut cost: chair backs in batches from a single mould, rosewood leaves laminated, then carved. That is *Dalbergia* in a process, not only in a parlor fashion (the Victorian draft). Gardner & Company’s doll’s chair of about 1875 and Isaac Cole’s 1874 all-plywood chair are the other V&A witnesses. Industrial flat boards expand in the 1880s. Prejudice against ply as cheap kept much of it hidden under other materials — Christopher Wilk’s point in the V&A exhibition texts.
Thonet’s No. 14 (V&A W.31-2011) is not plywood. It is six pieces of steamed solid beech. The parallel factory problem was how to make a seat or a back from leaves glued in a mould when you did not want, or could not get, a steam-bent solid. Molded ply and bent solid are cousins, not twins. Beech takes Thonet’s bend. Birch peels and glues for Aalto’s stack. Mahogany and rosewood take a mould if the leaves are thin and the glue holds. A solid flatsawn oak seat of the same compound curve would split.
## Aalto, then the splint, then the DCM
Aalto’s Paimio chair (1930, tuberculosis sanatorium) suspends a thin, curved birch seat between two frames. The V&A tells it as a plywood milestone; Artek’s factory made the bends a product; Finmar sold them into Britain in the 1930s. Casein glue in some of Artek’s cold-bend processes (Klim, WAG 1990) is a reminder that “plywood glue” is not one chemistry. Northern birch peels well and glues well. It is not silica-hard like teak, not tannic like oak. Thin leaves, stacked, take a bend a solid oak of the same thickness will not.
Charles and Ray Eames, with Eero Saarinen, tried compound-curved shells for MoMA’s 1940 Organic Design competition. The war interrupted, then supplied the 1942 moulded-plywood leg-splint contract for the US Navy (Engelbrecht on the 1946 chair; Kirkham). Later in the war they made plywood aircraft parts. The DCM (dining chair metal), 1946–47, wears a three-dimensionally moulded seat. Robin Day, via the V&A: every designer he knew had a picture of that Eames chair pinned to the drawing board. The face might be walnut, ash, teak, or a calico birch. The core is the process.
Wilk is careful, and so is this draft: the Eameses did not pioneer plywood, or plywood moulding, or the inflated rubber bag (the Loughead brothers used a bag in a cement mould for aircraft in 1919 `[CITE NEEDED: pin Wilk’s Loughead citation]`). They were the most influential furniture designers of the second half of the century, and they domesticated the moulded seat. Aalto had started the modern furniture argument. The Eames shop industrialized the compound curve.
Molded ply versus solid is a structural sentence. A solid member has long grain you can trust for a slender splat (mahogany after Bowett’s statute) and a movement you must allow across the width. A molded shell has no single “across.” It has layers, a glue line, a thickness that can be thin because the curve is the stiffness. You cannot draw-bore it. You cannot plane a shaving off a compound seat and call it a refinish without changing the section. Repair is specialist work. A pine block sistered onto a laminate scroll is not conservation.
## Core stock: the tree you were not sold
Kukachka’s imported-woods paper is a core-stock document as much as a show-wood one. Fuma (*Ceiba pentandra*) had been used primarily for corestock and was being replaced by lupuna (*Ceiba samauma*), firmer and more readily peeled. Cuangare (“virola” in the trade, *Dialyanthera*) for corestock, with a warning: “brownheart” wet zones collapse and make wavy panels; do not use that material for hot-press cores. Okoume as the great African plywood volume. Yellow-poplar as the American rotary core and crossband. Later, lauan and meranti as the tropical cores under walnut-look faces. Particleboard and MDF as the cores that are not veneer at all.
Void-core cheap ply telegraphs and loses a screw. Baltic birch and the many-ply clear cores do not. Count plies. Weigh the board. Interior furniture ply is often a cheaper glue than the phenolic films of 1930s aircraft and boat ply (Klim). Water still finds the cheap glue. Old furniture ply delaminates when the protein glue gives up in a damp room. Clamping and the right adhesive save some of it. A belt sander does not.
Screws in the edge of a cheap ply have nothing to hold but glue and a void. Screws in the face of a seven-ply birch hold if you do not oversize the hole. Confirmat screws and barrel nuts are the late-factory answers. A 1760 mahogany chair does not need them because the fiber is long in the right direction. A molded seat does not take a traditional corner glue-block the way a square rail does. The metal loop of a DCM is the joint. The birch knee of an Aalto stool is the joint. Do not treat those as failed mortises. They are different contracts.
Veneer matching — book, slip, radial — is a design choice as old as the 17th-century ébéniste. Plywood factories automated it and then abandoned it for random rotary. A radio of 1932 with a burl face that is book-matched and a back that is rotary lauan holds both habits in one box.
Boulle work is a different sandwich — brass, turtle, ebony — and belongs in the ebony draft. The piano case is a veneered box on a softwood or poplar ground, sometimes with ply in later instruments. Do not call a Steinway fallboard an Eames shell. Call it a leaf on a box. Do not call an Eames seat a Belter back. Call both molded leaves, a century apart, different genera on the face.
## Faces that sit under appendices
Decorative faces in *Dalbergia* and *Swietenia* sit under CITES when the species does. Neotropical *S. macrophylla* entered Appendix II on 15 November 2003 for logs, sawn wood, veneer, and plywood. *D. nigra* is Appendix I. The rest of *Dalbergia* went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15 as revised so finished musical instruments and small finished products would not freeze the concert hall. A rosewood-faced molded chair is not a jewelry box. A vintage Eames or Aalto already in the country is reuse of an already-cut tree. A new “walnut ply” is a specification: face species, core species, glue, certification.
Figure 1 puts the molded-ply hour and the Eames year on the same long clock as Bowett’s 1722 and the CITES marks. They are not a relay. A 1760 solid Jamaica leaf and a 1946 DCM are both furniture wood. The joint changed when the fiber was stacked.
Lacey (2008 amendment) and APHIS Phase VII (1 December 2024) still want names. “Plywood” is a process. *Betula*, Finland, or *Shorea*, unnamed, is the content.
## What to look for
An edge. A void. A printed grain that dies at a corner. A moulded seat whose underside shows layers. A Belter-type back that is several leaves. A Paimio scroll. A splint in a museum. A 1930s radio with a burl face and a cheap back. A 1950s dresser with rotary cathedrals on lauan. A poplar interior under an Empire flame — the ancestor, still at work.
Arkansas yellow-poplar is still core stock. Solid oak, walnut, and cherry are a different contract. Both can be named without apology. The sin is the single word “walnut” on a door that is 0.6 mm of face and a tropical core. The 500-year series needs this chapter because more people own ply than own joined oak. The physics is old. The factory is new. The label is where the trouble lives.
## Sources
V&A, “A short history of plywood in ten-ish objects”; V&A *Plywood: Material of the Modern World* (Wilk). V&A Thonet W.31-2011. Engelbrecht on the 1946 Eames chair; Kirkham, *Charles and Ray Eames*. Klim, “Composite wood materials,” WAG 1990. Aalto / Artek / Finmar notes. Kukachka, FPL-125 (okoume, fuma, lupuna, cuangare cores). USDA FPL-GTR-190, ch. 4. Bowett on the mahogany solid (contrast). CITES 2003 mahogany release; App. I *D. nigra*; *Dalbergia* App. II, 2 January 2017, Annotation #15.
See: `mahogany-regency-empire`, `rosewood-victorian`, `brazilian-rosewood-midcentury`, `veneer-versus-solid`, `conservation-today`.

item.title: The tropical hardwood peak around 1900
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# The tropical hardwood peak around 1900
By 1900 a Chicago or London factory could put Cuban mahogany, Bahia rosewood, Burma teak, and a strip of African ebony on the same invoice, and the woods would still mean the trees. Twenty years later the word mahogany had begun to leak toward *Khaya*. Forty years later lauan cores wore walnut photographs. The years on either side of 1900 are the last hour when the fashionable tropical names and the fashionable tropical genera still mostly matched — and the hour when the match was already breaking. Cuban *Swietenia mahagoni* in commercial furniture sizes was already a memory. Honduran *S. macrophylla* held the name. Brazilian *Dalbergia nigra* still arrived, thinner in log and thicker in veneer. Figure 1 is that crest: after Baltic oak and Bowett’s 1722 mahogany duty cut, before the CITES years.
![Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/timeline.svg)
*Figure 1. Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.*
![Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).](../assets/species-comparison/core-species-properties.svg)
*Figure 4. Mean Janka hardness and oven-dry density for ten species that anchor this series (USDA FPL / Wood Database means).*
## What “peak” means here
Not a single tonnage number I will invent. Peak means the last decades when piano factories, mail-order suites, world’s-fair displays, and city shops could still specify *Swietenia*, *Dalbergia*, *Tectona*, and *Diospyros* as ordinary luxury, while the source forests were already writing the shortage Kukachka would record in 1970. Pin a comparable import series at publication `[CITE NEEDED: a named UK or US tropical-hardwood import series, 1880–1914]`. The objects are evidence enough to start: rosewood parlor pianos, mahogany dining rooms still in the true genus, teak campaign leftovers, ebony stringing, satinwood revival desks.
Bowett’s English mahogany story is the start of this crest, not the crest itself. The Naval Stores Act of 1721, in force 1722, took the duty off British West Indian timber. Ripley told the Admiralty the wood would undercut deal and wainscot (*Georgian Group Journal*, 1997). Jamaica dominated the early furniture supply; Honduras bay-wood grew as volume. Customs values jumped in the 1720s. That statute made a tropical hardwood cheap enough to carve in the solid. The 1900 factory made it cheap enough to veneer onto every sideboard in a catalogue. Same genus, different conversion, a thinner leaf on a larger production.
Macquoid’s *Age of Mahogany* (to 1770) was already a periodization, not a law, when the Edwardian dining room still said mahogany and meant, if you were lucky, *S. macrophylla*. The Age had overflowed its dates. The tree had not overflowed its range.
## Four woods on one factory floor
Mahogany. Kukachka (FPL-125): *S. macrophylla* the commercial volume, Mexico to the Amazon; *S. mahagoni* and *S. humilis* generally heavier, by 1970 used almost entirely at home. *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190): pale pink to dark reddish brown, stable, durable, easy to work, premier veneer wood. Janka near 800 lbf, SG near 0.45–0.50. Strength in the neighborhood of cherry and paper birch. Figure 4 places that mid-density carvable wood among the anchors. A 1900 “mahogany” suite may still be this. A 1925 suite may be *Khaya*. Look at the ribbon and the pore.
Rosewood. Kukachka had no mechanical table for *D. nigra* and said so. Bahia to Rio, oily, fragrant, barely floatable dry, veneer for decorative plywood, *Machaerium* already mixing in. *D. latifolia* at about 53 pounds per cubic foot, compiled Janka near 2,440 lbf. Piano cases and parlor sets of 1880–1910 are the objects. Dean’s Atlantic-forest history is the background. The Victorian and Gothic-revival drafts take the silhouettes. Here the point is volume: more cases, thinner leaves, a forest that Kukachka would call nowhere abundant.
Teak. FPL: properties generally on par with U.S. oaks; compiled Janka near 1,070 lbf, SG near 0.55–0.66; silica dulls tools; oily; a dockyard wood that furniture inherited (the teak drafts). 1900 is still imperial deck and campaign chest more than Danish oil. The suburb comes later.
Ebony. African commercial *Diospyros* about 63 pounds per cubic foot; Ceylon about 73 (Kukachka). Inlay, keys, turnery. Not a carcase. The ebony draft is the millimeter. On the 1900 floor it is a strip in a drawer of parts.
Yellow-poplar and pine are on that floor too, as grounds. Crotch mahogany on poplar is an Empire inheritance the factory never retired. A 1900 sideboard with a flame face and a green tulip interior is the same sandwich Lannuier’s shop knew, run through a larger glue press.
## Joinery at factory scale
Solid dining leaves still exist. They still need to float. The rule joint still hides a gap. What multiplies is veneer: sliced faces, rotary faces for the cheap sides, cross-banding, a poplar or basswood or early plywood core. Figure 3’s cut geometry (in the glossary and the rosewood-Victorian draft) decides whether the face shows cathedrals or stripe. The factory prefers yield. Flatsawn and rotary win. Quartersawn mahogany ribbon is a special, not a default.
Piano-case construction is the high-volume version of the Empire sandwich: a stable box, a lockboard, a figured skin, hide glue giving way to earlier synthetics `[CITE NEEDED: a dated adhesive shift in piano-case shops]`. Boulle is not a factory product in 1900; ebonized finishes and gilt transfers are. Molded ply is already in the building — Belter’s 1858 patent is fifty years old; the V&A history treats 1850–1890 as the molded-ply hour — but the 1900 parlor still hides the layers under carving. Aalto and Eames are not yet born as furniture names. The core-stock habit is.
Screws, dowels, and machine-cut mortises replace draw-boring. The wood still moves. A glued-down breadboard on a mahogany top still splits it. Factories that forgot the 18th-century manners left a trail of cracked leaves.
Carving quality is the other factory tell. A Chippendale splat of 1760 is a gouge in the solid, oxidized brown. A “Chippendale” dining chair of 1900 may still be *Swietenia*, machine-cut piercing, a redder film. The wood can be true and the hour still be the peak, not the statute. Bowett’s Jamaica chair and the 1900 catalogue chair share a genus and fight about the tool. Look at the back of the splat. Tear-out from a router is not a gouge.
## Substitutes waiting in the yard
African mahogany (*Khaya*), sapele and utile (*Entandrophragma*), Philippine “mahogany” (lauan/meranti), Spanish cedar (*Cedrela*), toon (*Toona*). Okoume as a European plywood face (Kukachka: the most important African timber by volume for that use). Fuma and later lupuna as corestock. None of these are sins if named. They become the 20th-century default when the invoice still says the 18th-century word.
Satinwood revival desks of the 1890s–1910s may be *Chloroxylon swietenia* (Kukachka: about 60 pounds per cubic foot, almost twice sugar maple in side hardness, veneer only in the U.S.) or a dyed pale hardwood. A lens.
Do not invent a world’s-fair prize or a price list. The genera on the invoice and the secondary wood in the drawer are enough.
Grand Rapids, High Wycombe, the German bentwood towns, the Paris Faubourg, the New York piano loft: different clocks, the same tropical bills of lading. A mail-order suite of 1905 could offer “genuine mahogany” and mean *Swietenia*, or mean a hope. The surviving leaf is the test. A world’s fair display of 1893 or 1900 is a good place to see the names still attached to the trees — and to see the plywood and the composition ornaments already standing next to them. I will not invent a particular exhibit number. The catalogues exist; quote one at publication `[CITE NEEDED: a named 1893/1900 exposition furniture-wood catalogue page]`.
Railroad and steamship freight made the crest possible. A Bahia log and a Rangoon teak balk could meet a Michigan carcase plant in the same season. That is not a romance of globalization. It is a freight ledger and a forest ledger written on the same crate. Enslaved labor is earlier in the mahogany and rosewood stories; wage and coerced colonial labor is the 1900 version. The dining table does not become innocent because the legal form of the labor changed.
## The later brake, already latent
Figure 1’s right-hand marks are the papers the 1900 factory did not file. Neotropical *S. macrophylla* entered CITES Appendix II on 15 November 2003 (decision 2002; press release 11 November 2003), typically for logs, sawn wood, veneer, plywood. *D. nigra* went onto Appendix I on 11 June 1992. The rest of *Dalbergia* followed onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15 as later revised for instruments and small finished goods. Madagascar ebonies took their own listings. The U.S. Lacey Act as amended in 2008, and APHIS Phase VII (1 December 2024), make a binomial part of the crate.
A 1900 suite already in the country is usually legal to own. A new suite that borrows its names is a labeling problem. The peak is why the appendices exist. The appendices are not why the peak ended. Exhaustion and substitution ended it. The law arrived after the vocabulary had already slipped.
## What to look for
A dining room of 1900: oxidized mahogany that may still be *Swietenia*, a rosewood piano, oak in the hall, pine or poplar inside the cases, maybe an ebony line. A dining room of 1925: the same words, a different chance of *Khaya* and a print. A dining room of 1965: teak, a rosewood sideboard that may be *D. latifolia*, ply cores. Open an edge. Weigh a leaf. Read the invoice if there is one.
Arkansas was sending oak, gum, and pine into the same national catalogues. The tropical names on those pages were imports. A shop that works the domestic hardwoods now is not missing the peak. The peak was a matching of name and genus that lasted about two centuries after Bowett’s statute and then came apart. Name what you use.
A 1900 hotel lobby — mahogany counters, a rosewood piano, teak chairs from a leftover campaign vocabulary, oak wainscot that is still Baltic or American — is the mixed room this series keeps asking you to see. Macquoid’s staircase does not describe it. The invoice, if you could find it, would. The woods are still themselves. The peak is the last decade when that sentence was cheap to say.
## Sources
Bowett, *The English Mahogany Trade 1700–1793*; Ripley, *Georgian Group Journal* 7 (1997). Kukachka, FPL-125 (mahogany, rosewoods, ebonies, okoume, satinwood, corestock notes). USDA FPL-GTR-190. Dean, *With Broadax and Firebrand*. Macquoid (periodization). V&A plywood history (Belter / molded ply already present). CITES 2003 mahogany release; App. I *D. nigra*; *Dalbergia* App. II, 2 January 2017, Annotation #15. USDA APHIS Lacey Phase VII.
See: `mahogany-chippendale`, `rosewood-victorian`, `plywood-and-core-stock`, `cites-1973-convention`, `conservation-today`.

item.title: Conservation as a crate, 2024
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Conservation as a crate, 2024
A container lands at Savannah. The packing list says “wood furniture.” The HTS code is a furniture code. Until Phase VII, a lot of those codes did not require a Lacey declaration. On 1 December 2024 they did, unless the product is 100 percent composite or sits in a remaining exemption APHIS still lists. The Federal Register notice of 31 May 2024 is the dated instrument. USDA APHIS’s Lacey Act declaration pages are the living ones. Check the date. This chapter is the present tense of the timber appendices, the 2008 plant amendments, and a dining table on a drawing. It is not a permit.
![Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).](../assets/cites-conservation/furniture-timber-listings.svg)
*Figure 5. Illustrative origin regions for CITES-listed furniture timbers; confirm appendix status at publication time (cites.org).*
![Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.](../assets/timber-trade-500y/timeline.svg)
*Figure 1. Milestone years in the long furniture-timber trade, from Baltic oak through tropical hardwoods to CITES enforcement.*
## The wall of dates
Figure 1 is the long trade. The conservation end of that line is a cluster, not a single year.
CITES, signed Washington 3 March 1973, entered into force 1 July 1975. Appendix I is not a furniture plan for new wild specimens. Appendix II is a permit and a non-detriment finding. Appendix III is a Party asking for help. Annotations decide whether a finished chair is a specimen.
Neotropical *Swietenia macrophylla* went onto Appendix II on 15 November 2003, Annotation #6: logs, sawn wood, veneer sheets, plywood. *Dalbergia nigra* had already gone onto Appendix I on 11 June 1992. The rest of *Dalbergia* went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15, revised at CoP18 in 2019 so finished musical instruments and small finished products — wood of the listed species up to 10 kg per shipment — would not freeze concerts and jewelry boxes. Madagascar populations of *Diospyros* went onto Appendix II on 12 June 2013, Annotation #5. Figure 5 is a schematic of those origin regions. Confirm at publication.
The Lacey Act (16 U.S.C. §3371 et seq.), amended by the Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008 §8204, makes it illegal to trade plants taken in violation of U.S. or foreign law. It is the first comprehensive U.S. ban of that kind on illegal wood. Importers file a declaration: scientific name, country of harvest, quantity, value. Enforcement of declarations was phased. Phase VII, 1 December 2024, extends declarations to remaining plant-product HTS codes that are not 100 percent composite, including more furniture. APHIS later noted that furniture codes 9403409040, 9403409060, and 9403409080 were omitted from the first list and would need a later notice with six months’ lead. Check the current page.
Due care is the standard. A certificate on a website is not automatically due care. FSC is a useful risk tool. It is not a finding that Lacey has been met — APHIS and FSC both say versions of this. Composite exemptions exist for some mixed or unidentifiable cases. They are not a blanket for a solid “mahogany” table.
Stolen walnut trees exist. Domestic wood is not automatically innocent. A Boone County *Juglans nigra* log with a cloudy chain of custody is a Lacey problem if it crossed a line to get to the mill. The Arkansas chapter is a preference, not a halo.
## What a specifier can put on a sheet
Write binomials. *Quercus alba*, United States. *Juglans nigra*, United States. *Prunus serotina*, United States. *Tectona grandis*, plantation, country, certificate number. *Swietenia macrophylla* only with the permit path in the file — neotropical sawn wood is Annotation #6 paper after 15 November 2003, or a pre-Convention story USFWS will accept. *Dalbergia latifolia* as a finished sideboard is not a 10 kg jewelry box. *Shorea* spp. as a core only if you know the harvest country and you are willing to defend due care.
Prefer domestic hardwoods when the job allows: oak, walnut, cherry, maple, hickory, ash (while the dry stock lasts), pine. That is a specification, not a sermon.
For tropicals: old furniture already in the country, or new wood with boring paperwork. If the price of a “solid rosewood suite” is funny, the wood is funny. If the hangtag says mahogany and the pore looks like *Shorea*, the lauan chapter already told you.
For engineered goods: still ask the face species and the core species. Lauan cores have a forest. Foil has a name. CARB / TSCA Title VI is an emission stamp, not a harvest stamp. You want both conversations on the same purchase order.
## Antiques, exports, and the sideboard that cannot fly
Antique *Dalbergia* and *Swietenia* pieces are usually legal to own in the U.S. They can be complicated to export. Ask before you ship a 1960s rosewood sideboard to another country. Appendix I objects are the sharpest case. An 1880 Brazilian rosewood piano is a living-room object and a paperwork object at the border. Pre-Convention certificates and antique annotations exist; they are not a postcard you write yourself. USFWS will tell you. A dealer’s shrug will not.
Within the country, a 1962 Danish rosewood credenza can be bought and sold. Take a photograph of the grain. Keep the invoice. If you later want to send it to London, the file starts then, not at the airport.
A 1760 Jamaica chair in a collection is the ethical supply of the Chippendale look. A new “Chippendale mahogany dining set” from an unnamed exporter is a labeling problem before it is a style problem.
## Shop behavior that is not a halo
Keep a Species+ printout in the project file, dated. Keep the harvest country on the invoice. If you import, keep the APHIS declaration and any CITES permit. If you do not import, keep the mill’s chain-of-custody sheet anyway. An edge that matches the name is the object-level check: tyloses in white oak, the oily pore of teak, the tight diffuse face of maple, the printed cathedral that does not turn the corner.
A crate that says only “wood” is a refusal. A salesperson who says “it’s all mahogany” is a refusal. A funny price on a listed genus is a refusal.
Hide glue on a historic carcase can be reversed. Urea-formaldehyde on a particleboard carcase cannot. That is a conservation fact about objects, not about forests: repair culture is how a 1760 chair stays a chair. A cam-lock suite that swells under a sink is landfill. Design for a life that matches the glue. The engineered chapter takes the panel. This chapter takes the name on the panel.
Plantation teak and certified *S. macrophylla* from outside the Neotropics are real supplies. They are not automatically innocent. Ask for the country and the papers. IUCN status is not a CITES appendix. A Forest Stewardship Council claim is not a Lacey finding. The three stamps can sit on one invoice. None of them replaces the others.
## What this series will not do
It will not issue a permit. It will not update itself when CoP20 changes an annotation. It will not treat FSC as a halo. It will not treat domestic wood as automatically innocent. It will say: names, countries, papers, edges.
TRAFFIC and Chatham House’s five-taxa paper is the trade-analysis neighbor. Taylor Guitars’ CITES note is the instrument-industry walkthrough of Annotation #15; verify it against Species+. Furniture companies have less excuse than guitar companies. A dining table is not a Chapter 92 object.
Emerald ash borer (Detroit / southeastern Michigan, 2002) and Dutch elm disease (U.S. introduction, 1930s) are domestic conservation clocks that do not wait for an appendix. Ash chairs while the dry stock lasts. Elm Windsor seats from trees that are already down. Those are shop facts. They belong next to the tropical appendices so a reader does not think conservation is only a southern-hemisphere story.
## A drawing and a dock
On the drawing: *Quercus alba*, United States, quartersawn, floating panels, slotted screws in the breadboard, hide glue if the piece should come apart in a hundred years. On the dock: a crate that used to say “wood furniture” and now, after 1 December 2024, often needs a binomial and a harvest country. Those two sentences are the same job. Fashion without a paper trail is how *Swietenia* and *Dalbergia* got to the appendices. The 1973 Convention built the gate. The 2008 amendment and Phase VII put a declaration on more of the crates that walk through it.
## A kitchen door and a stolen walnut
Walk a 2012 kitchen. The door may be walnut veneer on MDF, or a foil, or a solid frame-and-panel in white oak. The carcase is often particleboard. CARB / TSCA Title VI may be stamped on the edge tape. That stamp does not name a forest. The face, if it is *Juglans nigra*, still wants a harvest country if the leaf was imported. If the face is domestic, it still wants a mill that can say so. Phase VII is an import declaration. It is not a domestic chain-of-custody law. Lacey still reaches interstate commerce in plants taken in violation of state law. A walnut log stolen from a fencerow and sold across a state line is the example APHIS trainers use `[CITE NEEDED: a named APHIS or DOJ case, not a training-room memory]`. The Arkansas preference does not wash that log.
Reclaimed oak beams and “barnwood” suites are a conservation fashion with their own lies. A beam can be a beam. A beam can be new oak beaten with a chain. Ask for the building and the date. The reclaimed-oak draft in this series takes that object. This chapter only says: old wood already in the country is usually the cleanest tropical look you can buy, and a new barnwood crate from an unnamed port is still a crate.
Plantation teak (*Tectona grandis*) and plantation *S. macrophylla* outside the Neotropics are the supplies that let a specifier write a tropical name without pretending the 18th century is still in force. They need country, certificate, and a will to defend due care. They do not need a sermon about “sustainability.” They need a file.
Look at the invoice the way you look at an end grain. Rings and a binomial are evidence. A color word is not. The interesting trees are in the other chapters. The dullness here is the point.
## Sources
CITES text 1973; EIF 1 July 1975. CoP12 *S. macrophylla* (15 Nov. 2003) Annotation #6. CoP8 *D. nigra* (11 June 1992). CoP17 *Dalbergia* (2 Jan. 2017) Annotation #15; CoP18 2019 revision (instruments / 10 kg). CoP16 Madagascar *Diospyros* (12 June 2013) #5. Species+. USFWS 50 C.F.R. 23. Lacey Act 16 U.S.C. §3371 et seq.; 2008 §8204; APHIS Phase VII (1 Dec. 2024); Federal Register 31 May 2024; APHIS omitted-code note (94034090xx). TRAFFIC / Chatham House five-taxa paper. Taylor Guitars CITES note (verify). USDA / APHIS EAB 2002; DED literature.
See: `cites-1973-convention`, `cites-swietenia-permits`, `cites-dalbergia-2017`, `cites-ebony-africa`, `intro-500-year-timber`.
